# Mistakes found in published sources

The atlas's workers read papers and books line by line to extract and plan their mathematics, and they record every mistake they find in them: misprints (slips whose intended meaning is clear), errors (false statements or steps that fail) and gaps (steps asserted without an adequate proof). A finding counts as confirmed once an independent reviewer has checked it at its locator. Each finding says where its worker looked for an existing correction; a new one is not corrected in any erratum or later version they found. Nothing here has been sent to the authors.

Collected by `scripts/errata.py` from the paper extractions and blueprint packets (research/blueprint/PROTOCOL.md, section 18); the data is in `data/source-issues.json`.

### Abdurrahman–Venkatesh, "Symplectic L-functions and symplectic Reidemeister torsion (mod squares)", Inventiones Mathematicae (2025) (`PAPER-ABDURRAHMAN-VENKATESH-25`)

- **Misprint** at §1.5 Notation, p. 8. The source says `"Sp2r(R) denotes the standard symplectic group, i.e., the automorphisms of the free R-module on generators e_i, f_i (1 ≤ i ≤ g) with form ⟨e_i, f_j⟩ = δ_ij and ⟨e_i, e_j⟩ = ⟨f_i, f_j⟩ = 1. … Sp(R) := lim_g Sp2r(R). … automorphisms of R^{2g}"`; it should be `⟨e_i, e_j⟩ = ⟨f_i, f_j⟩ = 0, with 1 ≤ i ≤ r, the limit over r and R^{2r}.`. With ⟨e_i, e_i⟩ = 1 the form is not alternating, so its automorphism group is not a symplectic group; the index g is the genus elsewhere in the paper, while the rank parameter is r. - **Misprint** at §6.4, end of the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, p. 60. The source says `"Σ_{x∈S°(Fq)} f(x)² = q²(1 + O(q^{−1/2})), using the fact that the dimension of invariants for geometric monodromy of S° on ρλ equals 1"`; it should be `… the dimension of invariants of the geometric monodromy of S° on ρ_λ ⊗ ρ_λ (≅ End ρ_λ, ρ_λ being self-dual) equals 1.`. f(x)² is the trace of Frobenius on ρ_λ ⊗ ρ_λ, and the H^4_c term of that sheaf is governed by its geometric invariants, one-dimensional by irreducibility and self-duality. The geometric invariants of ρ_λ itself are 0, since H^0 = 0. - **Error** at Appendix B.10, the functoriality statement and its proof, and the Claim's proof, pp. 85–86 (it affects a stated result). The source says `"This is functorial, i.e., if f : R → S is a homomorphism of normal integral rings then the associated class RT(M, ρ ⊗_R S) is simply the image of RT(M, ρ) under H^1(R, μ_2) → H^1(S, μ_2)." and "[the class of 𝔞] … agrees with it up to a sign depending only on the dimension data of the complexes"`; it should be `Base-change compatibility holds for the normalized class (−1)^{χ_{1/2}(M,ρ)/2}RT(M, ρ), not for RT(M, ρ): RT(M, ρ_L) = image(RT(M, ρ))·(−1)^{(χ_{1/2}(M,ρ_L) − χ_{1/2}(M,ρ_K))/2}. The sign relating 𝔞 to RT depends on the rank of the middle differential, not only on the ranks of the terms. The main text needs only the normalized class, which is what §2.4 uses to define 𝔑.`. (i) A symplectic example. Take the genus-2 mapping torus of t = T_3³T_5 (applied left to right) with ρ(b_1) = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] and ρ(a_1) = ρ(a_2) = ρ(b_2) = I, over R = Z_(3). Over Q the monodromy on H^1(S, ρ) has characteristic polynomial (x² + x + 1)², so H^1(M, ρ) = 0 and χ_{1/2} = 0. Over F_3, dim ker(1 − T̄) = 2, so χ_{1/2} = −2. (Checked independently by computer.) Theorem 2.1 and the naturality of c_et then force RT_{F_3} = −image(RT_Q), and −1 is a nonsquare in F_3. (ii) An orthogonal circle example, from the paper's own (B.30). V = H ⊕ H over R = Q[s]_(s) with A_s = diag(1 + s, (1 + s)^{−1}) ⊕ 1: over Q(s), h = 2 and RT = −(1 + s); at s = 0, h = 4 and RT = 1, while the specialization of −(1 + s) is −1. The existence Claim (B.38) is unaffected. The source says `"(C.2) (−1)^{h/2}RT(M, ρ) = det′(1 − T)·δ, … and δ is the determinant of the quadratic form restricted to H^1(S, ρ)^{T=1}"`; it should be `δ is the discriminant of the form on the generalized 1-eigenspace of T, which is what Zassenhaus's formula (B.31) gives.`. ### Alpöge–Bhargava–Shnidman, "Rank stability in quadratic extensions and Hilbert's tenth problem for the ring of integers of a number field", Inventiones Mathematicae (2026) (`PAPER-ALPOGE-BHARGAVA-SHNIDMAN-26`)

- **Error** at Proof of Proposition 2.5, case 𝔪 ≠ 1, p. 1137 (published version); the same text in arXiv v1 p. 7 (it affects the proof). The source says `"We need only check that the equation t_1x² + 2rγ^{nℓ}t_2y² = t_3z² has a solution modulo 𝔪 for some choice of units t_1, t_2, t_3 modulo 𝔪. Since we are free to assume t_1 = t_3, there is no local obstruction at 2-adic primes 𝔭 | 𝔪."`; it should be `With t_1 = t_3 there can be an obstruction at a 2-adic 𝔭 | 𝔪, whenever v_𝔭(2rγ^{nℓ}) < v_𝔭(𝔪). The conclusion still holds. Repair: replace r by rδ^ℓ, where δ ∈ 𝒪_F is divisible by 𝔭^{v_𝔭(𝔪)} for each 2-adic 𝔭 | 𝔪 and by no other prime (it exists because the class group is finite). Then C_{q^ℓr²δ^{2ℓ}} ≅ C_{q^ℓr²} (§2: C_n ≅ C_{nλ^{2ℓ}}), so Lemma 2.3 and the sets S′, S, Σ are unchanged. The clause r ∉ 𝔭 still holds at the odd ramified primes, where the smooth-conic argument uses it. Now β = 2rδ^ℓγ^{nℓ} ≡ 0 modulo the 2-adic part of 𝔪, so x = y = z = 1 solves the congruence there with t_1 = t_3. Alternatively, keep r and choose t_1 ≠ t_3.`. Take F_0 = ℚ, K_0 = ℚ(i) and ℓ = 3, which does not divide Disc = −4. §4 replaces these by F = ℚ(ζ_3) and K = F(i) = ℚ(ζ_12), and K/F is unramified above 3. The prime (2) is inert in F/ℚ, so F_(2) = ℚ_4 is unramified over ℚ_2 with residue field 𝔽_4. F_(2)(i)/F_(2) has conductor exponent 2, so 𝔪 = (4). Since (2) ramifies in K, (2) ∉ S and γ ∉ (2); and r ∉ (2) by Lemma 2.3. Hence v_2(β) = 1. Suppose t x² + βt_2y² ≡ t z² (mod 4) with x, y, z units. Then (z/x)² ≡ 1 + βt_2y²/(tx²) (mod 4), which is ≡ 1 mod 2 but ≢ 1 mod 4. But a unit w with w² ≡ 1 (mod 2) has w ≡ 1 (mod 2), since squaring is bijective on 𝔽_4, and then w² ≡ 1 (mod 4). This is a contradiction. An exhaustive search over the 12 units of ℤ[ζ_3]/4 confirms it. Inertness of a principal prime (p) in K is detected by χ(p) = (−1)^{(N(p)−1)/2}, where N is the norm to ℚ; this is the Hilbert symbol (p, −1) at (2), trivial on global units. For every unit value of β/2 there is no solution with t_1 = t_3 and χ(t_1) = χ(t_2) = −1. Yet admissible residues exist with t_1 ≠ t_3: for β ≡ 2, u_1 = u_2 = 1 + 2ζ_3 and u_3 = u_1 + βu_2 ≡ 3 + 2ζ_3 (mod 4), with norms 3, 3, 7 ≡ 3 (mod 4). ### André, "Le lemme d'Abhyankar perfectoïde", Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS (2018) (`PAPER-ANDRE-18`)

### Anschütz–Le Bras, "Prismatic Dieudonné Theory", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2023) (`PAPER-ANSCHUTZ-LEBRAS-23`)

- **Misprint** at Theorem 4.9.5 (published: Theorem 4.90), the statement; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version. The source says `Then the prismatic Dieudonné functor M_Δ(−) : BT(R) → DM^adm(R) from the category of p-divisible groups over R to the category of admissible prismatic Dieudonné crystals over R is essentially surjective.`; it should be `… to the category of admissible prismatic Dieudonné modules over R …`. R is assumed quasi-regular semiperfectoid and the displayed functor is the non-calligraphic M_Δ(−), which Definition 4.42 (arXiv Definition 4.2.8) defines as Ext^1_{(R)_qsyn}(G, O^pris) with values in prismatic Dieudonné modules over R; DM^adm(R) is used for both categories by the deliberate overloading of Definitions 4.8 and 4.19 (arXiv Definitions 4.1.8 and 4.1.15), but the words in the statement name the wrong one. The proof settles it: it begins 'let M ∈ DM^adm(R)' and speaks of 'a descent datum for expressing that it comes from an admissible prismatic Dieudonné module over R (namely, M)'. The crystal version of the same statement is Theorem 4.74 (arXiv Theorem 4.6.10), for a general quasi-syntomic ring. Recorded as `PAPER-ANSCHUTZ-LEBRAS-23/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: the arXiv listing and submission history of arXiv:1907.10525, read 22 September 2026: v1 (24 July 2019), v2 (6 February 2020), v3 (14 May 2021) and v4 (11 October 2022), the version read, whose comment records that the notion of filtered prismatic Dieudonné crystal was replaced by the equivalent notion of admissible prismatic Dieudonné crystal and that the proof of full faithfulness was corrected and simplified following a suggestion of Akhil Mathew; there is no later preprint version and no version carrying the erratum; the published version, doi:10.1017/fmp.2022.22 (Forum of Mathematics, Pi 11 (2023), e2, open access on Cambridge Core), read 22 September 2026, including its 'A correction has been issued for this article' notice; the erratum itself, Prismatic Dieudonné Theory – ERRATUM, doi:10.1017/fmp.2024.30 (Forum of Mathematics, Pi 13 (2025), e3, published 7 February 2025), read 22 September 2026: it is the only correction listed for the article; the numbering of the preprint against the numbering of the published version, statement by statement, in all six sections and the appendix; the two agree except that arXiv Remark 5.1.7, on Cartier duality for finite locally free group schemes, has no counterpart in the published version.

- **Misprint** at Example 6.0.4 (published: Example A.4), the displayed chain of equalities; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version. The source says `p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0`; it should be `p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i−1}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0`. The relations imposed are p x_{i,j} = f x_{i,j+1}. Substituting once gives p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}(p x_{i,0}) = p^{i−1} f x_{i,1}, and each further substitution trades one p for one f, so that the chain is p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}f x_{i,1} = p^{i−2}f^2 x_{i,2} = … = f^i x_{i,i}: the total degree in p and f is i throughout. As printed, the second term has degree i+1 and is in fact equal to f^{i+1}x_{i,i+1} = 0, since x_{i,i+1} = 0, which would contradict the assertion that the chain is non-zero. The next sentence, p^{i+1}x_{i,0} = f^i p x_{i,i} = 0, is correct. ### Antieau–Mathew–Morrow–Nikolaus, "On the Beilinson fiber square", Duke Mathematical Journal (2022) (`PAPER-ANTIEAU-MATHEW-MORROW-ETAL-22`)

- **Misprint** at Example 7.3, the two stated ranges in the computation of the cyclic homology of k over W(k); in arXiv v2, the version read (the published version could not be consulted). The source says `Using the filtrations of [antieauperiodic], we conclude for i ≤ 2p−1, π_i HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{s+1} if i = 2s ≥ 0, 0 otherwise. … Thus, in the range 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−2, we deduce that π_i HC((W(k),(p)/W(k)) ≅ p^{s+1}W(k) if i = 2s, 0 if i is odd.`; it should be `The two ranges should be i ≤ 2p−4 and 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−4 (equivalently i ≤ 2p−3, since the odd groups vanish).`. Both formulas are read off from the sentence immediately before them, that LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s} ≅ W(k)/p^s for s ≤ p−1, applied with s+1 in place of s: π_{2s}HC(k/W(k)) = LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s+1}. That needs s+1 ≤ p−1, i.e. i = 2s ≤ 2p−4. At the first excluded value, i = 2p−2 and s = p−1, the formula would give W(k)/p^p, but LΩ_k here is the p-completed divided power envelope of (p) ⊆ W(k) — that is, W(k) itself — and its Hodge filtration is the divided power filtration, whose p-th step is generated by γ_p(p) = p^p/p!, of p-adic valuation p − 1 since v_p(p!) = 1. So LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥p} = W(k)/p^{p−1} and π_{2p−2}HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{p−1}, not W(k)/p^p; correspondingly the relative group is p^{p−1}W(k), not p^pW(k). The conclusion of the example is unaffected: it is drawn in the range 1 ≤ i ≤ 2p−5, where the odd degrees used are i = 2s+1 ≤ 2p−5, so s ≤ p−3 and s+1 ≤ p−2, well inside the range where the de Rham formula holds. ### Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020) (`PAPER-BAKKER-KLINGLER-TSIMERMAN-20`)

- **Error** at Theorem 4.1, p.13 of the author copy (= arXiv 1810.04801v2, p.13); the JAMS typeset version was not collated (publisher PDF not obtainable here, verification gap G1) (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Theorem 4.1. Let V be a polarized variation of pure Hodge structures of weight k over the punctured polydisk (∆*)^n, with period map Φ: (∆*)^n → S_{Γ,G,M}. Then Φ is R_an,exp-definable." (∆ is the unit disk, p.4.)`; it should be `Definability holds only after shrinking. For some radius 0 < ρ < 1, the restriction of Φ to (∆*_ρ)^n is R_an,exp-definable, and then for every ρ < 1 by compactness of the remaining annular pieces. The reduction in §4.1 must use charts whose shrunken polydisks still cover the compactification.`. Counterexample (n = 1, trivial monodromy). Let f(z) = exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)) on the unit disk, so |f| < 1, and τ = 2i + εf with ε small, so that τ(∆) lies in a disk on which π: H → Γ\H is injective (Γ torsion-free, e.g. Γ(3)). τ is the period map of a polarized weight-one integral VHS. But Φ^{−1}(π(2i + ε/e)) contains the points z_n = 2πin/(2 + 2πin), n ≠ 0, where f = 1/e. These form an infinite discrete set accumulating at 1, which is impossible for a fibre of a definable map. The proof itself allows for this: it says 'after maybe shrinking the polydisk' (p.14), and its Siegel set S_H (y > 1) covers only |q| < e^{−2π}. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected, since §4.1 can use finitely many shrunken charts. Checked numerically: |f(z_n) − 1/e| < 1e−8 for 0 < |n| ≤ 2000. Noted by the extraction (item local-outer-boundary-obstruction). Recorded as `PAPER-BAKKER-KLINGLER-TSIMERMAN-20/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: The official erratum (JAMS 36 (2023), DOI 10.1090/jams/1025), read in full: it corrects only the maximal-compact dependence, morphisms and the Siegel-set pullback citation; arXiv 1810.04801 v2 (2020-06-22, the latest version): same wording at each locator; Benjamin Bakker's web page (author copy and erratum).
- **Gap** at Proof of Lemma 4.5, p.15 of the author copy (= arXiv v2 p.15); the JAMS typeset version was not collated (publisher PDF not obtainable here, verification gap G1) (it affects the proof). The source says `"Consider for each positive integer m and real number c the function f_{m,c} which we obtain from f by setting z_1 = mz_2 + c. Note that the assumptions of the lemma still apply to f_{m,c}, and it follows by induction on n that f_{m,c} ≪ 1 on all of Σ_{n−1}"`; it should be `State the lemma, and verify its curve hypothesis, on the wider sectors Σ_n^R = {|x_i| < R, y_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ y_n > 1} for every R, with constants depending on R. The substitution then maps Σ_{n−1}^{R′} into Σ_n^{mR′+c}, and the induction goes through unchanged. In the application in §4.5, the curve bounds come from Schmid's one-variable Corollary 5.29 and the norm estimates of Theorem 4.8, which hold for real parts in any bounded interval; Theorem 1.5 is already stated on H^n_{R,η} for all R.`. Σ_n is defined with 0 < x_i < 1 (Definition 4.4). The proof uses c = 0, 1, …, r_1 and m ≥ 1. For c ≥ 1, x_1 = mx_2 + c > 1, so Σ_n ∩ {z_1 = mz_2 + c} is empty. For c = 0 it is only the strip x_2 < 1/m. So the hypothesis gives no information about f_{m,c} on Σ_{n−1}. The functions extend there (the coefficients in O are periodic in x and f is polynomial in x), but the bound is assumed only on Σ_n. With the R-uniform hypothesis, the finite difference in c isolates the top x_1-degree, the Vandermonde step in m isolates each y-power, and |x_1| < 1 on Σ_n finishes the proof, as printed. Noted by the extraction (verification gap G4); the repair is given by this continuation. ### Bennett–Siksek, "A conjecture of Erdős, supersingular primes and short character sums", Annals of Mathematics 191 (2020), no. 2 (`PAPER-BENNETT-SIKSEK-20`)

- **Error** at Lemma 3.2, p.361, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 191 (2020), 355–392 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3920a752…). The source says `"Its discriminant is Δ_a = 64(a_a b_a c_a)² = (2⁸/g⁶)(n+id)²(n+jd)²(n+(2j−i)d)²."`; it should be `Δ_a = 16(a_a b_a c_a)² = (2⁶/g⁶)(n+id)²(n+jd)²(n+(2j−i)d)².`. For y² = x³ + a₂x² + a₄x, Δ = 16a₄²(a₂² − 4a₄). For E_a: Y² = X(X−a)(X+c), a₂ = c − a and a₄ = −ac, so Δ = 16a²c²(a+c)² = 16(abc)² since a+b+c = 0; with b_a = −2(n+jd)/g this is 2⁶/g⁶ times the product. The extraction found this (item 16, report D1); the review re-derived it. - **Error** at Theorem 5, equation (26), p.374, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 191 (2020), 355–392 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3920a752…). The source says `"Let χ be a primitive Dirichlet character of conductor N. ### Benoist–Wittenberg, "On the integral Hodge conjecture for real varieties, I", Inventiones Mathematicae (2020) (`PAPER-BENOIST-WITTENBERG-20`)

- **Error** at Inventiones mathematicae 222 (2020), Theorem 3.16 (ii), p. 55, and its introduction form Theorem A (ii), p. 4 (it affects a stated result). The source says `Theorem 3.16. Let X be a smooth, proper and geometrically irreducible variety over a real closed field R. Assume that dim(X) > 0, that H^2(X,O_X) = 0 and that X satisfies the real integral Hodge conjecture for 1-cycles. ... (ii) There exists a geometrically irreducible curve of even geometric genus in X if and only if the natural map Pic(X)[2^∞] → Pic(X_C)^G[2^∞] is onto. (Theorem A (ii) is the case R = ℝ, stated for "dimension d ≥ 1".)`; it should be `Part (ii) needs dim(X) ≥ 2 whenever X(R) ≠ ∅. The hypothesis dim(X) > 0 of Theorem 3.16, and the hypothesis d ≥ 1 of Theorem A, are too weak: the case dim(X) = 1 with X(R) ≠ ∅ must be excluded. Part (i) is not affected by this counterexample.`. Take X = E the elliptic curve y^2 = x^3 - x over R = ℝ, with its rational point at infinity. All the printed hypotheses hold: dim(X) = 1 > 0; H^2(X,O_X) = 0 because X is a curve; and the real integral Hodge conjecture for 1-cycles is the codimension-0 case, which holds trivially, since X is geometrically irreducible, so H^0_G(X(ℂ),ℤ(0)) = ℤ and the class of the codimension-0 cycle [X] generates it. The left-hand side of (ii) fails: the only integral closed subscheme of dimension 1 in a curve is the curve itself, and E has geometric genus 1, which is odd, so X contains no geometrically irreducible curve of even geometric genus. The right-hand side holds: by Hochschild–Serre, Pic(X) → Pic(X_ℂ)^G is injective with cokernel embedding in Br(ℝ), and that obstruction is killed by the real point, so the map is an isomorphism and is in particular onto on 2-primary torsion. Hence (ii) is false as printed. The source of the gap is visible in the proof: Theorem 3.16 is obtained by combining Theorem 3.3, Theorem 3.6 and Proposition 3.9, and it is Proposition 3.9 — "Let X be a smooth, proper and geometrically irreducible variety, of dimension ≥ 2 ... If X(R) ≠ ∅, then X contains a geometrically irreducible curve of even geometric genus" — that supplies the left-hand side when X(R) ≠ ∅, and it assumes dimension ≥ 2. Verified independently against both the published text (pp. 4, 51, 55) and the LaTeX source of arXiv:1801.00872v3, which carry the same hypotheses. The source says `"More generally, let D be a fixed divisor and let A be a semiample Q-Cartier Q-divisor such that A ∼_Q M + Λ, where M is an effective Cartier divisor with no exceptional curve of Y → X in its support, and −δD ≤ Λ ≤ δD for δ > 0. Take x ∈ F ∩ M of multiplicity k ∈ Z_{>0} in M. Then ε_sa(A; x) converges to k when δ → 0."`; it should be `Only a lower bound holds. For every rational γ with 0 < γ < k there is δ₀ > 0, depending only on f, D and γ, such that ε_sa(A; x) = ε(A; x) ≥ k − γ for all δ < δ₀ and all such A, M, Λ and x. Equivalently, liminf_{δ→0} ε_sa(A; x) ≥ k, uniformly. This is exactly what the printed proof establishes; there is no upper bound.`. Counterexample with Λ = 0. Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, X = A²_k, and f: Y → X the blow-up of the origin with exceptional curve E = F. Let M be the sum of the strict transforms of the two axes. Then M ∼ −2E, so M is effective, Cartier, globally generated over X (O_Y(−E) = m·O_Y) and has no exceptional component. Let x = E ∩ (strict transform of the y-axis), so mult_x M = 1 = k. Blow up x, with exceptional curve G and strict transform E′. Then E′² = −2, G² = −1, E′·G = 1 and π*M − tG ∼ −2E′ − (2+t)G, which has degree 2 − t on E′ and t on G. Hence ε(M; x) = 2. At t = 2 the ideal (x, y²) pulls back to O(−E′ − 2G) (charts x = ab, y = b, then a = c, b = cd, giving c²d, and a = ef, b = f, giving f²). So π*M − 2G ∼ −2E′ − 4G is globally generated and ε_sa(M; x) = 2. Taking A = M and Λ = 0 (any D), ε_sa(A; x) = 2 for every δ, not converging to k = 1. The proof only shows that π*A − (k − γ)E is nef. The consumers need only the lower bound: Proposition 8.15 (p.173) uses the first assertion ε_sa(M; x) ≥ 1, which is correct, and Claim 8.21 (p.178) needs ε_sa > 2 for k = 3. So the paper's results are unaffected. Checked on the page image and by exact arithmetic. ### Binyamini, "Point counting for foliations over number fields", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2022) (`PAPER-BINYAMINI-22`)

- **Misprint** at Lemma 15 and proof, (34)–(35), p.11 (published version). The source says `"S(X ∩ B², ε) ≤ (2^m/c(m)) vol(X)·ε^{−2m}" … "vol(X ∩ B_p) ≥ c(n)(ε/2)^{2m}"`; it should be `S(X ∩ B², ε) ≤ (2^{2m}/c(m)) vol(X) ε^{−2m}, from vol(X ∩ B_p) ≥ c(m)(ε/2)^{2m}.`. X has dimension m, so the Lelong bound involves c(m), the volume of the unit ball of ℂ^m. Dividing vol(X) by c(m)(ε/2)^{2m} gives the factor 2^{2m}. Only O_n-constants change. Recorded as `PAPER-BINYAMINI-22/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: arXiv 2009.00892 (v1, 2 September 2020, the only version); Forum of Mathematics, Pi 10 (2022) e6 article page (open access): no correction notice; Crossref metadata for 10.1017/fmp.2021.20: no update or correction relation.
- **Misprint** at §4.4, p.14 and proof of Proposition 22, p.15 (published version). The source says `"by a dimension-counting argument using Lemma 19, the codimension of π_Φ(Σ_Ṽ) is positive" … "Set Z = Clo π(Σ_{W̃_{k+1}}) … Z has positive codimension"`; it should be `Restrict to the part of Σ_Ṽ lying over M ∖ Σ_V (resp. over the p with dim(V ∩ L_p) < n − k): Z := Clo π_Φ(Σ_Ṽ ∖ π_M^{-1}(Σ_V)).`. Over points p ∈ Σ_V every Φ lies in Σ_Ṽ, so π_Φ(Σ_Ṽ) is all of M_D whenever Σ_V ≠ ∅. Lemma 19 and the target condition (44) concern only p ∉ Σ_V. - **Error** at Proposition 51 and Theorem 9, Appendix A, pp.36–37 (published version) (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Proposition 51. Suppose L is defined over a number field. Then inf_{φ ∈ Aut(ℙ¹)} ‖a₀(φ*L)‖ = e^{−poly_n(δ_L)}. Proof. … Now the operator L′ := L + 1 is also Fuchsian …"`; it should be `Assume in addition that L + 1 is Fuchsian. This holds when every finite zero of a₀ has order ≤ n and deg a₀ ≥ n, and in particular for the Legendre Picard–Fuchs operator (87), a₀ = λ(1−λ), n = 2, which is the only operator to which the paper applies Theorem 9. Under this normalization the proof of Proposition 51 is correct, and Theorem 9 follows as written.`. For a general Fuchsian operator, L + 1 need not be Fuchsian, and both statements fail. Take L = ∂_t, which is Fuchsian: its only singular point ∞ is regular singular (∂_t = −z(z∂_z), z = 1/t). Then φ(s) = κs gives φ*L = κ^{-1}∂_s and inf_φ ‖a₀(φ*L)‖ = 0. In Theorem 9 take b(t) = (t − t₀)/(2r) (|b| ≤ 1 on D^{1/2}) and f = (t − t₀)²/(4r), so j_z f(t₀) = 0 while |∂_z f(t₀ + r/2)| = r/4, unbounded in r. Here L + 1 = ∂ + 1 has an irregular singularity at ∞. Theorems 1–8 are unaffected. ### Böckle–Harris–Khare–Thorne, "Ĝ-local systems on smooth projective curves are potentially automorphic", Acta Mathematica (2019) (`PAPER-BOCKLE-HARRIS-KHARE-ETAL-19`)

- **Misprint** at Lemma 9.1(i), p. 51 (arXiv v2). The source says `"Suppose that ψ is surjective, even after restriction to π_1(Y_{F̄_q}, η_Y). Then Z_{ψ,φ} is a geometrically connected finite étale K-scheme."`; it should be `a geometrically connected finite étale **Y_K**-scheme.`. Z_{ψ,φ} is defined on p. 50 as Isom_{Y_K,H}(X_φ, X_ψ), the scheme of isomorphisms of two H-torsors over the curve Y_K, so it is finite étale over Y_K, not over K. The distinction is not cosmetic: the proof of Proposition 9.2 uses the lemma in the form "By the first part of Lemma 9.1, Z_{ψ,φ} is a smooth, geometrically connected curve over K", and a finite étale K-scheme has relative dimension 0 over K, so it could carry no such family of local points. (b) The assertion being justified is that the **Lie algebra** 𝔤 is self-dual as a G-representation, which needs an invariant form on 𝔤; [SS70, Lemma I.5.3] is about the Lie algebra. (e) Here φ : G × S → X and x ∈ X(k), so φ(x) is not defined; the hypothesis of Proposition 3.13 is that G_k·x is closed, and the point of G × S in play is (1, x), as the last line of the same proof writes. - **Misprint** at Proof of Theorem 2.1, pp. 514–515 (published offprint; identical in arXiv v1–v3). The source says `"(see [BLGGT14, Thm. 2.4.2] for a restatement in the precise form we use here; in the notation of that statement, we are taking l = p, n = p − 1, S = {p}, μ = ε^{1−n}, H_τ = {0, 1, . . . , n − 1})" and "(taking F = Q, l = p, n = p − 1, r = ρ, and μ = ε^{1−n}δ^n_{F/F^+})"`; it should be `In both parameter lists read n = n, that is n = p − 1 or n = p − 2 as in the statement of Theorem 2.1.`. With θ′ the induced representation has multiplier ε^{p(2−k)}ε^{1−p} = ε^{1−(k−1)p} and weights {pa + b} = {0, …, (k−1)p − 1}. With θ, as printed, it has multiplier ε^{2−k}ε^{1−p} = ε^{3−k−p} and repeated weights {a + b}; for p = 79, k = 38 the exponents are −114 against the required −2922. For an ordinary f the shape ρ̄_f|G_{Q_p} ≅ ψ̄ ⊕ ψ̄^{−1}ε̄^{1−k} determines k mod p − 1 up to replacing k by p + 1 − k (the companion), and gcd(p − 1, k − 1) = gcd(p − 1, p − k) is the same for both. At p = 151 the only ordinary level-one eigensystems with ρ̄_f|G_{Q_p} semisimple are the companion pair in weights 52 and 100 ([CG13] table: 151, C[52]). This was confirmed by matching the characteristic polynomials of T_2 and T_3 on S_52 and on S_100 (twisted by ℓ^{99}) mod 151; no other pair (k, 152 − k) with 12 ≤ k < 76 matches, and the self-pair k = 76 = (p+1)/2 has (150, 75) ≠ 1. Since (150, 51) = (150, 99) = 3, hypothesis (2) of Theorem 2.1 fails at 151. (Theorem 3.1 does apply at 151, through the non-ordinary pair (60, 94).) [CKPSS04, Thm. 7.2] describes the image of the global generic lift and says nothing about local components. [CKPSS04, §7.2] treats local lifts only through γ-factors and notes that local descent for SO_2n and Sp_2n was not yet available. So 'level one' for the representation of Sp_104, and with it H^*_cusp(𝒜_52, C) ≠ 0, is asserted without the needed local input. The conclusion is expected to hold. What the later reductions need is a statement about the t-birationally liftable (or birationally liftable) sections of a parabolic affine X, which have to be treated directly, including the case where X̄ ∖ X is a single point of degree 2. The reductions to non-parabolic X rest on this: "We may assume that X is non-parabolic" in the proof of Lemma 16, and "it is immediate to check that t-b.l. sections are quasi-t-b.l." after Definition 18, where the identity map is not available for parabolic X.`. Counterexample. Let k = Q and X = P¹_Q ∖ V(T² − 2). Then X is affine, of genus 0, with boundary a single point of degree 2, so it is parabolic. The paper defines a Galois section to be cuspidal if it is associated with a k-rational point of X̄ ∖ X (§1). The boundary has no Q-rational point, so X has no cuspidal sections. But 0 ∈ X(Q), so X has a geometric section. Schmidt's theorem concerns the existence of rational points and splitting; it does not make a degree-2 boundary point rational. The paper's Theorems A–C are not claimed to fail here, only this justification of the reduction. Noted by the extraction (item 77, with the reduction gap in items 81, 96 and 112). Theorem C assumes a prime 𝔭 of good ordinary reduction, and its proof uses ordinarity through [BK, Theorem 0.7(iii)] to get gr⁰ H²(V̄_𝔭, Q_p) ≠ 0. For a smooth projective V with H²(V, O_V) ≠ 0 (so H⁰(Ω²) ≠ 0 by Hodge symmetry), nothing in the paper supplies such a prime. Ordinarity is geometric and does not change under finite extension of L. The paper itself says, after Theorem C, that ordinary reduction at a positive density of primes is only conjectured in general (Joshi, attributing it to Serre), and known for abelian surfaces and K3 surfaces. So the claim holds only for varieties with an ordinary prime. The source says `"L′(g, U, 0) = 2^{2−4j} π^{−3/2−2j} Γ(2j + 1/2) / (m_0^j deg(Z(U))) · b(m_0, μ_0) L′(G, 1 + 2j)"`; it should be `L′(g, U, 0) = 2^{2−4j} √M π^{−3/2−2j} Γ(2j + 1/2) / (m_0^j deg(Z(U))) · b(m_0, μ_0) L′(G, 1 + 2j)`. The first formula of the lemma gives L′(g, U, 0) = C(0, j)(4πm_0)^{−1/2−j}L(χ_{D_0}, 1)^{−1}b(m_0, μ_0)L′(G, 1 + 2j) with C(0, j) = 2(4π)^{−j}Γ(2j + ½). The proof uses deg Z(U) = 2√|D_0|L(χ_{D_0}, 1)/π and |D_0| = 4Mm_0, so √|D_0| contributes 2√(Mm_0) and a factor √M survives. Theorem 6.5, which uses the first formula, has the √M correctly. - **Misprint** at Proof of Lemma 6.8, p. 743 (and the displayed identity on p. 744). The source says `"(1 − x)² P′′ − 2xP′ + 2j(2j + 1)P = 0 … a_{2m+2}/a_{2m} = −(2j − 2m)(2j + 2m + 1)/((2m + 2)(m + 1))" and "x^{(m+1)}_{s−1,+} + x^{(m+1)}_{s,−} = (2j − 2m)(2j + 2m + 1)/((2m + 2)(m + 1)) x^{(m)}_s"`; it should be `(1 − x²)P″ − 2xP′ + 2j(2j + 1)P = 0 and a_{2m+2}/a_{2m} = −(2j − 2m)(2j + 2m + 1)/((2m + 2)(2m + 1)); likewise (2m + 2)(2m + 1) in the identity on p. 744.`. ### Burungale–Kobayashi–Ota, "Rubin's conjecture on local units in the anticyclotomic tower at inert primes", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 3 (`PAPER-BURUNGALE-KOBAYASHI-OTA-21`)

- **Error** at Lemma 5.2(ii), p.956, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), 943–966 (Caltech repository copy of the publisher PDF, SHA-256 77ff3290…790e) (it affects a stated result). The source says `"(ii) The number of supersingular points in X₀(N)(F_{p²}) that correspond to supersingular elliptic curves over F_{p²} with the Frobenius trace a_{p²} = 2p or −2p and the j-invariant different from 0 and 1728 is at least µ(⌊(p−1)/12⌋ − 3/2 + (−3/p) + ½(−1/p)). In particular, there is a supersingular point with a_{p²} = 2p or −2p in X₀(N)(F_{p²}) over X(1)(F_{p²})∖{0,1728} that is unramified for π if p ≡ 1 mod 12 or p ≥ 31."`; it should be `The "in particular" follows for p ≡ 1 mod 12 and for p ≥ 31 with p ≠ 47. At p = 47 the displayed lower bound is 0 and gives nothing. The existence of an unramified supersingular point at p = 47 comes instead from Lemma 5.2(iii), since 47 ≡ 2 mod 3.`. The conclusion needs the lower bound to exceed the number of ramification points, which (i) bounds by µ/6. At p = 47: ⌊46/12⌋ = 3, (−3/47) = −1 (47 ≡ 2 mod 3) and (−1/47) = −1 (47 ≡ 3 mod 4), so the bound is µ(3 − 3/2 − 1 − 1/2) = 0 < µ/6. A computation over all primes 31 ≤ p ≤ 400 finds 47 as the only failure, and beyond that the floor term dominates. The main theorem is unaffected: Lemma 5.2(iii) covers p = 47, and Rubin's own verification (Remark 2.3) covers small p. Found by the review REV-PAPER-BURUNGALE-KOBAYASHI-OTA-21. ### Burungale–Tian, "A rank zero p-converse to a theorem of Gross–Zagier, Kolyvagin and Rubin", Annals of Mathematics 203 (2026), no. 1 (`PAPER-BURUNGALE-TIAN-26`)

- **Error** at Theorem 2.1 and footnote 3, p.4, in arXiv 2506.03465v2 (11 October 2025), the version read; the passage is the same in v1 (4 June 2025) (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Theorem 2.1. Let the notation be as above. Then we have ξ(h²_Q) = ξ((h¹/z)_Q), an equality of ideals in Z_p[[G_{p∞f}]]⊗Q." Footnote 3: "The formulation in Theorem 2.1 is then identical with the one in [11, §7.2]."`; it should be `ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(h²_Q)·∏_{𝔩|f, 𝔩∤p} ξ(Z_p[[G_{p∞f}/D_𝔩]]_Q), D_𝔩 the decomposition group of 𝔩; equivalently ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(H²_Q) with H² = lim_{K'} H²(O_{K'}[1/pf], Z_p(1)), which is the module of Johnson-Leung–Kings §7.2. The printed equality holds when every prime factor of f lies above p, and after localizing at height-one primes on components ramified at every 𝔩|f with 𝔩∤p.`. z is generated by the elliptic units of the single modulus p^n f (Kato §15.5), whose projection to a character χ carries ∏_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p}(1 − χ(𝔩)Frob_𝔩^{−1}) (Johnson-Leung–Kings Lemma 7.7); JLK accordingly pair it with H² over O_K[1/pf]. BT's h² is the class-group limit, which Kato (15.6.2) identifies at height one with H² over O_K[1/p]. By purity, 0 → H²(O[1/p]) → H²(O[1/pf]) → ⊕_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p} Z_p[[G/D_𝔩]] → 0, and since D_𝔩 has Z_p-rank one each term is torsion but not pseudo-null. On the trivial-character component 1 − Frob_𝔩^{−1} is a non-unit even after inverting p, so the printed equality fails whenever f has a prime factor not above p, and footnote 3's "identical" is false for h². The same imprecision is in Kato's quotation of Rubin (Astérisque 295, Theorem 15.2(2)); Rubin's elliptic units include all moduli g|f. Over 𝔽₅ the lemma holds: H¹(SL₂(ℤ), 𝔽₅) = 0 and H²(SL₂(𝔽₅), 𝔽₅) = 0 (Lemma 4.5.5) give vanishing invariants, and 3, 3′, 5 reduce to the Brauer irreducibles 3, 3, 5 of PSL₂(𝔽₅), none trivial. The source says `“By Lemma 5.2.6, the set {z ∈ D(0, 1) : |FN(z)| > e^M + 1} is contained in S(M, N)”`; it should be `… is contained in s·S(M, N), the image of S(M, N) under the order-2N rotation s of Lemma 5.2.6.`. On that set |1 − F_N^N| ≥ |F_N|^N − 1 > e^{MN}, so it is disjoint from S(M, N). By (5.2.7) it lies in s·S(M, N). Since s is a Euclidean rotation of D(0,1) about 0, s·S(M, N) also avoids the closed disc of radius r, and the conclusion stands. arXiv v1 (“contained in the rotation under s of the set S(M, N)”) and v3 (“contained in sS(M, N)”) had it right; the s was lost in v4. In the same proof the Shimizu bound is quoted for γ̃ ∈ Γ̃_N but used for γ ∈ Φ_N; Φ̃_N is discrete and contains t̃_N, so Shimizu's lemma gives the same bound. ### Calegari–Geraghty, "Modularity lifting beyond the Taylor-Wiles method", Inventiones Mathematicae (2018) (`PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-18`)

- **Gap** at Abstract (p. 298) and §1 Introduction (p. 305), compared with the §4.1 set-up for Theorem 4.8 (p. 361) and Lemma 4.11 (pp. 364–365). arXiv v2 has the same text ("completely solved", l. 316; same parenthetical on twisting before Thm 4.8). arXiv v1 is also the same: intro, and §3.8 Theorem 3.25 with the same twist-minimal hypothesis. (it affects a stated result). The source says `p. 305 (§1): "In the process of proving our main result, we also completely solve the problem (for p odd) of determining the multiplicity of an irreducible modular representation ρ̄ in the Jacobian J_1(N*)[m], where N* is the minimal level such that ρ̄ arises in weight two. In particular, we prove that when ρ̄ is unramified at p and ρ̄(Frob_p) is a scalar, then the multiplicity of ρ̄ is two (see Theorem 4.8). (In all other cases, the multiplicity was already known to be one—and in the exceptional cases we consider, the multiplicity was also known to be ≥2)." Abstract, p. 298: "Moreover, we also completely solve the problem (for p odd) of determining the multiplicity of an irreducible modular representation ρ̄ in the Jacobian J_1(N), where N is the minimal level such that ρ̄ arises in weight two." p. 361 (§4.1, set-up before Thm 4.8): "Assume that ρ̄ has minimal conductor amongst all its twists at all other primes (one can always twist ρ̄ to satisfy these condition)."`; it should be `In the abstract and introduction, limit the multiplicity claim to ρ̄ that have minimal conductor amongst their twists at primes ≠ p. That is the hypothesis of Theorem 4.8. Twist-minimality at p is automatic in the scalar case, where ρ̄|G_p is unramified. The alternative is to give a separate argument for non-twist-minimal ρ̄. Theorem 4.8 as stated in §4.1 needs no change.`. I rendered pp. 298, 305 and 361–366 and checked them against the text above.

1. The claims do not match. The abstract and introduction claim multiplicity two for every irreducible modular ρ̄ (p odd) at its own minimal weight-2 level. The classical multiplicity-one results cited in Remark 4.9 (Mazur, Gross, Edixhoven, ...) are stated without twist-minimality. Theorem 4.8, however, is proved only under the hypothesis that ρ̄ has minimal conductor among its twists. The only link between the two is the parenthetical "(one can always twist ρ̄ to satisfy these condition)". That remark is true, but it does not show that multiplicity is unchanged by twisting: ρ̄ and ρ̄⊗ψ̄ sit at different levels N(ρ̄)p and N(ρ̄⊗ψ̄)p, with different Jacobians and Hecke algebras.

2. The multiplicity depends on the Hecke algebra. The proof of Theorem 4.8 uses T_pG^0 ≅ T_m and T_pG^e = Hom(T_m, Z_p), so dim J[m] = 1 + (number of generators of ω_{T_m}). Multiplicity two therefore means T_m has type 3. This is a property of T_m, and T_m changes under twisting.

3. A concrete example where T_m changes. Let ρ̄ = ρ̄_0⊗χ̄, with ρ̄_0 twist-minimal and unramified at a prime v ∤ N_0 p, and χ̄ tame of conductor v. Then ρ̄^{I_v} = 0, so every lift has conductor exactly v² and every lift appears at level N(ρ̄)p, with U_v = 0. If ρ̄_0(Frob_v) has eigenvalue ratio ≡ v, then Ribet's level-raised forms (Steinberg at v, level N_0vp) twisted by χ̃ are extra newforms of conductor v² in T_m(ρ̄). They have no counterpart in T_{m_0}(ρ̄_0) at level N_0p. So T_m(ρ̄) corresponds to the unrestricted deformation problem at v, while T_{m_0}(ρ̄_0) corresponds to the unramified one.

4. The proof does not carry over word for word. The proof of Lemma 4.11 lists the non-smooth cases only under twist-minimality. In the example above, R_v ≅ R_v^unrestricted(ρ̄_0|G_v). Its unramified and Steinberg components meet at characteristic-0 points (unramified lifts with eigenvalue ratio v), where H^2(G_v, ad^0ρ) ≠ 0. So "R_v[1/p] formally smooth" fails, and that property is what the text uses when applying Kisin's method to get R̃[1/p] = T[1/p]. The paper's own remark on p. 363 also uses twist-minimality to exclude v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄^{I_v} = 0.

5. The result is probably still true. R_v is still a complete intersection, and weight-2 points avoid the intersection locus by Ramanujan. So multiplicity two is plausible at non-minimal level too, but the paper gives no argument for it.

Conclusion: this is a gap in the reduction to the twist-minimal case, and it affects the claim in the abstract and introduction. Theorem 4.8 itself, as stated, is correct. Defence tried and failed. (1) The quantity is not twist-invariant by any formal argument. Twisting ρ̄ = ρ̄_0⊗χ̄ (χ̄ of conductor x ≠ p) changes N(ρ̄), N*, the curve J_1(N*) and the Hecke algebra T. (2) If ρ̄ is not twist-minimal at x, then ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. Every lift then has conductor cond(ρ̄|G_x), so every lift of ρ̄|G_x shows up at level Γ_1(N). After twisting back, m at level N(ρ̄)p also sees non-minimal forms for ρ̄_0. Examples are χ-twists of forms that are Steinberg at x (conductor x²) when the level-raising condition holds, or of ramified principal series of p-power type when x ≡ 1 mod p. So T_m is not the twist of T_{m_0} at level N(ρ̄_0)p. When no such extra forms exist, a Chebotarev/trace argument does identify the two Hecke algebras, but not in general. (3) The paper's proof really does use minimality. On p. 362, Φ is 'the only twists' preserving minimal-conductor lifts only under minimality; when x ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ is non-minimal at x, the characters of Z_p⊗(Z/x)^× also qualify. On p. 363 the paper itself says the twist-uniqueness 'is not true when v ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ has trivial invariants under I_v' and removes this case by the minimality assumption. Lemma 4.11 lists only the non-smooth cases that can occur for twist-minimal ρ̄. For a non-minimal ρ̄|G_x = χ̄⊗(unramified, Frobenius-eigenvalue ratio ≡ x mod p), R_{x,φ} is isomorphic to the unrestricted fixed-determinant ring of an unramified representation. Its unramified and Steinberg components meet in the generic fibre at the points μ⊕με, where H²(G_x, ad⁰ρ) ≠ 0. So the claim that the generic fibre is formally smooth fails, and with it the stated input to Kisin's R[1/p] = T[1/p]. (4) No nearby statement closes the gap. Remark 4.12 concerns J_H, and the parenthetical '(one can always twist ρ̄…)' only says that a twist-minimal twist exists. The general statement is very plausibly true: the extra local rings are complete intersections of type 1, and modular points avoid the singular locus. But the paper gives no proof of it, so the introduction and abstract claim more than Theorem 4.8 proves. Consequences: §4.1 opens with 'Although this is not needed for our main results', and nothing later cites Theorem 4.8. Only the claim in the abstract and introduction is affected, and the proposed restriction is right and minimal. The parenthetical says condition H at primes where ρ̄|I_x is irreducible follows from det ρ = ε. The paper writes "absolutely irreducible" wherever it means that: at the opening of §5.1, on p. 379, and in Theorem 1.3(4) ("either ρ̄|D_x is reducible or ρ̄|I_x is absolutely irreducible"). So plain "irreducible" in (3)(a) and (8) means irreducible over k.

2. Absolutely irreducible case: the claim holds. Let J ⊂ I_x be the kernel of I_x → Z_p(1). Then ρ(J) ≅ ρ̄(J). ρ̄|J is still absolutely irreducible because p is odd. So ρ(J) spans M_2(R), and ρ(t_p)^n is a scalar a ≡ 1 with a^2 = det = 1, hence a = 1.

3. Irreducible over k but not absolutely irreducible: the claim fails. This happens for tame inertia whose eigenvalues α, α^{−1} lie in k' \ k. Write ρ(t) = s·u, where u ≡ 1 lies in the centraliser R[s] = R⊗W(k'). The determinant condition only gives N(u) = uσ(u) = 1, which does not force u = 1. Frobenius adds u^{N+1} = 1 if it swaps the eigenlines, or u^{N−1} = 1 if it fixes them.

Explicit check (python script in work/agents/vK6A/check.py). Take p = 3, k = F_3, R = F_3[e]/(e^2), ρ̄(t) = s = [[0,−1],[1,0]]. The polynomial x^2 + 1 has no root mod 3, so ρ̄|I_x is irreducible over F_3. Put ρ(t) = s(1 + e·s), which has det 1 and order 12.
- Swap case: N = 11 or 23 (≡ −1 mod 12), ρ(Frob) = diag(1,−1) with det −1 ≡ N mod 3.
- Non-swap case: N = 13 or 169 (≡ 1 mod 12), ρ(Frob) = 1.
In all four cases F t F^{−1} = t^N holds (also with N^{−1}), and det ρ = ε on D_x. Yet |ρ(I_x)| = 12 while |ρ̄(I_x)| = 4, so H fails.

The swap case is allowed by (3)(a) as printed. It is not caught by (3)(d), which asks ρ̄|I_x to be reducible. Here ρ̄|D_x is dihedral of order 8, hence absolutely irreducible, so x is a genuine vexing prime. A global example is E[3] of y^2 = x^3 + 11x at 11 over F = Q(√−2). This is exactly the case that v1 and Theorem 1.3(4) exclude.

4. Effect on the proof. Conjecture A(2) gives only types S and P. So "Properties (1)–(4) of Conjecture A then imply ... ϕ: R^min → T_{m∅}" (p. 379), and likewise Lemma 5.6, rely on H being automatic, and that is unjustified in this case. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected: its hypothesis (4) excludes the N ≡ −1 case, and the N ≡ +1 case is repaired by extending scalars. DEFENCE: with the absolute reading the parenthetical is correct. Let J = ker(ρ̄|I_x). Then ρ(J) is pro-p, so it factors through tame inertia. It is procyclic, generated by some u ≡ 1, and u is central in ρ(I_x): it commutes with t, and [P_x,u] ⊂ ρ(P_x)∩⟨u⟩ = 1. When ρ̄|I_x is absolutely irreducible, Nakayama gives R·ρ(I_x) = M_2(R), so u is scalar. Then det u = ε|I_x = 1 gives u² = 1, hence u = 1 since p is odd, and ρ(I_x) ≅ ρ̄(I_x).

LITERAL READING FAILS: suppose ρ̄|I_x is irreducible over k but not absolutely. Then the centraliser of the prime-to-p part s̃ of ρ(t) is R' = R⊗W(k'), and det gives u·σ(u) = 1. Two cases break the claim.

(B) Frobenius swaps the eigenlines. Then σ(u) = u^{N(x)}, and N ≡ −1 allows u ≠ 1. This is the candidate's case. Checked explicitly: p = 5, N(x) = 29, ρ̄(t) = [[0,−1],[1,−1]] (order 3, char. poly x²+x+1 irreducible mod 5), ρ̄(Frob) = [[1,−1],[0,−1]], image S_3, absolutely irreducible on D_x. Over F_5[ε] take ρ(t) = ρ̄(t)(1+εX) with X = [[1,−2],[2,−1]]. Then the relation Frob·t·Frob^{-1} = t^{29} holds, det ρ(t) = 1 and det ρ(Frob) = 29 mod 5, but ρ(t) has order 15. This x satisfies (3)(a) literally, and (3)(d) is vacuous for it over k.

(A) Not noted by the candidate: Frobenius centralises and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p. Then u^{N−1} = 1 and u·σ(u) = 1 again allow u ≠ 1. Checked explicitly: p = 3, N = 13, ρ̄(t) = [[0,−1],[1,0]], ρ̄(Frob) = 1, ρ(t) = ρ̄(t)(1+ε·ρ̄(t)) of order 12. This is realised locally, e.g. by y² = x³+13x+13² at 13, mod 3. Thm 1.3's hypotheses do not exclude case A. Under the absolute reading it is type P, covered by Conj A(2)(b).

WHY THIS IS A MISPRINT, NOT AN ERROR: the intended meaning is clear from context.
(i) Thm 1.3(4) says 'absolutely irreducible'.
(ii) The sentence right after (8) says the N ≡ −1 vexing primes 'have been eliminated'. That is true only if (3)(d)'s 'reducible' means 'over k̄'.
(iii) §3.9 defines vexing primes by 'ρ̄|I_x ≃ ξ⊕ξ^c is reducible', which is reducibility over k̄.
(iv) v1 states the hypothesis with 'absolutely'.
Under the absolute reading, case B with N ≡ −1 is excluded by (d), case B with N ≢ −1 is type M (automatic: u^{N+1} = 1), case A is type P, and H is automatic. So Conj A (1)–(4) do give ϕ on p. 379, and Thm 5.11 and Thm 1.3 stand as intended. 2. For v ∤ p, a p-power-order character ξ of O_v^× factors through (O_v/π_v)^×, so a nontrivial one exists iff p | N(v) − 1. Put χ″|O^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ.
- If a(ψ) ≥ 2, then ⟨ψ⟩ξ agrees with ⟨ψ⟩ on 1 + π^{a−1}.
- If a(ψ) = 1, then ⟨ψ⟩ξ is still nontrivial, because the orders of ⟨ψ⟩ and ξ are coprime.
Either way a(⟨ψ⟩ξ) = a(ψ). So π″ = π(χ″, χ″^{−1}) is irreducible with trivial central character and conductor 2a(ψ) = c. By Casselman its newvector is K_0(π^c)-fixed, hence Γ_p(v^c)-fixed.

3. Mackey check (script at work/agents/K6-1-A/mackey.py). Take N(v) = 7, p = 3, ψ quadratic, so c = 2. Double cosets B(O)\GL_2(O)/K_0(7^n) have representatives (1 0; 7^i 1), and the character condition becomes a(χ) ≤ min(i, n − i). For both the minimal χ = ⟨ψ⟩ (order 2) and the non-minimal χ″ = ⟨ψ⟩ξ (order 6):
- n = 1: no coset contributes.
- n = 2: only i = 1 contributes.
So each has exactly a 1-dimensional space of K_0(v²)-fixed vectors.

4. π″ reduces to ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1} on I_v, and T_∅ has no operators at v, so π″ lies in the m∅-part. Moreover ⟨ψ⟩ξ ∉ {⟨ψ⟩, ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}}, because ξ ≠ 1 has p-power order while ⟨ψ⟩ has prime-to-p order. So π″ is excluded by condition (6).

5. Existence of such forms. Take r̄ over Q with trivial character and weight 2, ℓ ≡ 1 mod p split in F, and r̄|I_ℓ = ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}. Lifts of prescribed type exist (Diamond–Taylor 1994; Gee 2011); take a newform f with type ⟨ψ⟩ξ ⊕ (⟨ψ⟩ξ)^{−1} at ℓ and minimal elsewhere. Then BC_F(f) is a cohomological cuspidal π″ at level K_∅. At the Q̄_p-point of T_{∅,m∅} it defines, the specialisation of ρ_m has the traces of r_f|G_F. So it is r_f|G_F, and by Carayol r_f|I_v has the non-minimal type, contradicting A(2)(b). In that case R^min ≅ T_m (Theorem 1.3) fails too, and the theorem survives only because its hypothesis, Conjecture A, is false.

6. §3 avoids this by twisting (p. 310: ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0) together with X_H / U_x at level x^{c_x}, c_x = a(ψ). That route is unavailable in §5, where det = ε is fixed on PGL_2.

7. Types M and H are fine: with fixed determinant ε, a non-minimal lift at a type-M prime needs p | N(v) + 1, which is excluded. A separate case, not checked in detail: when ψ is quadratic, a twisted Steinberg St⊗χ (conductor c) also sits at Γ_0(v^c) whatever N(v) is.

I classify this as an error rather than the candidate's "gap": Conjecture A as formulated at this level is false in cases where π″ occurs. Defence attempts, none of which works:
(1) Γ_p(v^c) is contained in Γ_0(v^c) by definition. Take π'' = π(χ'', χ''^{−1}) with χ''|O^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ, where ξ ≠ 1 is tame of p-power order. Then π'' has trivial central character and conductor 2a(⟨ψ⟩ξ) = 2a(ψ) = c. By Casselman newform theory, K_0(ϖ^c) acts on the newvector through ω(d) = 1, so the newvector is Γ_0(v^c)-fixed and hence Γ_p(v^c)-fixed. The restriction "d has p-power order" therefore removes nothing here.
(2) Explicit check in the induced model: at PGL-level {a ≡ d, c ≡ 0 mod ϖ^n}, π(χ, χ^{−1}) has vectors on which K_0 acts by χ^{±1}(a/d), and only when a(χ) ≤ n. The p-power restriction does separate ⟨ψ⟩ from ⟨ψ⟩ξ at n = a(ψ), but not at n = 2a(ψ), where both have Γ_0-fixed newvectors. The paper's own §5.5 (p. 380) says the level was chosen as the X_H(N) analogue to exclude such twists. v1's GL_2 version (type 1 ⊕ ψ, c = a(ψ)) does exclude them. Nothing in the hypotheses rules out p | N(v) − 1 at type-P primes: (3)(c) and Theorem 1.3(4) only exclude N ≡ −1 for vexing primes.
(3) Consequence. π'' has I_v-type ⟨ψ⟩ξ ⊕ (⟨ψ⟩ξ)^{−1}, which fails condition (6). If π'' is cohomological at level K_∅ with residual representation ρ̄, it contributes to T_{∅,m} ⊗ Q̄_p. Then Conjecture A(2)(b) for Q = ∅ contradicts local–global compatibility at v, even up to semisimplification.
Such π'' exist. Take the base change to F, with ℓ split, of a classical weight-2 form on Γ_0(ℓ²) with ℓ ≡ 1 mod p and local type ⟨ψ⟩ξ that is congruent to a minimal form of type ⟨ψ⟩; Carayol and Diamond–Taylor give such congruences. So Conjecture A as stated is false for such ρ̄, and Theorems 5.11 and 1.3 are vacuous for them.
Theorem 1.2 is unaffected: semistable minimal ρ has only type-S primes. The proofs of 5.11 and 1.3 use the level only through Conjecture A, so the patching argument survives once the level is corrected. However, the conclusion of Theorem 1.3 as stated, R^min ≅ T_m on H_1(Y_0(N)), is false in these cases.

The intended meaning is still clear. 𝒪_v is local, so Pic(𝒪_v) = 0 and PGL_2(𝒪_v) = GL_2(𝒪_v)/𝒪_v^×. That is the image of GL_2(𝒪_v) in PGL_2(F_v), the maximal compact subgroup that stabilises the lattice class [𝒪_v^2]. So the proposed correction to PGL_2(𝒪_v) is right, and it agrees with the finite-flat (unramified, maximal level at p) intent and with item (3) of §9.1 (PGL_n(𝒪_v) for v ∉ S ∪ Q, which includes v|p). The arXiv v2 text (§5.2.1) has the identical wording "GL2 (Ov)", so the slip was never corrected. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

- **Gap** at §5.3, Lemma 5.6 (statement and proof), published p. 375 (PDF p. 79); Conjecture A(3) runs from p. 374 to p. 375. arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2, §5.3, p. 58) has word-for-word the same text for Conjecture A(3) and Lemma 5.6. arXiv v1 does not contain this section. (it affects a stated result). The source says `Lemma 5.6 Assume Conjecture A. Assume that there exists a maximal ideal m of T_Q associated to ρ̄. Suppose that Q consists entirely of Taylor–Wiles primes. Then there exists a representation: ρ_Q : G_F → GL_2(T_{Q,m}) whose traces generate T_{Q,m} and such that ρ_Q is a minimal deformation of ρ̄ outside Q with cyclotomic determinant. Proof By Conjecture A, the representation ρ_Q := ρ_m to T_{Q,m} is such a representation. Moreover, assumption 3 above guarantees (by Hensel's Lemma) that the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces. [Conjecture A(3), same page: "... and so φ(Frob_v) mod m is well defined; assume that φ(Frob_v) ≢ ±1 mod m. Then ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}."]`; it should be `Lemma 5.6 needs one more hypothesis: for each v ∈ Q, U_v = T_{π_v} ≢ ±1 mod m, which is the same as φ_v(Frob_v) ≢ ±1 mod m. One way to guarantee this is to take m ⊇ (m_∅, U_v − α_v) with α_v a root of X² − T_vX + 1 mod m_∅, as in Lemma 5.8 and Theorem 5.11. The proposed correction is right and minimal for the Hensel step. Conjecture A(3) also takes "the image of φ mod m is unramified" "by assumption". If that phrase is read as a hypothesis too, the lemma also needs the diamond operators at v to be trivial mod m. That holds in Theorem 5.11, where the diamond operators act through the p-group Δ_N. The rest of the lemma does not use (3): the minimality and cyclotomic-determinant parts need no change.`. I rendered pp. 374–375 and read them. Conjecture A(3) is conditional: it gives ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1} only after "assume that φ(Frob_v) ≢ ±1 mod m". Nothing else in Conjecture A mentions v ∈ Q: (1) covers λ outside S ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}, (2) covers S(ρ̄) and (4) covers v|p. Lemma 5.6 allows any maximal ideal m of T_Q associated to ρ̄. By Definition 5.5, "associated to ρ̄" only constrains T_λ for λ outside S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}. "Taylor–Wiles primes" (§5.1 and Prop. 5.2) only means N(x) ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄(Frob_x) has distinct eigenvalues, which is a condition on ρ̄ and not on m. So nothing ensures U_v mod m ≠ ±1. The proof uses the conclusion of (3) without checking its hypothesis. Without that conclusion, the operators T_α at Q are not linked to ρ_m at all, so "traces generate T_{Q,m}" is not justified. Hensel's lemma alone splits ρ|D_x into two characters, but it cannot identify either character with the Hecke character φ.

I also checked whether the paper excludes such m elsewhere. It does not. Lemma 5.8, like Lemma 3.5 (pp. 305–307), treats only the m containing U_x − α_x. The step showing V[m] = 0 gives x·U_x² = ⟨x⟩, i.e. γ² ≡ α_xβ_x ≡ 1 for the eigenvalue γ of U_x on V. That contradicts γ = α_x (since α_x ≠ β_x), but it is consistent with γ = ±1. So "new at x" torsion with U_x ≡ ±1 (Steinberg type) is not ruled out without local–global compatibility at x, which Conjecture A deliberately leaves out.

The minimality part of the conclusion and the cyclotomic determinant (from (1) plus Chebotarev) do not use (3). Lemma 5.6 is never cited later. Theorem 5.11 repeats the argument itself for m ∋ U_x − α_x, where α_x ≢ ±1, and its step (a) invokes (3) correctly. So the main results are unaffected, and only Lemma 5.6 as stated overreaches. A charitable reading ("there exists m" meaning a suitably chosen m) does not help, because the conclusion is about T_{Q,m} for the given m and no choice of U_x-eigenvalue is specified. Defence tried and failed. (i) The "Taylor–Wiles primes" hypothesis (Prop. 5.2: N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, ρ̄ unramified at v, ρ̄(Frob_v) has distinct eigenvalues) is a condition on ρ̄, not on U_v mod m. It would give U_v ≢ ±1 mod m only through the conclusion ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}. Then the eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v) are φ̄(Frob_v)^{±1}, which are distinct iff φ̄(Frob_v) ≠ ±1, because ε(Frob_v) = N(v) ≡ 1. But that conclusion is exactly what (3) withholds when φ(Frob_v) ≡ ±1, so the argument is circular. (ii) "Associated to ρ̄" (Def. before Conj. A) constrains only T_λ for λ ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}. (iii) Nothing else in Conjecture A controls U_v mod m. (1) gives ρ_m mod m ≅ ρ̄, but no statement ties φ(Frob_v) to the eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v) in the ±1 case. (iv) No nearby result supplies the step. Lemma 5.8 and the Ihara argument in the proof of Lemma 9.6 deal only with m ∋ U_x − α_x where U_x² − 1 is invertible. They do not show that H_1(Y_1(Q))_m = 0 when U_x ≡ ±1. For torsion classes, nothing rules out "new at x" classes with U_x ≡ ±1. Such classes would be excluded under full local–global compatibility (Steinberg at v would force equal eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v)), but Conjecture A does not assume that. (v) T_{Q,m} is generated by the T_λ, which are traces by (1), together with U_v and the diamond operators at v ∈ Q. The only route to putting U_v in the trace subalgebra is Hensel applied to ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}, using the fact that the roots φε(σ) and φ^{-1}(σ) are distinct mod m. So for an m with U_v ≡ ±1 mod m, "traces generate T_{Q,m}" is not proved. The rest of the lemma does not use (3). Minimality outside Q holds because R_Q (§5.1) puts no condition at x ∈ Q, and L_{Q,x} is the full H^1. The determinant is cyclotomic by (1) and Chebotarev. Consequences: the paper never cites Lemma 5.6 by number (grep finds only its own statement). Its content is re-derived in the proof of Theorem 5.11 ("Applying Conjecture A to T_{Q_N,m}, we deduce the existence of a surjective homomorphism R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}", together with step (5a) using part (3)). There m ⊇ (m_∅, U_x − α_x), and by Lemma 5.8, which step (b) invokes, α_x is a root of X² − T_xX + 1 whose two roots are distinct mod m_∅. Since α_xβ_x ≡ 1 and α_x ≢ β_x, we get α_x ≢ ±1, so (3) applies. Theorem 5.11, Theorem 1.3 and §9 (Conjecture B, with m = (m, U_x − α_x) stated explicitly) are therefore unaffected. Only Lemma 5.6, as stated for an arbitrary m, overreaches. - **Misprint** at §5.3, Conjecture A(4), p. 375 (published version) (it affects the proof). The source says `(4) If v|p, then ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary.`; it should be `(4) If v|p and ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, then ρ|D_v is finite flat (that is, (ρ ⊗ T_{Q,m}/m^n)|D_v is finite flat for all n ≥ 1, as in §5.1 condition (3)); and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary. An equivalent phrasing is "If v|p, then ρ|D_v is finite flat if ρ̄|D_v is". Deleting the first bar alone would not fix it. An unconditional "ρ|D_v is finite flat" would force ρ̄|D_v to be finite flat, because finite flat representations are closed under quotients when e = 1 < p − 1 (Raynaud). That contradicts the allowed case where ρ̄ is ordinary but not finite flat.`. I checked the page images at 110 and 250 dpi. Conjecture A starts on p. 374 (PDF p. 78), and part (4) is at the top of p. 375 (PDF p. 79). It reads exactly: "(4) If v|p, then ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary." The first two ρ's have bars and the last one does not. arXiv v2 (p. 58, image checked) has the same text.

As printed, the first clause says something about the residual representation ρ̄ and nothing about ρ = ρ_m. Taken literally, it contradicts the paper's own setup:
- §5.1 hypothesis (2), p. 369: "ρ̄ is either ordinary or finite flat at v|p".
- Theorem 1.3(1): ρ̄ is "either finite flat or ordinary" at v|p.
- §5.2 level condition (4), p. 373: K_{Q,v} = GL2(O_v) "if ρ̄|D_v is finite flat. Otherwise … Γ0(v)".

So the printed conjecture would be false whenever ρ̄ is ordinary but not finite flat. When ρ̄|D_v is finite flat and not ordinary, it says nothing about ρ|D_v.

The conclusion that is missing is exactly what the proofs need. §5.1 deformation conditions (2) and (3), p. 369, require the reductions mod m^n to be finite flat or ordinary, and finite flat whenever ρ̄|G_v is finite flat. These conditions define R_Q and R^min. They are used in three places:
- Lemma 5.6, p. 375: "By Conjecture A, the representation ρ_Q := ρ_m … is such a representation", i.e. a minimal deformation.
- §5.4, p. 378: "Properties (1)–(4) of Conjecture A then imply that ρ_{m∅} gives rise to a homomorphism ϕ : R^min → T_{m∅}".
- §5.4, p. 379: the surjection R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}, which the proof of Theorem 5.11 uses. Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 are deduced from that result.

Under the printed wording, ρ_m need not satisfy condition (3), so ϕ is not justified. The intended meaning is clear, and the proofs work once (4) is corrected. So this is a misprint in the statement of an assumed conjecture that the proofs depend on. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

A side note on a separate issue: the pdftotext layer drops the ε in part (3). The image shows "ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}", which is correct as printed. - **Error** at §5.3.1, proof of Lemma 5.9(1) (and hence (2)), p. 377 (published version) (it affects the proof). The source says `Proof Consider part (1). By Nakayama’s Lemma, we reduce to the case when μ = k. Yet H_3(Y_0(Q), k) = 0 and the action of Hecke operators on H_0(Y_0(Q), k) (which preserve the connected components) is via the degree map, and this action is Eisenstein (in the sense that the only m in the support of H_0 are Eisenstein). [§5.3, proof of Lemma 5.9, p. 377 = PDF p. 81; identical wording in arXiv v2, line ~3114 of cg-v2.txt]`; it should be `Replace "H_3(Y_0(Q), k) = 0" by the localized statement "H_3(Y_0(Q), k)_m = 0". That is all the Nakayama/dévissage step needs. For p ≥ 5 the step holds as intended. A finite-order element of PGL_2(F) has order 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6, since ζ+ζ^{-1} ∈ F ∩ R = Q. So the lattices have no p-torsion, the orbifold homology with k-coefficients is the homology of a non-compact 3-dimensional quotient, and H_3 = 0 even before localizing. For p = 3 the paper gives no argument, although §5.1 and Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 allow p = 3. Two fixes are possible: (a) add the hypothesis p ≥ 5 to §5 and to Theorems 1.2 and 1.3; or (b) prove that the 3-primary Farrell classes vanish after localizing at m. These classes are carried by order-3 subgroups, whose centralizers are rank-one tori coming from F(√−3). My unproved assessment is that their Hecke eigensystems are induced from F(ζ_3). The standing hypothesis that ρ̄|G_{F(ζ_3)} is absolutely irreducible would then exclude them. Two corrections proposed earlier are not quite right: - H-part1b-13 calls these classes "Eisenstein". That is inaccurate, and m being non-Eisenstein is probably not enough on its own. - X-K6-10 suggests restricting to 3-torsion-free levels. That is not available in general, because the level is fixed by ρ̄ and by Γ_0(x) at Taylor–Wiles primes, where N(x) ≡ 1 mod 3.`. Checked on the page image of p. 377: the text is as quoted. The setting of §5 allows p = 3: §5.1 says "let p ≥ 3 be a prime that is unramified in F", and Thms 1.2 and 1.3 also take p ≥ 3. Remark 5.3 and §5.2.2 take (co)homology in the orbifold sense, i.e. group homology of the arithmetic lattices. Under that convention the step is false for p = 3 whenever a component lattice has 3-torsion. My own check of the candidate's example, F = Q(i) (3 is inert) and level PGL2(O_v) everywhere, so Γ = PGL2(Z[i]):
(i) g = [[0,−1],[1,1]] has order 3 in PGL2.
(ii) Its centralizer in Γ is Z[i][g]^×/Z[i]^× = Z[ζ12]^×/μ4 ≅ Z/3 × Z, because Q(ζ12) has unit rank 1.
(iii) h = [[0,1],[1,0]] conjugates g to g^{-1}.
(iv) Γ has 3-rank 1 and vcd = 3 − 1 = 2. By Brown's theorem, Ĥ^4(Γ,Z)_(3) contains Ĥ^4(C,Z)_(3)^{N/C} = H^4(Z/3,Z) = Z/3 ≠ 0. Aut(Z/3) acts trivially on H^4.
(v) By universal coefficients, H_3(Γ,Z)_(3) ≠ 0, so H_3(Γ,F_3) ≠ 0.
Independent cross-check: Fine's amalgam PSL2(Z[i]) = (S3 *_{Z/3} A4) *_{PSL2(Z)} (S3 *_{Z/2} D2) with Mayer–Vietoris gives dim H^3(PSL2(Z[i]),F_3) = 2. This matches Z/3 in integral degrees ≡ 0, 3 mod 4.
The failure does not depend on this particular example. Every allowed level has 3-torsion: Γ_0(x) for Taylor–Wiles x (N(x) ≡ 1 mod 3) and Γ_0(v) for v|3 contain conjugates of g, since g fixes a point of P^1(k_x). The candidate's p ≥ 5 claim and element-order list are also correct.
The localized statement Lemma 5.9(1) is probably still true under the paper's hypotheses, but the printed proof does not establish it for p = 3.
Dependencies: Lemma 5.9(2) uses the H_3 vanishing from (1). Prop. 5.10 uses 5.9(1) and (2), the latter to get H_2(Y_0(Q),O)_m free. Thm 5.11(c) uses Prop. 5.10. Thm 5.11(b) needs only the H_0 part, which is fine. Thm 1.3 follows from Thm 5.11. Remark 9.3 makes a related unproved claim ("may be verified directly" for GL(2)/F, F imaginary quadratic), but that is outside this item. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, ALL FAIL.
(i) Convention. Remark 5.3 (p. 372) says explicitly that for every K the cohomology of Y(K) is taken in the orbifold sense, i.e. as the cohomology of the arithmetic lattices. It adds that this can differ from the cohomology of the underlying space. The argument itself needs this convention: the Shapiro isomorphism H_1(Y_0(Q),O[Δ]) ≅ H_1(Y_Δ(Q),O) and the Hochschild–Serre sequences in Prop. 5.10 and Thm 5.11(b) hold for group homology. So H_3 cannot be read as homology of the coarse space.
(ii) Scope. §5.1 and Thms 1.2 and 1.3 take any p ≥ 3 unramified in F. So p = 3 is allowed for F = Q(i), Q(√−2), and so on.
(iii) 3-torsion is present. g = [[0,−1],[1,1]] ∈ SL_2(Z) has order 3 in every PGL_2(O_F). Its characteristic polynomial X²−X+1 splits mod x when N(x) ≡ 1 mod 3, which holds at every Taylor–Wiles prime for p = 3. So Γ_0(x) contains conjugates of g.
  Example: F = Q(i), p = 3, S(ρ̄) = ∅, ρ̄ finite flat at 3. Then Y = Y_0(∅) = PGL_2(Z[i])\H³.
(iv) H_3 ≠ 0 there. The lattice Γ = PGL_2(Z[i]) has vcd 2 and 3-rank 1. The centralizer of ⟨g⟩ is Z[ζ12]^×/Z[i]^× ≅ Z/3 × Z; mod torsion it is generated by 1−ζ12. Conjugation by h = [[0,1],[1,0]] acts as ζ12 ↦ ζ12^5, so N/C = Z/2 inverts both factors. It follows that Ĥ^n(N)_(3) = Z/3 for n ≡ 0, 3 mod 4.
  By Brown's p-rank-one theorem, H^4(Γ,Z)_(3) = Ĥ^4 ≠ 0. Hence H_3(Γ,Z)_(3) ≠ 0 and H_3(Γ,F_3) ≠ 0.
  Cross-check: Fine's amalgam PSL_2(Z[i]) = (S_3 *_{Z/3} A_4) *_{PSL_2 Z} (S_3 *_{Z/2} D_2) with Mayer–Vietoris gives dim H³(PSL_2(Z[i]);F_3) = 2.
  The example is not special to Q(i). For any F, the relative automorphism of F(√−3)/F inverts norm-one units, so Ĥ^4 ⊇ Z/3 for every component lattice with 3-torsion.
(v) Nothing nearby supplies the missing step.
  - Remark 9.3 concerns only low degrees, via the congruence subgroup property.
  - §9 assumes the needed vanishing as Conjecture B(4)(a).
  - Footnote 3 in §3 on X_H(13) shows the authors knew stacky p = 3 classes exist; that class is induced from Q(√−3).

So the printed statement H_3(Y_0(Q),k) = 0 is false, not merely unproved. Under PROTOCOL §18 that is a step that fails, hence "error". The lemma itself is not shown false.

CONSEQUENCES, for p = 3 only:
- Lemma 5.9(1) with i = 3 is left unproved.
- Lemma 5.9(2) is left unproved: its proof uses H_3(μ/ϖ)_m = 0.
- Prop. 5.10 depends on 5.9(2). It needs H_2(Y_0(Q),O)_m to be torsion-free in order to bound dim Tor_1/ϖ by r. This is a real gap, not a formality: unlocalized, H_2(Γ,Z) does have 3-torsion (Z/3 for PSL_2(Z[i])). The displayed Hochschild–Serre exact sequence itself needs only the i = 0 part.
- Thm 5.11(c) depends on Prop. 5.10.
- Thm 5.11(b) uses only the i = 0 vanishing (low-degree Hochschild–Serre terms) and is unaffected. X-K6-10 says (b) relies on the H_3 vanishing; that is slightly off.
- Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 for p = 3 therefore rest on an unproved step. For p ≥ 5 nothing is affected, and §9 is unaffected. - **Misprint** at §5.3.1, proof of Lemma 5.9(2), p. 377 (published version). The source says `Taking cohomology, localizing at 𝔪, and using the vanishing of H_3(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪 from part (1), we deduce that H^2(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪[ϖ] = 0, hence the result. [The display just before it, printed without a ϖ over the first arrow, is "0 → μ → μ → μ/ϖ → 0". §5.3.1, proof of Lemma 5.9(2), p. 377 = PDF p. 81. arXiv v2 has the same wording.]`; it should be `"Taking homology, localizing at 𝔪, and using the vanishing of H_3(Y_0(Q), μ/ϖ)_𝔪 from part (1) (applied to the finitely generated O[Δ]-module μ/ϖ), we deduce that H_2(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪[ϖ] = 0, hence the result."`. I checked the page image of PDF p. 81 (published p. 377), and the text is printed as quoted. Lemma 5.9(2) is about homology: "If μ is p-torsion free, then H_2(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪 is p-torsion free." Its only use, in the proof of Prop. 5.10 on p. 378, is also about homology: H_2(Y_0(Q), O)_𝔪 must be O-free. So "cohomology" and the superscript H^2 are slips. Throughout §5.3 the paper writes H_i for homology and H^i for cohomology. Cohomology would also give the wrong sequence: H^1(μ/ϖ) → H^2(μ) → H^2(μ) (the second map multiplication by ϖ) says nothing about H^2[ϖ].

I redid the argument myself. Multiplication by ϖ commutes with the Hecke operators, and localizing at 𝔪 is exact. The homology long exact sequence of 0 → μ → μ → μ/ϖ → 0 (first map multiplication by ϖ) therefore gives, after localizing:
H_3(μ)_𝔪 → H_3(μ)_𝔪 (multiplication by ϖ) → H_3(μ/ϖ)_𝔪 → H_2(μ)_𝔪 → H_2(μ)_𝔪 (multiplication by ϖ).
Hence H_2(μ)_𝔪[ϖ] is the image of H_3(μ/ϖ)_𝔪. If only H_3(μ)_𝔪 = 0, we get H_2(μ)_𝔪[ϖ] ≅ H_3(μ/ϖ)_𝔪, which need not be zero. So the fact actually needed is H_3(Y_0(Q), μ/ϖ)_𝔪 = 0. Part (1) supplies it, because μ/ϖ is a finitely generated O[Δ]-module and part (1) holds for all such modules. Since H_2(μ)_𝔪 is a finitely generated O-module, having no ϖ-torsion means it is p-torsion free.

This is the paper's own pattern done slightly wrong. In the parallel Lemma 3.7(1) (p. 316) the authors correctly use the quotient coefficients: "H^2(X_Δ(Q), L_k) vanishes". Lemma 5.9's proof looks adapted from it, with the words "Taking cohomology" left in and the coefficients left as μ instead of μ/ϖ.

The candidate's correction is accurate. This is not one of the 47 known bracket errors: the "[ϖ]" here correctly means the ϖ-torsion, not a mangled ⟦ ⟧.

On 'affects': the statement of Lemma 5.9(2) is correct, and the corrected proof is immediate from part (1). Prop. 5.10 and §5.4 use only the statement, so nothing downstream is affected. Yet H_3(Y_0(Q), k) = 0 and the action of Hecke operators on H_0(Y_0(Q), k) (which preserve the connected components) is via the degree map, and this action is Eisenstein (in the sense that the only m in the support of H_0 are Eisenstein).`; it should be `Minimal fix: make the clause restrictive again, as in v1: "the action on H_0(Y_0(Q),k) of those Hecke operators which preserve the connected components (e.g. T_λ for λ trivial in the component group F^×\A_F^{∞,×}/(A_F^{∞,×})^2 det(L_Q)) is via the degree map, T_λ ↦ N(λ)+1". Such λ are exactly the primes that split completely in the finite abelian (2-power) extension L that corresponds to the component group. So T_λ − 2 ∈ m for every λ outside the level that splits completely in L(ζ_p), and m is Eisenstein in the sense of Def. 5.5. I rendered pp. 373-377 and read them. (a) §5.2.2 on p. 373 says: 'The Hecke operators act on H•(Y(K), O) but do not preserve the homology of the connected components. The group of components is isomorphic, via the determinant map, to F^×\A_F^{∞,×}/A_F^{∞,×2} det(K).' T^univ (p. 376) is generated by the T_α for α trivial at Q ∪ S(ρ̄) ∪ {v|p}, together with the U_x. So it contains T_λ = T(diag(ϖ_λ,1)), where det g = ϖ_λ. (b) Here is a counterexample to the parenthetical. §5.1 lets F be any imaginary quadratic field, with p ≥ 3 unramified in F. Take F = Q(√−5), whose class group is Z/2 = Cl/Cl^2, and p = 7. Let λ = (3, 1+√−5), which has norm 3 and is not principal because a^2 + 5b^2 = 3 has no solution. Assume ρ̄ is unramified at 3; the primes above 3 are not in Q, since Q consists of primes with N(v) ≡ 1 mod 7. We have L_Q ⊆ ∏ PGL_2(O_v), so det(L_Q) ⊆ Ô^×·(squares). Hence A surjects onto F^×\A^{∞,×}/(A^{∞,×})^2 Ô^× = Cl/Cl^2 = Z/2. The class of ϖ_λ maps to the nontrivial element there. So T_λ carries each component to one with a different determinant class: T_λ[C] = 4[C'] with C' ≠ C, because the transfer on H_0 has total degree [K : gKg^{-1} ∩ K] = N(λ)+1 = 4. The parenthetical claim is therefore false, and 'the action is via the degree map' is only true up to this permutation of components. (c) The conclusion still holds. H_0(Y_0(Q), k) = k[A] with p odd, so it decomposes into χ-eigenspaces, and T_λ acts on them by χ(λ^{±1})(1+N(λ)). This equals 2 mod p whenever λ splits completely in F(ζ_p)·(class field of A), an abelian extension of F. That is exactly the form required by Definition 5.5, so the support of H_0 is Eisenstein. The v1 wording, with its restrictive clause, already gave this argument. The published version and v2 added parentheses, which turned the clause into a false general assertion. I classify this as an error in one step of the proof whose conclusion is unaffected; since v1 shows what was intended, one could also argue it is a punctuation-level misprint. The printed parenthetical is false. G = Res_{F/Q} PGL_2, and F is an arbitrary imaginary quadratic field in which p ≥ 3 is unramified (§5.1). Every double-coset representative of K diag(α,1) K has determinant in α·det(K). So T_α translates components by the class of α in the component group F^×\A_F^{∞,×}/(A_F^{∞,×})^2 det(K), which the paper identifies in §5.2.2. That group surjects onto Cl(F)/Cl(F)^2, which is nontrivial for most F (for example Q(√−5)). Then T_λ for a non-principal λ swaps components. The paper itself says so three pages earlier (§5.2.2, p. 373): "The Hecke operators act on H•(Y(K), O) but do not preserve the homology of the connected components."

Defence: the intended meaning is clear, and the argument is complete under it. arXiv v1 has the same sentence without parentheses, as a restrictive clause: only the Hecke operators that preserve components are claimed to act by degree. That is true. It is also enough, because Def. 5.5 only asks that T_λ − 2 ∈ m for almost all λ splitting completely in some fixed abelian extension of F. For λ trivial in the component group, T_λ acts on each component's H_0 = k by its degree N(λ)+1. That equals 2 in k once N(λ) ≡ 1 mod p. So every m in the support of H_0 is Eisenstein, and since m ∩ T^an = m_∅ is non-Eisenstein, H_0(Y_0(Q),k)_m = 0. The parentheses were added in revision (v2 and published) and turned a restrictive qualifier into a false blanket assertion.

This is a slip whose intended meaning is clear from context (v1 and §5.2.2), so it is a misprint rather than an error. The candidate's statement of the fact is right, as is its fix via characters χ, but the minimal correction is simply the restrictive reading.

Downstream: Lemma 5.9(1) feeds Lemma 5.9(2) (vanishing of H_3), Prop. 5.10 (balancedness) and the main §5 modularity argument. Its conclusion is true as stated, so nothing downstream changes. The proof also exhibits T_{∅,m∅} as a quotient of a power series ring in q − 1 variables by q elements. ... From these remarks we see that Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11." The level is fixed on p. 372: "Γ_p(v^c) = { g ∈ PGL_2(O_v) | g ≡ (1 *; 0 d) mod π_v^c, d has p − power order }". On p. 373: "(5)(b) If ρ̄ is of type P, M or H at v, then K_{Q,v} = Γ_p(v^c), where c is the conductor of ρ̄|D_v." Theorem 1.3 on p. 302: "there exists an integer μ ≥ 1 such that H_1(Y_0(N), O)_m is free of rank μ as a T_m-module. If H_1(Y_0(N), O)_m ⊗ Q ≠ 0, then μ = 1."`; it should be `Multiplicity one only gives μ = dim π_f^{K_∅} = ∏_{v of type P,M,H} dim π_v^{Γ_p(v^c)}. This value is the same for every contributing π, because a minimal lift fixes the inertial type. It is at least ∏_v (N(v)−1)_{p'}, so μ ≥ 2 whenever S(ρ̄) contains a P/M/H prime with v ∤ 2. The remark and Theorem 1.3's clause "then μ = 1" are therefore correct only when every prime of S(ρ̄) has type S. (Theorem 1.2 only has type S primes and does not claim μ = 1 anyway.) Two ways to repair it: (a) Add that restriction. (b) Replace H by its Δ-invariants, where Δ = ∏_v Γ_0(v^c)/Γ_p(v^c), which is equivalent to working at the literal Γ_0(v^c) level. Δ has prime-to-p order and commutes with T_∅, so H^Δ is a T_m-direct summand of the free module H, hence itself free. Its rank in characteristic 0 is ∏ dim π_v^{Γ_0(v^c)} = 1, and it is nonzero once H⊗Q ≠ 0. This restores "μ = 1" for the space Y_0(N) of literal Γ_0(N) level. Theorem 5.11 itself (R^min ≅ T and freeness) is not affected, and neither is the complete-intersection clause.`. I checked the printed text on the rendered PDF pages 84, 76, 77 and 6.

The group. In PGL_2, "g ≡ (1 *; 0 d)" only makes sense up to scalars. So Γ_p(v^c) is the set of g that are upper triangular mod π^c with d/a of p-power order. The map g ↦ d/a gives Γ_0(v^c)/Γ_p(v^c) ≅ (O_v/π^c)^×/Syl_p. Since π_v has trivial central character, π_v^{Γ_p} = ⊕_η π_v^{(K_0(v^c), η(d/a))}, where η runs over the characters of (O_v/π^c)^× of order prime to p.

The η-summand. Let η̃ be any extension of η to F_v^×. If v ∈ π_v transforms under K_0 by η(d/a), then as a vector of π_v⊗η̃ (central character η̃²) it transforms by η(d)². So the η-summand equals (π_v⊗η̃)^{K_1(v^c)}. By Casselman this has dimension max(0, c − a(π_v⊗η̃) + 1).

Tame η contribute. Let η be tame, of prime-to-p order. There are (N(v)−1)_{p'} such η.
- Types M/H: π_v is supercuspidal and a tame twist keeps the conductor, since the Swan conductor is unchanged and there are no inertia invariants. So a(π_v⊗η̃) = c.
- Type P: π_v = π(χ,χ^{-1}) with χ|O^× = ψ̃, and a(ψη) + a(ψ^{-1}η) ≤ 2a(ψ) = c.
Either way each such η contributes at least 1.

Brute-force check. I computed dim π^{K'} by Mackey double cosets on GL_2(Z/ℓ²) (script work/agents/k6v/ps.py).
- ℓ = 7, p = 3, ψ quadratic (a valid type P): dimension 4, as the formula predicts.
- ℓ = 7, p = 5, ψ of order 3: dimension 8, as predicted.
- The unramified test case also matches.

Global step. Localized at the non-Eisenstein m∅, H ⊗ Q̄ is the direct sum of the spaces π_f^{K_∅} ⊗ H^1(g,K;π_∞) over the π that contribute. Here m(π) = 1 and the (g,K) cohomology has dimension 1. Definition 5.4 builds T_∅ only from T_α with α trivial at S(ρ̄) ∪ {v|p}, so T_∅ acts on each π_f^K by a scalar. By strong multiplicity one, different π have different eigensystems. So T⊗Q̄ is a product of copies of Q̄, and freeness of rank μ forces μ = dim π_f^K ≥ (N(v)−1)_{p'}. For v ∤ 2 this is at least 2, because N(v)−1 is even and p is odd.

The extra vectors lie in the same π and have the same Hecke eigenvalues. Classically they correspond to the twists f⊗η: same level, nebentypus η². In §3 (GL(2)/Q, U_x with d of p-power order) and in v1 (GL(2)/F), the nebentypus is pinned instead, so no extra vectors arise there.

Hence the printed claim is false whenever S(ρ̄) has a P/M/H prime v ∤ 2 and H⊗Q ≠ 0. Theorem 1.3 inherits the error if "Y_0(N)" means the paper's Y, as the deduction "Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11" requires. If Y_0(N) is read literally as Γ_0(N) level, the μ = 1 clause can be rescued via the prime-to-p invariants, but that is not the argument the paper gives. (The separate issue that non-minimal type-P forms also appear at this level is candidate C-K6-1, not this one.) The defence fails.
(1) T_∅ is generated only by T_α with α trivial at Q ∪ S(ρ̄) ∪ {v|p} (Def. 5.4), and m_∅ involves only T_λ for λ ∉ S∪{v|p} (§5.4). T_α then acts on π_f^{K} = ⊗_w π_w^{K_w} by the characteristic function of K_λ g K_λ, which is a scalar on the whole space. So the T_∅-eigenspace of π in H_1(Y,K)_{m∅} has dimension dim π_f^{K_∅} · dim H^1(g,K;π_∞) = dim π_f^{K_∅}, and μ = dim π_f^{K_∅} (strong multiplicity one rules out any other π with the same eigenvalues).
(2) In PGL2, Γ_p(v^c) = {d/a ∈ Syl_p((O_v/π^c)^×)}, and Γ_0/Γ_p has prime-to-p order. Hence π_v^{Γ_p} = ⊕_η π_v^{(Γ_0, η(d/a))}, summed over characters η of prime-to-p order. Twisting by η̃ and conjugating by Atkin–Lehner, Casselman's theory gives dim of the η-summand = max(0, c − a(π_v⊗η̃^{-1}) + 1). With trivial central character, nothing forces η = 1. That is exactly what v1 had (GL2, central character in T) and v2 lost.
(3) For a minimal π_v, a(π_v) = c. For every tame η, a(π_v⊗η̃^{-1}) ≤ c:
- type P: a(χη̃^{-1}) + a(χ^{-1}η̃^{-1}) ≤ 2a(ψ) = c;
- types M and H: σ⊗η stays without inertia invariants and keeps its Swan conductor.
So each such η contributes at least 1, giving dim ≥ (N(v)−1)_{p'}, which is ≥ 2 for N(v) odd since p ≥ 3.
(4) I checked this numerically (principal series, computed as dim of K-invariants of Ind_{B(O)}^{GL2(O)}(ψ(a)ψ^{-1}(d)) by the character formula; script work/agents/K6-B/ps.py). Results:
- q=5, c=2, p=3, ψ of order 4: Γ_0-invariants 1, Γ_p-invariants 6;
- q=7, p=3, ψ quadratic: 1 and 4;
- q=13, p=3, ψ of order 4: Γ_p-invariants 6.
All three match the formula exactly.
(5) If H⊗Q ≠ 0, then under Theorem 5.11 every contributing π is a minimal lift, so μ ≥ 2 whenever there is a P/M/H prime with v ∤ 2. For H/M primes (not vexing), minimality is automatic, so Conjecture A is not contradicted and such cases can really occur.
Consequences: the remark is used only to deduce Theorem 1.3 ("From these remarks we see that Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11"). That deduction identifies H_1(Y_0(N),O)_m with H = H_1(Y,O)_{m∅} at Γ_p level, so the μ = 1 clause of Theorem 1.3 is false as the paper intends it. Nothing else in the paper uses μ = 1. The candidate's correction is right. Fix (b) above is a minimal alternative that keeps μ = 1.
Separate issue, not verified here and not part of this finding: at type P primes with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, the level Γ_p(v^c) already contains Γ_0(v^c)-newforms π(χ,χ^{-1}) with χ|O^× = ψε, ε of p-power order. These are non-minimal, which puts pressure on Conjecture A(2)(b) at this level.
