This is needed for every 𝔞 ∈ Cl_p(𝒪_F), or equivalently for the generators 𝔞_i (of orders h_i) of a cyclic decomposition. In that case x splits completely in the metabelian compositum of the fields F(α_i^{1/h_i}, ζ_{h_i}). The formula needs h | N(x)−1. This holds for Taylor–Wiles primes, where N(x) ≡ 1 mod p^N and p^N ≥ h. With no divisibility assumption the condition is α^{(N(x)−1)/gcd(h, N(x)−1)} ≡ 1 mod x. The printed p-th-power condition is necessary but not sufficient when h > p. It gives the right answer only when Cl_p(𝒪_F) has exponent p, for example the Z/pZ case discussed earlier in the paragraph.`. I checked the printed text on the rendered page (PDF p. 85 = p. 381). I redid the computation. Assume p ∤ |O_F^×|, as the paper does. Then tensoring O_F^× → (O/x)^× → RCl(x) → Cl(O_F) → 0 with Z_p gives 0 → G → RCl_p(x) → Cl_p(O_F) → 0, where G = ((O/x)^×)_p is cyclic of order p^v, v = v_p(N(x)−1).

Take the lift ã = [𝔞] of 𝔞. Every lift has the form ãu with u ∈ G, and (ãu)^h = [α]·u^h. So a lift of order h exists iff the image of α lies in G^h. In a cyclic group of order N(x)−1 this is the same as α being an h-th power, i.e. α^{(N(x)−1)/h} ≡ 1 when h | N(x)−1. It is not p-th power residuosity.

Explicit counterexample to sufficiency: Cl_p = Z/p^2, v ≥ 2, and α ≡ g^p for a generator g of G. Then the printed condition holds, but E ≅ (Z × Z/p^v)/⟨(p^2, −p)⟩. The Smith normal form of [[p^2, −p], [0, p^v]] gives E ≅ Z/p × Z/p^{v+1}, which is not Z/p^2 × Z/p^v. So the map does not split. Applying the printed condition to every element of Cl_p does not help: an element b with b^p = 𝔞 gives the same α.

Interpretive caveat: read literally, "The necessary condition" is true as a necessary condition, and the stated equivalence with splitting in F(α^{1/p}, ζ_p) (given N(x) ≡ 1 mod p) is correct. But the sentence is introduced by "Explicitly" as the explicit form of the Chebotarev condition equivalent to splitting ("corresponds to x splitting completely in a metabelian extension"). As that, it is wrong for h > p. It looks like a slip from generalising the Z/pZ example: h is introduced but only used to define α.

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It sits in an informal, hedged sketch ("It seems that…") of an alternative GL approach that the authors explicitly do not pursue ("We ultimately decided, however, to impose the simplifying assumption that det(ρ) is cyclotomic"). No theorem, lemma or proof uses it. I checked the printed text on the rendered page (PDF p. 85).

Setup. Assume p ∤ |𝒪_F^×|, as the paper does. Tensoring 𝒪_F^× → (𝒪/x)^× → RCl(x) → Cl(𝒪_F) → 0 with Z_p gives 0 → G → RCl_p(x) → Cl_p(𝒪_F) → 0, where G = (𝒪/x)^× ⊗ Z_p is cyclic of order p^v, with v = v_p(N(x)−1).

Why h, not p. The class ã = [𝔞] lifts 𝔞, and every lift of 𝔞 has the form ãu with u ∈ G. Then (ãu)^h = ι(α)·u^h. So a lift of order h exists iff α ∈ G^h. For a set Q of primes the kernel is ∏G_x, so the condition is imposed prime by prime. Because Cl_p is a direct sum of cyclic groups, the map splits iff this holds for the generators. So the correct condition is that α is an h-th power mod x, not a p-th power.

Group-theoretic counterexample. Take Cl_p = Z/p², v ≥ 2 and α = g^p, with g a generator of G. Then RCl_p ≅ Z²/⟨(p², −p), (0, p^v)⟩. Its Smith normal form is Z/p × Z/p^{v+1}, which is not Z/p² × Z/p^v, so the map does not split.

Concrete counterexample (python, ex.py in my work dir).
- F = Q(√−199), 𝒪_F = Z[ω] with ω² − ω + 50 = 0, and Cl ≅ Z/9. Take p = 3, which is prime to |𝒪^×| = 2.
- 𝔭' = (2, ω−1) has order exactly 9, and 𝔭'^9 = (21+ω), since the norm of 21+ω is 512. So h = 9 and α = 21+ω.
- Take x | 487 with ω ≡ 185, so N(x)−1 = 2·3^5.
- Then α^{162} ≡ 1 mod x, so the printed condition holds and x splits completely in F(α^{1/3}, ζ_3).
- But α^{54} ≢ 1 mod x, so α is not a 9th power. Hence RCl_3(x) ≅ Z/3 × Z/3^6 does not split over Z/9.
- Primes over 829 and 1009 behave the same way.

Defence attempts.
(i) Read literally, "necessary condition" is true. But the sentence opens with "Explicitly", continues "or equivalently", and is presented as the explicit form of the Chebotarev condition that "corresponds to" splitting. As that it is wrong for h > p. If the authors had meant only a necessary condition, h would still be introduced solely to define α, so the context does not show which reading was intended.
(ii) The printed condition is exactly the splitting condition for the pushout extension by G/G^p. That corresponds to Taylor–Wiles data Δ_N with N = 1. The text, however, speaks of RCl_p(Q) = RCl(Q) ⊗ Z_p, and Taylor–Wiles needs N → ∞. For the pushout to G/G^{p^N} the condition is α ∈ G^{p^{min(k,N)}} (where h = p^k), which is the h-th-power condition once p^N ≥ h. So neither reading saves the printed claim.
(iii) Because p appears consistently twice, this looks like a generalisation of the Z/pZ example rather than a one-character typo, and the intended meaning is not clear from context. That makes it an error rather than a misprint.

Consequences. The passage is an informal, hedged sketch ("It seems that…") of a GL approach that the authors explicitly abandon ("We ultimately decided, however, to impose the simplifying assumption that det(ρ) is cyclotomic"). No theorem, lemma, remark or proof cites it. §8.2 uses RCl(Q)/p^n, but not this splitting condition. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Read literally, (6) contradicts (1) and (2) when n ≥ 2. By (1) and (2), r|G_v is crystalline with Hodge–Tate weights 0, …, n−1 at each v | p, so r is ramified at v (an unramified representation has all HT weights 0). (6) would then force r|I_v to be unipotent. That makes r^ss|I_v trivial, so r^ss|G_v is unramified and all its Hodge–Tate weights are 0. Sen weights are additive in extensions, so this contradicts weights 0, …, n−1. The theorem would therefore be vacuous for n ≥ 2.

The context shows that x ∤ p is intended:
(i) The remark right after the theorem (p. 384) says "If conditions 1, 2, and 3 are satisfied, then conditions 5 and 6 are satisfied after a solvable extension which is unramified at p". That is impossible at primes above p under the literal reading.
(ii) The setting of §8.5 (p. 406), from which Theorem 5.16 is deduced, says "For each v ∤ p, r̄|G_v has at worst unipotent ramification…".
(iii) The definition of semi-stable before Theorem 1.2 (p. 301) asks for unipotence only "for all finite v not dividing p".
(iv) In §10 the theorem is applied to crystalline r with distinct weights.

Not a bracket error. A separate issue is whether the N(x) ≡ 1 mod p clause matches §8.5, which requires N(v) ≡ 1 mod p where r̄ is ramified. That is candidate X-K10-10, not this one. Rendered PDF p. 87 at 250 dpi. The text is exactly as printed above. [3] = CHT, whose Definition 2.5.1 defines bigness for a subgroup H ⊂ GL_n(k). The paper never defines "r̄ is big" (grep finds 'big' only at pp. 383, 410, 422, 425). The natural literal reading, r̄(G_F) big, is not the hypothesis the proof uses.

The theorem is said to "follow immediately from Theorem 9.19" (p. 384). §9.5 (p. 425) says "Theorem 5.16 follows from it immediately as a corollary". Theorem 9.19 is proved under the standing assumption "We assume also that r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big" (p. 425). It uses Proposition 8.5 (p. 410), "Assume that r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big", which follows CHT Prop. 2.5.9 and needs bigness over F(ζ_p).

Bigness of r̄(G_F) does not formally pass to the normal subgroup r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) of prime-to-p cyclic index, and the paper gives no argument that it does. The CHT conditions are not inherited in general: no p-power quotient; H^1(H, ad^0) = 0 (restriction only controls the H/H'-invariants); and condition (c) on irreducible submodules. Hypothesis (3) only says F(ad^0 r̄) ⊉ F(ζ_p); it does not make the intersection F(ad^0 r̄) ∩ F(ζ_p) trivial, so it does not close the gap.

The intended hypothesis is clear from §9.5 and Prop. 8.5, so this is a misprint or loose statement rather than a false theorem. The printed hypothesis must still be read with bigness over F(ζ_p). I give an abstract argument, not an explicit counterexample satisfying (1)–(8). Partly overlaps with X-K10-10. - **Error** at §6 (opening of Part 2, before §6.1 Patching), Lemma 6.1 and its proof, published p. 385 (PDF p. 89). arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2) has word-for-word the same statement and proof (Lemma 6.1, citing [Mat86] Thm 17.2). The lemma is not in arXiv v1. Its only use is in the proof of Lemma 6.2 on the same page ("the central inequality is Lemma 6.1").. The source says `Lemma 6.1 Let S be a Noetherian local ring. If N is an S-module with depth n, and 0 ≠ M ⊆ N, then dim(M) ≥ n. Proof Let 𝔭 be an associated prime of M (and hence of N). Then 𝔭 is the annihilator of some 0 ≠ m ∈ M, and it suffices to prove the result for M replaced by mS ⊂ M. On the other hand, for a Noetherian local ring, one has the inequality (see [69], Theorem 17.2) n = depth(N) ≤ min_{Ass(N)} dim S/𝔭 ≤ dim(M).`; it should be `Assume N is finitely generated: "If N is a finitely generated (finite) S-module with depth n, and 0 ≠ M ⊆ N, then dim(M) ≥ n." Nothing else needs to change. This is the minimal fix, and it is exactly the hypothesis of the cited result, Matsumura Thm 17.2 (depth M ≤ dim A/p for p ∈ Ass M, where M is a finite module over a Noetherian local ring). With it the proof is complete as printed.`. I rendered PDF page 89 and the printed text is as quoted. The Notation section adds no convention that modules are finitely generated, and elsewhere the paper states that hypothesis explicitly (for example Lemma 5.9, "Let μ be a finitely generated O[Δ]-module"). The cited result, Matsumura Thm 17.2 (depth M ≤ dim A/𝔭 for 𝔭 ∈ Ass M), is stated for finite modules, and its proof needs Nakayama on Hom(A/𝔭, M).

Without finite generation the lemma is false under every standard definition of depth (Ext, Koszul, or regular sequence). My counterexample: S = k⟦x,y⟧ and N = S ⊕ k((x)), where y acts as 0 and x acts invertibly on k((x)).
(1) (x, y) is an N-regular sequence. x is injective on both summands. N/xN = k⟦y⟧ ⊕ 0, and y is regular on it. N/(x,y)N = k ≠ 0.
(2) Ext^i_S(k, k((x))) = 0 for all i, because x acts on it both as 0 (through k) and invertibly. So Ext^i_S(k, N) = Ext^i_S(k, S), which is nonzero first at i = 2. Hence depth N = 2 under either definition.
(3) Take M = S·(0,1) ≅ S/(y) ≅ k⟦x⟧, a nonzero cyclic submodule of N. Then dim M = 1 < 2 = depth N, which contradicts the lemma.

The reader's own example (S = k⟦x⟧, N = M = k((x))) gives depth ∞ only under the Ext definition. Under the regular-sequence definition its depth is 0, so the example above is the sturdier one. Note that here M is even finitely generated, so the finiteness is needed on N specifically.

I class this as an error (the statement as printed is false) rather than a gap. The intended fix is clear from the citation, and one could argue the hypothesis is implicit, since Matsumura defines depth only for finite modules. That is why I rate confidence medium, not high. No stated result is affected: the lemma is used only in Lemma 6.2, with N = K^m = P^m/Im(δ^{m−1}), a cokernel in a perfect complex and hence finitely generated. This is not one of the 47 bracket defects. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED. (a) The paper sets no convention that modules are finitely generated. The Notation (p. 306) only defines a perfect complex as a bounded complex of finitely generated projective modules. Elsewhere, whenever finiteness matters the paper says "finitely generated" explicitly, e.g. Thm 6.3's P∞ "of finitely generated S∞-modules". (b) The paper never defines depth. The strongest defence is that the textbook definitions (Matsumura §16; Bruns–Herzog 1.2) define depth only for finite modules. On that reading "an S-module with depth n" tacitly means a finite one, and the lemma holds. So the intended meaning is clear. But the printed hypothesis says only "an S-module", and depth is routinely used for arbitrary modules (via Ext, local cohomology or regular sequences). Under those definitions the literal statement is false.

ROBUST COUNTEREXAMPLE, which works under every standard definition of depth, including the regular-sequence definition with no ∞ convention. Take S = k⟦x,y⟧ and N = S ⊕ k((x)), where y acts as 0 on k((x)). Take M = 0 ⊕ k⟦x⟧, which is finitely generated, or M = 0 ⊕ k((x)).
- dim M = dim S/(y) = 1.
- depth N = 2. x, y is an N-regular sequence: x is injective on S and invertible on k((x)); N/xN = k⟦y⟧, on which y is regular; and N/(x,y)N = k ≠ 0.
- Ext check: Ext^i_S(k, k((x))) = 0 for all i, because x acts on it both as 0 (through k) and invertibly (through k((x))). Hence Ext^i_S(k, N) = Ext^i_S(k, S), which is first nonzero at i = 2.
So depth N = 2 > 1 = dim M. The reporter's own example (S = k⟦x⟧, N = M = k((x)), depth ∞ via Ext) also works, but it depends on the convention for depth; the example above does not. The proof's step "depth(N) ≤ min_{Ass N} dim S/p" is exactly where it fails, because Matsumura 17.2 needs N finite.

CONSEQUENCES. Lemma 6.1 is cited only once, in the proof of Lemma 6.2 (p. 385: "where the central inequality is Lemma 6.1"). There it is applied with N = K^m = P^m/Im(δ^{m−1}) and M = H^m(P) ≠ 0. K^m is a quotient of the finitely generated projective module P^m, since P is perfect, so it is finitely generated. Lemma 6.2 is then used in the proof of Thm 6.3 (p. 389) with the perfect complex P∞. All uses therefore satisfy the added hypothesis, and no stated result beyond the literal Lemma 6.1 is affected.

CLASSIFICATION. It is "error" rather than "gap": with N finite the proof is complete, and without it the statement is false. It could also be seen as a misprint-level omitted word, since the intended meaning is clear. Either way it affects nothing. - **Error** at §6, Lemma 6.2 and proof, p. 385 (published version) (it affects a stated result). The source says `p. 385 (PDF p. 89): "Lemma 6.2 Let l0 ≥ 0 be an integer and let S be a Noetherian regular local ring of dimension n ≥ l0. Let P be a perfect complex of S-modules which is concentrated in degrees 0, . . . , l0. Then codim(H^*(P)) ≤ l0, and moreover, if equality occurs, then: (1) P is a projective resolution of H^{l0}(P), (2) H^{l0}(P) has depth n − l0 and has projective dimension l0." Proof: "Let δ^i : P^i → P^{i+1} denote the differential and let m ≤ l0 denote the smallest integer such that H^m(P) ≠ 0." (arXiv v2 has the same wording, cg-v2.txt l. 3400-3422.)`; it should be `Add the hypothesis H^*(P) ≠ 0, i.e. P is not exact, to Lemma 6.2. This is the minimal correct fix. Requiring only "P ≠ 0" is not enough: P = [S →id S] in degrees 0, 1 is non-zero but exact. The same non-vanishing (H ≠ 0, or equivalently T ≠ 0) is also implicitly needed in Theorem 6.3(iii), Theorem 6.4(2) and Proposition 6.6. Every application in the paper satisfies it.`. The page image matches the quoted text. The paper never defines codim. It uses codim(M) = n − dim(M) in the proof, and dim(0) is −1 or −∞ under any standard convention. So codim(0) is at least n+1 > n ≥ l0. Taking codim as the height of Ann(M) gives ht(S) = +∞, the same result. Counterexamples: P = 0, or P = [S → S] by the identity in degrees 0 and 1 with l0 ≥ 1. Both are perfect and concentrated in degrees 0..l0, but H^*(P) = 0 has codimension > l0. The claimed inequality therefore fails. The proof starts by choosing the smallest m with H^m(P) ≠ 0, which silently assumes H^*(P) ≠ 0. Lemma 6.1, used as the central inequality, explicitly requires 0 ≠ M.

I redid the proof with the extra hypothesis and it goes through:
- H^i = 0 for i < m makes 0→P^0→…→P^m→K^m→0 exact, so pd K^m ≤ m.
- Since 0 ≠ H^m ⊆ K^m, Lemma 6.1 and Auslander–Buchsbaum give codim H^m ≤ n − depth K^m = pd K^m ≤ m.
- codim H^* ≤ codim H^m.
- In the equality case m = l0 and H^{l0} = P^{l0}/Im δ^{l0−1} = K^{l0}.
The proposed correction is therefore right and sufficient.

Downstream, Theorem 6.3 (p. 387) is the only use. There P∞^□ is minimal, since P∞^□ ⊗ k ≅ T has d = 0, and H^{l0}(P∞^□)/a ≅ H. So when H ≠ 0 its cohomology is non-zero and the lemma applies as intended. The degenerate case H = 0 forces T = 0 and P∞^□ = 0. In that case Theorem 6.3(iii) (depth of the zero module) and Theorem 6.4(2) (the zero module is not nearly faithful) also fail as literally stated. Those theorems likewise implicitly need H ≠ 0, and in the §9 applications H is a non-zero localized cohomology module. Main results are unaffected. This is a degenerate missing non-vanishing hypothesis in a stated lemma, not a substantive mathematical error. I looked for a defence and found none.
- The paper never defines codim. The proof uses codim(M) = n − dim(M).
- For M = 0, every standard convention gives dim(0) = −1 or −∞, so codim(0) ≥ n+1 > l0. Reading codim as the height of Ann(M) gives +∞, and the minimum of ht over an empty support is also +∞. No reading makes codim(0) ≤ l0.
- Counterexamples: P = 0, or P = [S →id S] in degrees 0, 1 (with l0 ≥ 1). Both are perfect and concentrated in degrees 0..l0, and H^*(P) = 0 violates the inequality. Conclusion (2) also fails, since depth(0) ≠ n − l0.
- The proof starts by choosing "the smallest m such that H^m(P) ≠ 0", and no such m exists. The authors did put "0 ≠ M" into Lemma 6.1 but left the analogous condition out of 6.2.

With H^*(P) ≠ 0 added, I re-checked the proof and it goes through:
- 0 → P^0 → … → P^m → K^m → 0 is exact, so pd K^m ≤ m.
- K^m ⊇ H^m ≠ 0, so Lemma 6.1 and Auslander–Buchsbaum give codim H^m ≤ pd K^m ≤ m ≤ l0, hence codim H^* ≤ codim H^m ≤ l0.
- In the equality case, l0 ≤ codim H^{l0} ≤ pd K^{l0} ≤ l0. This forces m = l0 and H^{l0} = K^{l0}, since P^{l0+1} = 0. Both (1) and (2) follow.

Consequences. Lemma 6.2 is used only in the proof of Theorem 6.3 (p. 389), and through it in Theorem 6.4 and Proposition 6.6, whose proof is "much the same".
- There P∞^□ ⊗ k ≅ T has zero differential, so P∞^□ is minimal. By Nakayama, a minimal exact bounded complex of free modules is 0.
- If H ≠ 0, then H^{l0}(P∞^□)/a ≅ H forces H^*(P∞^□) ≠ 0, and the lemma applies as intended.
- If H = 0, then H^*(P∞^□) = 0: otherwise the corrected lemma plus Nakayama would force H ≠ 0. So T = 0 and P∞ = 0. That degenerate data satisfies every hypothesis of 6.3, for example R∞ = O⟦x_1..x_{q+j−l0}⟧, H = 0, D_N = 0.
- In that degenerate case, 6.3(iii) ("depth of H^{l0}(P∞) = 1+j+q−l0") fails. So does 6.4(2), because the zero module is not nearly faithful: Ann = R is not nilpotent. The proof of 6.4 in fact asserts "Since H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ {0}" without justification.

In the §8–9 applications, T is the mod-ϖ cohomology localized at a maximal ideal m in its support, so T ≠ 0 and hence H ≠ 0. The main theorems are therefore unaffected. This is a missing non-degeneracy hypothesis, not a substantive flaw. It is still a literally false stated lemma, so "error" (a false statement and a failing step) fits better than "gap". It is not among the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not mention it. (1) The printed (c) cannot hold for n > N. D_N is a complex of S_N/ϖ^N-modules, so ϖ^N kills it. For n ≥ N the termwise tensor product is D_N ⊗_{S_N} O/ϖ^n = D_N/(𝔞_N, ϖ^n)D_N = D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^N, which does not depend on n. A derived tensor product would not help either: its cohomology is still killed by ϖ^N. So (c) says ϖ^N kills H/ϖ^n for every n, i.e. ϖ^N H ⊂ ∩_n ϖ^n H. The compatibility clause gives the same thing, since the transition maps H/ϖ^{n+1} → H/ϖ^n would all be isomorphisms. Conclusions (ii) and (iv) make H ≅ H^{l0}(P∞^□)/𝔞 a finite module over the Noetherian local ring R∞. By Krull's intersection theorem ∩ ϖ^n H = 0, so ϖ^N H = 0; with N = 1, ϖH = 0.

(2) A minimal example shows this: take l0 = q = j = 0, R∞ = R = O, H = O, T = k, D_N = O/ϖ^N. Here (a), (b) and (d) hold, but (c) would need O/ϖ^N ≅ O/ϖ^n for all n, which fails for n > N. The expected conclusion (H free) is exactly what the corrected (c) gives.

(3) The application relies on the printed version holding. In the proof of Theorem 9.19 (pp. 426–427), D^1_N is the complex D̃_N/ϖ^N of S_N/ϖ^N-modules, and "its cohomology computes H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_m". That is true only for n ≤ N.

(4) The proof of Theorem 6.3 only uses n ≤ N. The level-N datum D_{M,N} uses ψ = the given isomorphism H^{l0}(D_M^□ ⊗ O/ϖ^N) ≃ H/ϖ^N with N ≤ M (p. 388). The datum definition only needs "each N ≥ n′ ≥ 1" (p. 387). Proposition 6.6 only needs n = 1. So the candidate's correction is sufficient, and it matches the application. Hypothesis (b)'s "each n ≥ 1" does no harm, because it only asks for compatible actions.

This is a genuine error in how the hypothesis is stated, not a bracket misprint. On 'affects': I disagree slightly with "a stated result". Theorem 6.3 and Prop. 6.6 are true as printed, just unusable, and no downstream statement is false. What is invalid as printed is the proof of Theorem 9.19 (and so the chain to Theorems 5.16/1.1), which checks a hypothesis that fails. The fix, weakening the hypothesis in the statements of Thm 6.3/Prop 6.6, repairs everything. I checked the rendered pp. 386–391 and 425–428 of the published PDF, the text of arXiv v2 (Theorem 6.3 and the proof of Theorem 9.19), and arXiv v1.

DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, ALL FAIL.
(i) The expression is well-defined for every n. The tensor product is over S_N, and the paper's own convention makes O/ϖ^n = S_0/ϖ^n a quotient of S_N for every n. So nothing in the notation limits n to n ≤ N.
(ii) Reading the tensor product as derived does not help. D_N is a complex of S_N/ϖ^N-modules, so multiplication by ϖ^N is zero on D_N, and hence on the cohomology of D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^n whether the tensor is termwise or derived. For n ≥ N, the termwise D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^n equals D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^N.
(iii) Take N = 1 in the printed (c). It gives ϖ(H/ϖ^n H) = 0 for all n, i.e. ϖH ⊂ ∩_n ϖ^n H. When H is finitely generated this intersection is 0 by Krull, so ϖH = 0. Finite generation is needed anyway: the conclusion H ≅ H^{l0}(P∞^□)/a forces it.
(iv) The simplest model case fails. Take l0 = q = j = 0, R∞ = R = O, H = O, T = k and D_N = O/ϖ^N. Then (1)–(3), (a), (b) and (d) hold, and the intended conclusion (H free) is true. But the printed (c) would need O/ϖ^{min(n,N)} ≅ O/ϖ^n for all n, which is false.

WHY IT MATTERS. The printed Theorem 6.3 and Prop 6.6 are not false: their proofs go through whenever the stronger hypothesis holds. But that hypothesis can never be met in the application. In the proof of Thm 9.19 (p. 427), D^1_N = D̃_N/ϖ^N, "whose cohomology computes H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_m", and H^1 = H^{q0}(Y,K/O)^∨_m, which is finite over O. By (iii), the printed (c) would force ϖH^1 = 0. Yet Theorem 9.19 concludes that H^1 is nearly faithful over R_S. Theorem 5.16 is deduced from this using the characteristic-0 point of R_S given by r, so ϖH^1 ≠ 0. The proof itself (p. 428) also uses p-torsion-freeness of H^{l0}(P∞^{1,□}). So "condition (c) is clear" is false as printed; it is true only for n ≤ N.

THE FIX SUFFICES. Every use involves only n ≤ N:
- D_{M,N} (p. 388) takes ψ to be the given isomorphism for D_M at n = N ≤ M.
- The patching datum (p. 387) records only "N ≥ n′ ≥ 1".
- The extra data and commuting square of Prop 6.6 use only n = 1 ≤ M.
- Hypothesis (b) also says "each n ≥ 1", but that is harmless there, because it only asks for compatible actions.

CLASSIFICATION. The intended range can be recovered from the patching-datum definition, so this is close to a misprint. I call it an error because it is not a one-character slip: the unbounded "n ≥ 1" is written deliberately in (b), (c), (d) and again in §9. As printed, the verification in Theorem 9.19 asserts a condition that fails.

AFFECTS: the proof. No stated result becomes false. Theorems 6.3 and 6.6 only get stronger under the fix, and their existing proofs support it. What fails is the proof of Thm 9.19, and through it the chain to Thms 5.16 and 1.1. The fix repairs it.

SEPARATE ISSUE, NOT PART OF THIS CANDIDATE. Thm 6.3(2) lets H be any R-module. ψ∞ comes from lim H/ϖ^{N_i}H, so it tacitly needs H to be finitely generated (and nonzero, for (iii)). For example, H = K with T = 0 and D_N = 0 satisfies all the hypotheses but not (iv). This is harmless in §9. (1) "M, N and n as above" points to (b): M ≥ N ≥ 0, M ≥ 1, n ≥ 1. Condition (c) defines φ_N only for N ≥ 1, so the printed (d) is meaningless when N = 0.
(2) The module H^*(D_M^□ ⊗ S_N/ϖ^n) belongs to level M. By (c), R∞ acts on its l0-part mod the augmentation ideal through φ_M. It does not give the φ_N version for M > N. I built a toy case to check: q = 0, j = 1, l0 = 0, R = H = O, D_M = O/ϖ^M, x acting as z + c_M. The corrected (d) holds for arbitrary c_M. The printed (d) forces c_N ≡ c_M mod ϖ^M.
Two points qualify the candidate's reason:
(a) For N ≥ 1 the printed hypothesis is stronger than needed, not weaker. At N = M the printed and corrected versions coincide, and in degree l0 that case already gives what the proof uses: H^{l0}(D ⊗ S_N) = H^{l0}(D ⊗ S_M) ⊗ S_N, and the R∞-actions are compatible by (b). So no conclusion of 6.3, 6.4, 6.6 or 9.19 becomes false. The damage is that the stated hypothesis is ill-formed at N = 0 and, for M > N, differs from what the application verifies.
(b) On p. 427 the application also writes the action on H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M)) through R_{S_{Q_N}} and R∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}}. That looks like a matching index slip (it should be Q_M) and could be a separate candidate. I checked the page image (PDF p. 90): the printed text reads exactly as quoted.

DEFENCE ATTEMPTS AND WHY THEY FAIL:
(1) "M, N and n as above" refers to (b): M ≥ N ≥ 0, M ≥ 1, n ≥ 1. But (c) defines φ_N only for N ≥ 1, so the printed condition has an undefined symbol φ_0 when N = 0.
(2) The module belongs to level M. By (c) at level M, together with the (b)-compatibility for the maps to N' = 0, R∞ acts on H^{l0}(D_M^□ ⊗ S_N/ϖ^n) modulo the augmentation ideal through φ_M. φ_N plays no part there.
(3) The proof (p. 388) builds the datum D_{M,N} with φ = (R∞ →φ_M R ↠ R/𝔡_N), and φ∞ = lim φ_{M_i} mod 𝔡_{N_i}. So the final step "image of 𝔞 … contained in that of ker(φ∞) by assumption (d)" (p. 389) directly calls for ker φ_{M_i}.
(4) The one-index model, Prop. 2.3(5a) (p. 307), pairs H_N with φ_N at the same level. The slip is what happens when that clause is carried over to two indices.
(5) One could try to defend the printed index by reading p. 427 literally: there R∞ acts on H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M)) through R∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}}. That reading does not hold up. R_{S_{Q_N}} does not act on level-Q_M cohomology, because Q_N and Q_M are different sets of primes; this is H-part2-27. The reading also contradicts (b)+(c).
(6) The printed condition is not the corrected one in disguise when M > N. I built a toy model satisfying (a)–(c): q = 0, j = 1, l0 = 0, R = H = O, R∞ = O⟦x⟧, D_M = O/ϖ^M, x acting as z + c_M, φ_N(x) = c_N ∈ 𝔪. The corrected (d) holds, since z = x − c_M. The printed (d) needs z ∈ (z + c_M − c_N)·(O/ϖ^m)⟦z⟧ with m = min(n, M). Comparing the constant and z-coefficients shows this forces c_N ≡ c_M mod ϖ^m. In §9 the surjections R∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}} are chosen independently for each N (via Prop. 8.5). So "Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B" (p. 427) proves the ker φ_M version, not the printed one for M > N. So the text as printed is wrong, and the defence fails.

CONSEQUENCES:
The proof uses (d) only in degree l0, through P_i = D_{M_i} ⊗ S_{N_i}/ϖ^{N_i} with N_i ≥ 1. It never uses N = 0. In degree l0, the N = M instance already gives every other case, and at N = M the printed and corrected conditions coincide. The reason: H^{l0} is a cokernel, so H^{l0}(D_M^□ ⊗ S_N/ϖ^n) = H^{l0}(D_M^□ ⊗ S_M/ϖ^n) ⊗ S_N. The quotient map is R∞- and S_M^□-equivariant by (b). And aug(S_M^□) maps onto aug(S_N^□). So an element of ker φ_M that acts like x̃ upstairs also acts like x downstairs.

It follows that:
- Theorem 6.3 as printed, restricted to N ≥ 1, is still true.
- Its proof needs only this one-line reduction.
- Theorem 6.4, Prop. 6.6 and the application in Theorem 9.19 all go through. The application verifies the corrected (d), which includes the N = M instances.
- No conclusion changes. The mathematics is right as intended.

The paper has no global rule that modules are finite: the Notation section only fixes C_O and says what "perfect complex" means. When finiteness is needed elsewhere the authors state it, as in Prop. 2.3(1). I redid the counterexamples.
(A) Finiteness. Take q = j = l0 = 0, so S∞ = S_N = O, O^□ = O and 𝔞 = 0. Take R∞ = R = O (Krull dimension 1 = 1+j+q−l0) and H = K. Then H/ϖ = 0, so T = 0 satisfies (3). Take D_N = 0 and φ_N = id. Conditions (a)–(d) hold trivially, since every cohomology group is 0 = K/ϖ^n K. Conclusion (iv) then gives H^0(P∞) ≅ K, but P∞ is a complex of finitely generated O-modules, so this is impossible. Theorem 6.4(1) applies (R∞ = O is p-torsion free and formally smooth) and would say that K is a free O-module, which is false. If l0 ≥ 1 is wanted, take q = 0 and j = l0; the same argument works with 𝔞 = (z_1..z_j).
The proof uses finiteness explicitly on p. 387: "(As in the proof of Theorem 2.3, one can take 𝔡_N to be the ideal generated by ϖ^N and Ann_R(H)^N)". That step relies on "R/Ann_R(H) ⊂ End_O(H) is finite as an O-module" (p. 307), which needs H finite over O. Finiteness is also needed to identify the limit of the H/ϖ^N H with H when building ψ∞.
(B) Non-vanishing. Take H = 0, T = 0, D_N = 0 and R∞ = R = O. The hypotheses of 6.4 hold and R∞[1/p] = K is irreducible. But 6.4(2) would make 0 a nearly faithful O-module, which is false because Ann = O is not nilpotent. The proof of 6.4(2) on p. 390 itself says "Since H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ {0}". Lemma 6.2's proof also assumes that some H^m(P) is non-zero.
Minor point: the proposed "equivalently T ≠ 0" works only through the theorem's own dimension argument. "H^{l0}(T) ≠ 0" is the cleaner equivalent.
Where the theorem is applied (Theorem 9.19, via Prop. 6.6), H = H^{q0}(Y,K/O)^∨_𝔪 is finite over O. It is non-zero because 𝔪 is a maximal ideal of the Hecke algebra, so T ≠ 0. The main results are therefore unaffected. What is wrong is the printed statements of Theorems 6.3 and 6.4 (and Prop. 6.6, which inherits the hypotheses): they are false as printed in these degenerate cases. **Defences tried.**
- **Global convention?** There is none. The Notation section (p. 299) only fixes C_O and defines "perfect complex". Elsewhere the authors state finiteness when they need it: in Prop. 2.3(1) (p. 307), and they write "finitely generated" for P∞ in the conclusion.
- **Does (3) force finiteness?** No. It only makes H/ϖ finite-dimensional; H itself need not be finite.
- **Do (a)–(d) force it?** No. They only constrain H/ϖ^n.

**(A) Finiteness fails.**
- Setup: take q = j = l0 = 0. Then S_N = S∞ = O, O^□ = O and 𝔞 = 0. Take R∞ = R = O (Krull dimension 1 = 1+j+q−l0), H = K, T = 0, D_N = 0 and φ_N = id. D_N = 0 is a perfect complex.
- The hypotheses hold: (a) holds because T = 0. (c) holds because H^0(0) = 0 = K/ϖ^n K. (b) and (d) hold trivially, since End(0) = 0.
- Conclusion (iv) would then give H^0(P∞) ≅ K, where P∞ is a perfect complex of finitely generated O-modules. That is impossible.
- Theorem 6.4(1) applies, since O is p-torsion free and formally smooth with 0 variables. It would say that K is a free O-module, which is false.
- For l0 ≥ 1, take q = 0 and j = l0. Then 𝔞 = (z_1..z_j), and H^{l0}(P∞^□)/𝔞 is finite over O, so it again cannot be ≅ K. Taking H = O ⊕ K shows that the proof really produces the ϖ-adic completion of H, not H.
- Two places in the proof use finiteness:
  - p. 387: "(As in the proof of Theorem 2.3 [sic, Prop. 2.3], one can take 𝔡_N to be the ideal generated by ϖ^N and Ann_R(H)^N)". Openness there depends on "R/Ann_R(H) ⊂ End_O(H) is finite as an O-module" (p. 308).
  - p. 388: ψ∞ is built from the H/ϖ^{N_i}H, so it identifies lim H/ϖ^N H with H.

**(B) Non-vanishing fails.**
- Setup: take q = j = l0 = 0, R∞ = R = O, H = 0, T = 0 and D_N = 0.
- R∞ is p-torsion free and R∞[1/p] = K is irreducible. So 6.4(2) says that 0 is a nearly faithful O-module.
- In Taylor's sense ([11]), nearly faithful means Ann is nilpotent. Here Ann_O(0) = O, so this is false.
- The proof on p. 390 itself uses "Since H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ {0}", and Lemma 6.2's proof needs some H^m(P) ≠ 0.
- In 6.3, (iv) together with Nakayama forces H^{l0}(P∞^□) = 0. Then (iii) asserts that depth(0) = 1+j+q−l0, which is false under the convention depth(0) = ∞ and undefined otherwise.

**Where the result is used.** Only in the outline of §8.1 (pp. 369–370) and in Theorem 9.19 (pp. 417–419), through Prop. 6.6 and Theorem 6.4(2) with i = 2 and conclusion (iv).
- There H^i = H^{q0}(Y,K/O)^∨_𝔪 (or its χ-version). This is the Pontryagin dual of a cofinitely generated module, so it is finite over O.
- It is non-zero because 𝔪 is a maximal ideal of the Hecke algebra acting on H^*(Y,O/ϖ^n). So T ≠ 0, the patched minimal complex P∞ (with P∞⊗k ≅ T) is non-zero, and by Lemma 6.2 H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ 0, hence H ≠ 0.
- So Theorem 9.19, Theorem 5.16 and Theorem 1.1 are unaffected.

Proof that it is not local:
- A = O⟦x⟧⊗_O O⟦z⟧ is O-flat, so it embeds in A⊗K = O⟦x⟧[1/p]⊗_K O⟦z⟧[1/p].
- That ring maps injectively to coefficient arrays K^{N^q×N^j}, and every element has a coefficient matrix of finite rank.
- The inverse of 1 − x_1z_1 in O⟦x,z⟧ is Σ(x_1z_1)^n. Its coefficient matrix contains an infinite identity block, so the inverse is not in A, and 1 − x_1z_1 is not a unit of A.
- But x_1z_1 lies in the maximal ideal ker(A → k). So the non-units of A do not form an ideal, and A is not local.

So, as printed, S∞^□ is not in C_O. It is not the Noetherian regular local ring that Lemma 6.2 requires ("let S be a Noetherian regular local ring"), and it has no "dim S∞^□ = 1+j+q". P∞ ⊗_O O^□ is likewise not the complete module whose cohomology carries the patched R∞-action.

1) Read literally, the definition fails. Even after Correction item (10) (O^□ = O⟦z⟧), M^□ is defined with the plain ⊗_O. Take q = j = 1: S∞ ⊗_O O⟦z⟧ = O⟦T⟧ ⊗_O O⟦z⟧, which embeds in O⟦T,z⟧. Its image consists of power series whose coefficient matrix (c_{a,b}) has finite rank over K. In O⟦T,z⟧ the inverse of 1 − Tz is Σ T^n z^n, whose coefficient matrix is the identity and has infinite rank. So 1 − Tz is not a unit in the plain tensor product. Tz is not a unit either. Hence the ring is not local, so it is not in C_O and not a Noetherian regular local ring. Its Krull dimension is also not 1 + j + q.

2) The proof needs the completed ring at every step:
- "dim R∞ = dim S∞^□ − l0" needs dim S∞^□ = 1 + j + q.
- "By Lemma 6.2 (with S = S∞^□ and P = P∞^□)": Lemma 6.2 needs S Noetherian regular local.
- "since S∞^□ is formally smooth over O, we can and do choose a homomorphism ı: S∞^□ → R∞ in C_O".
- (ii) asks H^{l0}(P∞^□) to be a finite R∞-module carrying an action of R∞ ⊗̂ S∞^□. That action arises as an inverse limit, so it lives on P∞ ⊗̂ O^□, not on P∞ ⊗_O O^□. The latter is in general not complete.

3) Defence tried and rejected. One could argue the paper uses ⊗ to mean ⊗̂ by convention. It does not: it writes ⊗̂ explicitly elsewhere, e.g. Lemma 4.2's B ⊗̂_O C, R_loc, and R∞ ⊗̂_O S∞^□ in the same theorem. So the plain ⊗ is a genuine slip and is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

4) The intended meaning is nonetheless unambiguous from context: the dimension count, formal smoothness, the use of C_O, Lemma 6.2, and p. 426, where R_{S_{Q_N}}⟦z_1,…,z_j⟧ is identified with "R^□_{S_Q} in the notation of Proposition 6.3". With the completed product, every step of Thms 6.3 and 6.4, Prop 6.6 and Thm 9.19 goes through unchanged. So this is a misprint, not a gap, and it affects nothing.

Here is an example that satisfies all of (1)–(3) and (a)–(d):
- q = 0, j = 1, l0 = 1, so S_N = S_∞ = O.

Now take N ≥ 2, n′ = 2 and I = (ϖz, z^2). Then (z^N) ⊂ I ⊂ (z), and B = O⟦z⟧/(ϖz, z^2, ϖ^2) = A·1 ⊕ k·z.

- Right side: H^0(Y)⊗_A B = k⟦z⟧/I = k[z]/(z^2). Here z acts nontrivially.
The two sides are not isomorphic even as O^□-modules. The natural map ϖ⊗z ↦ ϖz = 0 is neither injective nor surjective.

So the proof cannot get the required R_∞-action on the left side from (b) for such I. In this example an action exists anyway, since R_∞ = S_∞^□/ϖ. So this is a flaw in the argument, not a counterexample to the claim, and it is fixed by restricting to monomial I.

Other readings do not rescue the step:

- No nearby statement restricts I.
- In top degree l_0 the display does hold, by right exactness. But the proof needs every degree: it uses the dimension of H^*(P_∞^□) and then Lemma 6.2.

COUNTEREXAMPLE WITHIN THE HYPOTHESES. I checked this by hand; it is the example in H-part2-7's verdict.
- Take q = 0, j = 1, l_0 = 1. Then S_N = O and O^□ = O⟦z⟧.
- D_N = (O/ϖ^N →ϖ O/ϖ^N) and T = (k →0 k), R = H = k.
- R_∞ = k⟦z⟧, of Krull dimension 1 = 1+j+q−l_0. It acts on H^*(D_M^□/ϖ^n) ≅ k⟦z⟧ by z ↦ z. φ_N sends z to 0.
- Conditions (1)–(3) and (a)–(d) all hold.

Now take M ≥ N ≥ 2, n′ = 2, N′ = 0 and I = (ϖz, z^2). This I lies between (z^N) and (z). Then B = O⟦z⟧/(ϖz, z^2, ϖ^2) = A·1 ⊕ k·z.
- Left side: H^0 = ker(ϖ on B) = span(ϖ, z), and z acts as 0 on it.
- Right side: H^0(Y) ⊗ O^□/I = k[z]/(z^2), and z acts nontrivially.
The two sides are not isomorphic even as O^□-modules. The check with O = Z_3 is: 3(a + bz) = 3a in Z/9 ⊕ (Z/3)z.

X-K7-10's example I = (z^N, ϖz) has O^□/I ≅ O ⊕ k^{N−1}. It shows the same failure in general, but it was not checked against (a)–(d).

X-K7-10'S FINITENESS SUB-CLAIM IS WRONG. The groups depend only on I + ϖ^{n′}O^□, which contains (z_1^N,…,z_j^N, ϖ^N). So they correspond to ideals of the finite ring (O/ϖ^N)[z]/(z_i^N); k is finite by the paper's conventions. Two ideals I and I′ with the same I + ϖ^{n′} both map compatibly to I + I′, so they carry the same action. Hence the paper's claim of "finitely many patching data" is fine as it stands.

CONSEQUENCES. The false display is used only to check that D_{M,N} is a patching datum. After that, the proof uses only I = (z^{N_i}) and (z_1,…,z_j). So restricting to monomial or O-flat I repairs it with no change to any statement. The same applies to Proposition 6.6. Kind: an error, because the displayed identity is false for some admissible I. It is a local error with a routine fix, and it does not reach a stated result. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. In the application (§9.5, p. 426), j = n²|T| − 1 > 0.

- **Misprint** at §6.1, proof of Theorem 6.3, p. 388 (published version) (it affects the proof). The source says `• M_i ≥ N_i, M_{i+1} ≥ M_i, and N_{i+1} ≥ N_i for all i; [p. 388 (PDF p. 92), proof of Theorem 6.3, first of two bullets after "Since there are finitely many patching data of each level N ≥ 1, up to isomorphism, we can find a sequence of pairs (M_i, N_i)_{i≥1} such that"; checked on a 250 dpi page image. arXiv v2 text l. 3551 has the same weak inequalities. The analogous bullet in the proof of Proposition 2.3, p. 309 (PDF p. 13), reads "M_i ≥ N_i, M_{i+1} > M_i, and N_{i+1} > N_i for all i;", also in v2 l. 465.]`; it should be `Read "M_i ≥ N_i, M_{i+1} > M_i, and N_{i+1} > N_i for all i", exactly as in the proof of Prop. 2.3 on p. 309. The smallest fix is N_{i+1} > N_i, or just N_i → ∞. Together with M_i ≥ N_i this also forces M_i → ∞, so M_{i+1} > M_i is harmless but not needed. Such a sequence exists by the pigeonhole/König argument the text invokes: - D_{M,N} mod N' ≅ D_{M,N'} by construction. - So choose nested infinite sets I_1 ⊃ I_2 ⊃ … of M such that the class of D_{M,k} is constant on I_k. - Then take N_i = i and strictly increasing M_i ∈ I_i with M_i ≥ i.`. I checked the printed text on the page image. The weak inequalities are really printed on p. 388, and the same text is in v2. As written, the two bullets are satisfied by the constant sequence (M_i, N_i) = (1, 1): 1 ≥ 1, and D_{1,1} mod 1 is D_{1,1} itself, since "D mod N'" for N' = N is the identity operation defined on p. 387–388.

With that sequence the rest of the proof fails:
- ϕ∞ = lim ϕ_i is just ϕ_1 : R∞ ↠ R/𝔡_1, not a surjection onto R.
- The transition maps P_{i+1} → P_{i+1}/(ϖ^{N_i} + 𝔞_{N_i}) ≅ P_i are isomorphisms, so P∞ = P_1. That is a complex of S∞/(𝔞_1 + ϖ) = S_1/ϖ-modules, so it is not a complex of projective S∞-modules.
- ψ∞ only gives H^{l0}(P∞^□)/𝔞 ≅ H/ϖH, not H.
- H^{l0}(P∞^□) is killed by ϖ and 𝔞_1, so its dimension is at most j. The depth claim (iii), 1 + j + q − l0, therefore fails as soon as q ≥ l0.

So the claim "Then P∞ is a perfect complex of S∞-modules … ϕ∞ : R∞ ↠ R" does not follow from the bullets as printed. The argument needs N_i → ∞, which the parallel proof of Proposition 2.3 gets from strict inequalities. The intent is obvious and the fix is one character, so this is a misprint rather than a real gap. It is not one of the 47 known ⟦ ⟧ bracket errors.

The statement of Theorem 6.3 is still true: the corrected choice of sequence exists by the same finiteness argument. Theorem 6.4 and the applications in §9 use only the statement, so nothing downstream is affected. Defence attempted and failed.
- Nothing on pp. 387–389 forces N_i → ∞. The patching-datum definition, the D mod N' operation, the definitions of ϕ∞, P∞ and ψ∞, and the rest of the proof never pass to a cofinal subsequence.
- The inverse-limit construction is used as if the levels grow, but that is never stated.
- The bullets as printed allow the constant sequence (M_i, N_i) = (1, 1). Here 1 ≥ 1, and D_{1,1} mod 1 = D_{1,1}, since D mod N' is defined for 1 ≤ N' ≤ N, which includes N' = N.

With that sequence the conclusions of the proof fail:
- ϕ∞ = ϕ_1 : R∞ ↠ R/𝔡_1, not a map onto R.
- Every transition map P_{i+1} → P_{i+1}/(ϖ^{N_i} + 𝔞_{N_i}) ≅ P_i is an isomorphism, so P∞ = P_1. That is a complex of S∞/(𝔞_1 + ϖ)-modules, not a perfect complex of S∞-modules resolving anything of the stated depth.
- ψ∞ only gives an isomorphism onto H/ϖH, not onto H.
- H^{l0}(P∞^□) is killed by ϖ, so the depth claim 1 + j + q − l0 is false once q + j ≥ l0 ≥ 1.

So the step "Then P∞ is a perfect complex of S∞-modules …" does not follow from the text as printed. It does follow once N_{i+1} > N_i.

The intended meaning is clear:
- the identical construction in Prop. 2.3 uses strict inequalities;
- the authors fixed exactly this slip in §2 between v1 and v2;
- the claimed existence is just as easy with strict inequalities.

So this is a misprint rather than an error or gap. It is not one of the 47 known ⟦ ⟧ bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not mention it.

Downstream, the construction is used by:
- the proof of Theorem 6.4 (p. 389), which uses ι and ψ∞ "as in the proof of Theorem 6.3";
- Prop. 6.6, whose proof is omitted as "much the same way as Theorem 6.3";
- §8.1 (p. 5303 of the text file region), which cites the depth information "deduced in the proof of Theorem 6.3".

With the corrected sequence all of these go through unchanged. No stated result changes, because the statements of 6.3, 6.4 and 6.6 remain true.

On 'affects': the protocol's gloss "nothing (the mathematics is right as intended)" could support "nothing", since the intended mathematics is right. I record "the proof" because the proof as printed does not establish the theorem until the inequality is fixed. - **Error** at §2 (introduction), item (1), p. 306 (also §6 introduction, p. 384; same in arXiv v1, v2). The source says `p. 306 (PDF 10), §2 intro: "(1) is well behaved for non-reduced quotients of power series rings over O (like S_N)," where S_N := O[(Z/p^N Z)^q] (the same sentence appears again in §6, p. 384). p. 309 (PDF 13), proof of Prop. 2.3: "ψ : X/aX ~→ H/b_N to be the reduction modulo ϖ^N of the given isomorphism ψ_M : H_M/aH_M ~→ H;". p. 313 (PDF 17), §3.2.1, continuing from p. 312: "C_Q ⊂ E[Q] is a subgroup étale locally isomorphic to Z/QZ and such that the subgroup Q + α_N(μ_N) of E meets every irreducible component of every geometric fibre of E." p. 314 (PDF 18), §3.2.3: "the 'Fricke involution' w_x : X_Δ(Q; x) → X_Δ(Q; x) which is defined on the open modular curve Y_Δ(X; x)". p. 323 (PDF 27), proof of Prop. 3.8: "We have a second quadrant Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence [33, Theorem III.2.20, Remark III.3.8] H^i(Δ, H^j(X_Δ(Q), (Ω^1 ⊗ ω^{-1} ⊗ L^*)_{K/O})) ⟹ H^{i+j}(X_0(Q), (Ω^1 ⊗ ω^{-1} ⊗ L^*)_{K/O})." p. 324 then says: "Applying Pontryagin duality, we obtain a third quadrant spectral sequence". p. 330 (PDF 34), after Thm 3.14: "(The choice of H ensures that for each prime x ≠ p, det(ρ_{n,α})|I_x has order prime to p)."`; it should be `Change "non-reduced" to "non-regular" (or "singular", or "not necessarily regular"). For example: "(1) is well behaved for non-regular quotients of power series rings over O (like S_N)". S_N = O[(Z/p^N Z)^q] ≅ O⟦y_1,…,y_q⟧/((1+y_i)^{p^N} − 1) is reduced. It is a 1-dimensional complete intersection that is neither regular nor a domain. Its reductions k[Δ_N] and S_∞/b_N = (O/ϖ^N)[Δ_N] are the rings that are non-reduced. This is a one-word change, and it matches what "balanced" (Definitions 2.1 and 2.2) is built to handle: over a non-regular ring, projective dimension can be infinite, so Auslander–Buchsbaum cannot be used there.`. I checked all six passages on page images (PDF pages 10, 13, 17, 18, 27 and 34; pp. 313–314 at 250 dpi), and every quote matches. All six are also in arXiv v2, so none is a typesetting artifact, and none is one of the 47 bracket errors.

p. 313: Q is a squarefree integer, while C_Q ⊂ E[Q] was defined just before. The moduli condition clearly needs C_Q + α_N(μ_N). Clear misprint.

p. 314: X is the level-N curve, and "Y_Δ(Q; x)" appears on both sides of the slip. Clear misprint.

p. 323: both indices of the displayed spectral sequence are ≥ 0, so it is first-quadrant. The authors' own next sentence calls the dual "third quadrant", which fits only a first-quadrant original. Slip.

p. 306: I redid the check. O[G] ⊂ K[G] ≅ ∏ fields for G finite abelian in characteristic 0, so S_N is reduced. The informal phrase "non-reduced ... (like S_N)" is wrong. The intended property (not regular, not a domain) is clear, and nothing uses the phrase.

p. 330: Theorem 3.14 claims only conditions (2) and (4) of Def. 3.1. These concern x ∉ Q ∪ S(ρ̄) and x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄), where the claim is true: det is unramified at x ∤ NQp, and H is the p-part of (Z/N(ρ̄))^× (§3.3). For x | Q with x ≡ 1 mod p, which is the Taylor–Wiles case, the literal claim fails. So the correct range is x ∤ Qp, as the candidate says. One small point on the candidate's reason: in §3.2–3.3, Q is only squarefree and prime to Np. The failure happens exactly when some x | Q has x ≡ 1 mod p, and the sets Q_N (≡ 1 mod p^N) are such a case. Determinant condition (1) is never claimed for ρ_{n,α}; Thm 3.11 fixes the determinant by a twist. So nothing later depends on this.

p. 309, which I refute: b_N = (ϖ^N) + a_N and a_N ⊂ a. The paper already writes quotients like "H_M/b_N" for H_M/b_N H_M. H is an S_∞/a = O-module through ψ_M, so H/b_N H = H/ϖ^N H, exactly the target in the definition of a patching datum on p. 308. This is harmless shorthand, not an error.

Overall: a genuine but cosmetic bundle. It affects nothing. WHY THE PAPER IS WRONG. O is the ring of integers of a finite extension of Q_p (p. 305), so it has characteristic 0. Take Δ_N = (Z/p^N)^q. Then S_N = O[Δ_N] is free over O, so S_N ⊂ S_N ⊗_O K = K[Δ_N]. By Maschke's theorem in characteristic 0, K[Δ_N] is commutative semisimple, i.e. a finite product of fields. A subring of a reduced ring is reduced, so S_N is reduced. Smallest case, q = N = 1: O[T]/(T^p − 1). Over K, T^p − 1 = (T − 1)Φ_p(T) is separable (its discriminant is ±p^p ≠ 0), so K[T]/(T^p − 1) ≅ K × K(ζ_p) and there are no nilpotents.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. For q, N ≥ 1, S_N ≅ O⟦y⟧/((1+y_i)^{p^N} − 1). Each relation lies in m^2 of O⟦y⟧: the linear term is p^N·y_i with p ∈ m, the middle terms are divisible by p, and the top term is y_i^{p^N}. So embdim S_N = q + 1 > 1 = dim S_N, and S_N is not regular. It is also not a domain, because K[Δ_N] has more than one factor. Its special fibre k[y]/(y_i^{p^N}) is non-reduced. So "non-reduced ... (like S_N)" misnames the property. The candidate's reasoning and its correction are both right.

DEFENCES I TRIED, ALL FAILED. (a) "Non-reduced" might mean "not necessarily reduced". This strains the words, and even then S_N would not be an example of the feature being singled out. (b) S_N might be redefined somewhere as a torsion ring. It is not: every occurrence (Prop. 2.3(2), proof of Thm 3.14, §5, Thm 6.3, Prop. 6.6, §9) has S_N = O[Δ_N]. (c) Balancedness might be applied over non-reduced rings. The notion is used over S_N itself: Prop. 2.3(5c) says "H_N is finite and balanced over S_N", and later arguments say "d_{S_N}(H_N) ≥ 0". The non-reduced rings S_∞/b_N enter only through base change of the resulting presentation. No reading makes S_N non-reduced.

KIND. This is a false mathematical assertion (that S_N is non-reduced), not a typographical slip. It is repeated verbatim in §2 and §6, but that looks like a copy: the v1 wording "to find a find a" survives in the published §6. The intended word ("non-regular" or "singular") is fairly clear from context. So "misprint" is arguable, and that is how the p. 306 item in the H-part1a-15 bundle is classed. I class it as an error of the harmless kind.

CONSEQUENCES. This is motivational text in an introduction, and nothing refers back to it. Definitions 2.1 and 2.2 are stated for an arbitrary Noetherian local ring S, and no proof uses reducedness or non-reducedness of S_N. That covers Prop. 2.3, Theorems 3.14 and 5.x, Theorem 6.3, Prop. 6.6 and §9. Affects nothing.

RELATION TO H-part1a-15. That candidate bundles six slips. Its p. 306 item is exactly this finding, and its prior verdict already confirmed it with the same correction. Its other items (pp. 309, 313, 314, 323, 330) are separate and were not re-examined here.

SIDE NOTE. The §6 copy on p. 384 also has the duplicated words "to find a find a suitable notion" (also in v2 p. 65 and v1 p. 6). This is a trivial typo and separate from this candidate. I checked the rendered PDF page 93 (p. 389), including a 250 dpi crop. Theorem 6.4(1) reads "If R∞ is formally smooth over 𝒪, so R ≃ 𝒪[x_1,…,x_{q+j−l_0}], then H is a free R-module." arXiv v2 (cg-v2.txt, line ~3594) has the same wording, with correct brackets: "so R ≃ O[[x1,…,xq+j−l0]]".

In Theorem 6.3 (p. 386), R∞ and R are separate objects. Hypothesis (1) says R∞ ∈ C_𝒪 has Krull dimension 1+j+q−l_0. Hypothesis (2) says R ∈ C_𝒪 is just some other ring, with an R-module H. Part (iv) on p. 387 gives a surjection φ∞ : R∞ ↠ R. So a formally smooth R∞ is 𝒪⟦x_1,…,x_{q+j−l_0}⟧, since a power series ring over 𝒪 in n variables has dimension 1+n. The proof starts with the correct hypothesis: "Proof Suppose first of all that R∞ ≃ 𝒪[x_1,…,x_{j+q−l_0}]."

As printed, the claim about R is false in general. The proof shows R = R∞/ı(𝔞)R∞, with ker(φ∞) = ı(𝔞)R∞, where 𝔞 is generated by q+j elements. There is also a direct contradiction with the setup. Hypothesis (3) of Thm 6.3 gives H/ϖ ≅ H^{l_0}(T), which is a finite-dimensional k-vector space. Suppose H ≠ 0 were free over R ≅ 𝒪⟦x_1,…,x_m⟧ with m = q+j−l_0 ≥ 1. Then H/ϖ would be free over k⟦x_1,…,x_m⟧ and so infinite-dimensional. So the printed statement only makes sense when q+j = l_0. In the applications R is a Hecke algebra that is finite over 𝒪. The "R" in the "so" clause must therefore be a slip for "R∞". This is not a bracket error; only the [ ] → ⟦ ⟧ part of this line is covered by the 2022 Correction.

Dependence: the text cites Theorem 6.4 only on p. 391 (the paragraph after Prop. 6.6) and on p. 428 (the §9 proof: "by Theorem 6.4 H^{l_0}(P∞^{2,□}) is nearly faithful as an R∞^2-module"). Both uses are of the nearly-faithful parts (2)/(3), not part (1). The proof of (1) already uses the correct hypothesis on R∞, and its conclusion (H free over R, with R = R∞/ı(𝔞)R∞) is correct. Proof This can be proved in much the same way as Theorem 6.3; we omit the details."`; it should be `Add a compatibility hypothesis. For each M ≥ N ≥ 0 with M ≥ 1, the isomorphism θ_{M,N} at level (M,N), once reduced along S_N/ϖ → S_0/ϖ = O/ϖ (that is, θ_{M,N} ⊗_{S_N} O, which makes sense because H^{l0} is the top degree and so H^{l0}(D_M ⊗ S_N/ϖ) ⊗_{S_N} O = H^{l0}(D_M ⊗ O/ϖ)), should equal θ_{M,0}. Equivalently, the square should also commute when its top arrow is the map induced by θ_{M,N}. The candidate asks instead for compatibility with every natural surjection N → N' ≥ 0. That is a natural, slightly stronger version and it is also correct. Only the case N' = 0 is needed; compatibility across different M is not needed, because pigeonholing takes care of it.`. I rendered pp. 386–391 and 427–428 and checked them against the patching proof of Thm 6.3 (pp. 387–389).

1. The "same way as Theorem 6.3" proof: build a joint patching datum of level N from (φ^i, ψ^i, P^i) for i=1,2 plus the mod-ϖ isomorphism β, with D_{M,N} carrying β = α_{M,N}. Choose (M_i, N_i) with N_i → ∞ and take limits. The patched β_∞ on H^{l0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ is lim_i α_{M_i,N_i}. By right-exactness of top-degree cohomology, H^{l0}(P_∞)/(a+ϖ) is H^{l0}(D_{M_i}⊗_{S_{M_i}}O/ϖ). So β_∞ mod a equals α_{M_i,N_i}⊗_{S_{N_i}}O, and ψ^i_∞ mod ϖ is the (c) isomorphism of D_{M_i} with n=1.

2. The conclusion square therefore commutes exactly when ψ^2∘(α_{M_i,N_i}⊗O)∘(ψ^1)^{-1} = θ. The hypothesis only gives this for α_{M_i,0}, which never enters the patching because N_i → ∞. Nothing in the statement links α_{M,N} (N ≥ 1) with α_{M,0}. The third bullet only requires R_∞-linearity at each fixed (M,N). The authors state such compatibilities explicitly elsewhere: Thm 6.3 (b) says "compatible with the R_∞-actions" for N ≥ N', and (c) says "compatible for fixed N and varying n". So the omission here looks real, not a convention.

3. Explicit data where every hypothesis holds but the omitted argument gives a square that fails. Take q=1, j=0, l0=0 and R^i_∞ = O[[x,y]]/(y^2), which has dimension 2 = 1+j+q−l0. Take R^i = O, H^i = O^2 and T = k^2. Let D_N = (S_N/ϖ^N)^2 with x acting as [γ]−1 and y as ([γ]−1)·n, where n = [[0,1],[0,0]], and φ_N(x) = φ_N(y) = 0. Conditions (a)–(d) hold, with the same data for i=1,2. Take θ = Id and α_{M,0} = Id, so the square commutes. For N ≥ 1 take α_{M,N} = [[1,1],[0,1]]; this commutes with n, so it is R_∞⊗S_N-linear. The patched β_∞ then reduces to [[1,1],[0,1]] ≠ θ, and the square fails.

Here the literal existential conclusion still holds, because β = Id works. So I have not refuted the statement itself: it is a gap in the omitted proof, not a proven false statement. It does not affect Thm 9.19, where the needed compatibility holds by naturality. Defence attempted, and it fails.

(1) The omitted proof must patch θ as well as the rest. The conclusion needs one isomorphism Θ: H^{l0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ → H^{l0}(P^2_∞)/ϖ. This can only come from the level isomorphisms θ_{M,N}, which have to be added to the level-N patching datum of Theorem 6.3's proof (p. 391). Pigeonholing then picks pairs (M_i, N_i), and Θ is the limit of the θ_{M_i,N_i}. So Θ mod a is θ_{M_i,N_i} ⊗_{S_{N_i}} O.

(2) The vertical maps ψ^i_∞ mod ϖ are the n = 1 isomorphisms of hypothesis (c) for D_{M_i}. This uses (c)'s compatibility "for fixed N and varying n".

(3) The patched square therefore commutes exactly when β∘ψ^1 = ψ^2∘(θ_{M_i,N_i} mod a), where β: H^1/ϖ → H^2/ϖ. The hypothesis only gives this for θ_{M_i,0}. Nothing in the statement links θ_{M,N} to θ_{M,0}. Both are R_∞/ϖ-linear isomorphisms between the same two modules, so they differ by an arbitrary automorphism γ of H^1/ϖ as an R^1_∞/ϖ-module.

(4) The obvious repairs do not work in general. One could twist ψ^1_∞ by γ, but then γ must lift to an automorphism of H^1 as an integral R^1-module. One could twist Θ, but then γ must lift to an automorphism of H^{l0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ as an R_∞/ϖ-module. In general Aut_R(H) → Aut_{R/ϖ}(H/ϖ) and End_{R_∞}(M) → End(M/aM) are not surjective.

(5) A charitable reading does not help. Elsewhere the paper states such compatibilities explicitly: Theorem 6.3(b) covers N ≥ N' and n ≥ n', and (c) says "compatible for fixed N and varying n". Here the square is imposed only for "S_N/ϖ = O/ϖ", i.e. N = 0.

(6) Degenerate check: when q = j = l0 = 0 the conclusion holds trivially, since Θ := ψ^{2,-1}βψ^1 works. I have no counterexample to the statement as printed, so this is recorded as a gap, not an error.

Downstream use: the only use is the proof of Theorem 9.19 (pp. 426–427). There the level isomorphisms are the natural ones H^{l0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ) ≅ H^{l0}_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ), which exist because χ ≡ 1 mod ϖ. They are functorial in the covers, so they are compatible as N varies and reduce to the N = 0 isomorphism. The paper only says they "give rise to the commutative square required", but the added hypothesis does hold there. Theorem 9.19, and so the main theorems, are unaffected. - **Error** at §7.1, the sentence before Lemma 7.2 and Lemma 7.2, published p. 392 (PDF p. 96), proof on p. 393. The same issue is in §7.2, pp. 398–400. arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2) Lemma 7.2 and its proof have the same wording. arXiv v1 has no such section. (it affects a stated result). The source says `p. 392: "Let γ ∈ G(A^{∞,p}) with associated Hecke operator T_γ : H_*(X_Δ(Q), O/ϖ^N) → H_*(X_Δ(Q), O/ϖ^N) for N ≤ ∞ (where we define O/ϖ^∞ := O). Lemma 7.2 Let C be as in Lemma 7.1. Then the action of T_γ on homology may be lifted to a map T_γ : C → C of complexes of R-modules." Proof, p. 393: "Thus T_γ is induced by the corresponding composition of morphisms of complexes C(X_K) →^{tr} C(X_{K''}) →^{γ_*} C(X_{K'}) → C(X_K), (after tensoring over O with A). Denote this composition T̃_γ. Restricting to C ..., we obtain T̃_γ : C → C(X_K) which also gives rise to T_γ on homology. We thus have a diagram [C →^{T̃_γ} C(X_K) ← C] of complexes of R-modules with the vertical morphism being a quasi-isomorphism." Here R = O[Δ] (p. 392). §7.2 has the same claim: "The Hecke algebra will be generated by operators T_γ where γ ∈ G(A_F^{∞,p})" (p. 398); "we have an equality (of Hom's in the category D^b(R)) ... and we define an element of T̃_γ of the right hand side by composing • the pullback under π_1^* ⊗ (φ∘π_2^*) ..." (p. 399), then lifted to C_n^∨ (p. 400).`; it should be `Add a hypothesis to Lemma 7.2, and to the Hecke algebra T on p. 393 and the operators T_γ on p. 398: K_Δ(Q)γK_Δ(Q) must be stable under conjugation by K_0(Q), i.e. K_Δ(Q)δ^{-1}γδK_Δ(Q) = K_Δ(Q)γK_Δ(Q) for all δ ∈ K_0(Q). A sufficient condition is that γ commutes with some set of representatives in K_0(Q) of Δ = K_0(Q)/K_Δ(Q). Under this hypothesis the chain map T̃_γ is Δ-equivariant and the proof goes through word for word. The candidate's correction is correct and essentially minimal. The condition "T_γ commutes with Δ on homology" is necessary but does not by itself give a chain-level R-linear map, so the double-coset condition is the natural one to add. It holds for every operator the paper actually uses: good operators at v ∉ S_Q, where K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} and L_Q = ∏_v L_{Q,v}; the diagonal T_{α,k} = T(diag(α,…,α,1,…,1)), V_x and U_x at x ∈ Q in §9, which commute with the diagonal representatives of Δ; the diamond operators; and polynomials in these, such as the projectors P_x and P_i on pp. 394–395.`. R = O[Δ] acts on X_Δ(Q) = X_K by right translation by δ ∈ K_0(Q), which normalizes K = K_Δ(Q). If KγK is the disjoint union of the cosets γ_i K, then r_δ^{-1} T_γ r_δ sends xK to the sum of the x δ^{-1}γ_i δ K. So conjugating T_γ by δ gives T_{δ^{-1}γδ}, which in general is a different operator. If T_γ does not commute with Δ on H_*(X_Δ(Q), A), then no R-linear chain map C → C can induce it. The lemma allows any γ ∈ G(A^{∞,p}), and that includes components at the places v ∈ Q (they do not divide p).

Counterexample inside the paper's own §9 setting, with n = 2. At v ∈ Q, K_{Q,v} is the Iwahori subgroup and L_{Q,v} is the kernel of the character [[a,b],[c,d]] ↦ d/a mod π_v. The Atkin–Lehner element w = [[0,1],[π_v,0]] satisfies w^{-1}[[a,b],[c,d]]w = [[d, c/π_v],[bπ_v, a]]. So w normalizes K_{Q,v} and L_{Q,v}, K w K = wK, and T_w is right translation by w (K' = K'' = K and tr = id in the paper's proof). Since w^{-1} diag(a,b) w = diag(b,a), we get T_w⟨t⟩ = ⟨t^{-1}⟩T_w. Because w² is central, T_w is invertible. If T_w were R-linear, then ⟨t⟩ = ⟨t^{-1}⟩, so ⟨t⟩² = 1. Δ has odd p-power order, so Δ would act trivially on H_*.

But Δ does act nontrivially. Classical check: q = 31, p = 5, Δ = Z/5. By the dimension formula, dim S_2(31, χ) = 8/3 − 2/3 − 1 = 1 for each of the 4 characters χ of order 5. As a consistency check, 2·2 + 4·1 + 8·2 = 24 = g(X_1(31)) − g(X_0(31)) = 26 − 2. So H_1(Y_Δ, O) ⊗ E has χ-isotypic pieces with χ ≠ 1, and Lemma 7.2 fails for γ = w (N = ∞, or N large). Adding auxiliary level at another prime to make the quotient neat changes nothing.

The step of the proof that fails is the implicit claim that C(X_K) → C(X_{K''}) → C(X_{K'}) → C(X_K) is a diagram "of complexes of R-modules". Δ need not act on X_{K'} or X_{K''}, and even when it does, the maps need not be equivariant. The same unjustified R-linearity occurs in §7.2, where the pullback to Y^γ is treated as a morphism in D^b(R).

The paper is aware that the condition matters: p. 395 requires P_x to "commute with the action of the diamond operators". All operators actually used satisfy the condition: diagonal g in §9.2 commutes with torus representatives of Δ. So no main theorem is affected. I class this as an error in the stated generality, not merely a gap, because the lemma as printed is false for some allowed γ. Defence attempted and failed. An R-linear chain map C → C induces an R-linear map on H_*(C) = H_*(X_Δ(Q), A), and the R-action there is the Δ-action by right translation, because the map C → C(X_Δ(Q)) of Lemma 7.1 is R-linear. So the lemma forces T_γ to commute with Δ. Lemma 7.2 is stated for every γ ∈ G(A^{∞,p}), and that is false.

Counterexample inside the paper's own §9 setting. Take n = 2, x ∈ Q, and γ = w = (0 1; π_x 0) at x, trivial elsewhere (x ∤ p, so w ∈ G(A^{∞,p})). A direct computation gives w (a b; πc d) w^{-1} = (d c; πb a). So w normalizes K_{Q,x} (the Iwahori) and L_{Q,x} = {d/a ≡ 1}, and it acts on Δ by δ ↦ δ^{-1}. Hence K' = K'' = K and T_w = w_* is right translation, with w_*∘r_δ = r_{δ^{-1}}∘w_*. Also w^2 = π·I, which is central, so T_w is invertible. R-linearity would then force r_{δ^2} = id on H_*(X_Δ(Q), O). For p odd, δ ↦ δ^2 is bijective on Δ = (Z/p^N)^q, so Δ would act trivially on H_*(X_Δ(Q), O). Taking transfer, dim H_*(X_Δ, K) = dim H_*(X_0, K). That is false in general. For example, with F = Q allowed by the general setting of §7.1, the Euler characteristic gives χ(X_Δ) = |Δ|·χ(X_0) ≠ χ(X_0). In any case, patching needs Δ to act nontrivially.

The failing step in the proof is the claim that T̃_γ is a map of complexes of R-modules. C(X_{K'}) and C(X_{K''}) carry no Δ-action. Computed out, T̃_γ(σ) = Σ_{hK ⊂ KγK} σ·h. This commutes with r_δ exactly when δKγK = KγKδ, which is the candidate's condition. Under that condition the rest of the proof (Tag 08FQ over R) is fine.

The authors evidently meant only operators that commute with Δ: p. 394 says "In practice, the Hecke algebra T will be of the form T^an[U_x : x ∈ Q]", and p. 395 says "a projector P_x which commutes with the action of the diamond operators". The intro to §7.2 on p. 395 speaks of "'good' Hecke operators … together with certain operators at the primes in Q". §7.2 (pp. 398–400) has the same unrestricted γ, and its "element of the right hand side" in D^b(R) likewise needs Δ-equivariance.

Downstream uses:
- Lemma 7.3, Lemma 7.4 and the choice of T on pp. 394–395 use only operators that satisfy the condition.
- §9 (p. 425: "By Conjecture B and the results of Sect. 7.1") uses T_{Q,ψ}, which is generated by diagonal g (Def. 9.1), so the condition holds there.
- §7.2 feeds no stated theorem.

So Lemma 7.2 is false as stated and needs the added hypothesis. No later theorem changes. The minimal repair adds finite-dimensionality, which is available in the §7 setting ("covering space X_Δ(Q) → X_0(Q) of manifolds"). Route (a), which makes Lemma 1 unnecessary: Δ acts freely on the Borel–Serre compactification, a compact manifold with boundary. It is Δ-equivariantly homotopy equivalent to a copy of itself inside X_Δ(Q), obtained by removing a collar. Lift a finite triangulation of the quotient. The simplicial chains then form a bounded complex C of finite free R-modules, with a Δ-equivariant quasi-isomorphism C → C(X_Δ(Q)). Route (b): use dim X_0(Q) = d. Then H_i(C(X_Δ(Q)) ⊗_R M) = H_i(X_0(Q), local system M) = 0 for i > d and every R-module M. So the truncation τ_{≤d}C(X_Δ(Q)) is a bounded complex of flat modules with finitely generated homology. Apply Lemma 1 to it. The resulting map P → τ_{≤d}C lifts to P → C(X_Δ(Q)) because P is a bounded complex of projectives. In the next sentence, replace "bounded" by "bounded below (homologically)". Mumford's Lemma 2 still holds for such complexes by its mapping-cone proof: an exact complex of flat modules that is bounded above cohomologically has flat cycle modules. The finite generation of H_*(X_Δ(Q), O) is also needed and is not stated; it is standard via Borel–Serre. The "since R is local" remark needs no change. The §7 introduction (p. 391) fixes Δ = (Z/p^N Z)^q, and in any case a finitely generated flat R-module is projective. That is perfect in the sense of the Notation on p. 306.`. I rendered PDF pages 95–96 and read them; the quoted sentence is exactly as printed, and v2 has the same wording. In the same paragraph the paper uses "bounded" in the two-sided sense: "a perfect complex ... we mean a bounded complex of finite free R-modules". It also defines C(Y) as the complex of O-valued singular chains, which is non-zero in every degree ≥ 0 whenever Y is non-empty. So the statement that C(X_Δ(Q)) is bounded is false under the paper's own definitions. This is not one of the 47 known bracket errors (R = O[Δ] is a genuine finite group ring). The flatness claim is fine: the covering group acts freely, so C_i(X_Δ(Q)) is R-free. I re-derived the key step: a quasi-isomorphism between complexes of flat modules that are bounded below homologically stays a quasi-isomorphism after any base change (mapping cone plus flat cycle modules). So the displayed isomorphism, and both isomorphisms in Lemma 7.1, hold. The proposed correction is right in substance. I could not check the exact wording of Mumford's hypotheses (no copy was available). I am fairly, not fully, sure Lemma 2 there is stated with only K^p = K'^p = 0 for p > n; either way the argument works. I classify this as a minor error, not a misprint, and set "affects" to "the proof" rather than "nothing". The reason is that the same false boundedness is what the proof silently relies on when it cites Mumford Lemma 1 to get a bounded (perfect) C. For an unbounded complex, perfectness does not follow from a lemma about complexes alone; it needs the geometric finite-dimensionality argument described in the correction. The statement of Lemma 7.1 is true. Everything later (Lemma 7.2, the rest of §7.1, the patching in §9) uses only that statement, so no stated result is affected. I rendered PDF pp. 95–98 and read them; the text is exactly as quoted. The paper's own conventions rule out a charitable reading. "Bounded" is two-sided: the Notation on p. 306 defines a perfect complex as a "bounded complex of finitely generated projective R-modules", and the definition just before Lemma 7.1 uses "bounded" the same way. C(Y) is explicitly singular chains, which has a non-zero term in every degree ≥ 0. So the claim that C(X_Δ(Q)) is bounded is false.

Mumford's Lemma 1 requires K^p ≠ 0 only for 0 ≤ p ≤ n. I checked the statement and proof as reproduced in Schnell's lecture notes (Stony Brook MAT615, Lecture 9, Lemma 9.5, credited to Mumford's book). The construction is a descending induction, and the flat "final term" K^0 is a fibre product that uses the fact that nothing lies below degree 0. On a complex that is unbounded in that direction, the induction never ends.

The step is not merely missing a routine citation. As written, it uses only that the map is a covering with group Δ and that the homology is finitely generated. Those two facts would equally "prove" the claim for EZ/p → BZ/p, with Δ = Z/p and R = O[Z/p] local. There C(EZ/p) is a free R-complex with homology O in degree 0. It is not quasi-isomorphic to any perfect complex: otherwise Ext^i_R(O, k) = H^i(Z/p, k) would vanish for large i, but it is k for every i. So the missing ingredient is the finite-dimensional manifold structure of X_0(Q). The §7 setting assumes it, but the proof never uses it.

The rest of the passage is fine. The second sentence (Lemma 2) is correct once "bounded" is read as bounded below homologically. The objection in X-K7-13 that "since R is local" is unjustified does not hold: the §7 introduction on p. 391 says Δ has the form (Z/p^N Z)^q. The explicit "We now assume that Δ is of p-power order. Thus R = O[Δ] is local" on p. 394 only repeats this after the "somewhat general situation".

Consequences: the statement of Lemma 7.1 is true in the paper's setting, by either route in the correction. Everything later uses only that statement: Lemma 7.2 (lifting T_γ through the quasi-isomorphism C → C(X_K) because C is perfect), Lemmas 7.3 and 7.4, the complex D on p. 395, and §9 on p. 425 ("By Conjecture B and the results of Sect. 7.1, there exists a perfect complex D_N ..."). So only the proof of Lemma 7.1 is affected; no stated result is. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, because R = O[Δ] is a genuine finite group ring. - **Error** at §7.1, proof of Lemma 7.2, last sentences, published p. 393 (PDF p. 97). arXiv v2 has the same wording ("Since C is perfect, the morphism T̃_γ can be lifted to a morphism T_γ : C → C making the diagram commute. (See [Sta14, Tag 08FQ] for example.)"). arXiv v1 has no Lemma 7.2 in this form. The '§7.2, p. 400' part of the candidate is not a mistake. On p. 400 (PDF p. 104) the diagram is explicitly in D^b(R), and the text only says Tag 08FQ lifts T̃_γ "to a morphism of complexes T_γ : C_n^∨ → C_n^∨ that induces the operator T_γ on cohomology". That is correct.. The source says `of complexes of R-modules with the vertical morphism being a quasi-isomorphism. Since C is perfect, the morphism T̃_γ can be lifted to a morphism T_γ : C → C making the diagram commute. (See [70, Tag 08FQ] for example).`; it should be `'... can be lifted to a morphism T_γ : C → C making the diagram commute up to homotopy (equivalently, in the homotopy category K(R))'. This is minimal and suffices for everything later. Because C is a bounded complex of finite free modules, Hom_{K(R)}(C, C) → Hom_{K(R)}(C, C(X_K)) is bijective. So a lift exists that is unique up to homotopy, and it induces q_*^{-1} ∘ T_γ ∘ q_* on H_*(C ⊗ A) for every A = O/ϖ^N, since a homotopy survives tensoring.`. Rendered p. 393 and transcribed the passage above. The diagram is the triangle C --T̃_γ--> C(X_K) <--s-- C, described as a diagram "of complexes of R-modules", so "commute" literally means s∘T_γ = T̃_γ on the nose.
(1) The cited reference only gives homotopy. Stacks Tag 08FQ (Lemma 21.44.7, strictly perfect complexes) ends with "a dotted arrow ... making the diagram commute up to homotopy". Perfectness of C makes Hom^•(C,C) → Hom^•(C,C(X_K)) a quasi-isomorphism, which lifts cycles only up to boundaries (homotopy). It does not lift them strictly.
(2) The strict claim is false in general. Over any ring R, take P = R in degree 0 and M with M_1 = R, M_0 = R², d(a) = (a,0). Let s(1) = (0,1), which is a quasi-isomorphism since the cokernel is contractible. Let f(1) = (1,0), which is a chain map. Then s∘g = (0,g(1)) ≠ (1,0) for every g : P → P, so no strict lift exists, although f = d∘h ≃ 0 = s∘0. A strict lift would need, e.g., a surjective quasi-isomorphism, and s cannot be surjective: C is finite free while C(X_K) is free on uncountably many simplices.
(3) The strict claim also fails for some C that is "as in Lemma 7.1". Given any valid (C,s), add the contractible summand R --id--> R in degrees 1,0. Send its generators to a path σ from x to y and to y − x, extended R-linearly. The result is still a perfect complex with a quasi-isomorphism. For generic points x, y, the degree-0 chain T̃_γ(y − x) is supported on Hecke translates of x and y that lie outside the finite support of s(C_0) + R(y−x). So T̃_γ∘s does not factor through s.
Classification: the lemma's statement (the action on homology lifts to a chain map C → C) is true. The homotopy-commutative lift proves it, and later uses (polynomials in the T_γ, Lemma 7.3) need only an endomorphism of C inducing T_γ on homology. The missing "up to homotopy" is a slip whose intended meaning is clear from the cited Tag 08FQ, which states it. I therefore class it as a misprint (wording slip) with affects = nothing, rather than a substantive error. 1) The cited source gives only the weaker statement. Stacks Tag 08FQ is Lemma 21.44.7 (Cohomology on Sites, 'Strictly perfect complexes'). Its conclusion is a dotted arrow 'making the diagram commute up to homotopy', and the proof works in the homotopy category. So the paper's own citation supports only commutativity up to homotopy.

2) Strict commutativity is false in general. Toy example: C = R in degree 0; D_1 = R, D_0 = R⊕R with d(x) = (0,x); q(r) = (r,0), which is a quasi-isomorphism; f(r) = (0,r), which is a chain map. No g : C → C has q∘g = f, since f(C) is not contained in q(C). A strict lift needs something like a surjective quasi-isomorphism. Here q : C → C(X_K) goes from a finitely generated complex into singular chains, which are free of huge rank, so it is never surjective.

3) Strictness also fails for some C that Lemma 7.1 allows, and Lemma 7.2 is stated for any such C. Take any (C, q). Add the contractible summand R e_1 → R e_0 (d e_1 = e_0), sending e_1 to a singular 1-simplex σ and e_0 to ∂σ. This is still perfect with a quasi-isomorphism to C(X_K). Choose σ generic, away from the finite support of q(C_1), its Δ-translates, and the points fixed by the correspondence. Then T̃_γ(σ) is a nonzero positive combination of simplices, none of them in q(C_1) + Rσ, so no strict lift exists (for T_γ not the trivial correspondence).

Defence considered. The paper has no convention that diagrams of complexes commute up to homotopy. The diagram is explicitly one 'of complexes of R-modules', while §7.2 is careful to say 'in D^b(R)'. So as printed the sentence overstates, though the intent (up to homotopy) is clear from the citation. This could also be classed as a misprint.

Consequences. Lemma 7.2 itself only asks for a chain map lifting the action on homology, and the homotopy version gives exactly that. What uses the lift: expressing T ∈ T as a (not necessarily commutative) polynomial in the lifted T_γ; Lemma 7.3 (H_*(lim T^n C) = lim T^n H_*(C) by exactness); Lemma 7.4; the D at the end of §7.1 (H_n(D ⊗ O/ϖ^N) ≅ H_n(X_Δ(Q), O/ϖ^N)_m and so on); and §9's use of 'Sect. 7.1' (p. 431). All of these only need the induced maps on homology of C ⊗ A, and those are the same for homotopic maps. Nothing needs q∘T_γ = T̃_γ∘q on the nose, or the lifts to commute with one another.
