- **Error** at §7.1, Lemma 7.4, second sentence, p. 394 (published version) (it affects a stated result). The source says `p. 394 (PDF p. 98), Lemma 7.4, end of statement: "for all n. Moreover, the length of D is at most l_0, where l_0 is the range of cohomology groups such that lim_→ T^n H^*(C) is non-zero." Proof: "By Lemma 1 of Mumford ([43], Chap. II.5) again, one may find a perfect complex K quasi-isomorphic to C_T and such that K is bounded of length l_0. Assume that the differential d on D is non-zero modulo 𝔪_R from degree n + 1 to n. Then by Nakayama's Lemma, there exists a direct sum decomposition of perfect complexes of R-modules K ≃ L ⊕ J, ..." The arXiv v2 text is the same (Lemma 7.4, p. 72).`; it should be `Replace the "Moreover" sentence with: "Moreover, if H_n(C_T ⊗_R R/𝔪_R) = lim_→ T^m H_n(X_0(Q), k) vanishes for n outside an interval of length l_0, then D is concentrated in that interval, so its length is at most l_0." This is the X-K7-18 wording, and it follows at once from the first part of the lemma. It is also enough for the mod-ϖ homology of X_Δ(Q) to vanish outside that interval, because a minimal complex over the Artinian ring k[Δ] has non-zero homology in its top and bottom degrees. Integral vanishing alone only gives length(D) ≤ l_0 + 1. In the proof, the Mumford sentence should not claim length l_0: the bound comes out of the Nakayama reduction under the mod-𝔪 hypothesis. Also, "the differential d on D" should read "the differential d on K", because D is only produced at the end of the induction. The H-part2-9 correction says the same thing.`. I checked the page image and the v2 text. As printed, the lemma defines l_0 through the integral groups lim_→ T^n H^*(C), where C is the integral chain complex from Lemma 7.1. The paper uses "range/length l_0" to mean degrees q_0..q_0+l_0, so length means max − min.

The first part of the lemma, which is correct (the minimal-complex / Nakayama argument), forces dim D_n/𝔪_R = dim H_n(C_T ⊗ k). So D_n ≠ 0 whenever the mod-𝔪 homology is non-zero in degree n. Universal coefficients give 0 → H_n(C)⊗k → H_n(C⊗k) → Tor_1(H_{n-1}(C),k) → 0, so torsion in the top integral degree produces mod-ϖ homology one degree higher.

Counterexample (redone): take R = O (Δ trivial, which is of p-power order), T = 1, and C = [O --ϖ--> O] in degrees 1, 0. Then H_1(C) = 0 and H_0(C) = O/ϖ, so the integral range is 0. But C⊗k = [k --0--> k] has H_1 = H_0 = k. Any D as in the lemma must have rank 1 in degrees 1 and 0, so its length is 1 > 0.

A geometric instance: a Bianchi manifold with a non-Eisenstein 𝔪 such that H_1(X,O)_𝔪 is non-zero torsion. Then H_2(X,O)_𝔪 = 0, by Poincaré duality, vanishing boundary cohomology at 𝔪, and torsion-freeness of H^1. But H_2(X,k)_𝔪 ⊇ Tor(H_1,k) ≠ 0. The proof's claim that Mumford gives K "bounded of length l_0" fails for the same reason: any perfect complex quasi-isomorphic to C_T contains the minimal one as a summand.

"d on D" is a slip for "d on K", since D is only produced at the end of the induction.

Downstream: the bullets after the lemma on p. 395 use only the first part ("D_n ≠ 0 iff H_n(X_0(Q),k)_𝔪 ≠ 0"). §9.5 (p. 425) gets "D_N concentrated in degrees q_0,…,q_0+l_0" from Conjecture B(4)(a), which is stated with O/ϖ^m coefficients (reducible to k by dévissage, p. 413). So the main theorems are unaffected. Only the "Moreover" clause of Lemma 7.4 and its proof are wrong. The Correction (Invent. Math. 227) fixes brackets only, so this is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS
(1) The paper's convention, from the intro ("concentrated in l_0+1 consecutive degrees", "range of length l_0") and §9.5 ("q_0,...,q_0+l_0"), is that length = max − min. Counting terms instead makes no difference: the counterexample below fails under both conventions. It survives only if l_0 counts degrees while length(D) is max − min, and nothing in the paper supports mixing them like that.
(2) Standing hypothesis. §7 opens by saying that the cohomology localised at 𝔪 "is assumed to vanish outside a range of length l_0". Conjecture B(4)(a) is stated with O/ϖ^m coefficients, reducing to k by dévissage (p. 413). If that were the hypothesis, the lemma would be true. But the lemma defines l_0 itself, through the integral groups lim_→ T^n H^*(C). Here C is the O[Δ]-perfect complex of Lemma 7.1, quasi-isomorphic to C(X_Δ(Q)), so these are integral groups. They do not control the mod-𝔪 range.
(3) Reading H^* as cohomology of the dual complex does not help either (see below).

WHY THE PRINTED STATEMENT IS FALSE
The first part of the lemma is correct (minimal complex plus Nakayama). It gives D_n ≠ 0 exactly when H_n(C_T ⊗ k) ≠ 0. Universal coefficients give 0 → H_n(C_T)⊗k → H_n(C_T⊗k) → Tor_1(H_{n-1}(C_T),k) → 0, so torsion in the top integral degree creates mod-ϖ homology one degree higher.
- Abstract example: R = O (Δ trivial), T = 1, C = [O --ϖ--> O] in degrees 1, 0. The integral homology is O/ϖ in degree 0 only (range 0). But C⊗k has k in degrees 1 and 0, so every D satisfying the first part has length 1.
- Geometric example (Bianchi): Q empty, 𝔪 non-Eisenstein, H_1(X,O)_𝔪 non-zero torsion with no characteristic-zero classes at 𝔪 (the torsion phenomenon the paper is built around). Then H_0(X,O)_𝔪 = 0. Also H_2(X,O)_𝔪 = 0: it is torsion-free because X is homotopy equivalent to a 2-complex, and rationally it is H^1_c = H^1 at 𝔪, which is 0. So the integral homology sits in degree 1 only (range 0). But H_2(X,k)_𝔪 ⊇ Tor(H_1,k) ≠ 0, so length(D) = 1.
- Cohomology reading: with cohomology (or the dual complex), the torsion moves to degree 2 alone, so the range is again 0.
- General bound: over the depth-1 ring O[Δ], the bottom degree of D equals the bottom degree of H(C_T). Above the top homology degree, the complex is a finite free resolution of a submodule of a free module, which is free by Auslander–Buchsbaum. So length(D) ≤ l_0 + 1, and this is sharp.
- The proof's first sentence fails too: Mumford's Lemma 1 bounds K by the degree range of the complex it starts from, not by its homology. Any perfect complex quasi-isomorphic to C_T contains the minimal D as a direct summand, so no such K of length l_0 exists in the examples above.

CONSEQUENCES
- The bullets right after the lemma (p. 395) use only the first part ("D_n ≠ 0 iff H_n(X_0(Q),k)_𝔪 ≠ 0").
- §7.2 (the coherent case) does not use the "Moreover" clause.
- The only later use is §9.5 (p. 425): "By Conjecture B and the results of Sect. 7.1, there exists a perfect complex D̃_N ... concentrated in degrees q_0,...,q_0+l_0". That conclusion is true, because Conjecture B(4)(a) gives mod-ϖ vanishing, and together with the first part of Lemma 7.4 this yields the corrected clause. The main theorems are therefore unaffected. Only the "Moreover" clause of Lemma 7.4 and the corresponding proof step are wrong.

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors: the Correction (Invent. Math. 227) fixes brackets only.

VERDICT ON THE PROPOSED CORRECTIONS
Both are right and minimal. The X-K7-18 wording is good. H-part2-9 adds the correct "d on D → d on K" fix. I classify this as an error rather than a misprint because both the printed statement and a proof step fail. I redid the computation. Since f is étale, f^*Ω^1_X ≅ Ω^1_Y, so f^*ω_X ≅ ω_Y. Hence f^*ℱ ≅ (f^*ℰ)^* ⊗ ω_Y, and because f^*ℰ is locally free, Hom(f^*ℱ, ω_Y) ≅ f^*ℰ. Both the corrected sentence and the identification f^*ℱ = ℰ^*⊗ω_Y on Y are consistent. The slip is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. The same text appears in arXiv v2, so it is an authors' slip, not a typesetting defect. The source says `In Betti cohomology, the groups H^{q_0}(X, 𝓔/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 may be identified with the non-zero homology group of highest degree with coefficients in 𝒪, namely H_{q_0+l_0}(X, 𝒪)_𝔪. This means changing "homology" to "cohomology" and the subscript to a superscript. It keeps the justification "consequence of Poincaré duality, with the boundary killed by localization", because H^{q_0}(X,E/𝒪)^∨ ≅ H_c^{d−q_0}(X,𝒪) = H_c^{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪) and H_c ≅ H after localization at 𝔪 (with d = 2q_0+l_0). An equivalent fix is "the homology group of lowest degree, H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)", which follows from universal coefficients alone, up to the paper's usual loose 𝔪/𝔪* bookkeeping. The unrelated E/𝓔 font slip in the same sentence is a separate issue.`. Setting (§8/§9): dim_R X = 2q_0 + l_0. After localising at 𝔪, the cohomology is concentrated in [q_0, q_0+l_0] (assumption (4)(a) of §9), and boundary cohomology dies, so H^*_c(X)_𝔪 = H^*(X)_𝔪.
(i) K/𝒪 is divisible, hence injective over 𝒪, so universal coefficients give H^{q_0}(X, K/𝒪) = Hom(H_{q_0}(X,𝒪), K/𝒪). Therefore H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪. The paper says the same on p. 376 (proof of Lemma 5.8): "H^1(Y, K/𝒪) = H_1(Y,𝒪)^∨". Poincaré–Lefschetz duality then identifies H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 with H^{2q_0+l_0-q_0}_c(X,𝒪)_𝔪 = H^{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪. (ii) The printed group is torsion-free. By Poincaré–Lefschetz duality, H_{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 ≅ H^{q_0}_c(X,𝒪)_𝔪 = H^{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪. Its ϖ-torsion is the image of H^{q_0-1}(X,k)_𝔪 = 0, so it is torsion-free. It is the 𝒪-dual of H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪, not that module itself.
(iii) The paper's own Part 1 contradicts the printed identification. Take the Bianchi case q_0 = l_0 = 1, d = 3. Lemma 5.9(2) (p. 376, checked on the rendered page) says "If μ is p-torsion free, then H_2(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪 is p-torsion free." But the module that patches there is H^1(K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 = H_1(Y_Δ(Q),𝒪)_𝔪, which can have torsion; torsion classes are the point of the paper. Suppose H_1(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 is finite and non-zero. Then H_2(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 ≅ Hom(H_1(Y,𝒪)_𝔪, 𝒪) = 0, while H^1(Y,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 = H_1(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 ≠ 0. So the printed group is zero, and even the words "non-zero" fail.

No reading rescues the printed text. Borel–Moore H_{q_0+l_0} ≅ H^{q_0} is also torsion-free, and reading H_i as H^i(K/𝒪)^∨ would make the identification tautological and of degree q_0, not "a consequence of Poincaré duality".
The statement is false as printed. It sits in a motivational remark, though. Nothing later uses it: §9 works directly with H^{q_0}(Y,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 (e.g. Thm 9.19). So no proof or result is affected. Defence attempted and failed. (1) Universal coefficients: since K/𝒪 is injective, H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪) = Hom(H_{q_0}(X,𝒪), K/𝒪), so H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 (degree q_0, not q_0+l_0). The paper says the same on p. 376 (proof of Lemma 5.8): "H^1(Y,K/𝒪) = H_1(Y,𝒪)^∨". Its own convention in §7.2 also gives degree q_0: it defines homology as H_i := (H^i of the dual with torsion coefficients)^∨, so the dual of lowest-degree cohomology is lowest-degree homology. (2) Poincaré–Pontryagin duality gives H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)^∨ ≅ H_c^{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪) ≅_𝔪 H^{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪, which is cohomology, not homology. The only charitable reading that uses homology of degree q_0+l_0 drops the ∨ and keeps K/𝒪 coefficients: H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)_𝔪 ≅ H_{q_0+l_0}(X,K/𝒪)_𝔪. That is not what is printed. (3) The printed identification is false exactly where it matters. H_{q_0+l_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 is ϖ-torsion free, because its ϖ-torsion is the image of H_{q_0+l_0+1}(X,k)_𝔪 = 0. The paper proves this itself for Bianchi manifolds in Lemma 5.9(2): H_2(Y_0(Q),μ)_𝔪 is p-torsion free, where q_0 = l_0 = 1. By contrast, H^{q_0}(X,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H_{q_0}(X,𝒪)_𝔪 carries the torsion classes the paper is about. Take a Bianchi 𝔪 supported only on torsion. Then H_1(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 is finite and non-zero, while H_2(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 is torsion free of rank dim H_1(Y,K)_𝔪 = 0, so H_2(Y,𝒪)_𝔪 = 0. The printed statement would therefore force the patched module to vanish. The ranks over K do agree (by Poincaré duality and universal coefficients), so the claim fails only on torsion. A toy check without localization: for the lens space L(p,1), H^1(Q_p/Z_p)^∨ ≅ Z/p ≅ H^2(Z_p), but H_2(Z_p) = 0. The statement is correct only when l_0 = 0. It is not a single-character slip: both the words "homology ... of highest degree" and the formula H_{q_0+l_0} say the same wrong thing, so I classify it as an error rather than a misprint. Consequences: the passage is expository. It only motivates the name "coherent homology", and nothing later cites it. Every place the paper actually uses this module agrees with the correction. §5 patches H_1(Y_0(Q),𝒪[Δ])_𝔪 (degree q_0). §9 patches H = H^{q_0}(Y,K/𝒪)^∨_𝔪 (Theorem 9.19 and its proof, pp. 425–427), using complexes D_N whose homology in degrees q_0..q_0+l_0 is the homology of Y. Remark 9.2 refers to the cohomology module H_ψ^{q_0+l_0}(Y_1(Q),𝒪), matching the proposed fix. The 2022 Correction covers only the bracket errors, and this is not one of them. - **Error** at §7.2, pp. 399–400 (published version). The source says `• the duality isomorphism RHom(O_{Y^γ_A}, ω_{Y^γ_A}[d]) --∼--> A[0]. (§7.2 "The Coherent case", p. 400 = PDF p. 104. It is the third bullet in the definition of T̃_γ, after "the pullback under π_1^* ⊗ (φ ∘ π_2^*)" and "the composition morphism". The arrow is printed with a tilde over it. The v2 text, cg-v2.txt line ~4017, is identical.)`; it should be `Minimal fix, p. 400: "the trace (duality) morphism tr : RHom(O_{Y^γ_A}, ω_{Y^γ_A}[d]) = RΓ(Y^γ_A, ω_{Y^γ_A})[d] → A[0]", dropping the ∼ and the word "isomorphism". This is the counit Rπ_*π^!A → A of Grothendieck duality for the smooth proper map Y^γ_A → Spec A of relative dimension d. Equivalently, it is the composite of the canonical map K → H^0(K)[0], for K = RΓ(ω)[d] ∈ D^{[−d,0]}, with the trace H^d(Y^γ_A, ω_A) → A. Minimal fix, p. 399: "tr denotes the trace map H^d(Y^γ, (ω_{Y^γ})_A) → A". That map is an isomorphism only when Y^γ has geometrically connected fibres over O. Only a morphism is used in either place.`. Checked on the rendered page. The paper's own conventions make RHom a complex, not a Hom group. On p. 399, "Rπ_*(G) = RHom(O_{Y_A}, G)" is an object of D^b(R). Verdier duality is stated as an identity of complexes, RHom(RHom(O_{Y_A}, G), A[0]) = RHom(G, ω_{Y_A}[d]). The composition morphism in the preceding bullet uses ⊗^L of such complexes. So RHom(O_{Y^γ_A}, ω_{Y^γ_A}[d]) = RΓ(Y^γ_A, ω_A)[d], and I recomputed its cohomology: H^j of this complex is H^{j+d}(Y^γ_A, ω_A) for −d ≤ j ≤ 0.

Here Y^γ is smooth and proper over O of relative dimension d (p. 398), and ω is the top exterior power of Ω^1. By Serre duality, the map to A[0] can only be a quasi-isomorphism if H^i(Y^γ_A, ω_A) = 0 for all i < d, i.e. H^j(O) = 0 for j ≥ 1. This fails in general. Take the modular-curve instance of the setting, with d = 1 and genus g ≥ 1, which holds at the large levels in use once Taylor–Wiles primes are added. Then H^{-1} = H^0(Y^γ_A, ω_A) ≅ A^g ≠ 0. More generally, H^{-d} = H^0(Y^γ_A, ω_A), and this is typically nonzero for positive-dimensional Shimura varieties. So the ∼ and the word "isomorphism" are wrong; only a morphism exists. The candidate's correction and its degree computation (H^{i−d} = H^i(Y^γ_A, ω) for 0 ≤ i ≤ d) are correct.

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. A side remark, outside this candidate: the "trace isomorphism H^d(Y^γ, (ω)_A) → A" on p. 399 also assumes Y^γ is geometrically connected. I checked this on the rendered pages 399–400. I tried to defend the text, and none of the defences works.

(1) The paper's own conventions make RHom a complex. On p. 399 the paper writes "Rπ_*(G) = RHom(O_{Y_A}, G)" as an object of D^b(R). Verdier duality there is an identity of complexes. The preceding bullet takes ⊗^L of such RHom's. So RHom(O_{Y^γ_A}, ω[d]) = RΓ(Y^γ_A, ω_A)[d], and its cohomology in degree j is H^{j+d}(Y^γ_A, ω_A) for −d ≤ j ≤ 0. For a quasi-isomorphism with A[0], all of H^i(Y^γ_A, ω_A) for i < d would have to vanish. By Serre duality over the Gorenstein Artinian ring A = O/ϖ^n, H^i(ω_A) = Hom_A(H^{d−i}(Y^γ_A, O), A). So we would need H^j(Y^γ_A, O) = 0 for j ≥ 1, and also H^0 = A.

This fails in the paper's own motivating case: Y^γ is a modular curve (d = 1) at Taylor–Wiles level, of genus g ≥ 1. There H^{−1} = H^0(Y^γ_A, Ω^1) ≅ A^g ≠ 0, the weight-2 cusp forms. More generally H^{−d} = H^0(ω_A), and this is nonzero for positive-dimensional Shimura varieties of large level. The statement is also false for d = 0 whenever there is more than one point.

(2) Reading it as H^0 only, i.e. as the isomorphism Ext^d(O, ω) ≅ A, is ruled out. The paper treats RHom as a complex in the same paragraph, and the target is written A[0] with a tilde.

(3) Reading it as the genuine duality isomorphism RHom(O, π^!A) ≅ RHom_A(Rπ_*O, A) does not help. That has a different target. One reaches A[0] only by composing with restriction along the unit A → Rπ_*O, and that composite is not an isomorphism.

(4) The p. 399 claim is conditionally true. H^d(Y^γ_A, ω_A) = Hom_A(H^0(Y^γ_A, O), A), so it equals A exactly when the fibres are geometrically connected. That holds for X_1(N)-type modular curves, where det(L^γ) is surjective. It fails in the stated generality: "Shimura varieties associated to some reductive group G over a number field F", e.g. Hilbert modular varieties with several geometric components. There the trace is the sum map A^c → A.

So the text is genuinely wrong. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not mention it.

Consequences: every place where the paper uses the passage needs only a morphism. T̃_γ is defined as a composite of morphisms landing in Hom(RHom(O,G) ⊗^L RHom(G, ω[d]), A[0]). The claim that "T̃_γ induces the Hecke operator T_γ defined above" needs only that H^0 of the last arrow is the trace H^d(ω_A) → A used on p. 399. That holds for the trace morphism. The lift to C_n^∨ via Tag 08FQ and the localisation lim T^m C_n do not use invertibility. Perfect Serre/Verdier duality is needed only on Y, not on Y^γ, and it holds with the trace map without any connectedness hypothesis. §7.2 is also not used by any later theorem. The introduction (p. 300) says the Coherent case is confined to "constructing suitable complexes (see Sect. 7.2)". The weight-one results of §3 use their own modular-curve arguments, and "Sect. 7" is otherwise cited only through §7.1 (in §9). So the proposed correction is right and minimal. I classify it as an error, not a misprint: it is a false mathematical assertion, stated twice (in words and by the tilde), not a typographical slip. It affects nothing. I rendered pp. 402–404 and cropped them at high resolution; all three printed items match exactly, and arXiv v2 p. 78 is the same. (a) The Greenberg–Wiles formula compares H^1_L(F, M) with H^1_{L^*}(F, M^*). For M = F_p, M^* = μ_p. The sentence just before the display calls the dual Selmer group H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p), and items (1)–(3) and the conclusion dim H^1_L(F, F_p) − dim H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p) = −(r_1 + r_2 − 1) all use μ_p. So the F_p in the denominator is a slip. With μ_p, the arithmetic works out: +1 from the H^0 term (ζ_p ∉ F), −(r_1 + r_2) from the infinite places, and 0 from v|p. (b) F has characteristic 0, so H^1_fppf(F, μ_p) = H^1(G_F, μ_p) = F^×/F^{×p}. That is the whole group, not something that 'sits inside' it, as the next sentence says. The dual Selmer group is the set of classes that are unramified or flat at every place. That is H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p), which sits in the exact sequence 0 → O_F^×/p → H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p) → Cl(F)[p] → 0 given on p. 402. (c) U_Q is a subgroup of the finite ideles, obtained from U by changing O_v^× at v ∈ Q. So the printed Y_Q is not the level-Q analogue of Y = F^×\A_F^×/UK_∞, even though the text says Y = Y_0(Q) and Y_Q = Y_1(Q). The fibres of Y_Q are then described as components of the cokernel of O_F^× → R^{×r_1} × C^{×r_2}/K_∞, which is (S^1)^{r_1+r_2−1} × R, and that description divides by K_∞. I redid the dimension count. Without K_∞, the identity component R_{>0}^{r_1} × (C^×)^{r_2} modulo units and A^0_∞ has dimension r_1 + 2r_2 − 1. With K_∞ it has dimension r_1 + r_2 − 1 = ℓ_0, which is what the text uses. None of these is one of the 47 known bracket errors. None is correct under the paper's own conventions, since the paper itself writes the correct forms nearby. - **Error** at §8.2, p. 402 (last paragraph) (published version). The source says `We can, in fact, deduce this equality directly by computing both terms via class field theory. The first group has dimension dim Cl(F)/p. For the second, recall that for v|p the group L_v^* is one-dimensional and is dual to the unramified classes in H^1(F_v, F_p). This dual consists of classes which are finite flat. So we are interested in H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p), which sits in the exact sequence: 0 → O_F^×/O_F^{×p} → H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p) → Cl(F)[p] → 0`; it should be `Minimal fix: "recall that for v|p the group L_v^* ⊂ H^1(F_v, μ_p) = F_v^×/F_v^{×p} is the annihilator, under local Tate duality, of the one-dimensional space L_v of unramified classes in H^1(F_v, F_p). So L_v^* has codimension one, and the quotient H^1(F_v, μ_p)/L_v^* is dual to L_v. This annihilator is O_v^×/O_v^{×p}, which consists of the finite flat classes." The dimension of L_v^* is [F_v:Q_p] + dim H^0(F_v, μ_p). That equals 1 only when F_v = Q_p (p is odd because ζ_p ∉ F).`. I checked the rendered PDF page 106 (= p. 402, §8.2) at 200 dpi, and the sentence is printed as quoted. The arXiv v2 text (line 4115) is the same. The paper does not define L^* in §8.2. It is the dual Selmer condition in the Greenberg–Wiles formula displayed just above, and §8.3 writes L^⊥ for the same object. So L_v^* is the Tate annihilator of L_v.

I redid the computation. Kummer theory gives H^1(F_v, μ_p) = F_v^×/F_v^{×p}. By the local Euler characteristic formula, with h^2(μ_p) = h^0(F_p) = 1, this has dimension [F_v:Q_p] + 1 + h^0(F_v, μ_p). Here L_v is the unramified line, so dim L_v = 1 = h^0(F_v, F_p), and its annihilator has dimension [F_v:Q_p] + h^0(F_v, μ_p). Concretely, the Tate pairing sends (a, χ) to χ(rec(a)). Unramified characters kill exactly the classes with v(a) ≡ 0 mod p, so L_v^* = O_v^×/O_v^{×p}. Since O_v^× ≅ k_v^× × μ_{p^∞}(F_v) × Z_p^{[F_v:Q_p]}, the dimension agrees.

This is 1 only if F_v = Q_p and ζ_p ∉ Q_p. F is an arbitrary number field of signature (r1, r2), so the claim "L_v^* is one-dimensional" is false in general. For example, take F real quadratic with p inert, so F_v is unramified quadratic over Q_p and dim L_v^* = 2. The assumption ζ_p ∉ F does not force ζ_p ∉ F_v: for p = 3 and F = Q(√6), Q_3(√6) = Q_3(√−3). That is why the H^0(F_v, μ_p) term in the candidate's formula is needed. "Dual to the unramified classes" is also loose, since L_v^* is the annihilator of L_v, not dual to it. The authors probably had F_v = Q_p in mind, or meant the quotient H^1/L_v^*.

The candidate's correction and dimension formula are right. The slip changes nothing. The following sentence ("This dual consists of classes which are finite flat") is true, because H^1_fppf(O_v, μ_p) = O_v^×/O_v^{×p}. The direct computation uses only that identification plus the fppf sequence and Dirichlet's unit theorem, which give dim Cl(F)/p − (r1 + r2 − 1) − dim Cl(F)[p] = −(r1 + r2 − 1). The Greenberg–Wiles computation in item (3) uses dim L_v = 1, not dim L_v^*. §8.2 is an explicitly heuristic illustration ("ultimately somewhat circular"), and no later result uses dim L_v^*.

A separate small typo sits in the Greenberg–Wiles display on the same page: the denominator reads H^1_{L^*}(F, F_p) where the text around it has H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p). It is outside this item. I rendered PDF pp. 105–108 (published pp. 401–404) and confirmed the printed text.

Defence attempts, all failed:
(a) Notation. §8.2 never defines L^*. It is the dual Selmer condition in the Greenberg–Wiles formula displayed just above, and §8.3 writes the same object as L^⊥ (p. 408ff., e.g. Prop. 8.5). So the only faithful reading of L_v^* is the Tate annihilator of L_v. No other convention in the paper makes "one-dimensional" true.
(b) Direct computation. H^1(F_v, μ_p) = F_v^×/F_v^{×p}, which has dimension [F_v:Q_p] + 1 + h^0(F_v, μ_p) by the local Euler characteristic formula. The pairing of a with an unramified χ is χ(Frob)^{v(a)}, so L_v^⊥ = O_v^× F_v^{×p}/F_v^{×p} ≅ O_v^×/O_v^{×p}. Its dimension is [F_v:Q_p] + h^0(F_v, μ_p), since O_v^× ≅ (prime-to-p part) × μ_{p^∞}(F_v) × Z_p^{[F_v:Q_p]}.
(c) Is it one-dimensional anyway? Only when F_v = Q_p. The hypothesis ζ_p ∉ F forces p odd, because −1 ∈ F. Nothing restricts F to have its p-adic completions equal to Q_p: §8.2 takes "an arbitrary number field F". Counterexamples: F = Q(√2), p = 3 (inert, F_v = Q_9, dim L_v^* = 2). F = Q(√6), p = 3 (F_v = Q_3(√−3) contains ζ_3, dim L_v^* = 3).
(d) The phrase "is dual to the unramified classes" is also wrong. L_v^* is orthogonal to L_v, not dual to it. The object that is one-dimensional and dual to L_v is the quotient H^1(F_v, μ_p)/L_v^*. The authors apparently merged "the quotient by L_v^* is dual to the 1-dim L_v" into "L_v^* is 1-dim and dual to L_v", or had F_v = Q_p in mind. The sentence is a false mathematical assertion, not a typographical slip, so I class it as an error. It is harmless.

Consequences: none. The very next sentence, "This dual consists of classes which are finite flat", is correct: L_v^* = O_v^×/O_v^{×p} = H^1_fppf(O_v, μ_p). With the unramified condition at v∤p (and H^1(R, ·) = 0 for p odd), this gives H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p) = H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p). From there the fppf sequence and Dirichlet's unit theorem (ζ_p ∉ F) give dim Cl(F)/p − (r1 + r2 − 1) − dim Cl(F)[p] = −(r1 + r2 − 1). This matches the Greenberg–Wiles count, whose item (3) uses only dim L_v = dim H^0(F_v, F_p) = 1. The later use on p. 404 ("the dual Selmer group, which is H^1_{L^*}(F, μ_p) = H^1_fppf(F, μ_p)", choosing |Q| = dim H^1_{L^*}) needs only this identification, never dim L_v^*. §8.2 is explicitly a heuristic illustration ("ultimately somewhat circular"), and no numbered result depends on it.

Both candidates' corrections (H-part2-13, X-K8-1) are right. X-K8-1's wording ("codimension one; quotient dual to L_v; L_v^* = image of O_v^×/p, dim [F_v:Q_p] + h^0(μ_p)") is the most accurate minimal repair. The earlier verdict on H-part2-13 is consistent with this.

Page 403 (PDF p. 107) was rendered and read, and the text was transcribed above. v2 has the same text. The passage is not one of the 47 bracket errors: the Correction lists none in §8.2, and a group ring of a finite group rightly uses single brackets.

2. The component group, computed directly. U_Q is open, so the image of (F⊗R)^{×,0} is open and connected. Hence π_0(X_Q) = A_F^×/F^× U_Q (F⊗R)^{×,0}. The quotient map U_Q → U induces a surjection π_0(X_Q) → A^×/F^×U(F⊗R)^{×,0} = Cl^+(F). So for every Q, the exponent of π_0(X_Q) is a multiple of the exponent of Cl^+(F). It cannot be a group of exponent p^n (in particular not RCl(Q)/p^n) when Cl(F) has an element whose order does not divide p^n.

3. Explicit counterexample, computed. I wrote a Python composition of binary quadratic forms (…/work/agents/xk84A/cl.py). It gives h(−199) = 9 with exponent 9, so Cl(Q(√−199)) ≅ Z/9. Take F = Q(√−199), p = 3, n = 1; ζ_3 ∉ F, and l_0 = 0. For Q = ∅, X = F^×\A^×/U C^× is the 9-point space Cl(F) ≅ Z/9. Then H^0(X, Z_3)_m = Z_3[Z/9]. The paper's formula instead gives Z_3[Cl/3] = Z_3[Z/3]. The rank over Z_3 is 9, not 3. For nonempty Q the group still surjects onto Z/9, so the claim fails for every Q. Prime-to-p examples also break the unlocalised statement: for Q(√−23) with p = 5, the component group has order 3, while its maximal exponent-5 quotient is trivial.

4. The paper contradicts itself. At the end of §8.2 it concludes R^unr ≃ Z_p[Cl(O_F) ⊗ Z_p]. That is the full p-part of the class group, not Cl/p^n, and it is what the correct π_0(X) gives at Q = ∅. At Q = ∅ the printed formula would even depend on n, which is absurd.

5. Charitable reading. "And exponent p^n" might be meant to describe the local ramification at Q, cut to exponent p^n. Under that reading the group is right. But the notation RCl(Q)/p^n literally means RCl(Q) modulo p^n-th powers, and "maximal quotient ... of exponent p^n" naturally means the same thing. As printed, the statement is false.

6. Impact. §8.2 is a heuristic sketch. The later steps do not use the exponent claim: Hecke operators act through [π_v], R_Q → T_{Q,m} is a surjection, and the final isomorphism uses the correct group. So nothing downstream is affected. 1. What the definitions give. Since A_∞^0K_∞ is connected, π_0(X_Q) = A_F^×/F^×U_Q(F⊗R)^{×,0}. Here U_{Q,v} = (O_v^×)^{p^n} has index p^n, and the quotient is taken only at the places v ∈ Q. So π_0 = RCl^+(Q)/⟨image of ∏(k_v^×)^{p^n}⟩, which sits in 0 → Δ_Q/(image of units) → π_0 → Cl^+(F) → 0. The printed text says instead that π_0 is the maximal exponent-p^n quotient, and writes H^0 = Z_p[RCl(Q)/p^n].

2. Defences I tried.
(a) Reading "exponent p^n" as "inertia of exponent p^n". This would make the words true, but the grammar does not support it: "maximal quotient of G" needs a qualifier, and the displayed "RCl(Q)/p^n" can only mean G/p^nG.
(b) Localising at m. This removes the prime-to-p part, so it answers the candidate's example with h=3, p=5 only up to localisation.
(c) Taking n large. This answers the objection "Cl_p has exponent > p^n".
Neither (b) nor (c) saves the statement. The Taylor–Wiles condition in §8.2 itself forces RCl_p(Q) → Cl_p to be non-split, and then the p-parts differ as well.

Explicit example, with every hypothesis of §8.2 satisfied:
- F = Q(√−23), h = 3, p = 3, n = 1. ζ_3 ∉ F and ℓ_0 = 0.
- The dual Selmer group is H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_3) ≅ Cl[3], spanned by α = (3+√−23)/2, where 𝔭_2^3 = (α) (norm 8).
- Take Q = {v}, v | 13. Then N(v) = 13 ≡ 1 mod 3, and α ≡ 10 mod v is not a cube (computed: 10^4 ≢ 1 mod 13). So v is exactly the kind of Taylor–Wiles prime §8.2 asks for.
- The sequence ±1 → k_v^× → RCl(v) → Cl → 0 gives |RCl(v)| = 12·3/2 = 18.
- The cube of a lift of [𝔭_2] is the image of α, which generates (k_v^×/±1)_3. So RCl(v)_3 ≅ Z/9.
- U_Q contains (k_v^×)^3, which has order 4 and trivial 3-part, and its image in k_v^×/±1 has order 2. So π_0(X_Q) ≅ Z/9: X_Q has 9 components.
- Therefore H^0(X_Q, Z_3) = H^0_m = Z_3[Z/9]. The printed formula gives Z_3[RCl(v)/3] = Z_3[Z/3].
- On the Galois side, R_Q = Z_3[Z/9], which matches the correct answer, not the printed one.
The same failure occurs for every n: with Cl_p = Z/p and a Taylor–Wiles prime, π_0⊗Z_p = Z/p^{n+1} while RCl(Q)/p^n = Z/p^n. With Q = ∅ the printed formula does not even make sense, since n plays no role there. Note also that Remark 5.11 (p. 381) says this non-splitting happens.

3. Consequences. §8.2 is an explicitly heuristic, "somewhat circular" illustration. Remark 5.12 cites it only as "some indication". No lemma, theorem or proof uses RCl(Q)/p^n: the only other occurrence is [π_v] ∈ RCl(Q) on the next line. The section's final conclusion, R^unr ≃ Z_p[Cl(O_F)⊗Z_p], is stated correctly and agrees with the correct π_0 (for Q = ∅, π_0 = Cl^+ and p is odd), not with the printed formula. So the mistake affects nothing.

4. Classification. This is a false mathematical claim rather than a typographic slip, so it is an error; calling it a misprint would be a borderline reading. The candidate's own counterexamples are valid as unlocalised statements. The example above shows the statement fails even after localisation and even for large n. I rendered PDF p. 110 and transcribed the text as above. Setup: c_v^2 = 1 and char ≠ 2, so c_v is diagonalisable with eigenspace dimensions a, b (a + b = n). Its centraliser in ad has dimension a^2 + b^2 and contains elements of trace 1. Hence dim H^0(F_v, ad^0 V) = a^2 + b^2 − 1 = (n^2 + d^2)/2 − 1, where d = a − b. The printed formula is the case |d| ≤ 1. In characteristic ℓ, however, Trace(c_v) = d mod ℓ.

Counterexample (within the printed hypotheses): F = Q, n = 2, coefficient field F_3, V with c acting trivially. Then Trace(c) = 2 = −1 in F_3, so V counts as "odd". But dim H^0(R, ad^0 V) = dim ad^0 = 3, while the display gives r_1(n^2/2 − 1) = 1. Also l_0 = r_1(n−2)/2 = 0, so the right side of (1) is 1·1 + 0 = 1 ≠ 3.

A Python sweep over n ≤ 14 and primes ℓ < 40 confirms that the trace criterion fails exactly when ℓ ≤ n + 1 (n even) or ℓ ≤ n (n odd). With p > n, the failures are (n, p) = (2,3), (4,5), (6,7), (10,11), (12,13), … The case matters for the paper: §8.5 imposes "r̄|_{G_v} is odd" on r̄ : G_F → GL_n(k) with p > n. For example, n = 4, p = 5, r̄(c_v) = ±I has trace ±4 ≡ ∓1 mod 5. It is also compatible with the determinant, since ε^{6}(c_v) = 1. So r̄ meets the printed hypothesis, but (1) fails for it (15 versus 7 per real place).

How far it reaches: Theorem 5.16(5) defines oddness for O-valued (characteristic-0) representations, where the trace criterion is correct. Its residual r̄ then has the same eigenspace dimensions, so the main theorems are unaffected. The proof of Prop. 8.5(4) invokes (1), but it only needs Σ h^0 ≥ [F:Q]n(n−1)/2 + l_0. That inequality holds for every involution, since (n^2 + d^2)/2 − 1 is smallest at |d| ≤ 1. A larger h^0 only lowers the variable count, and a quotient of a power series ring in fewer variables is a quotient of one in more. So Prop. 8.5(4) remains true. The false statement is confined to the displayed formula and equation (1) (and the "Explicitly…" gloss) in small characteristic. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Suppose c_v has ±1-eigenspaces of dimensions a and b, with a + b = n. Then dim H^0(F_v, ad^0 V) = a² + b² − 1 in any characteristic other than 2, and Trace(c_v) = a − b computed in the field. In characteristic ℓ the trace condition only forces a − b ≡ −1, 0, 1 (mod ℓ).

Counterexample: take F = Q, n = 2, ℓ = 3 and V trivial, so c = I. Then Trace = 2 = −1 in F_3, so V is "odd" as printed. But Σ dim H^0 = 3, while the display gives r_1(n²/2 − 1) = 1, and (1) gives [F:Q]·1 + l_0 = 1 + 0 = 1.

This also happens inside §8.5's setting: n = 4, p = 5, F = Q, r̄(c) = ±I. The trace is ±4 = ∓1 in F_5, and det = 1 = ε(c)^6 matches ξ = ε^6. Here Σ h^0 = 15, but (1) gives 7.

A brute-force check over n ≤ 12 and primes ℓ < 40 shows the trace criterion fails exactly when ℓ ≤ n+1 (n even) or ℓ ≤ n (n odd). So the candidate's description is right.

- The only earlier definition of "odd" (p. 383) is for O-valued representations. There the trace is the integer a − b, and the criterion is correct.
- For a field of characteristic ℓ, the "Explicitly…" sentence is the only definition given. The text explicitly allows any characteristic other than 2, so the literal claim is false. Reading "Trace" as the integer a − b is not supported by the text.

Printed text confirmed from the page images. The cited sources do not give flatness. [11] is Taylor, IHES 108. I checked Prop. 3.1 in the author copy (…/agents/k8check/twugkfin.txt). It says only: Spec R^loc/I^χ is irreducible, its generic point has characteristic 0, and it has dimension n^2+1; for R^loc/I^{(1,…,1)}, all components have dimension n^2+1 and characteristic-0 generic points. Its proof shows only (R^loc/I^χ)_red is O-flat. Only the separate Steinberg quotient is "by definition flat over O". [76, Lemma 3.3] is BLGHT, CY II (…/k8check/cy2fin.txt). Its part 3 assumes O-flat inputs, and parts 5 and 7 are about minimal primes.

The statement is also false. Take n ≥ 2, p > n, v ∈ R with r̄|G_v trivial and q = N(v) ≡ 1 mod p; this is the intended Ihara-avoidance setting. Let Φ = ρ(φ_v) and Σ = ρ(σ_v) be the universal matrices over R^1_v, with φσφ^{-1} = σ^q in the tame quotient. Put N = log Σ; this is fine since (Σ−1)^n = 0 by Cayley–Hamilton and n < p. Then ΦNΦ^{-1} = qN. Taking traces, tr(ΦN) = q·tr(ΦN), so (q−1)·tr(ΦN) = 0. For n = 2 simply N = Σ−1, S² = 0 and Σ^q = 1+qS.

Now tr(ΦN) ≠ 0. Take B = O⟦u⟧[Y]/(Y², (q−1)Y) with c = ξ(φ_v) ≡ 1. Set Φ = diag(1+u, c/(1+u), 1, …) and Σ = diag(1+Y, 1−Y, 1, …), with σ_v^a ↦ diag(1+aY, 1−aY, …). This is a valid framed lift of determinant ξ. It reduces to 1, commutes, and Σ^q = Σ because (q−1)Y = 0. Every inertia element has characteristic polynomial (X−1)^2 − a²Y² = (X−1)^2 (times (X−1)^{n−2}). So there is a map R^1_v → B, and tr(ΦN) maps to ((1+u) − c/(1+u))·Y ≠ 0. This is because B ⊃ (O/(q−1))⟦u⟧·Y and the u-coefficient 1+c ≡ 2 is a unit.

So R^1_v has non-zero p-power torsion. The same holds for R^1_loc, via R^1_v → R^1_loc → B ⊗_O O' using O'-points of the other factors. Hence Lemma 8.2(1) fails for R^1_loc. For comparison, at points where Φ is regular semisimple the local ring is smooth ⊗ O[Y]/(Y², (q−1)Y), the same phenomenon.

The candidate is therefore genuine, and stronger than a gap: the claim is false. Downstream, only characteristic-0 minimal primes are used, so Theorem 9.19 stands after the repair. The cited sources give only characteristic-0 generic points, never p-torsion-freeness. I checked this in the texts. Taylor [11, Prop. 3.1] states: for distinct χ, Spec R^loc_v/I^χ is irreducible with generic point of characteristic zero; for (1,…,1), all components have dimension n^2+1 with characteristic-zero generic points. Its proof shows only that "(R^loc_v/I^χ)_red is flat over O". The only ring that is O-flat "by definition" is the separately saturated Steinberg quotient. BLGHT [76, Lemma 3.3](3) proves A⊗̂B is O-flat only for O-flat inputs. BLGHT's own use of the lemma for Taylor's ring R^{2T}_{χ,∞} derives irreducibility, dimensions and characteristic-0 generic points, never flatness. Taylor's main argument (p. 36) also asserts only these.

The claim is in fact false for R^1_loc. Take r̄|G_v trivial and q = N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. This is exactly the setting of [11, §3], so the citation applies, and N(v) ≡ 1 mod p is already required for v ∈ R. Take n = 2 and write Φ = ρ(φ_v), Σ = 1 + S = ρ(σ_v). The condition char Σ = (X−1)^2 gives tr S = det S = 0, so S^2 = 0 by Cayley–Hamilton and Σ^q = 1 + qS. The tame relation ΦΣΦ^{-1} = Σ^q then gives ΦS = qSΦ. Taking traces, (1−q)·tr(ΦS) = 0 in R_v^1, where 1−q = p^s·unit with s ≥ 1.

Now tr(ΦS) ≠ 0 in R_v^1. The lift Φ = diag(1+X, δ/(1+X)) (δ = ξ(φ_v)) and Σ = diag(1+α, 1−α), valued in A = O⟦X⟧[α]/(α^2, (q−1)α), is a valid point of R_v^1:
- Σ^q = Σ, since (q−1)α = 0;
- every inertia element acts by diag(1+mα, 1−mα), which has characteristic polynomial (X−1)^2 and determinant 1;
- det Φ = δ.
Under this point, tr(ΦS) maps to α((1+X) − δ/(1+X)). That is non-zero in (O/(q−1))⟦X⟧·α, and even modulo ϖ.

For general n with p > n, the same argument works with N = log Σ (so ΦN = qNΦ) and Σ = diag(1+α, 1−α, 1, …, 1). Since the other factors have O'-points, the p-torsion survives in R^1_loc = (⊗̂R_w)⊗̂(⊗̂R_v^1) and in R^1_∞. So (1) fails for R^1_loc whenever R ≠ ∅ in the cited setting, and even more so in the non-trivial cases raised in X-K8-12.

Defence attempt: read R_v^1 as the O-flat closure. That fails too. The torsion element is non-zero mod ϖ, so the flat closure's special fibre is a proper quotient of R_v^1/ϖ = R_v^χ/ϖ, and Noetherian rings are Hopfian, so (2) would then fail. §8.5.2 also makes the rings represent CHT-style deformation problems, which is the naive, non-saturated reading. For comparison, for n = 2 and trivial r̄ I checked that R_v^χ is O-flat: it is O⟦α,β,γ,u,y,z⟧ modulo the 2×2 minors and α^2+βγ−e, a hypersurface in an O-flat determinantal CM ring. So the defect is specific to R^1.

Consequences: Prop. 6.6 and Thm 6.3 need only dim R_∞ = 1+q+j−l_0, not torsion-freeness. The R^1 step (p. 428) explicitly uses only "all such primes have characteristic 0" plus [11, Lemma 2.2(2)]. Nothing in the Notation section restricts 'character' to finite order.

Counterexample: take n = 2 and p ≥ 3, and let v ∈ R. R may contain any prime with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, so it can be nonempty. Since v ∤ p, the maximal pro-p quotient of I_v is Z_p(1), and Frobenius acts on it by t ↦ t^{q_v}. Let t be a generator. Define the continuous character χ_1 : I_v → Z_p(1) → 1 + pZ_p by t ↦ 1 + p, and set χ_2 = χ_1^{-1}. These are distinct characters with trivial product, so they are admissible as printed.

Now take a Q̄_p-point ρ of R_v^{χ_v}, choose σ ∈ I_v mapping to t, and let φ be a Frobenius lift. Then φσφ^{-1} ∈ I_v, and ρ(φσφ^{-1}) is conjugate to ρ(σ), so the two have the same characteristic polynomial. The defining condition then forces {x, x^{-1}} = {x^{c}, x^{-c}}, where x = 1 + p and c = q_v^{±1}, depending on which way Frobenius is normalized. But x has infinite order in Z_p^×, so this needs c = ±1, which is impossible because q_v ≥ 2. As a sanity check with p = 3 and q_v = 7: 4^7 = 16384 is neither 4 nor 4^{-1}. So R_v^{χ_v}[1/p] = 0.

On the other hand, R_v^{χ_v} is not zero. Since r̄ is at worst unipotently ramified at v and det r̄ = ξ̄, r̄|_{G_v} is a k-point: its characteristic polynomial (X−1)^2 equals ∏(X − χ̄_i). Hence p^N R_v^{χ_v} = 0 for some N, with R_v^{χ_v} ≠ 0. The completed tensor product R^χ_loc is then killed by p^N and still surjects onto k. So it is nonzero and not p-torsion free, and Lemma 8.2(1) is false for this admissible choice.

The alternative reading, where R_v^{χ_v} is the maximal O-flat quotient, fails too. Then R_v^{χ_v} = 0, so R^χ_loc = 0, which breaks the dimension claim in (1) and also (2), because R^1_loc/ϖ ≠ 0.

Finite order is not enough on its own either. If p^2 ∤ q_v − 1, an order-p^2 character of I_v fails in the same way. The Frobenius-invariance supplied by ψ ∘ Art^{-1} is exactly what is missing.

The proof's citation, [11, Prop. 3.1] (Taylor), concerns characters of the residue field (via Art) and does not cover the printed generality. The main theorems are unaffected, since §9 only uses characters of k_v^× via Art (p. 413: 'ψ_v = χ_v'). But Lemma 8.2 as stated is false under the printed hypothesis. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The literal statement is false.

1. **Only certain characters of I_v can occur for a characteristic-zero lift.**
   - A continuous χ : I_v → 1 + m_O factors through the pro-p quotient Z_p(1) of tame inertia (v ∤ p). Write u_i = χ_{v,i}(t) for a generator t.
   - For a lift ρ over a finite extension of Q_p, ρ(φtφ^{-1}) = ρ(t^{q_v}) is conjugate to ρ(t). So the multiset {u_i^{q_v}} must equal {u_i}.
   - Hence some power u_i^{q_v^m − 1} = 1, so each u_i is a root of unity. For n = 2 and χ_2 = χ_1^{-1}, the condition forces u^{q_v − 1} = 1, i.e. χ factors through the p-part of k_v^×.
   - Counterexample: I_v ↠ Z_p(1) ≅ Z_p → 1 + pZ_p, t ↦ (1+p)^t, of infinite order. It is continuous, into 1 + m_O, distinct from its inverse, and the product is trivial, so it meets every printed condition.
   - Finite order is not enough either. With p = 3 and q_v = 7, the order-9 characters satisfy all printed conditions but are not Frobenius-stable. A script (work/agents/lensB-K8-11/chk.py) confirms the stable ones are exactly those with a(q_v − 1) ≡ 0 mod N.

2. **Lemma 8.2 then fails.** For such χ_v, R_v^{χ_v} has no Q̄_p-points, so R_v^{χ_v}[1/p] = 0 and the ring is killed by some p^N. It is still non-zero, because r̄|_{G_v} is a k-point: its inertia has characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^n, and ∏(X − χ_{v,i}(σ)) ≡ (X − 1)^n mod m_O. So R^χ_loc is non-zero and p-power torsion, and Lemma 8.2(1) ("p-torsion free and equidimensional of dimension …") fails. If R^χ_v is instead defined as the p-torsion-free closure of its Q̄_p-points, it is 0, and parts (1) and (2) fail anyway.

**Defence considered.** The notation section (p. 297) defines I_v ⊂ G_v as the full inertia group. So "characters of I_v" cannot faithfully be read as characters of the inertia of G_v^{ab}. The intended meaning can be recovered, but only from elsewhere:
- the proof of Lemma 8.2 cites [76, Lemma 3.3] and [11, Prop. 3.1], which are stated for characters of O_K^× via Art;
- §9.1 fixes ψ_v on (k_v^×)^n/(k_v^×);
- Conjecture B(3) uses ψ_{v,i}(Art_v^{-1}(σ)), and p. 415 identifies "ψ_v = χ_v".

So the defence fails for the statement as printed, but it shows the intended mathematics is correct.

**What depends on it.**
- Lemma 8.2 is used in Proposition 8.4/8.5 (R^χ_{S_Q}-type rings over R^χ_loc) and in the proof of Theorem 9.19 (pp. 425–427). There R^2_∞ = R^χ_loc⟦x_1..x_g⟧ is asserted p-torsion free, equidimensional and irreducible "by Lemma 8.2", and R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ.
- Theorem 9.19 also uses "the local system associated to our choice of characters χ = (χ_v)", which only makes sense for characters of Iw(v)/Iw_1(v) ≅ (k_v^×)^n/k_v^×. So the χ_v actually used are of the corrected form.

**Classification.** Main results unaffected; Lemma 8.2 needs a corrected hypothesis. I record this as an error in the hypothesis of a stated result. A reviewer could reasonably downgrade it to misprint/nothing, since §9 fixes the intended meaning.

I rendered PDF pp. 110–112 and read the printed text. Section 8.5 lets R be any finite set of primes that contains the ramified primes of r̄ and satisfies N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. Counterexample to (3), checked from scratch. Take n = 2 (so p ≥ 3) and v ∈ R with r̄ unramified at v, r̄(Frob_v) with eigenvalues α ≠ β, and q = N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. Let O contain ζ_p. Take χ_1 a non-trivial p-power-order character of k_v^× (via Art) and χ_2 = χ_1^{-1}; these are distinct because p is odd.
- Every lift is split. Diagonalise r(Frob) = diag(A, B) by Hensel's lemma and write r(t) = 1 + M. By Cayley–Hamilton, the off-diagonal entries of (1+M)^q are c·M_12 and c·M_21, where c ≡ q ≡ 1 mod m. The relation Frob·t·Frob^{-1} = t^q gives (A/B − c)M_12 = 0, and A/B − c ≡ α/β − 1 is a unit, so M_12 = 0; likewise M_21 = 0. Wild inertia maps to a pro-p group, so it acts trivially.
- So r = γ_1 ⊕ γ_2 with γ_2 = ξγ_1^{-1}, and γ_1|I_v = γ_2|I_v^{-1} because ξ|I_v = 1. The element u = γ_1(t) = tr(r(t)P), where P = (r(Frob) − B)/(A − B), is well defined in R^{χ_v}_v.
- The characteristic-polynomial condition gives (u − χ_1(t))(u − χ_2(t)) = 0. Since χ_1(t) − χ_2(t) is a non-zero element of O, e = (u − χ_2(t))/(χ_1(t) − χ_2(t)) is an idempotent of R^χ_loc[1/p].
- e is neither 0 nor 1. Both loci have Q̄_p-points: γ_1 = (unramified lift of the α-character) × (extension of χ_i to G_v^ab), with γ_2 = ξγ_1^{-1}. For i = 1, 2 this has determinant ξ and inertial eigenvalues {χ_1(σ), χ_2(σ)}.
- Hence Spec R^χ_loc[1/p] is disconnected. If (1) and (3) both held, then p-torsion-freeness would put every minimal prime in characteristic 0, so Spec R^χ_loc[1/p] would be irreducible and hence connected. That is a contradiction. If another factor had no characteristic-0 points, (1) would fail instead.

Counterexample to (1) with the paper's literal definition, same v. The framed ring is R^□_v = O⟦X,a,b⟧[Y]/((1+Y)^{p^a} − 1), where p^a is the p-part of q − 1. The condition "char poly (X−1)^2 on I_v" is (1+Y) + (1+Y)^{-1} = 2, i.e. Y^2 = 0. So R^1_v = O⟦X,a,b⟧[Y]/(Y^2, p^aY), and p^{a−1}Y is a non-zero element killed by p.

A setup of this kind is realisable: Chebotarev gives primes ≡ 1 mod p with r̄(Frob) of distinct eigenvalues, and §8.5 lets such primes be added to R. The cited inputs ([11, Prop. 3.1]; BLGHT's R-primes) are for residually trivial r̄|G_v, and in that case e does not exist because nothing labels the two eigencharacters. So the one-line proof does not cover the stated generality. Theorem 9.19 uses (1) and (3) directly ("By Lemma 8.2, Spec R^2_∞ is irreducible"). DEFENCE FAILS. (a) The cited [11] = Taylor, Publ. IHES 108 (2008); I fetched it and checked §3. Its setting is 'r̄ : G_{F_v} → {1_n} ⊂ GL_n(k) denote the trivial representation', with #k(v) ≡ 1 mod l. The rings are the literal quotients R^loc_v/I_v^χ. Prop 3.1 concludes: Spec irreducible 'and its generic point has characteristic zero'; R^χ/λ = R^1/λ; components of dimension n^2+1 whose 'generic points all have characteristic zero'. It never states p-torsion-freeness. [76, Lemma 3.3] (BLGHT II, also checked) only concerns completed tensor products: flatness for flat inputs, and minimal primes. Nowhere in §8.5, §8.5.2 or §9.5 is r̄|G_v assumed trivial for v ∈ R. §8.5 explicitly puts the primes where r̄ ramifies into R, and Theorem 5.16(6) allows r̄ to be ramified, or unramified but nontrivial, at such primes. So the hypothesis is not 'clear from context'; the setup contradicts it. COUNTEREXAMPLE (checked): take n = 2, and an extra v ∈ R where r̄ is unramified, r̄(Frob_v) has eigenvalues α ≠ β, and q_v ≡ 1 mod p. By Chebotarev such v exist, and §8.5 allows them. Every lift is γ1 ⊕ ξγ1^{-1}; by Hensel and Nakayama the off-diagonal inertia entries vanish. γ1|I_v factors through the cyclic p-part of k_v^× (order p^a), so u = γ1(t) satisfies u^{p^a} = 1. Take χ_{v,2} = χ_{v,1}^{-1} ≠ χ_{v,1}, with c = χ_{v,1}(t). Then R^χ_v = O[Y]/((Y−(c−1))(Y−(c^{-1}−1)))[[X,z1,z2]]. This ring is O-flat with two minimal primes. Suppose Spec R^χ_loc were irreducible. Then one factor Y−(c^{±1}−1) would be nilpotent, and evaluating at an O'-point of the other type gives c = c^{-1}, a contradiction. So (3) fails. R^1_v = O[Y]/(Y^2, (1+Y)^{p^a}−1)[[X,z]] = O[Y]/(Y^2, p^aY)[[X,z]], and Y is p-torsion, so the literal (1) fails. If R^1_v is read as the flat quotient, then R^1/ϖ = k[[X,z]] ≠ k[Y]/(Y^2)[[X,z]] = R^χ/ϖ, so (2) fails instead. Either way the lemma is false. The same thing happens inside the hypotheses of Theorem 5.16, for both (8a) and (8b). Take n = 3 and r̄|G_x = Sp_2(β̄) ⊕ ᾱ' (ramified or not) with ᾱ' ≠ β̄. Lifts split as ρ1 ⊕ ρ2, and ∏_j(ρ2(t) − χ_j(t)) = 0. That gives three disjoint nonempty characteristic-0 loci, so Spec R^χ_x is reducible. CONSEQUENCES: the proof of Theorem 9.19 uses (3) ('By Lemma 8.2, Spec R^2_∞ is irreducible' → Theorem 6.4(2)). It also uses (1) (p-torsion free, and minimal primes of characteristic 0) and (2). Theorem 5.16 follows 'immediately' from 9.19, so the gap reaches a stated theorem in those configurations. The theorem is probably still provable by the repairs above. Theorem 1.1 is probably safe, because L can be chosen so that r̄ is trivial or regular there, but the paper does not say so. Lemma 8.2 itself is a false stated result. - **Error** at §8.5 (Deformations of Galois representations), published p. 407 (PDF p. 111), 4th line of the page, right after the two bullets defining ξ. arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2, §8.5, PDF p. 81) has the same sentence word for word. arXiv v1 has no n-dimensional §8.5, so the sentence does not appear there.. The source says `[p. 406, end:] "We also fix a continuous character ξ : G_F → O^×" [p. 407, top:] "lifting det(r̄) and with • ξ|_{I_v} = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for all v|p, and • ξ|_{I_v} = 1 for all v ∤ p. For example, we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}."`; it should be `Minimal fix: "For example, if det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2} (as under Theorem 5.16(7)), we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}." General choice: ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}·[χ̄], where χ̄ := det(r̄)·ε̄^{−n(n−1)/2} and [·] is the Teichmüller lift into W(k)^× ⊂ O^×. This works because χ̄ is unramified at every finite place. At v|p, Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1] makes det(r̄)|_{I_v} = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}|_{I_v}, which is the convention the paper's own bullet ξ|_{I_v} = ε^{n(n−1)/2} presupposes. At v∤p, unipotent ramification makes det(r̄)|_{I_v} = 1. So [χ̄] is unramified at all finite places, and ξ lifts det(r̄) and meets both inertia conditions. The correction proposed in the candidate is therefore correct.`. I rendered p. 407 and read the text there; it matches arXiv v2 exactly. The §8.5 hypotheses on r̄ are: absolutely irreducible; Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1] at v|p; at worst unipotent ramification at v∤p, with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p where r̄ ramifies; odd at the real places. None of these fixes det(r̄). They only force det(r̄)|_{I_v} to be ε̄^{n(n−1)/2} at v|p and trivial at v∤p. So det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}·χ̄, where χ̄ is unramified at every finite place, and χ̄ need not be trivial.

The hypotheses are unchanged by twisting with an everywhere-unramified character η: G_F → k^× (whose order is automatically prime to p):
- Fontaine–Laffaille-ness and the weights survive an unramified twist.
- r̄|_{I_v} is unchanged, so unipotence holds and the set of ramified primes is the same.
- At a real place, Trace(c_v) only changes by the sign η(c_v) = ±1, so it stays in {−1,0,1}.
- Absolute irreducibility is preserved.
But det(r̄⊗η) = det(r̄)·η^n.

Concrete instance: F = Q(√−47) (class number 5), n = 2, p = 3, r̄ = E[3]|_{G_F} with E = 11a1.
- 3 splits in F, so it is unramified.
- E has good reduction at 3, which gives Fontaine–Laffaille weights [0,1] ⊂ [0,p−2].
- E has split multiplicative reduction at 11 with ord_11(Δ) = 5, so r̄ is unipotently ramified at 11. Also 11 is inert in F (since (−47/11) = −1), so N(v) = 121 ≡ 1 mod 3.
- r̄ is irreducible: 2 splits in F, and Frob_2 has characteristic polynomial X²−X−1, which is irreducible mod 3. (Absolute irreducibility follows from Serre's result that ρ_ℓ is surjective for 11a1 when ℓ ≠ 5. I did not recheck that here.)
- det r̄ = ω, the mod-3 cyclotomic character.
Now twist by a character η of order 5 of the class group, with values in F_81. Then r̄⊗η satisfies every §8.5 hypothesis, and det = ω·η² ≠ ω. So ξ = ε does not reduce to det(r̄⊗η), and the "for example" fails.

I call this an error with no downstream effect. A suitable ξ always exists (the Teichmüller-twisted choice above). The paper only applies §8.5 when det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}: Theorem 5.16(7) assumes det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2}, and §9.5 assumes r̄ ≅ r̄_m for PGL_n cohomology. So in that setting the example is valid and the results are untouched. The slip is the missing hypothesis in a general setup that deliberately allows any ξ lifting det(r̄). I looked for a defence and found none that covers §8.5 as stated. §8.5 assumes only: absolute irreducibility, Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0..n−1] at v|p, at most unipotent ramification (with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p if ramified) at v∤p, and oddness at real places. Nothing in §8 (§§8.1–8.4 included) fixes det(r̄). Those hypotheses force only that χ̄ = det(r̄)ε̄^{−n(n−1)/2} is unramified at every finite place, and such a χ̄ can be nontrivial when F has nontrivial narrow class group.

Explicit failure: take any r̄ satisfying §8.5 and an everywhere-unramified character η: G_F → k^× with η^n ≠ 1 (order necessarily prime to p). Then r̄⊗η still satisfies every §8.5 hypothesis. The unramified twist keeps it Fontaine–Laffaille with the same weights and keeps the ramification unipotent on the same primes. Trace(c_v) only changes sign, so it stays in {−1,0,1}. Irreducibility is kept. But det(r̄⊗η) = det(r̄)·η^n, so det(r̄) and det(r̄⊗η) cannot both equal ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}. For n odd, a character that is unramified at all finite places but nontrivial at a real place already works. The claim does hold automatically over F = Q, where such a χ̄ must be trivial, but the paper allows an arbitrary number field F.

So "we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}" is false as stated: that ξ meets both inertia conditions but need not lift det(r̄).

Why it is harmless: §8.5.1 and §8.5.2 (R_v, R_v^1, R_v^{χ_v}, the data S_Q) and Conjecture B / Theorem 9.19 all use only "a fixed ξ with the listed properties", never the specific example. The only route to a stated result is Theorem 5.16 ("follows immediately from Theorem 9.19"). There hypothesis (7) says det(r) = ε^{n(n−1)/2}, so det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2} and the example choice is valid. The PGL(n) automorphic side (§9, G = Res PGL(n)) also forces the determinant of r_m to be a fixed cyclotomic power, so in the application ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2} is the choice actually needed.

In short, this is an illustrative remark with a missing hypothesis. It is false in the generality of §8.5, but the mathematics is right as intended and in every place it is used. Its remark that the equality is used only for the Q given by Prop. 8.5(3) is also right.`. The statement is false under the hypotheses as printed. Let v ∈ Q and q = N(v). Then v ∤ p and r̄ is unramified at v, because R contains every prime where r̄ ramifies and Q is disjoint from R. Take a lift ρ to k[ε] of type D_v. Wild inertia is pro-ℓ, so its image in the p-group ker(GL_n(k[ε]) → GL_n(k)) is trivial, and ρ|I_v factors through the Z_p(1) quotient of tame inertia. Let σ be a generator there. Then ρ(σ) = diag((1+εa)·1_{s}, (1+εb)·1_{ψ}) with (n−1)a + b = 0, because det = ξ is unramified at v. Since ρ(σ) is block-scalar it commutes with ρ(Frob_v), so the relation Frob σ Frob^{-1} = σ^q forces (q−1)a = 0 in k.

Case q ≢ 1 mod p: then a = b = 0, so every lift of type D_v is unramified. Conversely every unramified lift is of type D_v, because the 1-dimensional generalized eigenspace lifts by Hensel's lemma. Hence L_v = H^1_ur(G_v, ad^0 r̄), and for the procyclic quotient G_v/I_v, dim H^1_ur = h^0. So the difference is 0, not 1. Check with n = 2: let Frobenius have eigenvalues α ≠ β and suppose q ≢ 1 mod p. Then h^0 = 1. Also Hom(G_v, k) = Hom(F_v^×, k) has no ramified part, because k_v^× ⊗ F_p = 0. So L_v = H^1_ur has dimension 1 and the difference is 0.

Case q ≡ 1 mod p: the framed tangent space with fixed determinant has dimension (n^2−1) + 1 = n^2. It equals dim L_v + (n^2 − 1 − h^0), so dim L_v − h^0 = 1, as the paper claims.

Defence considered: the sentence "Q will consist of Taylor–Wiles primes" and the heuristic of §8.2, where a Taylor–Wiles prime has N(v) ≡ 1 mod p^n, show what the authors meant. Against this, the formal hypotheses in §8.5.1 ("Let Q denote a finite set of primes ... disjoint from R ∪ S_p"; "For each v ∈ Q, we assume that: •...") leave the congruence out. Prop. 8.5 then lists "(3) N_{F/Q}(v) ≡ 1 mod p^N" as a separate property, so the paper itself does not treat the congruence as automatic. The analogous passages in §3 and §5 do state "Suppose that x ≡ 1 mod p". So the printed claim is a genuinely missing hypothesis. The meaning is recoverable from context, which puts it on the border between error and misprint.

Consequences: Prop. 8.4 is stated for general Q and keeps the term Σ_{v∈Q}(dim L_v − h^0) unevaluated, so it does not use the claim. The only use is the last line of the proof of Prop. 8.5: "the fact that dim_k L_v − h^0(G_v, ad^0 r̄) = 1 if v ∈ Q". There Q satisfies (3), N(v) ≡ 1 mod p^N, so the equality holds. The exact sequence with the map φ ↦ tr(e_v φ(Frob_v)) in the same proof also relies on (3). The later uses (§9.4.2, §10, the condition "r_m|G_v is of type D_v") involve only Taylor–Wiles sets Q_N from Prop. 8.5. No stated result is affected. The same sentence ("Let K_Q = ∏_v K_{Q,v} and L_Q = ∏_v L_{Q,v} denote the open compact subgroups of G(A) such that:") appears in §5.2.1, p. 372 (PDF p. 76).`; it should be `"... denote the open compact subgroups of G(A^∞) such that:" (G(A^∞) = PGL_n(A_F^∞); likewise in §5.2.1 with PGL_2).`. G(A) = G(R) × G(A^∞), and G(R) = PGL_n(R)^{r_1} × PGL_n(C)^{r_2} is non-compact for n ≥ 2, so G(A) has no compact open subgroups. The groups are products of local factors at the finite places v of F, all subgroups of PGL_n(𝒪_v), and they are fed into Y(K), which was defined only for compact open K ⊂ G(A^∞) in the preceding paragraph. So G(A^∞) is intended. X-K8-17 is the same finding. It is not a bracket error. The source says `H_{•,ψ}(Y(K), O) → H_{•,ψ}(Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K_Q), O) → H_{•,ψ}(Y(K ∩ g^{−1}Kg), O) → H_{•,ψ}(Y(K), O), [displayed in §9.2 'Hecke operators', bottom of p. 412 (PDF p. 116), after 'For K ⊂ G(A^∞) a compact open subgroup of the form K_Q or L_Q, the Hecke operator T(g) is defined on the homology modules H_{•,ψ}(Y(K), O) by considering the composition:'; the sentence continuing on p. 413 reads: 'the first map coming from the corestriction map, the second coming from the map Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K, O) → Y(K ∩ g^{−1}Kg, O) induced by right multiplication by g on G(A)']`; it should be `In the second term, read H_{•,ψ}(Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K), O) instead of H_{•,ψ}(Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K_Q), O). This matches the next sentence on p. 413 ('Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K, O) → Y(K ∩ g^{−1}Kg, O)') and the same definition in §5.2.2, p. 373, which prints H_•(Y(gKg^{−1} ∩ K), O). arXiv v2 (§9.0.2) has the same misprint, 'Y(gKg−1 ∩ KQ)'.`. I rendered p. 412 at 300 dpi. The printed subscript really is K_Q, but the very next sentence (p. 413) uses gKg^{−1} ∩ K, and so does §5.2.2 (p. 373, checked on the page image). The paper allows K = K_Q or K = L_Q. When K = K_Q the two groups are the same. When K = L_Q, the corestriction H(Y(K)) → H(Y(K')) only makes sense if K' ⊂ K. Also, right multiplication by g sends level H to level g^{−1}Hg. For H = gKg^{−1} ∩ K_Q that level is K ∩ g^{−1}K_Q g, not the printed K ∩ g^{−1}Kg. For the composition to hold together, H has to be gKg^{−1} ∩ K. I checked by hand that the printed group can fail to lie in L_Q. Take v ∈ Q and let g_v be the permutation matrix w that swaps e1 and e2. Take x ∈ L_{Q,v} with x ≡ (a 0 *; 0 b *; 0 0 C) mod π_v, normalised so that b·det C/a^{n−1} ≡ 1. Then wxw^{−1} lies in K_{Q,v}, and the character K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^× takes the value a·det C/b^{n−1} = (a/b)^n on it, which need not be 1. So in general the printed group is not a subgroup of K = L_Q, and the printed diagram does not make sense. This is a genuine inconsistency and not one of the 47 known ⟦ ⟧ bracket errors. It is harmless, though. At places outside Q, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v}. For the diagonal g actually used (g = diag(α,…,α,1,…,1) for T_{α,k} and for the T_α at places in Q in Def. 9.1), conjugating by g leaves the (1,1) entry and the determinant of the lower (n−1)×(n−1) block unchanged. So gL_Qg^{−1} ∩ K_Q already lies in L_Q, and the printed and corrected groups coincide. The candidate's reason is correct in substance, though loosely worded. A line-stabilizer mod π_v is of the form (a ∗; 0 D) with D ∈ GL_{n−1}(k_v), and dividing by the scalar a normalizes the corner entry to 1 in PGL. The map (a ∗; 0 D) ↦ det D / a^{n−1} is well defined modulo scalars and maps onto k_v^×. Its kernel is the (1 ∗; 0 SL_{n−1}) form, which matches "quotient group k_v^×". No N is defined at this point in §9. The letter N appears later only as the Taylor–Wiles index (Q_N, Δ_N = (Z/p^N Z)^q) and in norms N(x). So GL_{N−1} and SL_{N−1} are misprints for GL_{n−1} and SL_{n−1}. (b) §9 opens with "Let S = S_p ∪ R and S_Q = S ∪ Q be as in Sect. 8", and §8.5 defines S = S_p ∪ R and S_Q = S ∪ Q. - **Misprint** at §9.1 (Arithmetic quotients), definition of K_Q = ∏_v K_{Q,v} and L_Q = ∏_v L_{Q,v}, condition (3), published p. 412 (PDF p. 116). The definition starts at the foot of p. 411. arXiv v2 §9.0.1(3), p. 85, has the same text: "(3) If v ∉ S_Q K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v)". arXiv v1 has no §9 or PGL_n material (it covers only the GL(2) part), so it cannot be compared.. The source says `(3) If v ∉ S_Q K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v). [context, p. 411: "Let S = S_p ∪ R and S_Q = S ∪ Q be as in Sect. 8." (1),(2) are "If v ∈ Q, ..."; (4) is "If v ∈ R, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = the Iwahori Iw(v) subgroup ofPGL_n(O_v) associated to the upper triangular unipotent subgroup."]`; it should be `"(3) If v ∉ R ∪ Q, then K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v)." Equivalently, keep (3) and add "If v | p, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_n(O_v)." This is the hyperspecial level at p, which makes sense because p is unramified in F. Only the index set changes (and a missing comma is added), so this is the minimal fix. Both readers' corrections (X-K9-3, C-K8-4) agree with this. I record it as a misprint, not the "gap" in C-K8-4: no proof step is missing, the definition just leaves out one case, and the intended value is clear from context.`. Sect. 8.5 (p. 409) defines S_p as the set of primes of F above p, R as disjoint from S_p, and Q as disjoint from R ∪ S_p. It sets S = S_p ⊔ R and S_Q = S ⊔ Q, and §9 says this notation carries over. In §9.1, conditions (1) and (2) cover v ∈ Q, (4) covers v ∈ R, and (3) covers v ∉ S_Q. So a prime v | p (v ∈ S_p) falls under none of the four conditions, and K_{Q,v}, L_{Q,v} are never defined there. The definitions of K_Q, L_Q, and therefore of Y = Y(K_∅), Y_0(Q), Y_1(Q), are incomplete as printed.

I searched the rest of §9 (Hecke operators, Conjecture B, Lemma 9.6, §9.4–9.5, Thm 9.16, Thm 9.19) and none of it fixes the level at p. By contrast, §5.2.1(4) on p. 330 does state the level at v | p explicitly for the GL_2 case.

The intended meaning is clear from context:
- p > n and p is unramified in F, so PGL_n(O_v) is hyperspecial.
- Conjecture B(1) and the local rings R_v are Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0, …, n−1], i.e. crystalline of trivial weight, which matches hyperspecial (spherical) level at p.
- The coefficients are trivial (O or O(ψ), with ψ supported on R).

So "v ∉ S_Q" is a slip for "v ∉ R ∪ Q". This is a misprint rather than a gap: it is an incomplete definition, not an unproved step. The minor typography on the same page (the missing comma after S_Q, "GL_{N−1}" in (2), "PGL(O_v)" in (1)) is separate and not part of this candidate. None of this is one of the 47 bracket errors. As printed, a place v | p is covered by none of the four conditions. §8.5 defines R as a finite set of primes "disjoint from S_p" and Q as disjoint from R ∪ S_p, so S_Q = S_p ⊔ R ⊔ Q. Conditions (1) and (2) cover v ∈ Q, (4) covers v ∈ R, and (3) excludes every v ∈ S_Q, including S_p. So the factor K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} at v | p is never specified, yet Y = Y(K_∅), Y_0(Q) and Y_1(Q) all need it.

Defence attempts that fail:
(a) §9 cannot be using a different S_Q. The §9 preamble explicitly takes S_Q = S_p ∪ R ∪ Q from §8, and Definition 9.1 uses "α which are units at primes in S_Q", which excludes the Hecke operators at p. That only makes sense if S_Q contains S_p.
(b) Reading "such that" as allowing any level at p does not rescue the text. Conjecture B(1) asserts that r_m|G_v is Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1] for v | p. At deeper level at p, for example Iwahori, the Hecke algebra would also see semistable, non-crystalline lifts, and (1) would fail. The patching in Theorem 9.19 likewise uses the Fontaine–Laffaille rings R_v of Lemma 8.2 at v | p.
(c) No later passage in §9 fixes the level at p. Lemma 9.6 talks only of "congruence subgroups commensurable with PGL2(O_F)", and §9.5 just uses Y = Y(K_∅).

The intended level (hyperspecial at p) is clear from context:
- Conjecture B(1).
- Theorem 5.16: (1)–(2) crystalline with Hodge–Tate weights 0,…,n−1 and p unramified in F; (8a) "good reduction at all v | p"; (8b) Serre-modular of minimal level N(r̄), which is prime to p.
- The parallel published §5.2.1(3)–(4) and arXiv v1 §4.2.1, which both give the level at v | p explicitly. Presumably the p-clause was lost when that template was rewritten as the S_Q-based (3).

The source says `p. 412 (PDF p. 116), §9.2: "We recall the construction of the Hecke operators. Let g ∈ G(A^∞) be an invertible matrix trivial at each place v ∈ R. This is consistent with the construction of T(g) and with the next paragraph's 'α is 1 for each component dividing the level'. Alternatively, extend the construction to g_v ∈ Iw(v) by letting g_v act on 𝒪(ψ) through ψ_v. The other reading ('trivial at primes in S_Q', as in Definition 5.4) is not a misprint fix: it would remove the diamond operators at Q from T^an_{Q,ψ}, which is the substantive question in the related gap (C-K9-0 / H-part2-18).`. R ⊂ S_Q. The construction of T(g) on p. 412 is stated only for g trivial at each v ∈ R. That restriction is needed because on the ψ-twisted local system the operator depends on the representative g, not just the double coset. If α_v ∈ 𝒪_v^× with α_v ≠ 1 at some v ∈ R, then g_v = diag(α_v, ..., α_v, 1, ..., 1) is a non-trivial element of Iw(v), and it maps non-trivially to Iw(v)/Iw_1(v) ≅ (k_v^×)^n/k_v^×. So T_{α,k} is not covered by the stated construction, and Definition 9.1 as printed refers to operators the paper has not defined. The mismatch is harmless. With the natural extension (right translation by g_v is a deck transformation of Ỹ → Y and acts on 𝒪(ψ) by ψ_v(g_v)^{±1}), such a T_{α,k} is a unit scalar in 1 + 𝔪_𝒪 times T_{α',k}, where α' has v-component 1. So the 𝒪-algebra generated is unchanged. At v|p a unit α_v gives g_v ∈ PGL_n(𝒪_v), which is harmless. At v ∈ Q a unit α_v gives the diamond operators through K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^×. The printed 'units' includes these deliberately or not; the minimal correction keeps them, as printed. Whether they should be in T^an is the separate gap about local–global compatibility at Q, and it does not affect this verdict. It is not a bracket error. (E, α_NQ) has two entries, and a few lines later the text itself calls it 'a pair (E, α_NQ)'; the word 'triple' is appropriate only for (E, α_N, C_Q) on X_1(N; Q). Note that 'triple' occurs twice: 'triples (E, α_NQ)' and 'Given such a triple'. The curve is written X_1(N; Q) with a semicolon everywhere else, including later in the same sentence ('X_1(NQ) → X_1(N; Q)') and on p. 313 ('resp. X_1(N; Q)'), so 'X_1(N, Q)' is a notational slip. - **Error** at §9.2, p. 413 (definition of T_{a,k}) together with §9.3, Conjecture B, p. 414 (characteristic polynomial) (published version) (it affects a stated result). The source says `p. 413 (§9.2, just after Definition 9.1): "If 𝔞 ⊆ O_F is an ideal prime to the level, we may define the Hecke operator T_{𝔞,k} as (1/N_{F/Q}(𝔞)^k)T_{α,k} where α ∈ A_F^{×,∞} is any element which represents the ideal 𝔞 and such that α is 1 for each component dividing the level." p. 414 (§9.3, Conjecture B): "... if λ ∉ S_Q is a prime of F, then r̄_𝔪 is unramified at λ, and the characteristic polynomial of r̄_𝔪(Frob_λ) is X^n − T_{λ,1}X^{n−1} + ··· + (−1)^i N_{F/Q}(λ)^{i(i−1)/2} T_{λ,i} X^{n−i} + ··· + (−1)^n N_{F/Q}(λ)^{n(n−1)/2} T_{λ,n}, in T^an_{Q,ψ}/𝔪[X]." arXiv v2 has identical wording (v2 p. 86, §9.1).`; it should be `Define T_{𝔞,k} := T_{α,k}, i.e. drop the factor 1/N_{F/Q}(𝔞)^k. This is the §5 convention: Definition 5.4 has "T_𝔞 as T_α" and Conjecture A(1) has X^2 − T_λX + N(λ). With it, the Conjecture B polynomial becomes the standard one. An equivalent fix is to keep the normalisation and change the i-th coefficient to (−1)^i N(λ)^{i(i+1)/2} T_{λ,i}, which gives the same polynomial. Either change is a one-symbol fix. After it, det r_𝔪 = ε^{n(n−1)/2}, as ξ (§8.5), Theorem 5.16(7) and §5.5 ("PGL ... forcing the determinant to be cyclotomic") require. Nothing else in §9 needs to change.`. I checked this against the page images (PDF pp. 116–118 = pp. 412–414) and the text. It holds.
(1) §9 takes G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) (p. 411). T_{α,k} is the double coset operator for g = diag(α,…,α,1,…,1) with k copies of α, and k = n is allowed (Definition 9.1). For k = n, g is scalar, so it is the identity in PGL_n and T_{α,n} = id. Under the printed normalisation T_{λ,n} = N(λ)^{−n}. The constant term (−1)^n N^{n(n−1)/2} T_{λ,n} then gives det r̄_𝔪(Frob_λ) = N(λ)^{n(n−1)/2−n}.
(2) Frob_v is the arithmetic Frobenius (Notation, p. 306), so det r̄_𝔪 = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2−n} by Chebotarev.
(3) §8.5 fixes r̄ as Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1]. It also fixes ξ lifting det r̄, with ξ|I_v = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for v|p and ξ|I_v = 1 for v∤p. Theorem 5.16(7) has det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2}. Conjecture B supposes r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄ and concludes that r_𝔪 is a deformation of type S_Q, so it has determinant ξ. §9.5 assumes a maximal ideal 𝔪 with r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄. Together these force ω^{−n} = 1 on I_v for v|p. Since p is unramified in F, that means (p−1) | n. With p > n this happens only when p = n+1. So for p ≥ n+2, the printed Conjecture B, part 1, rules out every 𝔪 with r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄.
(4) Independent check. The un-normalised T_{α,k} acts on constant classes by its degree, the q-binomial [n,k]_q. I verified numerically that q^{i(i−1)/2}[n,i]_q = e_i(1,q,…,q^{n−1}). So without the factor, the formula gives 1⊕ε⊕…⊕ε^{n−1}, which has weights 0,…,n−1 and determinant ε^{n(n−1)/2}, as the paper's conventions require. With the factor, every root is multiplied by N^{−1}, so the formula describes r⊗ε^{−1}. For n = 2 it gives X^2 − (T_α/N)X + N^{−1}, which contradicts Conjecture A for the same T_α. For n ≥ 3 the determinant is wrong whichever sign or Frobenius convention is used. Lemma 9.6 also uses the un-normalised T_x (roots α_x, β_x with α_xβ_x = N(x)).
Two small problems with the candidate's reasoning:
- The mod-𝔪 contradiction needs p ≥ n+2, not just p > n. When p = n+1 one needs 𝔪-adic or characteristic-zero information instead.
- Printed B is not literally self-contradictory. Its part-3 hypothesis (and §9.5's standing assumption) simply cannot be met, so Theorem 9.19 becomes vacuous. The proof of 5.16 also fails: by the standard normalisation, the 𝔪 coming from π_0 would give r̄⊗ε̄^{−1}, not r̄.
Theorem 1.1 applies 5.16 to Sym^{2n−1} in dimension 2n with large p, so it is affected. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. I checked the page images: PDF pp. 115–118, pp. 77–79 and 87–88, and v2 p. 86.

Defences tried, and why each fails:
(a) Is T_{α,n} = id? Yes. §9 takes G = Res_{F/Q}PGL(n) (p. 411), and for k = n the matrix g = diag(α,…,α) is scalar, hence trivial in PGL_n. So under the printed normalisation T_{λ,n} = N(λ)^{−n}. The constant term then says det r̄_𝔪(Frob_λ) = N(λ)^{n(n−1)/2−n} = N(λ)^{n(n−3)/2} for every λ ∉ S_Q. This does not depend on how T_{α,k} is read for k < n: using α^{-1} just swaps T_k with T_{n−k}, and the determinant is unchanged.
(b) Frobenius convention. The Notation on p. 306 says Frob_v is the arithmetic Frobenius. Chebotarev then gives det r̄_𝔪 = ω^{n(n−3)/2}. Using the geometric Frobenius instead gives ε^{−n(n−3)/2}. That agrees with ε^{n(n−1)/2} on inertia only if ε^{n(n−2)} = 1, so it helps only when n = 2. The paper uses the arithmetic Frobenius anyway: Conjecture A has X^2 − T_λX + N(λ), and Lemma 5.6 has cyclotomic determinant.
(c) The paper's own T(g), defined by corestriction, then translation, then pushforward, acts on constant classes by its degree, the q-binomial [n,k]_q. I checked numerically (q = 5, 7, 9; n = 2..5) that q^{i(i−1)/2}[n,i]_q = e_i(1,q,…,q^{n−1}). So the unnormalised operators give 1⊕ε⊕…⊕ε^{n−1}, as intended. The printed normalised operators give roots q^{−1},1,…,q^{n−2}, which is r⊗ε^{−1}. No convention in the paper supplies the factor N^{−k}. Lemma 9.6 itself uses the unnormalised T_x: φ^∨∘φ = [[N(x)+1, T_x],[T_x, N(x)+1]] with α_xβ_x ≡ N(x).

Consequences. Conjecture B assumes r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄. Here det r̄ = ξ̄ with ξ|I_v = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for v | p, and p is unramified, so ω(I_v) = F_p^×. The printed text would therefore force (p−1) | n, which for p > n means p = n+1. So for p ≥ n+2 no 𝔪 satisfies r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄. Parts (1)–(5) of B become vacuous, and the standing assumption of §9.5 (p. 425, "a maximal ideal 𝔪 of T with r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄") can never hold. When p = n+1, part (1) (Fontaine–Laffaille weights [0..n−1]) fails at any characteristic-0 point instead, because of the ε^{−1} twist.

The deduction "Theorem 5.16 follows immediately from Theorem 9.19" also breaks. The 𝔪 attached to π_0 in hypothesis (8a) would, under the printed normalisation, have r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄⊗ω^{−1}, not r̄. And with B vacuous, 5.16 would claim far more than is proved. Theorem 1.1 applies 5.16 to Sym^{2n−1} (dimension 2n) at large p, so it inherits the problem.

Unaffected: Conjecture B(5) and Lemma 9.6. They only involve Taylor–Wiles primes, where N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, and the projectors lim Q_x(V_x)^{k!} do not change when V_x is scaled by a unit ≡ 1.

Remark on the kind: the intended normalisation is recoverable from §5, so some would call this a slip. But the printed definition, which introduces a deliberate normalisation, makes the hypothesis of 5.16/9.19 unsatisfiable. The correction is right and minimal.
