- **Gap** at §9.3, Conjecture B, p. 414, and the sentence after (5), p. 415 ('In this case, we obtain a surjection R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,m}'); used in §9.5, p. 427 ('Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B') (published version) (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 414 (PDF p. 118), Conjecture B: "(2) If v ∈ Q, then r_𝔪|_{G_v} is a lifting of type 𝒟_v where 𝒟_v is the local deformation problem specified in Sect. 8.5.1." p. 427 (PDF p. 131), proof of Theorem 9.19: "Thus condition (b) of Proposition 6.3 is satisfied for both sets of patching data. Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B, while condition (c) is clear." (Both passages read the same in arXiv v2.)`; it should be `Add to Conjecture B a local–global compatibility clause at the Taylor–Wiles primes. This is the GL(n) analogue of Conjecture A(3), where T_α uses g = diag(α,1). Proposed clause: for v ∈ Q and α ∈ O_v^×, the operator T_{α,1} acts on H^*_ψ(Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^m)_𝔪 as the scalar by which r_𝔪(Art_v(α)) acts on the lift ψ_v of the line ψ̄_v. Here Art is normalised as in (3), with the transpose/inverse when one passes to the dual/homology side (𝔪*). Why this is the right form: identify K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} with k_v^× by g ↦ det(B)·a^{1−n}, where g ≡ [[a,*],[0,B]]. Then diag(α^{(k)},1^{(n−k)}) has class α^{k−n}, and T_{α,1} has class α^{1−n}. Since p > n, the T_{α,1} run over the whole p-part of Δ_Q. So the clause fixes the diamond action of S_N = O[Δ_N]; equivalently, a diamond operator acts by the inertial scalar on s_v. With the clause, R_{𝒮_Q} → T is a map of O[Δ_Q]-algebras. The diamond operators lie in the image of R_{𝒮_Q}, so the p. 415 surjection holds even though T^an contains them. The augmentation ideal maps into the image of ker(R_{𝒮_Q} → R_𝒮), which gives both halves of Theorem 6.3(d). A relation "diamond = inertial character to a fixed power prime to p" would do just as well; this is all that is needed. Alternative for Definition 9.1: read "units" as "trivial" at Q, as in Def. 5.4. That saves the p. 415 surjection but not (d); the clause is still needed. Comments on the reporters' versions. X-K10-9's form (T_{α,1} ↔ ψ_v∘Art_v) is correct, but its cross-reference "p. 378" should be pp. 374–375. C-K9-0's phrase "ψ_x∘Art_x ... should match the Hecke action of the T_{α,k}" holds only for k = 1. Under the expected compatibility, T_{α,k} with α ∈ O_v^× acts by (ψ_v∘Art_v)^{(n−k)/(n−1)}, and T_{α,n} = 1. H-part2-18's "diamond character, or its inverse" is right only for a suitable choice of the unspecified isomorphism K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^×.`. I checked the printed text on the page images and it matches the quote.

1. What Theorem 6.3(d) asks for (p. 386, checked on the image). "the image of S_M^□ in End_O(H^*(D_M^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ^n)) is contained in the image of R_∞ and moreover, the image of the augmentation ideal of S_N^□ ... is contained in the image of ker(φ_N)." In §9.5, S_N = O[Δ_N] acts through the deck group of Y_{Δ_N}(Q) → Y_0(Q). That group is a quotient of K_Q/L_Q ≅ ∏ k_x^×, so S_N acts by diamond operators. R_∞ acts through R_{S_Q} → Hecke. The map φ_N sends R_∞ onto R_S, and ker(R_{S_Q} → R_S) is generated by the condition that inertia at Q acts trivially.

2. What Conjecture B gives at v ∈ Q. Only (2): r_𝔪|_{G_v} has type 𝒟_v. In §8.5.1 (p. 408), 𝒟_v is purely Galois-theoretic: "I_v acts via (possibly different) scalars on s_v and ψ_v". Clauses (1) and (3)–(5) are about v|p, v ∈ R, vanishing, and Y_0(Q) respectively. None of them ties the inertial scalars at v ∈ Q to the diamond operators. r_𝔪 is determined by Frobenius at λ ∉ S_Q, so its inertial character at v is a well-defined object. Saying that this character equals the diamond character is extra local–global content. Without it, nothing stops r_𝔪 from being unramified at v while ⟨δ⟩ ≠ 1. The second half of (d) then fails, and so can the first half. Conclusion (iv) of Theorem 6.3, which is used to finish the proof of Thm 9.19, needs the second half.

3. The paper's own GL_2 argument uses exactly this input. Conjecture A(3) (pp. 374–375) is local–global compatibility at Q. The proof of Lemma 5.6 says "assumption 3 above guarantees ... that the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces". On p. 380 the authors write: "The image of S_N ... is contained in the image of R_∞ by Conjecture A, because it is given by the image of the diamond operators. The second part of condition (5a) follows from Conjecture A part (3)". Conjecture B has no counterpart to A(3).

4. The claimed surjection R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,𝔪}. As printed, Definition 9.1 allows α that are only units at primes in S_Q. For α ∈ O_x^× with x ∈ Q, diag(α^{(k)}, 1^{(n−k)}) lies in K_{Q,x}. By my computation it acts on Y_1(Q) as a diamond operator (class α^{k−n}). So T^an contains the diamond operators, and surjectivity from the trace algebra again needs the missing compatibility. If "units" was meant to be "trivial", as in Def. 5.4, then the first half of (d) needs it instead.

5. Independent corroboration. Khare–Thorne, "Potential automorphy and the Leopoldt conjecture" (arXiv 1409.7007), which uses the Calegari–Geraghty method, builds this into its setup. It defines D_v^TW so that "C_i|_{I_{F_v}} agrees, on composition with the Artin map, with the ith canonical character" of Δ_v, makes R_{S_Q} an O[Δ_Q]-algebra, and puts the requirement in a separate Conjecture 6.27. Its Remark 6.28 calls that conjecture "a form of local-global compatibility ... at the places of S_p ∪ Q".

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The O[(Z_p)^q] on p. 427 is one of those and is a separate matter.

On "affects": the proof of Theorem 9.19 has a gap. Theorems 5.16 and 1.1 are deduced from it assuming Conjecture B, so their hypothesis must be strengthened by the clause above for the proof to go through. Nothing shows the conditional statements are false, so "the proof" is the right classification. Defence attempts. None of them works.

(a) The other clauses of Conjecture B. Clause (1) concerns v|p. Clause (3) gives inertia compatibility only at v ∈ R, with fixed O-valued Iwahori characters. Clause (4) is about vanishing. Clause (5) concerns only Y_0(Q), where the diamond operators act trivially. Clause (2) says only that the lift has type 𝒟_v, which is a purely Galois-side condition: "I_v acts via (possibly different) scalars" (p. 408). Nothing ties those scalars to the deck group Δ_Q of Y_1(Q) → Y_0(Q). r_𝔪 is pinned down by its Frobenius traces at λ ∉ S_Q, so its inertial scalar at v ∈ Q is a definite object. Saying that it equals the diamond character is an extra assertion, and Conjecture B does not make it. In particular, clauses (1)–(5) do not rule out r_𝔪 being unramified at v while a diamond operator ⟨δ⟩ ≠ 1.

(b) The GL(1) and central-character mechanisms. In the GL(1) model (PDF 108), and for classical X_1(N), diamond operators come from Frobenius classes through class field theory or the central character. Here G = PGL_n, so T_{λ,n} = 1 and det = ξ carries no diamond information. The p-part of Δ_Q is therefore not in the closed algebra generated by traces unless one assumes something more.

(c) A charitable reading of the authors' intent. Remark 9.5 (p. 417) says the real difficulty lies in "proving local-global compatibility, especially at v|p". So the authors think of local–global compatibility as part of the conjecture's content. But the stated clause at Q is only (2). The proof says "Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B" and gives no argument.

(d) Deriving it from clause (3). One could try to treat Q as additional R-primes with character twists and then decompose. That is not in the paper. It would also fail integrally: patching needs O/ϖ^n and O[Δ]-coefficients, where eigen-decomposition by O-valued characters is not available.

(e) The same step in §5. The paper's GL(2) proof needed exactly this input and said so. The proof of Lemma 5.6 says "assumption 3 above guarantees (by Hensel's Lemma) that the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces". On p. 380: "The image of S_N ... is contained in the image of R_∞ by Conjecture A, because it is given by the image of the diamond operators. The second part of condition (5a) follows from Conjecture A part (3)". Here T_α uses g = diag(α,1) (§5.2.2), which is T_{α,1}. Conjecture B has no counterpart of A(3).

What the gap breaks.
- As printed, Definition 9.1 lets α be units at Q. For α ∈ O_v^×, diag(α^{(k)},1) ∈ K_{Q,v} normalises L_{Q,v}. So T_{α,k} is the deck transformation of class α^{k−n}. T^an_{Q,1} therefore contains the diamond operators, and the p. 415 surjection R_{𝒮_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,𝔪} does not follow for Q ≠ ∅. For Q = ∅ it is fine, and that case is the only one used as a surjection in §9.5 (R_𝒮 ↠ T_𝔪).
- Theorem 6.3(d) (p. 386) has two halves. Both need the compatibility.
  - The first half says the image of S_M lies in the image of R_∞. It is used on p. 388 to make H^*(P_∞) finite over R_∞.
  - The second half says the augmentation ideal maps into the image of ker φ_N. It gives conclusion (iv). The last lines of the proof of Thm 9.19 (p. 428) use (iv) to pass from near-faithfulness of H^{l0}(P_∞) to that of H^{q0}(Y,K/O)^∨_𝔪. Knowing only that ker φ kills H, a quotient of P/𝔞P, is not enough.

Consequences. The proof of Theorem 9.19 is incomplete. Theorem 5.16 is deduced from 9.19 ("follows ... immediately"), and Theorem 1.1 (§10) from 5.16, both under "Assume Conjecture B". Their proofs go through once Conjecture B is strengthened by the clause above. Nothing shows the conditional statements are false, so the affected thing is the proof.

Separate from this candidate: in the same step, condition (b) needs R_{𝒮_Q} to act on the intermediate covers Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M). Conjecture B is stated only for Y_1(Q). - **Misprint** at §9.3, paragraph after Conjecture B, p. 415 (published version). The source says `By dévissage, conditions 4 and 5 are satisfied if and only if they are satisfied for n = 1, e.g., with coefficients in the residue field k = O/ϖ.`; it should be `"... are satisfied if and only if they are satisfied for m = 1, i.e., with coefficients in the residue field k = O/ϖ." The only change needed is n to m. "e.g." should arguably also read "i.e.", but that is stylistic.`. I checked the page image. On PDF p. 119, which is published p. 415 (§9.3, the last sentence of the paragraph after Conjecture B), the text reads "for n = 1". A 300 dpi zoom confirms the letter is n. The arXiv v2 text has the same sentence (cg-v2.txt l. 4604-4606), so this is not a typesetting defect and is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

Conjecture B (pp. 414-415) uses its letters consistently. n is the rank: r̄_m : G_F → GL_n(T^an_{Q,ψ}/m), the characteristic polynomial X^n − ..., and condition (1) "weights equal to [0,1,...,n−1]". The coefficient exponent in conditions (4)(a), (4)(b) and (5) is m: H^i_ψ(Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^m)_m, H^i_ψ(∂Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^m)_m, and H^*_ψ(Y, O/ϖ^m)_m → H^*_ψ(Y_0(Q), O/ϖ^m)_{m_Q}. Read literally, "n = 1" would mean GL_1, which makes no sense here. The phrase "with coefficients in the residue field k = O/ϖ" shows the exponent 1 is intended.

Elsewhere the paper sometimes uses n as a coefficient exponent too. For example, the proof of Lemma 9.6 on p. 416 uses O/ϖ^n while n = 2 is the rank. So the letters are loose in places, but the sentence explicitly refers to conditions 4 and 5, which are written with ϖ^m.

I redid the dévissage myself, and the claim is correct with m. Take the exact sequences 0 → O/ϖ^{m−1} → O/ϖ^m → O/ϖ → 0, where the first map is multiplication by ϖ. The long exact sequences in cohomology are Hecke-equivariant, and localization at m is exact. So by induction, vanishing for m = 1 gives vanishing for all m in (4)(a) and (4)(b). For (5), the maps lim_k ∏ Q_x(V_x)^{k!} come from Hecke operators on complexes, so they commute with the connecting maps. The five lemma then carries the m = 1 isomorphism to all m. The converse direction is trivial.

- **Misprint** at §9.3 (after Conjecture B), Remark 9.3, published p. 415 (PDF p. 119). arXiv v2 (p. 87, Remark 9.3) has the identical text, including the superscript q_0−1 in all three places. arXiv v1 has no Conjecture B or Remark 9.3 (it covers only Part 1, l0 = 1).. The source says `Remark 9.3 ... In the latter two cases (where (q0, l0) = (2, 2) and (2, 1) respectively), the key point is that the lattices in question satisfy the congruence subgroup property [77], which yields vanishing for both (H^1)_𝔪 and (by duality, considering both 𝔪 and 𝔪^*) (H_c^{q_0−1})_𝔪 where 𝔪 is a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal. On the other hand, the vanishing of (H_c^{q_0−1})_𝔪 also implies the vanishing of (H^{q_0−1})_𝔪 after localization at 𝔪, since the cohomology of the boundary vanishes after localization at 𝔪.`; it should be `In all three places, replace the degree q_0−1 by q_0+l_0+1, which equals 2q_0+l_0−1 = d−1 = dim Y here because q_0 = 2. The text then reads "(by duality, considering both m and m^*) (H_c^{q_0+l_0+1})_m ... the vanishing of (H_c^{q_0+l_0+1})_m also implies the vanishing of (H^{q_0+l_0+1})_m". Concretely, this is H_c^5 and H^5 for GL(2)/F with F a quartic CM field, and H_c^4 and H^4 for GL(3)/Q. The candidate's proposed correction, d−1 = 2q_0+l_0−1, is the same thing and is right and minimal.`. I checked the rendered page and the transcription above matches it. §8.4 and §9 of the paper say that Y has real dimension d = 2q0+l0, and that Part (4)(a) of Conjecture B asks for H^i_𝔪 = 0 when i ∉ [q0, q0+l0]. By §8.4's formulas, GL(2) over a CM quartic field (r2 = 2) has l0 = 2 and d = 6, so q0 = 2. GL(3)/Q has l0 = 1 and d = 5, so q0 = 2. In both cases H^{q0−1} = H^1. Poincaré/Verdier duality (see the paper's own use of it in §9 and Remark 9.5) pairs H^i(Y,k)_{𝔪^*} with H_c^{d−i}(Y,k)_𝔪. So "by duality, considering both 𝔪 and 𝔪^*" turns the vanishing of H^1 given by the congruence subgroup property into the vanishing of H_c^{d−1}, not H_c^{q0−1} = H_c^1. The next sentence ("the vanishing of H_c^{q0−1} implies the vanishing of H^{q0−1}", because the boundary cohomology vanishes at 𝔪) is then circular as printed: H^{q0−1} = H^1 is exactly what the congruence subgroup property already gave.

The degree that actually needs this argument is never treated. For GL(2) over a CM quartic field, the range is [2,4] and d = 6. H^0_𝔪 = 0 because 𝔪 is non-Eisenstein. H^6 = 0 by virtual cohomological dimension: vcd = d − (Q-rank) = 6 − 1 = 5. But H^5 is not automatic, and it needs exactly the duality step with degree d−1 = 5 = q0+l0+1. For GL(3)/Q, vcd = 5 − 2 = 3, so H^4 happens to vanish anyway, but the argument as intended still concerns degree d−1 = 4. With the correction, the remark reads coherently: H^1_𝔪 = 0 (congruence subgroup property), so H_c^{d−1}_𝔪 = 0 (duality over 𝔪 and 𝔪^*), so H^{d−1}_𝔪 = 0 (boundary vanishing at 𝔪).

Each printed sentence is literally true: H_c^1_𝔪 ≅ H^1_𝔪 = 0 via the boundary sequence. The fault is the index, which makes the duality step misattributed and leaves the top degree out. The intended meaning (the Poincaré-dual degree of 1) is clear from "by duality", so I class it as an index misprint; "error" is also defensible, since the printed step fails to cover degree d−1. It sits in a remark supporting a conjecture, so nothing proved in the paper depends on it. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The paper sets up Y(K) for G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) in §9, and §8.4 says dim Y = 2q_0+l_0. For GL(2) over a quartic CM field (r_2 = 2) this gives l_0 = 2 and d = 6. For GL(3)/Q it gives l_0 = 1 and d = 5. So q_0 = 2 in both cases, as the remark says.

Part (4)(a) needs the localized cohomology to vanish outside [q_0, q_0+l_0]:
- GL(2)/F: degrees 0, 1, 5 and 6.
- GL(3)/Q: degrees 0, 1, 4 and 5.

H^0_m = 0 because m is non-Eisenstein. H^d = 0 because Y is non-compact. The congruence subgroup property gives H^1_m = 0 for every non-Eisenstein m, including m^*.

Poincaré duality is Hecke-equivariant up to replacing m by m^*: (H_c^{d−i})_m is dual to (H^i)_{m^*}. That is why the text says "considering both m and m^*". So from H^1 it gives vanishing of H_c^{d−1} = H_c^{q_0+l_0+1}, not of H_c^{q_0−1} = H_c^1. The boundary sequence then turns this into (H^{d−1})_m = 0.

As printed, q_0−1 = 1, so the remark fails in two ways:
- Duality is credited with giving H_c^1. H_c^1 does vanish, but through the boundary sequence, not through duality.
- The next sentence concludes (H^1)_m = 0, which was the starting point, so it is circular.
- Degree d−1 is never treated. This matters for GL(2)/F: the virtual cohomological dimension is 6 − 1 = 5 = d−1, so H^5 does not vanish for free. (For GL(3)/Q it is 5 − 2 = 3, so H^4 would vanish anyway.)

Defence considered: no convention in the paper shifts the indexing of H_c. Remark 9.5 uses the same duality, which reverses degrees between cohomology and compactly supported cohomology. No reading makes "q_0−1" the degree that duality produces. The only intended degree consistent with the words "by duality, m and m^*" and with the goal of (4)(a) is d−1 = q_0+l_0+1. The intended meaning is therefore clear from context. It is a wrong-index slip, the protocol's example of a misprint. It could also be called an error with affects = nothing, since the argument as printed does not close; the candidate chose that.

Consequences: Remark 9.3 is cited nowhere else in the paper. The §9 results (Theorem 9.19 etc.) assume Conjecture B outright. The later Ihara-type argument uses the congruence subgroup property of the S-arithmetic group PSL_2(O_F[1/x]) on its own, not this remark. The remark's claim, that (4)(a) can be checked in these cases, is true once the degree is corrected. - **Gap** at §9 (Conjecture B discussion), Remark 9.3, published p. 415 (PDF p. 119). arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2) has identical text, citing [BMS67]. arXiv v1 ("... I") has no such remark. Serre's 1970 SL_2 paper is not in the bibliography of either version; the only other Serre item nearby is [78], Arbres, amalgames, SL_2.. The source says `Remark 9.3 Part (4)(a) of Conjecture B may be verified directly in a number of small rank cases, in particular for GL(2)/F when F is CM field of degree either 2 or 4, or for GL(3)/Q. In the latter two cases (where (q_0, l_0) = (2, 2) and (2, 1) respectively), the key point is that the lattices in question satisfy the congruence subgroup property [77], which yields vanishing for both (H^1)_m and (by duality, considering both m and m^*) (H_c^{q_0-1})_m where m is a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal. [Bibliography] 77. Bass, H., Milnor, J., Serre, J.-P.: Solution of the congruence subgroup problem for SL_n (n ≥ 3) and Sp_2n (n ≥ 2). Inst. Hautes Études Sci. Publ. Math. 33, 59–137 (1967)`; it should be `Cite Serre's paper as well: J.-P. Serre, "Le problème des groupes de congruence pour SL2", Ann. of Math. (2) 92 (1970), 489–527. Suggested wording: "...satisfy the congruence subgroup property ([77] for GL(3)/Q; Serre, Ann. of Math. 92 (1970) for GL(2)/F with F CM of degree 4)". Serre proves that the congruence kernel of SL2(O_S) is finite when |S| ≥ 2, that is, when O_F^× is infinite. For a CM quartic field the unit rank is r1+r2−1 = 1, so this applies. For a totally imaginary F the kernel is μ(F), which is finite but not trivial. So "congruence subgroup property" here has to mean a finite kernel. The proposed correction is right and minimal.`. I rendered PDF p. 119 and read the text: "the latter two cases" are GL(2)/F with F CM of degree 4 ((q_0,l_0)=(2,2)) and GL(3)/Q ((2,1)), and the paper cites only [77] for both. [77] is Bass–Milnor–Serre, whose title and content restrict it to SL_n with n ≥ 3 and Sp_2n with n ≥ 2. Since Sp_2 = SL_2 is excluded, SL_2 is not covered. For the GL(2)/F case the lattice sits in G = SL_2 over F (the restriction of scalars of SL_2 from F), and no isogeny turns this into SL_n with n ≥ 3 or Sp_2n with n ≥ 2. I checked the attribution in the survey by Prasad–Rapinchuk, "Developments on the congruence subgroup problem after the work of Bass, Milnor and Serre" (arXiv:0809.1622), §2.3: "The results obtained in [3] exhibited two possibilities for C^S(G) for G = SL_n (n ⩾ 3) and Sp_2n (n ⩾ 2) ... Subsequently, it was shown in [49] that this description of C^S(G) remains valid for G = SL_2 if |S| > 1." Here [3] is BMS and [49] is Serre 1970. §5.6 of the same survey calls the SL_2 case with |S| > 1 "established first by Serre in [49]". BMS §15 only states the metaplectic conjecture for SL_2. For F a CM quartic field, S is the set of archimedean places, which are 2 complex places, so |S| = 2 and Dirichlet gives unit rank 1. Serre's theorem therefore applies and gives C ≅ μ_F. The mathematical claim in the remark is true, but the reference given does not prove it for one of the two cases it is cited for. That is an asserted step without adequate support, i.e. a citation gap. It sits in a heuristic remark and the statement is true, so nothing downstream is affected. The case for the paper is only partly sound. For GL(3)/Q the lattices are commensurable with SL3(Z), and [77] proves a trivial congruence kernel there, so the citation fits. For GL(2)/F with F a quartic CM field, the lattices are commensurable with SL2(O_F), or equivalently with arithmetic subgroups of SL2(C)^2. [77] cannot cover them. Its title and theorems are limited to SL_n with n ≥ 3 and Sp_2n with n ≥ 2, which excludes Sp_2 = SL2. The SL2 case was left open there and settled later by Serre (Ann. Math. 1970), who showed the kernel is finite exactly when |S| ≥ 2. The fact the remark asserts is true: F has 2 complex places, so |S| = 2 and CSP holds with kernel μ(F). The imaginary-quadratic case is correctly left out of "the latter two cases", since |S| = 1 there and CSP fails. So the mathematics is right, but half of its stated justification is missing. This matches the repo's precedent of recording a missing or wrong citation as "gap / nothing". It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Consequences: [77] is used only in this remark, nothing in the paper refers back to Remark 9.3, and the remark is a side comment on how plausible Conjecture B is. All later results in §9 assume Conjecture B as a hypothesis. Side note, not verified: for totally imaginary F the kernel μ(F) is nontrivial, so the "yields vanishing of (H^1)_m" step may need extra care when p divides |μ(F)|. The remark is informal ("may be verified directly"), and this candidate does not claim that. - **Error** at §9.3, Conjecture B, the italic paragraph after the display in (5), published p. 415 (PDF p. 119). arXiv v2, p. 87 has the same text. arXiv v1 (Part I) has no §9 and no Conjecture B. The surjection is used in the proof of Theorem 9.19, p. 426: "By Conjecture B, we have surjections R_S ↠ T_m and R_{S^χ} ↠ T_{χ,m}". The freedom in ξ comes from §8.5, p. 407.. The source says `(Italic, inside Conjecture B, after the display in (5).) "It follows that r_m is a deformation of r̄ of type S_Q (resp. S_Q^χ) if each ψ_v is the trivial character (resp. ψ_v = χ_v for each v ∈ R). In this case, we obtain a surjection R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,m} (resp. R_{S_Q^χ} ↠ T^an_{Q,χ,m})."`; it should be `Either add "(when ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2})", which is the choice forced in Theorem 5.16 by (7), or, keeping ξ general, replace the claim by: "It follows that r_m ⊗ θ^{1/n}, where θ := ξε^{−n(n−1)/2}, is a deformation of r̄ of type S_Q (resp. S_Q^χ) ...". Here θ is unramified everywhere, trivial mod m_O and of p-power order, and θ^{1/n} is well defined because p > n. The surjection R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,m} then holds as printed. The candidate's correction (add the hypothesis ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}) is right and minimal.`. I checked the rendered pages 407, 408, 412, 413, 414 and 415.
(i) In §9, G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) (p. 412). So g = diag(α,…,α) is trivial in G(A^∞), and T_{α,n} = T(1) = id. The normalised T_{λ,n} is therefore a scalar: N(λ)^{−n} as printed, or 1 with the §5 normalisation. The constant term of the characteristic polynomial in Conjecture B then makes det r_m(Frob_λ) a fixed power of N(λ). By Chebotarev, det r_m = ε^k with k fixed; k = n(n−1)/2 once the normalisation is repaired (X-K9-0, a separate issue).
(ii) Type S_Q requires "(2) it is of determinant ξ" (§8.5.2, p. 408). The local rings R_v, R_v^1, R_v^{χ_v} and D_v also fix the determinant as ξ.
(iii) §8.5 (p. 407) fixes ξ only as a continuous lift of det r̄ with ξ|_{I_v} = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for v | p and ξ|_{I_v} = 1 for v ∤ p. It then says "For example, we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}". Nothing in §9 or §9.5 specialises ξ; the only occurrences of ξ are in §8.5. So θ = ξε^{−n(n−1)/2} is unramified at every finite place, hence a character of the narrow class group, and θ ≡ 1 mod m. It can be non-trivial.
Concrete admissible data: F = Q(√−23) (h = 3), p = 3 > n = 2, where 3 is unramified and split, and O = Z_3[ζ_3]. Take θ a non-trivial character Cl(F) → μ_3 and ξ = εθ. This satisfies every condition of §8.5. Then det r_m = ε ≠ εθ = ξ in T_m^× whenever θ is non-trivial in T_m, for example when m supports characteristic-0 cohomology, as with π_0 in Theorem 5.16(8a). In that case r_m is not of type S_Q, so "It follows" fails.
The fix is harmless. Theorem 5.16(7) forces ξ = det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2} when Theorem 9.19 is applied. Alternatively, twisting by η restores a type-S_Q lift, and the surjection survives because the η(Frob_λ) are units.
This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It is also distinct from X-K9-0: after that correction the issue remains unless ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}. As an alternative classification, this is a missing hypothesis, which could be recorded as a gap. I checked all three passages against the page images (PDF pp. 111, 112, 118, 119).

(1) What the determinant of r_m is. In §9, G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) (p. 411). T_{α,n} is the Hecke operator for diag(α,…,α), which is trivial in PGL_n, so T_{α,n} = id. With the unnormalised operators, the constant term of the characteristic polynomial in Conjecture B gives det r_m(Frob_λ) = N(λ)^{n(n−1)/2} for all λ ∉ S_Q. Chebotarev then gives det r_m = ε^{n(n−1)/2}. This uses the correction of X-K9-0 / H-part2-17. With the printed 1/N(a)^k normalisation one gets ε^{n(n−3)/2}, which is a separate error. Either way, det r_m is a fixed power of ε and has nothing to do with ξ.

(2) What type S_Q requires. It requires det = ξ (condition (2), p. 408). §8.5 allows any ξ lifting det r̄ with the stated restrictions on inertia. Since r̄_m ≅ r̄ gives det r̄ = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}, the character θ = ξε^{−n(n−1)/2} is unramified at every finite place and trivial mod m_O. It is also trivial at real places, because p is odd. So θ is a character of Cl_F of p-power order. It can be non-trivial whenever p | h_F and ζ_p ∈ O. The paper forces ζ_p ∈ O as soon as R ≠ ∅, since the distinct χ_{v,i}/ψ_v factor through (k_v^×)^n/k_v^× into 1+m_O. Example: F = Q(√−23), h_F = 3, p = 3 > n = 2, 3 splits in F, O ∋ ζ_3, θ : Cl_F ↠ μ_3, ξ = εθ. Every §8.5 condition holds, but det r_m = ε ≠ ξ. So "It follows that r_m is of type S_Q" fails for this choice of ξ. If p ∤ h_F, ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2} is forced and the sentence is correct. Nothing in §9 fixes ξ.

(3) The defence, and why nothing downstream breaks. θ has p-power order and p > n, so θ^{1/n} exists, is unramified everywhere and is ≡ 1 mod m_O. The twist r_m ⊗ θ^{1/n} reduces to r̄ and has det ξ. At v|p it is still Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1], since the twist is unramified and within the FL range. At v ∈ R its inertial characteristic polynomials are unchanged. At v ∈ Q it is still of type D_v. So it is of type S_Q (resp. S_Q^χ). Its trace algebra equals that of r_m, because tr(r_m⊗θ^{1/n})(g) = θ^{1/n}(g)·tr r_m(g) with θ^{1/n}(g) ∈ O^×. So R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,m} still exists.

Where the sentence is used:
- §9.5, p. 426: "By Conjecture B, we have surjections R_S ↠ T_m and R_{S^χ} ↠ T_{χ,m}".
- Theorem 9.19 and its proof, p. 427, where R_{S_{Q_N}} acts on cohomology "by Conjecture B".
All of these survive if one uses the same fixed twist for every N and for both the 1- and χ-versions; the twist also commutes with the diamond and inertia data at Q. Theorem 5.16 assumes det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2} (hypothesis (7)), and r must be of type S, so ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2} there and the printed sentence is literally correct. Theorem 1.1 goes through 5.16.

So the paper's text is a genuine, harmless slip: the asserted step fails for some ξ that §8.5 allows. The candidate labels it a gap; 'error' fits PROTOCOL §18 slightly better, because the step is false rather than merely unproved. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The source says `"such that the composition φ^∨ ∘ φ is the matrix ( N(x)+1 T_x ; T_x N(x)+1 ), which has determinant T_x^2 − (1 + N(x))^2. With a = N(x)+1 and b = T_x this gives (1+N(x))^2 − T_x^2. The paper prints T_x^2 − (1+N(x))^2, which is the negative, so this is a real sign slip. The matrix is taken exactly as printed, so no convention in the paper makes the stated sign right. The expression is used only once afterwards, to say it is not in 𝔪, and so φ^∨∘φ is invertible after localizing. That property does not depend on the sign. Mod 𝔪 we have T_x ≡ α+β and N(x) ≡ αβ ≡ 1, so the expression reduces to ±(1−α)(1−β)(1+α)(1+β). This is nonzero exactly when α, β ≢ ±1, which is the Taylor–Wiles condition. A search of the text finds the expression nowhere else. The 47 known bracket errors are unrelated. - **Gap** at §9.3, proof of Lemma 9.6, published pp. 417–418 (PDF pp. 121–122), checked on the rendered pages. The arXiv v2 text is word for word the same (v2 p. 89, cg-v2.txt ll. 4689–4717). arXiv v1 has no amalgam or Lyndon argument: a grep finds neither word. (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 417: "For convenience, let us also assume that x is trivial in the ray class group corresponding to the component group of Y (this is equivalent to imposing a further congruence condition on x, but is imposed only for notational convenience in the argument below). ... (Without the extra assumption on x, one would have to amalgamate different pairs of lattices Γ_i occurring in the decomposition of Y according to the action of the ray class group, cf. Sect. 4.1.4 of [6]. The argument would then proceed quite similarly, but it would require more notation)". p. 418: "We claim that this sequence is equivariant with respect to the Hecke operator U_{x^2}, which acts on H^*(G, O/ϖ^n) by 1. First, recall the definition of U_{x^2}. It is defined to be 1/N(x)^2 times the operator induced by taking the double coset operator for Γ^1_0(x) corresponding to the matrix: (π_x^2 0; 0 1). ... g := (π_x 0; 0 π_x^{-1}). With this normalization, the matrix g lies in G. In particular, the corresponding map on H^*(G, O/ϖ^n) is given by multiplication by the degree of this operator on Γ^1_0(x), which is N(x)^2, and thus (after normalizing) it follows that U_{x^2} acts by 1."`; it should be `The proof needs the following, all of which can be supplied by standard arguments. (a) Realise the Lyndon sequence as the Ext_G(−, O/ϖ^n) sequence of 0 → C_1(T) → C_0(T) → Z → 0, where T is the Bruhat–Tits tree at x. Then U_{x^2} on H^*(Γ^1_0(x)) is induced by the G-endomorphism T_1 of C_1 ≅ Z[G/Γ^1_0(x)] that sends an edge to the N(x)^2 edges two steps from it. There is a unique G-endomorphism T_0 of C_0 with ∂T_1 = T_0∂: A(v) = v − N·S_1(v) + S_2(v) on one vertex type and B(w) = S_1(w) − N·w on the other. On the Γ^1-terms this is the 2×2 Hecke matrix [[T_x^2 − N, −N T_x],[T_x, −N]], i.e. U_x^2 on oldforms. Its augmentation is 1, so the sequence is equivariant and the un-normalised double coset acts on both H^*(G)-terms by 1. With the paper's 1/N(x)^2 normalisation, U_{x^2} therefore acts on H^*(G) by N(x)^{-2}, not by 1 as printed. This is harmless because N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, so U_{x^2} − N(x)^{-2} is a unit exactly when U_{x^2} − 1 is. (b) For general x: the operator diag(ϖ_x, ϖ_x^{-1}) ∈ SL_2(F_x) preserves components, and the same tree argument applies to each component's S-arithmetic group. Its two vertex stabilisers are the Γ^1-lattices of the components paired by [x], as in [6, §4.1.4]. (c) Also needed: the Φ-invariants and T^an-localisation bookkeeping behind "repeat this argument for each lattice Γ_i".`. 1. I rendered pp. 416–418 and transcribed the text above. The v2 text is the same, so this is not a bracket defect.

2. The proof asserts equivariance of the whole Lyndon/Mayer–Vietoris sequence, including the connecting map H^{i-1}(Γ^1_0(x)) → H^i(G). It never defines U_{x^2} on H^*(Γ^1)^2 or on H^*(G). Its only justification is that g ∈ G, so "the corresponding map on H^*(G) is multiplication by the degree N(x)^2". What this argument actually proves is U_{x^2}∘res^G_{Γ_0} = res^G_{Γ_0}. That is not a map in the sequence: the composite H^i(G) → H^i(Γ^1)^2 → H^i(Γ_0) is res − res = 0.

3. I checked from scratch which action the sequence really carries. G = Γ^1 *_{Γ^1_0} Γ^1 acts on the (q+1)-regular tree with quotient one edge. The sequence comes from 0 → Z[E] → Z[V] → Z → 0 via Ext_G(−, M), using Shapiro for compact induction. The Hecke operator T is the G-endomorphism of Z[E] described in the correction, and its image T(e) has q^2 terms. A G-equivariant lift T_V to Z[V] with T_V∂ = ∂T must be a finite combination of distance spheres. Solving the coefficient equations forces T_V(v0) = v0 − qS_1(v0) + S_2(v0) and T_V(v1) = −qv1 + S_1(v1). The lift is unique because G has no nonzero invariants in Z[V]. Using the other translation direction gives the mirror formulas. In both cases εT_V(v0) = 1 − q(q+1) + q(q+1) = 1 and εT_V(v1) = −q + (q+1) = 1. By naturality of connecting maps, δ∘T = δ, so T acts on H^*(G) by 1, not by N(x)^2.

4. A python check on tree balls for q = 2, 3, 4 confirms ∂T = T_V∂ and ε∘T_V = 1 (tree.py in my agent folder).

5. A degree-0 sanity check with trivial coefficients: T acts on H^0(Γ_0) by q^2. On H^0(Γ^1)^2 the lift gives the matrix [[1+q(q+1), −q(q+1)], [q+1, −q]], whose eigenvalues are 1 (on the diagonal, which is the image of H^0(G)) and q^2.

6. No other equivariant structure can give N(x)^2 on H^*(G) in general. It would need (N(x)^2 − 1)δ = 0, which fails for O/ϖ^m once m is large relative to the Taylor–Wiles level.

7. So the printed claim "U_{x^2} acts by 1" is literally wrong by the unit N(x)^{-2} ≡ 1 mod p, and the equivariance it rests on is asserted, not shown. The conclusion still holds, because only invertibility mod ϖ is used and α_x ≢ ±1.

8. The restriction to x trivial in the ray class group is acknowledged and the general case is waved at [6, §4.1.4]. I could not consult [6], which is cited as a Calegari–Venkatesh preprint.

Overall the candidate's description (equivariance asserted, not shown; the general case of x only sketched) is accurate. Lemma 9.6 itself is not in doubt. Defence first.
- The lemma is true, and the authors flag the argument as "implicit in … Chapter 4 of [6]".
- They explicitly reduce to x trivial in the ray class group and point to [6, §4.1.4] for the general case, which is indeed only notational (see (b)).
- The equivariance also holds. I checked the chain-level identity ∂T_1(e) = B(v_1) − A(v_0) by script on (N+1)-regular trees for N = 2, 3, 4, for both the forward and the backward double coset. It holds, with aug A = aug B = 1 and exactly N^2 edges in T_1(e).

The objection still stands, for two reasons.
1. The paper never defines the U_{x^2}-action on the middle term H^*(Γ^1)^2 and never proves that the maps of the sequence commute with it. The one justification it gives ("g ∈ G, so the map on H^*(G) is multiplication by the degree N(x)^2") computes [KgK]∘res^G_{Γ^1_0(x)}. That is not a map in the sequence: the composite H^*(G) → H^*(Γ^1)^2 → H^*(Γ^1_0(x)) is zero.
2. That justification also gives the wrong scalar. By naturality of the connecting map for the endomorphism (T_1, T_0, id_Z), δ∘[KgK] = δ. So on the image of δ the compatible scalar is 1 for the un-normalised operator, i.e. N(x)^{-2} for the paper's U_{x^2}. This differs from the printed 1 in O/ϖ^n whenever ϖ^n does not divide N(x)^2 − 1. It is harmless for the localisation, since N(x) ≡ 1 mod p.

So the key step is asserted without an adequate proof, and the stated result is not in doubt. The general-x case and the per-component and Φ bookkeeping are only sketched, but they are routine.

Consequences: Lemma 9.6 is cited nowhere else. Only Remark 9.8 discusses it. Theorems 9.19, 5.16 and 1.1 assume Conjecture B in full (including part 5) for each Q_N. The gap therefore affects only this proof.

- F totally real cubic: the fibres are 2-tori.
- The statement is literally true only when r1+r2 = 2.

A non-standard choice such as K_∞ = SU(n) at complex places changes the count, but it still does not give circles in general.

So the fibre dimension is r1+r2−1 (or r1+r2 without the R_{>0} quotient). It is 1 only for r1+r2 = 2, e.g. a real quadratic field or a cubic field with one complex place. No ordering is specified, so n-ind(χ^w) is that same π. Lemma 9.10 and Definition 9.11 also treat 𝒞 as a block with the single irreducible π.

(2) Directly: the normalized Jacquet module of n-ind(χ^w) has constituents χ^v (v ∈ W), each once. These are pairwise distinct on the uniformizers, so Ext^i vanishes between them (the paper says this itself) and the Jacquet module is a direct sum. So χ is a quotient, and Frobenius reciprocity gives a nonzero map n-ind(χ^w) → n-ind(χ). Both sides are irreducible (Lemma 9.9; with q ≡ 1 mod p the reducibility condition χ_i/χ_j = ν^{±1} reduces to χ_i = χ_j, which does not occur). So the map is an isomorphism. By exactness of n-ind, every constituent of n-ind M^w_B is ≅ π, for every w.

The inference the paper needs is this: M has only π-constituents, so its projections to the w ≠ id summands are zero, so injectivity into ⊕_W gives injectivity into the id-summand. That inference rests entirely on the false clause. Injectivity of M → ⊕_W n-ind M^w_B does not rule out a kernel of the id-projection. I found no charitable reading: "distinct from π" can only mean non-isomorphic, and no nearby statement supplies the missing step.

The paper's own tools repair the step: the same adjunction and kernel argument, restricted to the id-eigenspace. Length equality holds as the paper says: length_A(M_B) = length_G(M), and n-ind(χ) = π is irreducible. So the lemma is true.

Downstream uses: Lemma 9.12 is not cited by number. It is used implicitly in Cor. 9.13 (n-ind gives an equivalence with R-modules), in Lemma 9.14 ("Using this description of 𝒞"), and in the proof of Thm. 9.16 ("we may assume that M = n-ind^G_B M_B"). All of these need only the true statement, so no stated result is affected. §9.4 is also explicitly labelled an "informal approach". This is not one of the 47 bracket defects.

(a) GL2/Q: rank G = 2, rank O(2) = 1, Q-rank = 2, so l0 = −1, which is impossible.
(b) Res_{F/Q}GL2 with F imaginary quadratic: complexified Lie algebra gl2 ⊕ gl2 has rank 4, rank U(2) = 2, Q-rank = 2, so l0 = 0 instead of 1.
(c) Res_{F/Q}PGL2 with F imaginary quadratic, the paper's own Part 1 case: 2 − 1 − 1 = 0, but the paper treats this case as l0 = 1 (Part 1 "l0 equals 1"; §8.3 "n = 2 and l0 = 1").

With A taken as the Q-split torus in the centre, every value comes out right: GL2/Q gives 0, GL2 over imaginary quadratic F gives 1, PGL2 gives 1 (trivial central torus), and Res GL1 gives r1 + r2 − 1, matching §8.2. So the printed definition is wrong as stated and the fix is the missing "in the centre". It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It is also in the accepted arXiv v2, so it is not a production artifact. On length, the paragraph does say "length l0 + 1" and then "length l0", but each use is correct under its own meaning: number of degrees versus length of the interval. That part is a stylistic inconsistency, not an error. The paper's main convention elsewhere is "range of length l0", including p. 300 below, and Part 2's "degrees of arbitrary length l0" and "range of degrees of length l0". - **Misprint** at §9.4.1, Remark 9.15, p. 422 (published version). The source says `Remark 9.15 Since the group U(x) is pro-p, the higher cohomology of U(x) vanishes. Hence, for any subgroup U(x) ⊂ Γ ⊂ G(O_x), by Hochschild–Serre there are identifications H^i(Γ, M) ≃ H^i(Γ/U(x), M^{U(x)}). [published p. 422 = PDF p. 126, §9.4.1; arXiv v2 p. 92 has the identical wording "Since the group U(x) is pro-p, the higher cohomology of U(x) vanishes."]`; it should be `Replace "pro-p" with "pro-ℓ, where ℓ ≠ p is the residue characteristic of x (so U(x) is pro-prime-to-p)". The phrase "the higher cohomology of U(x) vanishes" should say "with coefficients in any M ∈ 𝒞" (these are smooth, p-power-torsion A = O/ϖ^k-modules). Nothing else in the remark needs to change. Both candidates propose this correction. It is correct and minimal.`. Checked on the rendered page images (published PDF p. 126 = p. 422, and v2 p. 92): "pro-p" is printed as quoted, with no lost prime such as p′. Setup (§9.4.1, p. 421): x is a prime of F with N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, and U(x) ⊂ G(O_x) = GL_n(O_x) is the full congruence subgroup of level x. Let ℓ be the residue characteristic of x, so N(x) = ℓ^f. If ℓ = p, then N(x) ≡ 0 mod p, which contradicts N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, so ℓ ≠ p. U(x) = 1 + ϖ_x M_n(O_x) has successive quotients (1+ϖ^i M_n)/(1+ϖ^{i+1} M_n) ≅ M_n(O_x/x), which are elementary abelian ℓ-groups. So U(x) is pro-ℓ and not pro-p. The coefficient modules M lie in C, which consists of smooth modules over A = O/ϖ^k, so they are p-power torsion and ℓ acts invertibly. For a pro-ℓ group, H^i(U(x), M) = lim H^i(U(x)/V, M^V) is then 0 for i ≥ 1, which is the vanishing the remark needs. The stated reason would give the opposite: a nontrivial pro-p group U has H^1(U, F_p) = Hom(U, F_p) ≠ 0, and U(x) is infinite. So the sentence as printed is false, but the intended meaning (pro-prime-to-p) is clear from context and from the correct conclusion. That makes it a slip rather than a failed argument, so I class it as a misprint under PROTOCOL §18; "error" is also defensible, since "U(x) is pro-p" is a false statement. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, which the 2022 Correction lists and which concern only ⟦ ⟧. Only the stated reason is wrong. The conclusion (U(x)-cohomology vanishes, so Hochschild–Serre gives H^i(Γ,M) ≃ H^i(Γ/U(x), M^{U(x)})) is correct. So the later use of the remark still holds: identifying R^kF ≃ H^k(G(O_x),M) and R^kG ≃ e_α H^k(U_0(x),M) on p. 422, and hence Theorem 9.16 and §9.4.2. Two small comments on the candidate: its locator (§9.4.1, Remark 9.15, p. 422; same in v2) is correct. Its correction is right, though the letter ℓ is also used for the invariant l_0 elsewhere in the paper, so "pro-prime-to-p" may be clearer. Defence attempted and failed. In §9.4.1 (p. 421), p is the paper's fixed global prime: x is a prime of F with N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, π is a mod-p representation, and 𝒞 is the category of locally admissible G-modules over A := O/ϖ^k. There is no local convention under which p could mean the residue characteristic of x. U(x) is the full congruence subgroup of level x in G(O_x) = GL_n(O_x), so U(x) = 1 + ϖ_x M_n(O_x). Its successive quotients are ≅ M_n(O_x/x), which are elementary abelian ℓ-groups, where ℓ is the residue characteristic of x. Since N(x) = ℓ^f ≡ 1 mod p, we get ℓ ≠ p. So U(x) is infinite and pro-ℓ, and not pro-p. The stated reason would in fact give the opposite conclusion: a nontrivial pro-p group U has H^1(U, F_p) = Hom(U, F_p) ≠ 0.

The conclusion is nonetheless true for the right reason. Take M ∈ 𝒞, which is smooth and p-power torsion. Then H^i(U(x), M) = colim_V H^i(U(x)/V, M^V) over open normal V. Each U(x)/V is a finite ℓ-group, and |U(x)/V| acts invertibly on M, so this is 0 for i ≥ 1. U(x) is normal in G(O_x), hence in every Γ between U(x) and G(O_x), so Hochschild–Serre gives H^i(Γ, M) ≃ H^i(Γ/U(x), M^{U(x)}) as printed.

The slip may have come from the paragraph on p. 421, where "pro-p image" is correctly said of the deformation χ̃ restricted to D(O_x). Only the justifying adjective is wrong, and the intended meaning (pro-prime-to-p) is forced by the correct conclusion. So I class it as a misprint under PROTOCOL §18. "Error" is also defensible, since "U(x) is pro-p" is literally false; the candidates chose that label.

Consequences. Remark 9.15 is used on p. 422 to identify R^k𝓕(M) ≃ H^k(G(O_x), M) and R^k𝓖(M) ≃ e_α H^k(U_0(x), M). It is used again implicitly in Remark 9.18 (p. 424) for R^1𝓕(π) ≃ H^1(GL_n(k), π^{U(x)}) and R^1𝓖(π) ≃ e_α H^1(U_0(k), π^{U(x)}). Through these it feeds Theorem 9.16 and §9.4.2. All of these uses need only the vanishing of U(x)-cohomology on 𝒞, which holds. So no statement or proof is affected. - **Gap** at §9.5, opening sentences, p. 424 (PDF p. 128). Also: the sentence after Theorem 5.16 on p. 384; Theorem 5.16(4) and (6) on p. 383; the §8.5 standing hypotheses and the definition of R on pp. 406–407; the §9.5 bigness hypothesis on p. 425. arXiv v2 has the same text: Theorem 5.16(4),(6) are identical (it cites [CHT08] Def. 2.5.1), and so are §8.5 ("N_{F/Q}(v) ≡ 1 mod p if r̄ is ramified at v") and "We note that Theorem 5.16 follows from it immediately as a corollary." arXiv v1 has no Part 2, so no counterpart. The 2022 Correction concerns only the brackets. (it affects a stated result). The source says `§9.5, p. 424: "In this section we prove our main theorem on modularity lifting. We note that Theorem 5.16 follows from it immediately as a corollary." Theorem 5.16, p. 383: "(4) In the terminology of [3], Definition 2.5.1, r̄ is big." and "(6) If r is ramified at a prime x, then r|I_x is unipotent. Moreover, if, furthermore, r̄ is unramified at x, then N(x) ≡ 1 mod p." (The bar is on r in the second sentence; checked at 300 dpi.) p. 384: "This theorem will follow immediately from Theorem 9.19, proved below." §8.5, p. 406: "• For each v ∤ p, r̄|G_v has at worst unipotent ramification and N_{F/Q}(v) ≡ 1 mod p if r̄ is ramified at v." p. 407: "Let R denote a finite set of primes of F disjoint from S_p that contains all primes at which r̄ ramifies and is such that N_{F/Q}(v) ≡ 1 mod p for each v ∈ R." §9.5, p. 425: "We assume also that r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big."`; it should be `State in Theorem 5.16 the hypotheses under which Theorem 9.19 is proved. (6) should read "If r is ramified at a prime x, then r|I_x is unipotent and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p", i.e. delete the proviso "if, furthermore, r̄ is unramified at x". (4) should read "r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big (in the sense of [3, Definition 2.5.1])". This is exactly what §8.5 (p. 406 bullet; R ⊇ ramification primes of r̄ with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p), Proposition 8.5 and §9.5 assume. The alternative is a separate argument for primes where r̄ is unipotently ramified and N(x) ≢ 1 mod p. In case (8a) that could be a solvable base change followed by descent, which is not "immediate". In case (8b) it is unavailable, since the authors themselves note 8b is not obviously preserved under base change. The candidate's proposed correction is right and essentially minimal.`. Checked from the page images. Theorem 9.19 is proved inside the §8.5/§9.5 setup. That setup explicitly assumes N(v) ≡ 1 mod p at every v ∤ p where r̄ ramifies. It also needs a set R that contains all primes where r̄ ramifies and has N(v) ≡ 1 mod p for each v ∈ R.

This congruence is actually used. Lemma 8.2, whose conclusion "Spec R^χ_loc is irreducible" is needed for Theorem 6.4, rests on [76, Lemma 3.3] and Taylor's [11, Prop. 3.1]. Those are Ihara-avoidance local computations in the setting q_v ≡ 1 mod p. The characters χ_{v,i} of p-power order that the rings R_v^χ need must also be nontrivial.

Theorem 5.16(6) imposes N(x) ≡ 1 mod p only where r is ramified and r̄ is not. Where r̄ is ramified, it asks nothing. Such cases exist. Take n=2 and E an elliptic curve with multiplicative reduction at x, p ∤ ord_x(Δ_E) and N(x) ≢ 1 mod p. By Tate-curve theory, r̄ = E[p] is ramified at x and r|I_x is unipotent, so (6) holds, but no R as in §8.5 can exist. So Theorem 9.19 does not apply, and the claim that Theorem 5.16 is "immediate" fails in this case.

This is not just a formality for n ≥ 3. Take n = 3, q = N(x) ≢ 1 mod p, and r̄|I_x unipotent of Jordan type (2,1), with Frobenius eigenvalues a, aq on the block and b ≡ aq² on the rest. Then there are unipotent lifts of type (2,1) and of type (3), so R_x^1[1/p] can have more than one component. Without the nontrivial χ_{x,i}, Ihara avoidance is not available, and nothing in the paper handles this. Hypothesis 8b does not exclude it, since r may still be non-minimally ramified at primes where r̄ ramifies.

Secondary point: (4) says only "r̄ is big" (CHT Def. 2.5.1 applies to subgroups), while Prop. 8.5 and §9.5 assume r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big. Bigness does not obviously pass to the normal subgroup of prime-to-p index: H^1(H, ad^0) = H^1(H', ad^0)^{H/H'} does not force H^1(H', ad^0) = 0. This part could be read as loose wording, and I did not build an explicit counterexample.

Theorem 1.1 is likely unaffected. In §10, Theorem 5.16 is applied over fields L chosen by Moret–Bailly, and there these extra conditions can be arranged. What is affected is Theorem 5.16 in the generality stated. Defence attempted, and it fails.

(a) Congruence condition. The whole proof of Theorem 9.19 lives in the §8.5 setting. There R must contain every prime where r̄ ramifies and have N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. The Hecke side (§9.1) uses Iwahori level at v ∈ R with characters ψ_v of Iw(v)/Iw_1(v) = (k_v^×)^n/k_v^× → 1+m_O, and these are trivial unless p | N(v)−1. Lemma 8.2, which gives irreducibility of Spec R^χ_loc for Taylor's trick, is proved via [11, Prop. 3.1], which assumes q_v ≡ 1 mod p.

Theorem 5.16(6) imposes the congruence only where r is ramified and r̄ is not. So it admits r̄ that is unipotently ramified at x with N(x) ≢ 1 mod p. Example: n = 2, E semistable with multiplicative reduction at x, p ∤ ord_x(Δ). Case (8b) makes this especially clear: r is then ramified only where r̄ is, so (6) imposes no congruence at all. Such x cannot lie in R, so Theorem 9.19 does not apply.

Putting x in R with trivial χ_x does not repair the argument when n ≥ 3. Example: n = 3, q̄ = N(x) mod p with q̄, q̄² ≠ 1, r̄|G_x with Frobenius eigenvalues ᾱ, q̄ᾱ, q̄²ᾱ and rank-1 monodromy. Unipotent lifts then lie on two distinct components of R^1_x[1/p], one with regular N and one with rank-1 N. Without Ihara avoidance, r and r_p(π_0) may lie on different components.

The condition in (6) mirrors the n = 2 condition of Part I, which is harmless there because the unipotent ring at a ramified r̄ is just the Steinberg component. For general n it is not.

(b) Bigness. CHT Definition 2.5.1 defines bigness of a subgroup of GL_n(k), so "r̄ is big" literally means r̄(G_F) is big. Prop. 8.5 and §9.5 need r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) to be big, and (3) does not bridge the gap. Computation (script h1.py in my scratch dir): take p = 7, n = 3, r̄ = Sym² ρ̄ with ρ̄(G_F) = GL_2(F_7), det ρ̄ = ε̄, and F linearly disjoint from Q(ζ_7).
- H^1(GL_2(F_7), ad^0 Sym²) = 0, so r̄(G_F) is big (the other conditions are easily checked).
- H^1(SL_2(F_7), ad^0 Sym²) has dimension 1, so r̄(G_{F(ζ_7)}) is not big.
- (3) still holds.
- r = Sym² of an elliptic curve's 7-adic representation satisfies (1), (2), (5) and (7).
Taken alone, (4) could be read charitably as a slip for the standard hypothesis. Together with (a), though, the claimed "immediate" deduction does not cover the stated generality.

Consequences: only Theorem 5.16 as stated is affected. Its only later use is the sketch in §10 (proof of Theorem 1.1, potential modularity and Sato–Tate). There the stronger hypotheses can be arranged: take p large and L linearly disjoint, so the image of G_{L(ζ_p)} contains Sym^{2n−1} SL_2(F_p), which is big. Then a further solvable base change, unramified at p, makes N(x) ≡ 1 mod p at the finitely many ramified primes, and the paper notes this preserves 8a. So Theorem 1.1 is unaffected, but Theorem 5.16 is proved only under the corrected hypotheses. (1) Q_N versus Q: §9.5 introduces only the sets Q_N ('For each integer N ≥ 1, let Q_N be a set of primes …'). Δ̃ is declared to be the Galois group of Y_1(Q_N) → Y_0(Q_N), and Δ_N = (Z/p^N)^q with q = |Q_N|. The Hecke projector in the display acts on the cohomology of Y_{Δ_M}(Q_N). The proof of Theorem 9.19 on p. 427 keeps the indices correctly (Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M)). This is a dropped index with a clear intended meaning, so it is a misprint. I agree with the earlier refutation of H-part2-25 on this point, so that part of the candidate is not a new mistake. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Nothing downstream changes. After these two changes, the claim on p. 427 that "the cohomology of D^2_N computes H^*_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_𝔪" holds. Checked on the page images at PDF pp. 116, 129, 130 and 131, and at arXiv v2 p. 95.

1. The paper's definition (§9.1, p. 412) is H_{i,ψ}(Y_i(Q), O) := H_i(Y_i(Q), O(ψ)). Here a section of O(ψ) is an f on π^{-1}(U) with f(γu) = ψ(γ)f(u). So "H_{∗,χ}" means homology with coefficients in O(χ) itself, not in its dual.

2. Recomputation. Let A = O/ϖ^n, which is self-injective. Let C = C_*(Ỹ), a finite free Z[Γ]-complex (via Borel–Serre), and M the monodromy module. Then Hom_A(Hom_{Z[Γ]}(C, M), A) ≅ C ⊗_{Z[Γ]} Hom_A(M, A), and Hom_A(−, A) is exact. So H^i(Y, L)^∨ ≅ H_i(Y, L^∨) canonically. The transpose of T(g) is T(g^{−1}), which gives 𝔪 ↦ 𝔪^∗. Sections g with g(γu) = χ(γ)^{−1}g(u) pair with O(χ) into O, so O(χ)^∨ = O(χ^{−1}). This gives H^*_χ(..)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H_{∗,χ^{−1}}(..)_{𝔪^∗}. Equivalently, the printed right-hand side H_{∗,χ}(..)_{𝔪^∗} is (H^*_{χ^{−1}}(..)_𝔪)^∨.

3. The cited Conjecture B part (4) only covers vanishing outside degrees [q0, q0+l0] and vanishing of boundary cohomology. It cannot turn χ^{−1} into χ.

4. Is the printed isomorphism accidentally true? For n = 2, yes, though not for the reason given. Then χ_{v,2} = χ_{v,1}^{−1}, so χ^{−1} is the Weyl swap of χ. The Iwahori normaliser [[0,1],[ϖ_v,0]] identifies O(χ) with O(wχ) compatibly with Hecke operators away from R. For n ≥ 3 this fails in general. The normaliser only gives cyclic rotations, and a generic tuple of distinct p-power-order characters with trivial product has {χ_i^{−1}} ≠ {χ_i}. So the two sides involve different Bernstein components and inertial types at v: ∏(X−χ_{v,i}) versus ∏(X−χ_{v,i}^{−1}).

5. Where it is used. The proof of Theorem 9.19 (p. 427, first bullet) says the cohomology of D^2_N = D̃^χ_N/ϖ^N computes H^*_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_𝔪, and makes this an R_{S_χ}-module. As printed, D̃^χ_N computes instead the dual of H^*_{χ^{−1}}, which is naturally an R_{S_{χ^{−1}}}-module. So one step of the proof is wrong as printed. The fix is a pure relabelling.

6. The trivial-coefficient analogue on p. 425 is fine. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

On 'affects': I choose "the proof" rather than the candidate's "nothing", because a step of the proof of Theorem 9.19 literally depends on this false identification. No stated result changes: Theorem 9.19 concerns H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪 with trivial coefficients, the χ-side is auxiliary, and the argument survives the relabelling. I tried to defend the printed text, then checked the page images of PDF pp. 116, 117, 129, 130 and 131, and v2 p. 95.

(1) Definitions (p. 412). H_{i,ψ}(Y_i(Q),O) is defined as H_i(Y_i(Q), O(ψ)). Sections of O(ψ) satisfy f(γu) = ψ(γ)f(u). So the subscript χ on H_{∗,χ} means coefficients in O(χ) itself; no convention hides a dual. The pointwise product of an O(ψ)-section and an O(ψ')-section is constant on fibres exactly when ψψ' = 1, so O(χ)^∨ = O(χ^{-1}).

(2) Universal coefficients. A = O/ϖ^n is self-injective, and Hom_A(C_*(Ỹ) ⊗_Γ M, A) = Hom_Γ(C_*(Ỹ), Hom_A(M, A)). This gives H^i(Y, L)^∨ ≅ H_i(Y, L^∨), with T(g) dual to T(g^{-1}), which accounts for 𝔪 ↦ 𝔪^∗. Using Poincaré duality, as in Remark 9.5, still leaves the dual local system. Conjecture B(4) is about vanishing outside degrees [q0, q0+l0] and about the boundary. It cannot change χ^{-1} into χ.

(3) Strongest defence, which works only partly. H^*_χ ≅ H^*_{wχ} holds Hecke-equivariantly away from R for every Weyl permutation w, not just cyclic rotations. The reason is that the Iwahori intertwiners T_s satisfy T_s' T_s = ±q_v, which is a unit because v ∤ p; I checked this numerically for GL_2(F_5). So the printed identity is true whenever {χ_{v,i}^{-1}} = {χ_{v,i}} for every v ∈ R, and in particular always when n = 2, since χ_{v,1}χ_{v,2} = 1. This is not the reason the paper gives. In §8.5.1, however, χ_v is an arbitrary tuple of distinct characters with trivial product. For n ≥ 3 that generally fails the condition. For example, take n = 3, χ_v = (a, a^2, a^{-3}) with a of order p ≥ 5; then {a^{-1}, a^{-2}, a^3} ≠ {a, a^2, a^{-3}}.

(4) Why the printed identity fails in that case. The two sides are Hecke modules of different inertial types, ∏(X−χ_{v,i}) and ∏(X−χ_{v,i}^{-1}) (Conjecture B(3)), and strong multiplicity one separates their rational eigensystems. The printed right-hand side is really (H^*_{χ^{-1}})^∨_𝔪, which is naturally an R_{S^{χ^{-1}}}-module. There is also a semilinear isomorphism through an automorphism σ of O with σχ = χ^{-1}, but it is not O-linear, so it does not rescue the O-linear R^2_∞-structure that patching needs.

(5) Consequences. The only place the paper uses this passage is the proof of Theorem 9.19 (p. 427). There, D^2_N = D̃^χ_N/ϖ^N is said to compute H^*_χ(…)^∨_𝔪, and that identification is used to transport the R_{S^χ_{Q_N}}-action (and hence the R^2_∞ = R^χ_loc[[x]]-action). As printed, that step fails for general χ when n ≥ 3. After relabelling χ to χ^{-1} in the homology, everything goes through: the degree bounds, the minimal complex, and the mod-ϖ identification H^{l0} ≅ H^{l0}_χ, since χ ≡ 1 mod ϖ. Theorem 9.19 concerns H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪 with trivial coefficients, so no stated result changes.

(6) This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The trivial-coefficient analogue on p. 425 is correct.

On classification, I keep 'error' rather than 'misprint'. The subscript χ appears consistently in two displays (the D̃^χ_N definition and the note), and it comes with a justification that does not address the coefficients. So the intended meaning cannot be read off from context; the reader has to redo the duality. I choose 'the proof' rather than the candidate's 'nothing', because a step of the proof as written fails, even though the fix is a relabelling. The arXiv v2 text is the same (v2 p. 95).`; it should be `T^i = H^{q_0+l_0−i}(Y, O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪 for 0 ≤ i ≤ l_0, with zero differentials, so that T^{l_0} = H^{q_0}(Y, O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H/ϖ. Turning the homological complex D̃_N, which sits in degrees q_0, …, q_0+l_0, into a cohomological complex in degrees 0, …, l_0 means taking D^i = D̃_{q_0+l_0−i}. This is a reflection, not a shift by q_0. Hence H^i(D^1_N) ≅ H^{q_0+l_0−i}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_𝔪, and likewise for D^2_N with H_χ. The same slip occurs in the display at the bottom of p. 427 (also in v2). There, "H^{l_0}((D^1_M)^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ) = H^{l_0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^□ ≅ H^{l_0}_χ(…)^□" should read H^{q_0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^{∨,□}_𝔪 ≅ H^{q_0}_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^{∨,□}_𝔪.`. I checked this against the page images at 250 dpi and against the paper's own requirements. (1) Theorem 6.3(3) (p. 344) requires T to live in degrees 0, …, l_0 with d = 0 and H^{l_0}(T) ≅ H/ϖ. Here H = H^{q_0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪. Conjecture B(4)(a) says localized cohomology vanishes outside degrees [q_0, q_0+l_0], so H^{q_0−1}(Y, K/O)_𝔪 = 0. With the long exact sequence for 0 → O/ϖ → K/O → K/O → 0 this gives H/ϖ ≅ H^{q_0}(Y, O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪. (2) As printed, T^i = H^{i−l_0}(…)^∨ is nonzero only when q_0 ≤ i−l_0 ≤ q_0+l_0, that is, for i between q_0+l_0 and q_0+2l_0. In the required range 0 ≤ i ≤ l_0 the degree i−l_0 runs from −l_0 to 0, where this cohomology vanishes (q_0 ≥ 1 for n ≥ 2). So the printed T is 0 in degrees 0, …, l_0. That contradicts both T^{l_0} ≅ H/ϖ ≠ 0 and D^i_N ⊗ k ≅ T, since D̃_N ⊗ k has zero differentials and homology H_c(Y, k) ≅ H^c(Y, k)^∨_𝔪. The printed formula also increases in i where it should decrease, so no reading of it works. (3) D̃_N is homological, with d: D_c → D_{c−1}. Re-indexing it cohomologically with increasing differentials forces i = const − c, so it cannot be a shift. The paper's own claim that condition (c) is clear needs H^{l_0}(D^1_N ⊗ O/ϖ^n) ≅ H/ϖ^n = H_{q_0}. So homological degree q_0, the cokernel end, must become cohomological degree l_0, the top degree, as Lemma 6.2 and Theorem 6.3(i) require. That gives i = q_0+l_0−c, exactly as the candidate says. A plain shift by q_0 would put H^{q_0+l_0} in degree l_0, which is wrong. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The candidate's quotation and locators are right (§9.5, proof of Theorem 9.19, p. 426 and p. 427; same in v2). The fix is purely notational: with the corrected T and indexing, every hypothesis of Proposition 6.6 and Theorem 6.3 holds as the authors intend, and nothing later uses the printed indexing. Theorem 9.19 and its consequences (Theorem 5.16) are unaffected, so 'affects: nothing' is right. - **Gap** at §9 (subsection 9.5 in the published numbering), proof of Theorem 9.19, published p. 427 (PDF p. 131). The hypothesis being checked is in Proposition 6.6, p. 390. arXiv v2 has the same text (proof of Theorem 9.19, v2 p. 96). arXiv v1 has no such argument: the Ihara-avoidance/level-changing section is not in v1. (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 427 (PDF p. 131): "• Choose representatives for the universal deformations of type S_{Q_N} and S^χ_{Q_N} which agree modulo ϖ. This gives rise to isomorphisms R^{□_T}_{S_{Q_N}} ⥲ R_{S_{Q_N}}[z_1,…,z_j], R^{□_T}_{S^χ_{Q_N}} ⥲ R_{S^χ_{Q_N}}[z_1,…,z_j]. In the notation of Proposition 6.3, the rings on the right hand side can be written R^□_{S_{Q_N}} and R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}}. By Proposition 8.5, we can and do choose surjections R^1_∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}} and R^2_∞ ↠ R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}}. Composing these with the natural maps R^□_{S_{Q_N}} ↠ R_{S_{Q_N}} ↠ R_S = R^1 and R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}} ↠ R_{S^χ_{Q_N}} ↠ R_{S^χ} = R^2, we obtain surjections φ^1_N : R^1_∞ ↠ R^1 and φ^2_N : R^2_∞ ↠ R^2." ... "H^{l0}((D^1_M)^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ) = H^{l0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^□ ⥲ H^{l0}_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^□ = H^{l0}((D^2_M)^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ) for all M ≥ N ≥ 0 with M ≥ 1. These isomorphisms are compatible with the actions of R^i_∞ and give rise to the commutative square required by Proposition 6.6."`; it should be `Add a condition to the choice. For each N, choose the surjections R^1_∞ = R^1_loc⟦x_1,…,x_g⟧ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}} and R^2_∞ = R^χ_loc⟦x_1,…,x_g⟧ ↠ R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}} so that their reductions mod ϖ agree. They must agree under the fixed N-independent isomorphism R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ (Lemma 8.2(2) with x_i ↦ x_i) and the isomorphism R^□_{S_{Q_N}}/ϖ ≅ R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}}/ϖ (the global rings agree mod ϖ, and the representatives agree mod ϖ). Such a choice exists. Take any surjection on side 1 as in Prop. 8.5(4); it is an R^1_loc-algebra map. On side 2, use the natural map R^χ_loc → R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}}, which reduces mod ϖ to the side-1 map. Send each x_i to any lift of the image of x_i mod ϖ. The resulting map is surjective mod ϖ, so it is surjective by complete Nakayama, since it is surjective on reduced cotangent spaces. Strictly, only equality of the induced actions on H^{l_0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M),O/ϖ)^□ is needed, and this choice is a sufficient way to get it. (Separately, the actions on H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M),…) should come from R_{S_{Q_M}} and R^i_∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_M}}; the printed index is Q_N, which is an index misprint.)`. Proposition 6.6 (p. 390) needs, for each M ≥ N, an isomorphism H^{l0}(D^1_M⊗S_N/ϖ) ⥲ H^{l0}(D^2_M⊗S_N/ϖ) that becomes an isomorphism of R^1_∞⊗_O S^□_N/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞⊗_O S^□_N/ϖ-modules. The ring identification is the fixed one from the first bullet, and it must work at every level for the patching to go through.

In the proof of Theorem 9.19, the R^i_∞-actions come from the chosen surjections R^i_∞ ↠ R^□. The paper makes the framings agree mod ϖ but puts no condition on these surjections: it just says "we can and do choose". It then states without argument that the isomorphisms are compatible with the R^i_∞-actions.

That statement fails for some choices the text allows. Take g ≥ 1, which is the usual case since q can be taken large. Let f^1, f^2 be a compatible pair, and change f^2 to x_1 ↦ f^2(x_1) + z_1^2. Since z_1^2 lies in m^2, the new map still hits generators of the cotangent space, so it is still a surjection as Proposition 8.5 provides. Here j = n^2|T|−1 ≥ 1. On H^{l0}(...)^□ ⊗ k = H⊗k[[z_1,…,z_j]], a nonzero free k[[z]]-module, the element z_1^2 acts injectively. So x_1 acts differently on the two sides by the nonzero operator z_1^2, and the required equivariance fails.

The other ingredients do match mod ϖ. The maps R^1_loc → R^□_{S_Q} and R^χ_loc → R^□_{S^χ_Q} both come from restricting the same mod-ϖ framed deformation. The Hecke/Galois actions on H(O/ϖ) ≅ H_χ(O/ϖ) agree by Carayol/Chebotarev. So the only missing condition is compatibility of the images of the x_i. The authors took this care for the framings ("agree modulo ϖ") but not for the surjections.

This is an omitted but necessary condition behind an asserted step, so it is a gap. It is easily repaired by the Nakayama argument above, and Theorem 9.19 stays true. Prop. 6.6 (p. 390) takes as input one fixed isomorphism R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ. It also needs, for each M ≥ N, isomorphisms H^{l_0}((D^1_M)^□⊗S_N/ϖ) ⥲ H^{l_0}((D^2_M)^□⊗S_N/ϖ) "of R^1_∞⊗S^□_N/ϖ ⥲ R^2_∞⊗S^□_N/ϖ-modules". In the proof of Thm 9.19, R^i_∞ acts on these groups only through the chosen surjections R^i_∞ ↠ R^□ followed by Conjecture B. The paper fixes the representatives so that they agree mod ϖ, but it puts no condition on the surjections: it says only "By Proposition 8.5, we can and do choose surjections". Prop. 8.5(4) says only that R^□ is a quotient of R_loc⟦x_1,…,x_g⟧, a non-canonical choice made separately on each side and for each N.

The R_loc part is compatible automatically, because the natural maps R^1_loc → R^□_S and R^χ_loc → R^□_{S^χ} agree mod ϖ. The images of the x_i are free. For example, swap the images of x_1 and x_2 on side 2 only, or add to one of them a non-zero element mod ϖ of the maximal ideal. Both give valid surjections, but then x_1 acts differently on the two sides, and the Hecke/z-module H^{l_0}(…)^□ does not generally make the two actions agree. So the claim "These isomorphisms are compatible with the actions of R^i_∞" does not follow from the choices as stated.

Defences tried:
- The "natural" isomorphism R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ cannot be adjusted per N to absorb the mismatch, because Prop. 6.6 fixes it independently of N.
- Nothing nearby in the paper supplies the condition. A search for "compatib" finds no such statement, and the Correction (Invent. Math. 227) is only about brackets.
- A charitable reader would read "we can and do choose" as meaning a compatible choice, and that choice is easy to make (see correction). So this is a small omitted condition plus an unjustified compatibility claim, not a false result.

The step matters. The compatibility is exactly what gives the R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ-module isomorphism H^{l_0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ ≅ H^{l_0}(P^2_∞)/ϖ on p. 428. That isomorphism, with [11, Lemma 2.2] and Lemma 8.2, gives near-faithfulness over R^1_∞, and then over R_S by Prop. 6.3(iv). Theorem 9.19 in turn gives Theorem 5.16 ("This theorem will follow immediately from Theorem 9.19") and hence Theorem 1.1. With the compatible choice described above, the proof goes through, so no stated result is affected.

On the candidate's correction: it is right and essentially minimal, except that "Only with this choice" overstates it. Agreement of the maps mod ϖ is sufficient, while what is necessary is only agreement of the induced actions. - **Error** at §3.2.3, p. 315 (definition of W_x on H^0(X_Δ(Q;x), ω_A^n)) (published version). The source says `p. 315 (PDF p. 19), §3.2.3: "We define the operator W_x on H^0(X_Δ(Q; x), ω^n_A) by setting W_x to be the composite H^0(X_Δ(Q; x), ω^n_A) --w_x^*--> H^0(X_Δ(Q, x), π_2^* ω^n_A) --φ_12^{⊗n}--> H^i(X_Δ(Q; x), ω^n_A). Explicitly, we have: W_x f(E, α_{NQ}, C_x) = φ^* f(E/C_x, α'_{NQ}, E[x]/C_x). Thus, using the identification x : E/E[x] ⥲ E together with the fact that we have an equality w_x^2(E, α_{NQ}, C_x) = ⟨x⟩(E, α_{NQ}, C_x), we see that: W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩. We will use this fact below"`; it should be `In the display the target should be H^0(X_Δ(Q; x), ω^n_A), not H^i; the "(Q, x)" in the middle term should also read "(Q; x)", which is cosmetic. On weight-n sections the identity should read W_x^2 = x^n⟨x⟩, which is the printed x⟨x⟩ only when n = 1. Stating the identity only for n = 1 would be an equally minimal fix, since every use is in weight one.`. I checked the page image at 250 dpi. It shows exactly H^i as the target and "W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩". The arXiv v2 text (cg-v2.txt, lines 675-692) reads the same, and the 2022 Correction covers only the ⟦ ⟧ brackets, so this is not a known error. The paper defines W_x on H^0 in both the sentence before the display and the source of the display. Both maps in the composite (w_x^* and φ_12^{⊗n}) send H^0 to H^0, so the "H^i" target is a slip.

I redid the W_x^2 computation from the paper's own definition, W_x = φ_12^{⊗n} ∘ w_x^*. For a Katz-style section f with f(E, α, C) ∈ ω_E^{⊗n}:
- W_x^2 f(E, α, C) = φ^* ψ^* f(E/E[x], α'', C''), where φ: E → E/C and ψ: E/C → E/E[x], so ψφ is the quotient q: E → E/E[x].
- Let ι: E/E[x] ⥲ E be the identification with ι∘q = [x]. Transported by ι, (E/E[x], α'', C'') becomes (E, x∘α, C). By isomorphism invariance, f(E/E[x], α'', C'') = ι^* f(E, xα, C).
- Hence W_x^2 f(E, α, C) = [x]^* f(E, xα, C).
- [x]^* multiplies invariant differentials by x, so it multiplies sections of ω^{⊗n} by x^n.
- The paper's ⟨a⟩ is pullback along ⟨a⟩ using the canonical identification ⟨a⟩^*ω ≅ ω, so (⟨x⟩f)(E, α, C) = f(E, xα, C).
- Therefore W_x^2 = x^n⟨x⟩. The same thing in sheaf terms: φ_12 ∘ w_x^*(φ_12) is pullback along E → E/E[x], and after (w_x^2)^* = ⟨x⟩^* this is [x]^* = x^n on ω^{⊗n}.

This is consistent with the classical picture: the unnormalized Atkin–Lehner operator in weight k squares to x^k⟨x⟩. The same scalar appears in the paper's own weight-one computation U_x∘V_x = π_1^*⟨x⟩ (p. 319), which uses "x⟨x⟩ f(E, α_N)".

The printed claim is stated in a setting of general weight n: §3.2.3 defines the Hecke action for L = ω^{⊗n} or ω^{⊗n}(−∞), and W_x on ω^n_A. So as a general statement it is false for n ≠ 1. It is correct in weight one, which is what the authors intend.

Every use is in weight one:
- Lemma 3.5, pp. 317–320, on H^0(X, ω_{K/O}): the lower-right matrix entry on p. 318, and "Since W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩, we deduce that xU_x^2 f = ⟨x⟩f" on p. 320.
- Lemma 3.6, pp. 320–321, whose proof reuses Lemma 3.5.
- Theorem 3.30, proof step (1), in §3.9.2 on p. 350: there W_x on ω⊗L_σ is induced from the weight-one W_x on H^0(X_{V_0(x)}, ω_{K/O}).
I found no other occurrence of W_x or of the Fricke map (a grep for W_x, Fricke and Atkin found nothing else). So no proof or stated result is affected, and the proposed correction is right.

I chose "misprint" (a missing exponent n and a wrong index H^i for H^0; the meaning intended is clear in weight one). The W_x^2 part could also be classed as an "error", since it is false as stated for weight n ≠ 1. Defence first. I looked for a reading under which the paper is right.
(a) Could n be fixed to 1 here? No. §3.2.3 (pp. 313–314) says it defines the Hecke action on H^i(X_Δ(Q), L_A) for L = ω^{⊗n} or ω^{⊗n}(−∞), and W_x is defined on H^0(X_Δ(Q;x), ω^n_A). Remark 3.4 on p. 316 then works in general weight n (T_x f = (1+χ(x)x^{n−1})f).
(b) Could the normalisations absorb the factor? No. The φ_12^{⊗n} normalisation is the unnormalised pullback. I checked it on the Tate curve: Σ_C φ_C^* f(E/C) has q^m-coefficient x·(a_{mx} + x^{n−1}a_{m/x}). So xT_x as defined gives the classical T_x in every weight, and the diamond identification ⟨a⟩^*ω ≅ ω is the identity on E. Nothing rescales W_x.
(c) Could "x" mean the operator [x]^* induced by the identification x: E/E[x] ≅ E? That operator equals x^n on ω^{⊗n}, so under this reading the formula would be right. But the paper uses x as a scalar: the matrix entry ⟨x⟩(x+1) on p. 318, and "x^2U_x^2 f = W_x^2 f … we deduce that xU_x^2 f = ⟨x⟩f" on p. 320. So this reading is not faithful for n ≠ 1.

Computation from the paper's own definition. Write W_x f(E,α,C) = φ^* f(E/C, α', E[x]/C). Then W_x^2 f(E,α,C) = φ^*φ'^* f(E/E[x], α'', C''), where φ'φ = q: E → E/E[x]. Take the isomorphism ι: E/E[x] ≅ E with ι∘q = [x]. It carries α'' to x∘α. It carries C'' = (E/C)[x]/(E[x]/C) = {y : xy ∈ C}/E[x] to C. So, by isomorphism invariance, W_x^2 f(E,α,C) = [x]^* f(E, xα, C) = x^n f(E, xα, C) = x^n (⟨x⟩f)(E,α,C). This is consistent with the classical picture: the unnormalised Fricke operator in weight k squares to x^k times a diamond operator. The paper's own weight-one count on p. 319 ("can be identified with x f(E, x∘α_N) = x⟨x⟩f(E, α_N)") shows the same factor [x]^* = x. The H^i target contradicts the sentence just before it and the fact that both maps preserve H^0, so it is a plain slip.

Consequences. W_x appears only on pp. 314–315, 318, 320 and 350 (I grepped for W_x, Fricke and w_x).
- Lemma 3.5 (pp. 317–320) uses W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ on H^0(X_0(x), ω_{K/O}), which is weight 1: in the lower-right matrix entry on p. 318, and in the step xU_x^2 f = ⟨x⟩f on p. 320.
- Lemma 3.6 (p. 321) reuses that proof.
- Theorem 3.30, step (1) on p. 350, gets W_x on (ω⊗L_σ)_{K/O} from the weight-one W_x on H^0(X_{V_0(x)}, ω_{K/O}).
- p. 344 defines only T_x on ω^n⊗L_σ, not W_x.
- p. 376 ("proceed as in the proof of Lemma 3.5", for homology of Y_0(x)) does not invoke this formula.
So every use is in weight 1, where the printed identity is correct, and no proof or stated result is affected. Both readers' correction (x^n⟨x⟩) is right and minimal.

The mismatch is real: the bullet assumes N_2 > n, while the next paragraph and condition (4) use N_2 > n + 1. The deeper problem is that "N_2 > n + 1" is copied from [76] = BLGHT II without changing its n. I checked a local copy of BLGHT II (cy2fin.pdf). Its Theorem 6.4 reads: "n is an even positive integer ... l + 1 = N_1N_2 ... Suppose that N_2 > n + 1" with "r : Gal(F̄/F) → GSp_n(Z_l)". So n there is the dimension of r. The proof then says "apply the results of section 4 with N = N_2". Section 4 starts: "Let N > n + 1 denote positive integers with n even and N odd", and by Lemma 4.1 the piece V_λ has rank n. In CG §10, r = Sym^{2n−1}ρ takes values in GL_{2n}, and M/Q has degree 2n, which CG did adjust. So the n of BLGHT equals 2n here, and the hypothesis needed is N_2 > 2n + 1. Neither N_2 > n nor N_2 > n + 1 gives this. For example, with n = 3 (dimension 6), N_2 = 5 satisfies N_2 > n + 1, but the degree-5 Dwork family has no rank-6 piece. So the candidate is right that the text is inconsistent, but wrong that the fix is N_2 > n + 1 and that nothing is affected. The repair is routine: N_2 can be taken as large as needed, since p, or A and p in the general case, are chosen freely via Moret–Bailly/Chebotarev. It is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. A side note: BLGHT also needs N_2 odd and prime to S, where S contains 2. CG only says "prime to the conductor of A", which is another imprecision in this sketch.
