No minimal form is lost. A minimal lift has Teichmüller determinant, so its nebentypus has prime-to-p order and is trivial on the p-power diamonds. Reading "reducible" in the definition of P(ρ̄) as "ρ̄|I_x reducible" does not fix the problem on its own (see the reason).`. I transcribed the text from the page images of pp. 340–342 and p. 318. The candidate's example is valid under the natural reading of P(ρ̄), where 'reducible' means ρ̄|G_x reducible, as in Def. 3.1(4) and §3.1.

The example, redone:
- p = 3, F = Q(i). ψ is a Hecke character mod 7 of order 4, trivial on μ_4 and nontrivial on the norm-kernel μ_8 of F_49^×, so ψ^7 = ψ^{-1} ≠ ψ.
- ρ̄ = Ind ψ̄. At 7: ρ̄|G_7 is irreducible, ρ̄|I_7 is reducible, 7 ≡ 1 mod 3, so 7 is not vexing. At 2: ρ̄|G_2 is reducible with ρ̄^{I_2} ≠ 0, as §3.1 requires.
- For a cubic character χ mod 7, the forms θ_{ψ·χ^j∘N} (j = 0, 1, 2) have conductor 7² at 7 (tame twist of an unramified induction). They are newforms of level 196, congruent mod m, with nebentypus changed by χ^{2j}. Their T_ℓ-eigenvalues are distinct: take ℓ split with ψ(λ) = 1 and χ(ℓ) ≠ 1.
- With U_7 = U_1(49), all three occur in T_m. Twisting to fixed determinant uses η = χ^{-j}, so all three give the same point of R^min. Hence φ: R^min → T_m is not surjective. The step "easily seen to be surjective" (p. 339) holds only because H removes p-power nebentypus.
- Theorem 3.30 is the result stated for X_U. For it to fail, T ≠ ∅ is needed, and the candidate's example has T = ∅. Adding a vexing prime fixes this: also ramify ψ at 23 (inert in Q(i), 23 ≡ −1 mod 3) with a tame order-4 character, trivial on μ_4 and nontrivial on μ_8. Twisting by χ keeps the type at 23, so all three forms stay σ-isotypic and Theorem 3.30 still fails.

The candidate's remark "contradicting p. 340" is loose. Page 340 simply defines X_U := X_1(N)/H for the case T = ∅. The real inconsistency is with §3.9's U.

Under the I_x reading, the problem persists for odd x ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_x irreducible (see the correction). So the printed definition is wrong under either reading, not merely ambiguous. I have classified it as an 'error' rather than a 'gap'. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Defence attempted and failed. The standing assumptions (§3.1, p. 318: p ≥ 3, ρ̄ odd, absolutely irreducible, unramified at p, and ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0 when ρ̄|G_x is reducible) do not stop a prime x in S − (T ∪ P) from satisfying x ≡ 1 mod p.

(a) Natural reading: "reducible" means ρ̄|G_x reducible, as in Def. 3.1(4). Example: p = 3, ρ̄ = Ind_{Q(i)}^Q ψ, where ψ is a character mod 7 with ψ(g) = i on F_49^× = ⟨g⟩. It has order 4, is trivial on μ_4 = ⟨g^12⟩, and ψ(g^6) = −1 on the norm kernel μ_8, so ψ^7 = ψ^{-1} ≠ ψ.
- At 7: ρ̄|G_7 is irreducible and ρ̄|I_7 is reducible. Since 7 ≡ 1 ≢ −1 mod 3, 7 is not vexing and lies in S − (T ∪ P).
- At 2: ρ̄|G_2 = ψ̃ ⊕ ψ̃ε is reducible with ρ̄^{I_2} ≠ 0, so 2 ∈ P. Then N = 196 and the printed X_U is X_1(196), not X_1(196)/H with H ≅ Z/3.
- For a cubic character χ mod 7, the forms θ_{ψ·(χ^j∘N)} (j = 0, 1, 2) are newforms of level 196. The twist stays tame and cannot factor through the norm, so the conductor at 7 stays 2. They are congruent mod m. Their nebentypus changes by χ^{2j}, which has nontrivial 3-part, so they appear on the printed X_U. Their T_ℓ eigenvalues differ: take ℓ split in Q(i), with a_ℓ ≠ 0 and χ(ℓ) ≠ 1.
- The normalising twist of Thm 3.11 has η = χ^{-j}, the unique p-power square root of χ^{-2j}. So all three forms give the same point of R^min, and φ: R^min → T_{∅,m∅} is not surjective.
- To make T ≠ ∅, so that Theorem 3.30 (p. 350) itself fails, also ramify ψ tamely at 23. This prime is inert in Q(i) and 23 ≡ −1 mod 3; use an order-4 character trivial on μ_4 and nontrivial on μ_24, so 23 is vexing. χ is unramified at 23, so the twists keep the inertial type there and stay σ-isotypic.

(b) Reading "reducible" as "ρ̄|I_x reducible" does not save the text. For odd x with ρ̄|I_x irreducible (wild dihedral case) the same failure occurs. Example: p = 3, ρ̄ = Ind from Q(√−7) of an order-7 ray class character of conductor 𝔭_7² (the ray class group has a Z/7 quotient). Complex conjugation acts by −1 on (1+𝔭)/(1+𝔭²), so ρ̄|I_7 is irreducible. Here c_7 = 3, (Z/343)^× has 3-part Z/3, and cubic twists keep the conductor at 7^3.

This also refutes H-part1a-8's claim that S − (T ∪ P) would then contain only x = 2.

Why the paper's argument breaks: in §3.8 (p. 339), φ is "easily seen to be surjective" only because X = X_1(N)/H kills the p-power diamond operators. Then η = 1 and T is generated by the images of the traces. Theorem 3.30's proof says it "is the same as the proof of Theorem 3.26", with ρ'_Q := ρ_Q ⊗ η "defined as before" (item (4), p. 353). With the printed U, η is nontrivial and surjectivity fails.

Nothing nearby supplies the missing quotient. The only uses of P(ρ̄) are the U-bullets and the cusp remark ("∏_{T} GL_2(Z_x) × ∏_{P} Z_x^× acts transitively", p. 351). Enlarging the group there to ∏_{S−T} Z_x^× only helps transitivity, so the correction is compatible with it.

The P/non-P split looks deliberate, so the intended group is not clear from context. It is an error, not a misprint. X-K4-2's correction and the earlier verdict on H-part1a-8 agree with mine, and theirs is the minimal change. H-part1a-8's first fix (the I_x reading) is insufficient, as shown in (b); its alternative fix (p-power d at every x in S − T) is correct. I transcribed the text from a 200 dpi render of p. 346. The proof speaks of "stalks at points of X − Y", L_{σ,x} and O_{X,x}, so the rings are Zariski local rings; Lemma 3.28 separately says "along the formal completions at x" when it means completions. For a finite map f, the Zariski stalk (f_*O_{X(V)})_x is the semilocal ring of X(V) along the fibre over x. It equals ⊕_{x′↦x} O_{X(V),x′} only when the fibre points lie on different connected components.

Here G = ∏_{x∈T} GL_2(Z/x^{c_x/2}), and when T ≠ ∅ several fibre points lie on the same component. Let C be the component through x′ and H its stabiliser in G. H contains S = ∏ SL_2(Z/x^{c_x/2}), which acts through det-trivial elements and so fixes each geometric component. H also contains the inertia group I(x′/x). The fibre points on C are H·x′, and under the paper's residue-field assumption the decomposition group equals I. So C contains |H|/|I| of them. That number is greater than 1 because S is nonabelian (SL_2(F_ℓ) is nonabelian for every ℓ, including SL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3) while I is abelian ([42, VI.5]). The semilocal ring of C at these points is a normal domain, so it is not the product of its localisations.

Worse, O_{X(V),x′} is then not finite over O_{X,x}. It contains inverses of functions that vanish at another point x″ over x, so it is not inside the integral closure of O_{X,x} in K(C), which is that semilocal ring. So the claim "O_{X(V),x′,χ} is free over O_{X,x}, being a summand of a free module" is false as written. A toy model with the same shape: t = s^2 at t = 1 over a field of characteristic ≠ 2 (a Z/2 cover). Here k[s] localised at (s−1) contains 1/(s+1), which is not integral over k[t]_{(t−1)}, and the semilocal ring at {±1} is a domain, not a product.

Lemma 3.27(1) is still true, and the standard completion/henselisation argument plus faithfully flat descent proves it. So the text asserts the key step with an invalid justification, and the descent step is missing. That is a gap, with no effect on any result. It is unrelated to the 47 bracket errors. The same text appears in arXiv v1 and v2 and in the published version. Defence attempted: nothing in the paper's conventions rescues the Zariski reading. Lemma 3.28 explicitly writes 𝒪^∧_{X,x} for completions, so 𝒪_{X,x} and 𝒪_{X_V,x′} mean Zariski local rings. The stalk 𝓛_{σ,x} is also a Zariski stalk ("its stalks at points of X − Y are free"). Taken literally, the displayed equality is false. (f_*𝒪_{X(V)})_x = 𝒪(X(V)) ⊗ 𝒪_{X,x} is the semilocal ring of X(V) along f^{-1}(x). Because X(V) is normal, it is a product of normal domains, one for each irreducible component through the fibre. In this setting a component C has several points over x. G acts transitively on the fibre, and the stabiliser of x′ is I(x′/x) (the residue fields agree), which is cyclic of order e prime to p (cusp inertia). The stabiliser of C contains a copy of SL_2(Z/x^{c_x/2}), whose order is much larger than e. So the semilocal ring has a domain factor with at least two maximal ideals, and it is not ⊕_{x′} 𝒪_{X(V),x′}. The claim "𝒪_{X(V),x′,χ} is free over 𝒪_{X,x}, being a summand of a free module" also fails. 𝒪_{X(V),x′} is not a summand of the stalk and is not finitely generated. If it were free it would have finite rank, hence be integral over 𝒪_{X,x}. But it contains 1/s for some s in the maximal ideal of another point x″ of C over x, and 1/s is not integral. After completion (or henselisation) every step is correct, and freeness descends, so Lemma 3.27(1) is true. Other fixes also work but take more effort: - Keep the statement general and define R^min in the Diamond sense, i.e. ρ(I_x) ≅ ρ̄(I_x) at such x, as in Cor. 1.5(1). The Hecke side then needs a new type-cutting bundle at those x, e.g. U_x = K_0(x^{max(a1,a2)}) with the character ψ̃1(a)ψ̃2(d). - State the Hecke side for the twist ρ̄⊗χ̄, with N, X_U, T and m taken from the twist. Corollaries 1.5 and 1.6 then each need a one-line twisting reduction, which is valid: weight-one modularity, finite image, the minimality in Cor. 1.5(1) and R^min are all unchanged by twisting by the Teichmüller lift of a character unramified at p.`. I checked the page images at pp. 303, 310–311, 338, 340 and 342 against the text. The same wording is in arXiv v2.

(1) Theorem 1.4 as printed covers every odd irreducible ρ̄ that is unramified at p. The whole proof runs under the §3.1 standing assumption. §3.8 (p. 340) says "We now deduce Theorem 1.4, under Assumption 3.9 … we take X_U = X = X_1(N)/H". §3.9.2 (p. 342, and p. 354) removes only Assumption 3.9, the vexing primes. The §3.1 assumption is never removed; the only thing said about it is the one-line twisting remark.

(2) For ρ̄|G_x ≅ ψ̄1⊕ψ̄2 with both characters ramified, ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. So Definition 3.1(4) already fails for ρ̄ over k, and the functor is empty. The R^min of the introduction then has to mean Diamond-minimal (ρ(I_x) ≅ ρ̄(I_x); compare Corollary 1.5(1)), and the §3 machinery does not apply to it directly.

(3) On the Galois side, twisting by the Teichmüller lift of χ̄ does give R^min(ρ̄) ≅ R^min(ρ̄⊗χ̄). The determinant condition and the inertia condition both carry over. On the Hecke side, the Serre level drops at x (from x² to x or 1), and X_U changes with it. The Hecke algebra of ρ̄' = ρ̄⊗χ̄ has no maximal ideal for ρ̄: ρ̄ cannot occur at level N' < N. So the twist does not directly give "X_U a quotient of X_1(N), m corresponding to ρ̄".

(4) Taking the paper's own level structure directly does not work either. For P(ρ̄) (p. 342) the paper uses U_x = {g ≡ (∗ ∗; 0 d) mod x^{c_x}, d of p-power order}, which here has c_x = 2. Take x ≡ 1 mod p and θ a nontrivial character of Z_x^× of p-power order and conductor x. The representation π(ψ̃1θ, ψ̃2θ^{-1}) has conductor 1+1 = 2 and central character ψ̃1ψ̃2, which is trivial on elements d of p-power order. Its newvector is therefore U_x-invariant, it is congruent to ρ̄, and it is non-minimal. Under the §3.1 assumption, by contrast, ψ̄1 is unramified, and such twists raise the conductor to 1+c_x, which excludes them. So the assumption is really used.

Conclusion: the statement of Theorem 1.4 goes beyond what is proved. The theorem is probably still true with a different choice of X_U and L_σ, so this is a gap, not an error. It is minor, and the fix is routine.

Dependencies: Corollaries 1.5 and 1.6 are unchanged by twisting, so they survive. §4 assumes minimal conductor among twists (p. 351), which implies the §3.1 condition. Only Theorem 1.4's generality is affected. Defences I tried, and why each fails. I checked page images for pp. 303, 310, 311, 340 and 342 and read the text of pp. 325–330 and 350–354.

(1) "R^min refers to §3, so the §3.1 assumption is implicit." Theorem 1.4 lists its hypotheses explicitly: p ≥ 3, odd, irreducible (which gives absolute irreducibility for p odd), and unramified at p. These are all the §3.1 standing assumptions except the twist condition. Under the paper's own Def. 3.1(4), a ρ̄ with ρ̄|G_x ≅ ψ̄1⊕ψ̄2, both characters ramified, has ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. No lift then satisfies (4), so the functor is empty and "R^min" means nothing. The intro must therefore intend Diamond-minimality, which is the reading of Cor. 1.5(1): "ρ(I_v) ≅ ρ̄(I_v) or dim ρ^{I_v} = dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1". The §3 proof never treats that notion.

(2) "By twisting, WLOG." On the Galois side this works. There is a global χ̄ with χ̄|I_x = ψ̄1^{-1}, ramified only at such x, and R^min(ρ̄) ≅ R^min(ρ̄⊗χ̄). On the Hecke side it does not. The twist has a smaller Serre level N' (the x-part drops from x^{a1+a2} to x^{cond(ψ̄2/ψ̄1)}), and its m' corresponds to ρ̄⊗χ̄. Theorem 1.4 requires m to correspond to ρ̄ itself, and ρ̄ does not occur at level N'. The paper says nothing beyond the one-line remark on p. 310, which is the only occurrence of "twist" in §3 apart from the remark on p. 334 about twisting a scalar local ρ̄ to trivial.

(3) "The paper's own X_U works anyway." It does not in general. §3.3 (p. 325) takes X = X_1(N)/H with H the p-part of (Z/N)^×, and §3.9 (p. 342) takes U_x = {g ≡ (* *; 0 d) mod x^{c_x}, d of p-power order} for x ∈ P(ρ̄). Suppose x ≡ 1 mod p and θ is a p-power-order character of Z_x^× of conductor x. Then π(ψ̃1θ, ψ̃2θ^{-1}) has conductor exponent a1+a2 = c_x, because ψ̃iθ^{±1} is still ramified with the same conductor. Its central character ψ̃1ψ̃2 has prime-to-p order, so it is trivial on p-power d, and the newvector is U_x-invariant. This representation is congruent to ρ̄ but not minimal. So Theorem 3.14 ("follows from the choice of N and H") and the p. 341 claim "all minimal lifts … appear in H^0(X_U, ω)" do not give R^min → T_m. Under the §3.1 assumption, ψ̄1 is unramified and such twists raise the conductor, so the assumption is really used. A concrete case exists: p = 3, x = 13, ρ̄|I_x ≅ χ̄ ⊕ χ̄^{-1} with χ̄ of order 4.

(4) Where the proof ends. §3.8 deduces Theorem 1.4 "under Assumption 3.9", and §3.9.2 removes only that assumption (vexing primes). The §3.1 assumption is never removed.

Consequences:
- Only the generality of Theorem 1.4 is affected. The theorem is very likely true with a type-cutting L_σ built with the paper's own §3.9 formalism, so this is a gap rather than a false statement.
- Cor. 1.5 and 1.6 ("immediately deduce") still hold after a routine twist.
- §4 assumes minimal conductor among twists (p. 361), which implies the condition, so it is unaffected.
- The proposed correction (add the hypothesis) is right and minimal.
- A side observation, not part of this candidate: p. 340's "if x^2|N, then U_x = 0" fits the both-ramified case but misses a wildly ramified ψ̄2 under the §3.1 assumption. U_x ∈ T_m still follows from the invariant-line argument in that case. Theorem 1.4 is existential in L_σ and survives after the repair. 1. What acts on H_0 (defence fails). By the paper's own definition, H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) = H^0(X_U,(ω⊗L^sub_{σ^*})_{K/O})^∨, with the dual Hecke action (p. 351; §3.2.4). By Lemma 3.27(2), (H^0(X_V,ω(−∞))⊗W_{σ^*})^G = Hom_G(W_σ, S_1(V)). So T_∅ is the Hecke algebra of the W_σ-part. Step (3) says this itself: 'dim H_0(…,ω⊗L_σ)_m = dim H^0(…,ω⊗L^sub_{σ^*})_m = dim H^0(…,ω⊗L_{σ^*})_m'.
2. Where the Galois representations are built. Step (4) builds them only on the Hecke algebra of H^0(X_{U_1(Q)},(ω⊗L_σ)_{K/O}) = Hom_G(W_σ^*, ·), the W_σ^*-part. So the 'same proof as Theorem 3.26' has no map R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m} for the patched modules H_0(…,ω⊗L_σ)_m, and no φ for T_∅. Nothing nearby bridges the two parts:
- the contragredient in step (3) sends the W_σ^*-part at m to the W_σ-part at m*, not m;
- the 'self-dual up to twist' remark in v1 changes ρ̄ to a twist of ρ̄.
3. Which side is right: I checked [15] (CDT, Taylor's copy).
- In §5.1, σ_{S,p} = Θ(χ_p), with ρ̄|I_p ≅ χ̄_p∘η_{p,2} ⊕ χ̄_p∘Frob∘η_{p,2}.
- Lemma 5.1.1: π ∈ N_S iff Hom_{U_S}(σ_S, π^∞) ≠ 0.
- CDT's Notation fixes η_1 = ε^{-1}, with the arithmetic-Frobenius normalisation.
- Θ(χ) has central character χ|Z_x^×.
Now take a minimal lift f. Then det ρ_f|I_x = χ|Z_x^× ∘ ε^{-1}, so the x-part of the nebentypus of f is (χ|Z_x^×)^{-1}. That character is how scalars of G act under the moduli action α ↦ α∘g. It is the central character of σ_x^*. So under the paper's moduli action, minimal forms lie in the W_σ^*-part: p. 341 and step (4) are right, and the statement of Theorem 3.30 is the slip.
4. The two parts really differ. Hom_G(W_σ, π) ≅ Hom_G(W_σ^*, π^∨), and CDT Lemmas 3.2.1(2) and 4.2.4(3) apply. Together they show the W_σ-part contains only forms of the dual type, whose reduction is ξ^{-1}⊕ξ^{-x}. That is ≇ ξ⊕ξ^x unless det ρ̄|I_x = ξ^{1+x} = 1.
- Example: p = 3, x = 5, ξ of order 8 on F_25^×; then ξ^5 ≠ ξ and ξ^6 ≠ 1.
- A dihedral ρ̄ = Ind_K ψ is one realisation.
In such a case H_0(X_U, ω_K⊗L_σ)_{m_∅} = 0 (in fact T_{∅,m_∅} = 0, by step (4)'s Hasse-invariant argument). But R^min ≠ 0, and it has a characteristic-zero point when there is a minimal weight-one lift. So Theorem 3.30 as printed is false.
5. What uses it. Theorem 3.30 is used only to deduce Theorem 1.4 (p. 354), and Corollaries 1.5 and 1.6 come from Theorem 1.4. Theorem 1.4 is existential in the bundle and still holds for L_σ via form (b). So the stated result that fails is Theorem 3.30 (and the rank-one remark); Theorem 1.4 and its corollaries are unaffected.
Confidence: the σ/σ^* mismatch is certain. The direction (the statement is wrong, not step (4)) rests on the normalisation check in point 3. I rendered p. 351 and p. 316 and transcribed the text. The claim is refuted by an equivariant projection. Here V_Δ(Q) = ∏_{x∉Q} V_x × ∏_{x∈Q} (a group between U_{1,x} and U_{0,x}), and patching needs Q ≠ ∅. Fix x ∈ Q and let W' = ∏_{y≠x} GL_2(Z_y) × U_{0,x}. Then W' contains V_Δ(Q), and it also contains the group K' = ∏_{T} GL_2(Z_y) × ∏_{P} Z_y^×, whose components all lie at primes other than x. The projection X_{V_Δ(Q)} → X_{W'} = X_0(x) is therefore K'-equivariant. K' acts trivially on X_0(x) because it lies inside W': on cusps, [h]_V ↦ [hg]_V maps to [hg]_{W'} = [h]_{W'}. The projection is surjective on cusps, and X_0(x) has two cusps, 0 and ∞. So K' has at least two orbits on the cusps of X_{V_Δ(Q)}. Equivalently, the local Bruhat type in B(Q_x)\GL_2(Q_x)/U_{0,x}, which has 2 elements, is an invariant that K' preserves. The same happens even when Q = ∅, at primes in S − (T∪P) with U_1(x^{c_x}) level.

Remark 3.4 fails in the same way. The diamond operators commute with X_Δ(Q) → X_0(NQ), which has at least 2 cusps when NQ > 1. Its consequence is also false: a Hecke eigenvector can vanish at the ∞-type cusps and have eigenvalue ψ_1(x) + ψ_2(x)x^{n−1} ≠ 1 + χ(x)x^{n−1}. An example is the constant-term vector of E_n^{χ,1} for n ≥ 3 and nontrivial χ.

The target conclusion (the boundary term is Eisenstein) is still true by the standard constant-term argument. So a false assertion is used as a proof step, while the result survives. arXiv v1 simply asserted the Eisenstein property without this faulty justification. Defence attempts. (a) Could "cusps in X_{V_Δ(Q)}" mean only the cusps over a fixed cusp of X_{U_Δ(Q)}? G acts transitively on those fibres, but then the factor ∏_P Z_x^× would be pointless, and the text says "the set of cusps". Also the argument of Remark 3.4 needs a global statement: an eigenvector is non-zero at '∞', and its eigenvalue is read off there. (b) Could "cusps" mean Galois orbits? Galois acts through det, i.e. by upper-triangular matrices, which preserve the types. Neither reading rescues the claim.

Why it is false. Adelically, cusps = B(Q)\GL_2(A^∞)/V = ({±1}^2·N(Ẑ))\∏_x GL_2(Z_x)/V_x. The listed group acts only on the T- and P-components on the right. At x ∈ Q, where V_x lies between U_{1,x} and U_{0,x}, the invariant N(Z_x)\GL_2(Z_x)/U_{0,x} = N\P^1(F_x) has two values. Neither the global ±1 nor the group can change it. At x ∈ P, the Z_x^× action is by elements of U_0(x^{c_x}), which preserve the c_x+1 ≥ 2 valuation types.

Brute-force check (script work/agents/vK4-9B/cusps57.py): p=3, vexing t=5 (5≡−1 mod 3, V_t=Γ(5)), Q={7} (7≡1 mod 3) with U_{1,7}-level. There are 288 cusps. GL_2(Z/5) has 6 orbits on them, and adding the diamonds at 7 still leaves 2 orbits.

So the claim fails whenever Q≠∅, P≠∅, S≠T, or the auxiliary Γ_1(q) level is used. It holds only in the degenerate case S=T, Q=∅ with no auxiliary level, which footnote 4 says needs that level anyway. Patching uses #Q_N = q ≥ 1, so the claim is false exactly where it is used.

Nuance on the candidate's reason: its example has T=∅, but §3.9.2 assumes T≠∅. The failure persists with T≠∅, as above.

Consequences. Item (2) is used in item (3): "which in turn, by point (2) above, is equal to". Through that it feeds the analogue of Prop 3.8 and the patching proof of Thm 3.30, and hence Thm 1.4. The conclusion of item (2) is true by the standard type-by-type computation, so no stated result changes. Only the given justification fails, so 'affects' is 'the proof'. The discrepancy is real in general. α(⟨x⟩) is the reduction of the nebentypus, which is det ρ̄(Frob_x) in weight 1, and it has order > 2 in general. So α(⟨x⟩)^2 is not identically 1, and read literally, the printed m* makes both the step "RHS = dim H^0(...)_{m*}" and the contragredient step false.

The error is in β, not in T_x^t = ⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x: the Ψ relations and the contragredient check both force the corrected β. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not cover it.

Scope: m* and β appear only in this item, and nothing later uses the formula. With the obvious fix, the argument goes through exactly as the authors intend, so no stated result is affected. As the candidate noted, I did not check the scalar normalisation of T_x^t from [31]. It would only change x-power factors, which are trivial when n = 1.

A separate small slip that is not part of this item: the display at the foot of p. 352 has "ω^n ⊗ L_σ" where n = 1 is meant. Defence attempted and it fails. Two independent checks both force the corrected β.

(1) The paper's own relations with n = 1, the case in use. Take v in H^0(ω⊗L_σ) with T_x v = τv and ⟨x⟩v = δv, and put w = Ψ(v). Then T_x w = Ψ(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x v) = δ^{−1}τ w and ⟨x⟩w = Ψ(⟨x^{−1}⟩v) = δ^{−1}w. For w to lie in the m-part we need δ^{−1} ≡ α(⟨x⟩) and δ^{−1}τ ≡ α(T_x). So τ ≡ α(⟨x⟩)^{−1}α(T_x) = α(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x). The same computation gives β(⟨a⟩) = α(⟨a⟩)^{−1} and β(U_y^t) = α(U_y), exactly as printed. So only β(T_x) is off, by a factor α(⟨x⟩)^2.

The printed β cannot be rescued by reading T_x^t = ⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x differently. That formula follows from the paper's own isogeny argument (φ^t : (E,α) → (E', x∘α')) with the moduli convention ⟨a⟩f(E,α) = f(E,aα). It also agrees with v1, which has D(T_x c) = ⟨x⟩^{−1}T_x D(c).

(2) The paper's final step, which does not depend on Ψ. The proof says that taking contragredients swaps H^0(ω⊗L_σ)_{m*}⊗C and H^0(ω⊗L_{σ*})_m⊗C, so m* must be the contragredient eigensystem of m. The paper's convention (p. 326) is that m_∅ is generated by ϖ, T_x − tr ρ̄(Frob_x) and ⟨x⟩ − det ρ̄(Frob_x); item (4) likewise uses X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩. Since ρ̄^∨ ≅ ρ̄ ⊗ det^{−1}, the contragredient has T_x ↦ t_x/d_x and ⟨a⟩ ↦ d_a^{−1}, where d = det ρ̄(Frob). This is again the corrected β. The printed m* would instead need a residual representation with trace d_x t_x and determinant d_x^{−1}. Its trace is that of ρ̄⊗det ρ̄, whose determinant is d^3, so this is impossible unless (det ρ̄)^4 = 1. The printed and corrected ideals differ as soon as d_x^2 ≠ 1 and t_x ≠ 0 for some x, which happens in general, since det ρ̄ can have order > 2. Read literally, then, the claim "RHS = dim H^0(...)_{m*}" is false and the contragredient step fails.

Why this is a misprint and not an error. It is a single inverted exponent. The correct value follows at once from the displayed relations just above it. The earlier version (v1) states the correct ideal, and the argument goes through verbatim with it.

Consequences. m* and β occur only in this item; the other m* on pp. 417 ff. and in §9 are unrelated. The item proves that H_0(X_Δ(Q), ω⊗L_σ)_m is balanced, which is then used in patching for Theorem 3.30, i.e. Theorem 1.4 with vexing primes. With the fix, that conclusion stands, so no stated result is affected. The mathematics is right as intended, so under PROTOCOL §18 'affects' is 'nothing'. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not cover it. A separate cosmetic slip: the display "dim_K H^0(X_{U_0(Q)}, ω^n ⊗ L_σ)_{m*}" has ω^n where n = 1 is meant. The text is exactly as quoted. The accepted arXiv version 1207.4224v2 has the same wording, so this is not one of the 47 bracket errors. By the paper's own conventions the printed statement is wrong:
(i) Item (4) is "the analogue of" Theorem 3.11. That theorem says ρ_Q is unramified outside NQ, i.e. outside S(ρ̄) ∪ Q, which includes being unramified at p. The printed version swaps Q for {p}. It also claims ρ_Q is unramified at every x ∈ Q.
(ii) It contradicts the next sentence. η is the square root of ν = det ρ̄ · det(ρ_Q)^{-1}, which is "unramified outside Q". The paper then says ρ'_Q = ρ_Q ⊗ η is minimal outside Q. By Definition 3.1(2), that requires ρ'_Q to be unramified at every x ∉ Q ∪ S(ρ̄), p included. So ρ_Q must be unramified at p. On the other hand, ramification at Q is exactly what "minimal outside Q" allows. T_m is built from H^0(X_{U_1(Q)}, ...), on which the diamond operators at x ∈ Q act, and these give the ramification at Q used in patching.
(iii) The trace condition is ill-posed at Q. p. 345 (PDF p. 49) says that on X_{U_i(Q)} the operators are T_x for x ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {p}, and U_y for y ∈ Q. Item (4) itself defines T using "T_x, U_y and ⟨a⟩" and m using U_x − α_x for x ∈ Q. So "trace T_x for all x ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ {p}" refers to operators T_x (x ∈ Q) that are not defined in T, and to Frob_x at primes where ρ_Q may ramify.
The proof that follows establishes the corrected statement: it constructs ρ_Q so that ρ'_Q satisfies the conditions of Definition 3.1, using Sections 3.3–3.7, the unramified-at-p argument. The error is a slip in writing the analogue's statement, not a mathematical gap. The proposed correction is right. - **Error** at §4.1, Lemma 4.2 ('Moreover…') and its proof, p. 355 (same in arXiv v2, §4.1) (it affects a stated result). The source says `p. 355 (PDF p. 59), §4.1: "Lemma 4.2 If B is a complete local Cohen–Macaulay O-algebra and admits a dualizing module ω_B with μ generators, then the same is true for the power series ring A = B[T1, . . . , Tn]. Moreover, the same is also true for B⊗̂_O C, for any complete local O-algebra C which is a complete intersection. Proof For power series rings this is a special case of the discussion above. Consider now the case of B⊗̂_O C. By assumption, C is a quotient of O[T1, . . . , Tn] by a regular sequence. Hence B⊗̂_O C is a quotient of B[T1, . . . , Tn] by a regular sequence, and the result follows from the discussion above applied to the maps B[T1, . . . , Tn] → B and B[T1, . . . , Tn] → B⊗̂_O C respectively." The single brackets are among the 47 known bracket errors and should read ⟦T1,…,Tn⟧; arXiv v2 prints B[[T1,…,Tn]] and O[[T1,…,Tn]].`; it should be `Add a Tor-independence hypothesis, for example: "…for any complete local O-algebra C which is a complete intersection, provided that B or C is flat over O." Over the DVR O, this is equivalent to Tor_1^O(B,C) = 0, which is exactly the condition the proof needs. If B is O-flat: (ϖ, T1, …, Tn) is a regular sequence on B⟦T⟧, so Tor_1^{O⟦T⟧}(k, B⟦T⟧) = 0. By the local flatness criterion, B⟦T⟧ is then flat over O⟦T⟧. If C is O-flat: write B = O⟦S⟧/I. Then Tor_i^{O⟦S,T⟧}(C⟦S⟧, B⟦T⟧) = Tor_i^{O⟦S⟧}(C⟦S⟧, B). This is 0 for i > 0, because C⟦S⟧ is O⟦S⟧-flat by the same criterion. In either case, a regular sequence f in O⟦T⟧ with C = O⟦T⟧/(f) stays regular on B⟦T⟧, and B⟦T⟧/(f) = B⊗̂_O C, so the printed proof then works. "B or C" is better than "B O-flat" alone, because it also covers the remark after the lemma (B⟦Δ⟧ for arbitrary B, where C = O⟦Δ⟧ is O-flat).`. I checked the counterexample independently. The paper's conventions allow it: C_O is "complete Noetherian local O-algebras with residue field k" and nothing requires flatness. The proof also defines "complete intersection" only as "a quotient of O⟦T1,…,Tn⟧ by a regular sequence".

Take B = k = O/ϖ. It is complete local, Cohen–Macaulay of dimension 0, with ω_B = k, so μ = 1. Take C = O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ, xz−ϖ).
- In the regular local ring O⟦x,y,z⟧ with maximal ideal (ϖ,x,y,z), xy−ϖ lies in m but not in m². So R = O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ) is regular of dimension 3, hence a domain.
- In R, xz−ϖ = x(z−y). Both factors are nonzero, as their images in k⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy) show. So xz−ϖ is a nonzerodivisor, and C is a complete intersection of dimension 2.
- B⊗̂_O C = C/ϖC = k⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy,xz) = k⟦x,y,z⟧/((x)∩(y,z)). Its associated primes are (x) and (y,z), with dim R/(y,z) = 1. Since depth ≤ dim R/p for every associated prime p, the depth is 1 while the dimension is 2. So the ring is not Cohen–Macaulay.
- The proof breaks exactly at "quotient of B⟦T⟧ by a regular sequence": in k⟦x,y,z⟧, xz times y lies in (xy), but y does not. So xz is a zero-divisor mod xy.
- Necessarily C here is not O-flat: ϖ = xy lies in the minimal prime (x) of C.

The second assertion of Lemma 4.2 is therefore false as printed. It is not a bracket misprint.

Downstream effect: Lemma 4.2 is cited only in §4.1 (pp. 363–364).
- For R_loc⟦x1,…,xn⟧, B = R̃†, which the proof of Thm 4.3 states is O-flat.
- For T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O⟦Φ⟧, B = T_{1,m} is O-flat and C = O⟦Φ⟧ is O-flat.
- The B⟦Δ⟧ remark holds because C = O⟦Δ⟧ is O-flat. The candidate's line that "every application has B O-flat" is slightly wrong for this remark, where B is arbitrary. The remark is still true through the C-flat variant.

The paper also says §4.1 is "not needed for our main results". Beyond what the candidate addressed, the R_loc application also needs C = ⊗̂_v R_v⟦x⟧ to be a complete intersection. That implicitly uses the R_v being O-flat, which I did not check further. So the flaw is in a stated result, Lemma 4.2, and the paper's conclusions stay intact. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, all of which fail.
(a) No flatness convention. The Notation section (p. 305) defines C_O as "complete Noetherian local O-algebras with residue field k", with no flatness. §4.1 adds none. B = k and B = O⟦x⟧/(ϖx) are allowed.
(b) "Complete intersection" cannot be read as "O-flat relative CI". The paper uses the term in the absolute sense for non-flat rings: Thm 1.3 (p. 302) and p. 380 say "If dim(T_m)=0, then T_m is a complete intersection", and there T_m is Artinian. The proof's own gloss, "a quotient of O⟦T1,…,Tn⟧ by a regular sequence", is satisfied by the counterexamples below.
(c) No nearby statement supplies the missing Tor-vanishing.

COUNTEREXAMPLES (checked by hand).
1. X-K4-14: B = O⟦x⟧/(ϖx).
- B is a hypersurface of dimension 1, hence CM and Gorenstein (ω_B = B, μ = 1). It is CM because ϖ+x lies in neither associated prime (ϖ), (x).
- C = O⟦y⟧/(ϖy) is a CI.
- B⊗̂_O C = O⟦x,y⟧/(ϖx,ϖy) = O⟦x,y⟧/((ϖ)∩(x,y)). Its minimal primes have coheights 2 and 1, so it is not equidimensional and not CM.
- The step that fails: ϖy·x = 0 in B⟦y⟧ with x ≠ 0.
2. H-part1b-1 / X-K5-0: B = k (CM, ω = k, μ = 1) and C = O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ, xz−ϖ), or (xy−ϖ, xz).
- xy−ϖ ∉ m², so O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ) is a regular domain, and x(z−y) and xz are nonzero in it. So C is a CI of dimension 2.
- C/ϖC = k⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy,xz) has associated primes (x) and (y,z).
- It has depth 1: y+x is regular, and modulo it x ≠ 0 is killed by m. Its dimension is 2, so it is not CM.
In all of these, neither B nor C is O-flat. As shown in the correction, flatness of either one is enough.

CONSEQUENCES. Lemma 4.2 is cited only on pp. 365–366.
- (i) R_loc⟦x⟧ = R̃† ⊗̂ (⊗̂_v R_v)⟦x⟧, with B = R̃†. The proof of Thm 4.3 (p. 356) says it is O-flat.
- (ii) T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O⟦Φ⟧. Here B = T_{1,m} is O-flat because the forms are ϖ-torsion free, and C = O⟦Φ⟧ is O-flat.
- The remark after the lemma, "B⟦Δ⟧ for any B", holds because C = O⟦Δ⟧ is O-flat.
So the multiplicity-two conclusion survives with the corrected lemma. Also, §4.1 is "not needed for our main results" (p. 355).

A side point that is independent of this candidate: application (i) also needs ⊗̂_v R_v⟦x⟧ to be a CI, which implicitly uses O-flatness of the R_v. The R_v are O⟦Δ⟧-power-series rings or O⟦x1..x4⟧/(r) with r = C(T)−T; I did not check further whether ϖ ∤ r.

Verdict: the second assertion of Lemma 4.2 is false as printed. It is not a bracket misprint, and the 2022 Correction does not fix it. v1 and v2 have the same text. - **Error** at §4.1, Lemma 4.4 (first sentence), p. 357 (published version) (it affects a stated result). The source says `Lemma 4.4 Let x ∈ 𝔪^d. Keep "if and only if" only in the 'Moreover' clause, where R ≃ gr(R), meaning R is the completion of its associated graded ring, and x is pure of degree d. A true 'iff' also holds in the ungraded case if "x is regular" is replaced by "the degree-d initial form of x is a regular element of gr(R)". That is not what the paper intends, though: its remark uses "regular" to mean regular in R.`. I checked the rendered PDF pages 61–62 (pp. 357–358). The first sentence of the statement really does say "equality holds if and only if x is a regular element", with no graded hypothesis. The setup on p. 356 is just "a complete local k-algebra (R, 𝔪) with residue field k". The authors' remark right after the proof ("in the non-graded case, the converse is not true") gives a counterexample to that first sentence.

I redid the computation myself with a Python script over the semigroup ⟨6,7,15⟩, using the m-adic order of φ^s = the maximal number of generators summing to s.
- H_R = 1+3t+4t^2+5t^3+5t^4+6t^5+6t^6+…, so (1−t)H_R = 1+2t+t^2+t^3+t^5.
- The Apéry set of the semigroup with respect to 6 is {0,7,14,15,22,29}, with orders 0,1,2,2,3,3. So H_{R/φ^6} = 1+2t+2t^2+t^3 and H_{R/x}/(1−t) = 1+3t+5t^2+6t^3+6t^4+….
- This is strictly larger than H_R at t^2, t^3 and t^4, and equal at t^0, t^1 and from t^5 on.
- R is a domain and x = φ^6 ≠ 0 lies in 𝔪 (d = 1), so x is regular while the inequality is strict. That breaks the 'if' direction of the first sentence.
- The script also shows that the initial form of φ^6 is not regular in gr(R): the order jumps by 2 at s = 15, 22, 29. This matches the authors' explanation.

The proof establishes only two things: (a) if x is not regular, the inequality is strict (Krull intersection argument); (b) if x is regular and R ≃ gr(R), equality holds. The 'Moreover' clause would be redundant if the first sentence were meant as 'iff', which confirms the intended reading is 'only if'. arXiv v2 (line 2332) has the same wording.

Downstream: the lemma is used only in Lemma 4.6 (p. 358–359). There it is applied (i) explicitly "in the graded case" to get H_{B/I} = H_B(1−t)^3 for a regular sequence of pure degree-one elements in B ≃ gr(B), and (ii) for "H_{B/I} = 1+3t ⇒ regular sequence", which is the direction that is true in general. Neither use relies on the false ungraded 'if' direction. So the misstatement affects Lemma 4.4 as stated, but not the proof or any later result. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors: the only bracket error nearby is k[φ^6, φ^7, φ^15] in the remark, which is already known. Defence attempted and failed. The setup on p. 356 is only "a complete local k-algebra (R, 𝔪) with residue field k", with no grading. "Regular element" gets no special definition. The remark after the proof uses it in the usual sense: x = φ^6 is regular because R is a domain. Read this way, the first sentence claims regular ⇒ equality for every such R. The paper's own remark refutes exactly that ("in the non-graded case, the converse is not true").

Independent check with python3 on the semigroup ⟨6,7,15⟩. For a monomial, ord_𝔪(φ^s) is the largest number of generators summing to s.
- H_R has coefficients 1,3,4,5,5,6,6,…, so (1−t)H_R = 1+2t+t^2+t^3+t^5.
- The Apéry set with respect to 6 is {0,7,14,15,22,29}, with orders 0,1,2,1,2,3. So H_{R/x} = 1+2t+2t^2+t^3, and H_{R/x}/(1−t) has coefficients 1,3,5,6,6,….
- This is strictly larger than H_R at t^2, t^3 and t^4, although x ∈ 𝔪 (d = 1) is regular.
- The initial form of x is a zero-divisor in gr(R): ord(s+6) ≠ ord(s)+1 at s = 15, 22, 29.
These values match the paper's printed series. A small side note: the earlier verdict gave the Apéry orders as 0,1,2,2,3,3, which is wrong because 15 has order 1. Its Hilbert series was still right.

The proof gives only two things: (a) x not regular ⇒ strict inequality (Krull intersection argument), which is the 'only if' direction and holds in general; and (b) x regular and R ≃ gr(R) ⇒ equality. The 'Moreover' clause would add nothing if the first sentence were a true 'iff'. So the intended statement is clear, but the printed one is false.

Consequences: Lemma 4.4 is cited only in the proof of Lemma 4.6 (p. 360). There it is used in two ways:
- (i) Explicitly "in the graded case", to get H_{B/I} = H_B(1−t)^3 for a pure degree-one regular sequence in B ≃ gr(B). This is the valid 'Moreover' direction.
- (ii) To deduce, from H_{B/I} = 1+3t, that three pure degree-one generators form a regular sequence. This uses the chain H_{B/I}/(1−t)^3 ≥ H_{B/(x1,x2)}/(1−t)^2 ≥ H_{B/x1}/(1−t) ≥ H_B = (1+3t)/(1−t)^3, which forces equality at each step. Then equality ⇒ regular, the direction that is true in general.
Neither use needs the false ungraded 'if' direction, so Lemmas 4.6 and 4.7 and Theorem 4.3 are unaffected. The damage is confined to the statement of Lemma 4.4. That is why affects = 'a stated result': the lemma as stated is false, but no later proof or result is.

Kind: this is a false mathematical claim (an overstated 'iff'), not a slip of notation, so I classify it as an error, even though the intended weaker statement can be recovered from the remark. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors; the only bracket error nearby is k[φ^6, φ^7, φ^15] in the remark, which is already known. - **Misprint** at §4.1, Lemma 4.4 (the 'Moreover' sentence) and the last step of its proof, published p. 357 (PDF p. 61); the same notation is used for B on p. 358. arXiv v2 p. 44 has the same displayed formula R ≃ gr(R) = ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1}. arXiv v1 does not contain this lemma, since the Hilbert-series argument of Lemmas 4.4–4.7 is new in v2.. The source says `Lemma 4.4 Let x ∈ 𝔪^d. We have H_{R/x}(t)/(1 − t) ≥ H_R(t) · (1 − t^d)/(1 − t), and equality holds if and only if x is a regular element. Moreover, if there is an isomorphism R ≃ gr(R) = ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1}, and x is pure of degree d, then equality holds if and only if x is a regular element. [proof:] "Finally, assume that x is a regular element, and that R ≃ gr(R)." [p. 358:] "All the relations in B are pure of degree two, and hence there is an isomorphism B ≃ gr(B)."`; it should be `Read the hypothesis as: R is isomorphic to the 𝔪-adic completion ∏_n 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1} of gr(R). In other words, R ≅ k⟦x_1,…,x_r⟧/I with I generated by homogeneous polynomials, and 'pure of degree d' refers to that grading. The same reading applies to 'B ≃ gr(B)' on p. 358.`. The setup on p. 356 makes R a complete local k-algebra (R, 𝔪). The ring B that the lemma is applied to is a quotient of the power series ring k⟦a,b,c,φ1,φ2,φ3⟧ (printed with single brackets, which is one of the known bracket errors). By Lemma 4.6/4.7, B has Krull dimension 3.

The displayed ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1} = k[a,…,φ3]/(homogeneous quadrics) is a finitely generated k-algebra of positive dimension. It therefore has infinitely many maximal ideals, so it is not local and not 𝔪-adically complete, and no ring isomorphism B ≃ ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1} exists. As printed, the hypothesis can only hold for Artinian R, and the claim 'B ≃ gr(B)' is literally false.

The intended meaning is clear, and the paper uses it elsewhere: the proof of Lemma 4.6 begins 'Let R be a complete local Cohen–Macaulay Noetherian graded k-algebra' and then invokes 'Lemma 4.4 (in the graded case)'.

With the completed reading, the proof works. Take R = Ĝ with G standard graded and x ∈ G_d regular. Then R/𝔪^{m+d} = ⨁_{j<m+d} G_j, and x·y ∈ 𝔪^{m+d} forces the components y_j with j < m to vanish. So the kernel is exactly 𝔪^m/𝔪^{m+d}, as the proof claims. B satisfies this reading because its defining relations are homogeneous quadrics. The induction in Lemma 4.6 keeps the reading, since quotients by homogeneous elements stay completions of graded rings.

This is an abuse of notation, not a wrong idea, so it is a misprint that affects nothing. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It is also separate from the 'if and only if' problem in the first sentence of Lemma 4.4 (candidates X-K5-1 / H-part1b-0). Confidence is medium only because some readers treat 'R ≃ gr(R)' for complete local rings as standard shorthand. The explicit '= ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1}' makes the printed statement literally wrong. - **Misprint** at §4.1, last sentence of the proof of Lemma 4.7, published p. 361 (PDF p. 65), top of the page. arXiv v2 has the same wording ('the Hilbert polynomial of C is 1 + 3t', v2 text line 2485). arXiv v1 does not contain Lemma 4.7.. The source says `On the other hand, since all the relations are trivial in 𝔪^2, we have dim(𝔪/𝔪^2) = 3. Hence the Hilbert polynomial of C is 1+3t, and the sequence is regular in A.`; it should be `"Hence the Hilbert series H_C(t) of C is 1 + 3t"`. The only notion the paper defines is the Hilbert series H_R(t) = Σ dim_k(𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1}) t^n (p. 356). Lemma 4.6 is stated in terms of H_{B/I}(t) = 1+3t, and the proof of Lemma 4.7 itself opens with 'it suffices to show that the Hilbert series of B/I … is 1+3t'.

C = B/I is a quotient of k⟦x,y,z⟧/(x^2,y^2,z^2,xy,xz,yz) with dim 𝔪/𝔪^2 = 3, so C ≅ k⟦x,y,z⟧/(x,y,z)^2. It is Artinian with Hilbert function 1, 3, 0, 0, …. Its Hilbert series is therefore 1+3t, while its Hilbert polynomial in the standard sense (the polynomial agreeing with the Hilbert function for n ≫ 0) is 0.

The word 'polynomial' is a terminology slip for 'series' (the series happens to be a polynomial here). The computation and the comparison with Lemma 4.6 are correct under the intended reading. I also rechecked the relations of C from those of B (a = 0, φ3 = −φ2, φ1 = −(b+c)): they match the printed list, and they give xz = yz = xy = x^2 = y^2 = z^2 = 0. This is not a bracket error. - **Misprint** at §4.1, p. 361 (setup before Theorem 4.8) (published version). The source says `p. 361 (PDF p. 65): "One knows that ρ̄ occurs as the mod-p reduction of a modular form of weight 2 and level N*, where N* = N if k = 2 and Np otherwise." p. 362 (PDF p. 66): "For φ ∈ Φ̂, and let χ_φ denote the character ε · ⟨ρ̄ε^{−1}⟩φ of G_Q." p. 363 (PDF p. 67): "Let ψ denote the restriction of χ to Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x∤M}(Z/xZ)^×, which we may regard as a character of G_Q. After twisting ρ by ψ^{−1/2}, we obtain a Galois representation G_Q → GL_2(T^an_{φ,m}) with determinant χ_φ = ε · ⟨ρ̄ε^{−1}⟩φ which is classified by R = R_φ." (The same text is in arXiv v2, pp. 47–49.)`; it should be `Replace ⟨ρ̄ε^{−1}⟩ with ⟨det(ρ̄)·ε̄^{−1}⟩ in both places, on p. 362 and p. 363. This gives χ_φ = ε·⟨det ρ̄·ε̄^{−1}⟩·φ = ε·ω^{−1}·⟨det ρ̄⟩·φ. There are also two minor fixes. On p. 361, "N* = N if k(ρ̄) = 2" is meant: k is the residue field, and the Serre weight is k(ρ̄). On p. 363, the product should be ∏_{x|N, x∤M}. The factor at x = p is irrelevant because Z_p ⊗ (Z/pZ)^× = 0.`. I checked the page images at 250 dpi, and the printed text is as quoted. The main point is a real misprint. The Notation section on p. 305 defines ⟨χ⟩: G → O^× only for a character χ: G → k^×. But ρ̄ε^{−1} is a 2-dimensional representation, not a character. Elsewhere the authors write the determinant explicitly: "ν := ⟨det ρ̄⟩ det(ρ_{Q,m})^{−1}" on p. 332, and ⟨det(ρ̄)⟩ in §3.4 of arXiv v2. So here the word "det" has been dropped, and it is dropped in both occurrences.

I redid the bookkeeping. For weight-2 forms with nebentypus χ, det ρ = ε·χ, so ε^{−1} det ρ = χ, as the paper says. Reducing, χ ≡ det ρ̄·ε̄^{−1} mod m. So χ = ⟨det ρ̄ ε̄^{−1}⟩·χ_p, where χ_p is the p-power-order part, a character of Z_p⊗(Z/NpZ)^×. Since p ∤ N, this group is Z_p⊗(Z/NZ)^× = Φ × Z_p⊗∏_{x|N, x∤M}(Z/xZ)^×. On Φ, χ_p = φ; on the other factor, χ_p = ψ. After twisting by ψ^{−1/2}, det = εχψ^{−1} = ε·⟨det ρ̄ ε̄^{−1}⟩·φ. This reduces to det ρ̄, and on G_p it equals εω^{−1} times an unramified character, as the ordinary ring R† of §3.7 needs. So the proposed correction is right.

The other two parts of the candidate are much weaker. "k = 2" is a notation clash with the residue field k, but the meaning k(ρ̄) = 2 is clear: the text later says "Thus N* = pN (since p is odd)", which uses k(ρ̄) = p. "∏_{x∤M}" is shorthand, since χ is a character of (Z/NpZ)^×, so x | Np is implicit. Neither needs its own entry.

Nothing depends on the misprint. The intended meaning is clear from the notation convention and the computation. Neither the statement of Theorem 4.8 nor the proof that follows (Lemma 4.11 uses χ_φ only as the fixed determinant) is affected. - **Misprint** at §4.1, proof of Theorem 4.8, published p. 362 (display defining Φ) and p. 363 (definition of ψ) (PDF pp. 66–67). arXiv v2 and v1 have the identical formulas.. The source says `p. 362 (display): "Φ := Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x|M} (Z/xZ)^×"; p. 363: "Let ψ denote the restriction of χ to Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x∤M}(Z/xZ)^×, which we may regard as a character of G_Q."`; it should be `Φ := Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x | M, x prime} (Z/xZ)^× (= Z_p ⊗ (Z/MZ)^×). ψ is the restriction of χ to Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x | N, x prime, x ∤ M} (Z/xZ)^×, the p-part of (Z/NpZ)^× at the non-harmless primes.`. The candidate's premise holds. At a harmless prime v, ρ̄|G_v is absolutely irreducible, so ρ̄^{I_v} = 0 and the conductor exponent is at least 2. Hence v^2 | N and M is never squarefree when M > 1. Read with x ranging over all divisors of M, the first product is the wrong group: for M = v^2 it gives two copies of the p-part of (Z/vZ)^×. The usual convention that the index x is prime fixes the first formula. Under that convention it equals Z_p ⊗ (Z/MZ)^×, since for x ≠ p the tensor Z_p ⊗ (Z/x^eZ)^× equals Z_p ⊗ (Z/xZ)^×. The second product is genuinely wrong as printed even with x prime. It runs over all primes not dividing M, so it is infinite. It must be cut down to primes x | N (x = p adds nothing because p is odd). Only then is 'the restriction of χ', a character of (Z/NpZ)^×, meaningful. The intended meaning is clear from context, so this is a misprint that affects nothing. Confidence is medium only because the Φ half could be defended as an abuse of notation. The ψ half cannot. - **Error** at §4.1, proof of Theorem 4.8, published p. 363 (PDF p. 67), paragraph beginning "The reason for dealing with the harmless primes". arXiv v2 (p. 49) has the same text. arXiv v1 has the first sentence (the ring isomorphism "up to unramified twists") but not the "Equivalently…" or "The only time…" sentences, and it defines "harmless" differently. (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 363 (PDF p. 67), first paragraph, read from the page image: "The reason for dealing with the harmless primes in this manner is as follows. For all non-harmless v ≠ p, the conductor-minimal deformation ring of ρ̄|G_v (which classifies deformations which appear at level Γ_1(N)) is isomorphic to the ring R_{v,φ} (up to unramified twists). Equivalently, for non-harmless primes, any characteristic zero lift ρ of ρ̄ is uniquely twist equivalent to a lift of minimal conductor. The only time this is not true is when v ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ has trivial invariants under I_v. Since we are assuming that ρ̄|_{G_v} is minimally ramified amongst all its twists, this only happens when ρ̄|_{G_v} is absolutely irreducible and v ≡ 1 mod p." The next paragraph, which depends on it, reads: "Kisin's improvement of the Taylor–Wiles method yields an isomorphism R_φ[1/p] ≃ T^an_{φ,m}[1/p]." On p. 362: "(2) When v ≠ p, R_v = R_{v,φ} is the unrestricted framed deformation ring with determinant χ_φ|G_v."`; it should be `The exceptional set is wrong. Uniqueness of the minimal-conductor twist, and the claimed isomorphism with R_{v,φ} up to unramified twist, also fail at the non-harmless primes of Lemma 4.11 case (3): v ≡ 1 mod p, ρ̄^{I_v} one-dimensional and ρ̄^{ss}|G_v unramified. Take a lift in R_{v,φ} with ρ|I_v ≅ ψ ⊕ ψ^{-1}, where ψ ≠ 1 has p-power order (one of the (q−1)/2 non-Steinberg components in footnote 5). It has two minimal-conductor twists by characters ≡ 1 mod ϖ, namely ρ⊗ψ (ψ² ⊕ 1 on I_v) and ρ⊗ψ^{-1} (1 ⊕ ψ^{-2} on I_v). These two twists are not related by an unramified twist. The correct statement is: uniqueness holds except when v ≡ 1 mod p and either ρ̄|G_v is absolutely irreducible (harmless) or ρ̄|G_v is, up to unramified twist, a ramified non-split extension of 1 by 1 (case (3)). The candidate's correction of the claim is right and minimal. Its assessment of the consequences is not. The proof also needs the twisting map (eigenforms in S_φ) → (points of R_φ) to be injective, and at case-(3) primes it is not. Primes of type (3) therefore need a separate treatment in the proof of Theorem 4.8. For example, one could use at v the ring of lifts with conductor exponent ≤ 1 and p-power inertial determinant, taken over O[Δ_v], instead of R_{v,φ}, or handle these primes differently from the ψ^{-1/2} twist.`. I checked this from scratch using the page images (PDF pp. 65–70).

**Setup.** R_{v,φ} is the full fixed-determinant ring. For non-harmless v, χ_φ|I_v is trivial (φ is ramified only at harmless primes). In case (3), after an unramified twist, ρ̄|G_v = (1 *; 0 1) with * ramified.

**The non-Steinberg lifts exist.** Take ρ(σ) = (ζ 1; 0 ζ^{-1}) with ζ ≠ 1 of p-power order dividing v−1, and ρ(Frob) = a·I. Then ρ(σ)^v = ρ(σ). The lift reduces to (1 1; 0 1), and its determinant is unramified and adjustable through a. For example p=3, v=7, ζ a cube root of 1. The paper itself describes these points on p. 365 ("χ_φψ ⊕ ψ^{-1} with ψ|I_v of p-power order") and in footnote 5 (the (q−1)/2 components).

**Twists of such a lift.** Let η ≡ 1 mod ϖ, so ρ⊗η still lifts ρ̄. Then ρ⊗η has conductor exponent 1 = a(ρ̄) exactly when η|I_v ∈ {ψ, ψ^{-1}}. That gives two minimal twists. They differ by ψ², which is ramified and nontrivial because p is odd. So neither "uniquely twist equivalent" nor the claimed ring isomorphism holds. The ring statement fails under either reading:
- If "conductor-minimal" fixes the determinant up to unramified twist, it gives only the Steinberg component, one of (q+1)/2.
- If the determinant is free, it gives q components mapping 2:1 onto the non-Steinberg ones.

**Impact on the proof.** This is more than motivation. Take a newform f ∈ S_{φ,m} with ρ_f|I_v ≅ 1 ⊕ η, η ≠ 1 (the paper needs such forms: every component of R_{v,φ} must be in the support of S_φ). Let Θ be a Dirichlet character of conductor v and p-power order with Θ|I_v = η^{-1}, and let g = f⊗Θ. Then:
- g has the same level N*, is still ordinary, and lies in the same m.
- χ_g|Φ = χ_f|Φ = φ, because Θ is trivial on the harmless part.
- ψ_g = ψ_f Θ², so ρ_g⊗ψ_g^{-1/2} = ρ_f⊗ψ_f^{-1/2}.
- ρ_g ≇ ρ_f, since the inertial types 1⊕η^{-1} and 1⊕η differ, so g and f have different T_l eigenvalues for some l.

So two points of Spec T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] map to one point of Spec R_φ[1/p]. Hence R_φ → T^an_{φ,m} is not surjective, and the asserted R_φ[1/p] ≃ T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] is false whenever such a prime occurs. The same holds for R̃ ≃ T_{φ,m} (p. 365): U_p eigenvalues also agree after the twist. The 2:1 fibres are exactly what the "uniqueness" claim was meant to rule out.

**Status of Theorem 4.8.** The theorem is probably still true via a double-cover local ring, which is still a complete intersection. So only the proof is affected. I did not build an explicit global ρ̄ satisfying the scalar hypothesis with a case-(3) prime. I disagree with the reader's "affects: nothing". 1. The claim is false.

Case (3) primes are non-harmless because ρ̄|G_v is reducible. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|G_v ≅ (unramified) ⊗ (1 *; 0 1), * ramified. p. 365 (Lemma 4.11) itself says the generic fibre of R_{v,φ} contains lifts 'χ_φψ ⊕ ψ^{-1} with ψ|I_v of p-power order'. Footnote 5 says it has (q+1)/2 components.

- A twist ρ⊗θ with θ ≡ 1 mod ϖ has conductor exponent 1 (minimal) exactly when θ|I_v = ψ or θ|I_v = ψ^{-1}.
- These two twists differ by ψ², which is ramified. Since p is odd and ψ ≠ 1, ψ² ≠ 1 and ψ² ≠ ψ^{-2}. So the minimal twist is not unique, not even up to unramified twist.
- The rings do not match either. The conductor-minimal ring with free determinant has 1 + (q−1) = q generic components (Steinberg, and θ ⊕ 1 for each θ ≠ 1). With determinant fixed to χ_φ|G_v, which is unramified here, it has only the Steinberg component. R_{v,φ} has (q+1)/2. So no reading of 'isomorphic up to unramified twists' works.
- Cross-check of the other v ≡ 1 mod p cases: in case (1), ρ̄|I_v ≅ χ̄ ⊕ 1, the other twist would be by a character ≡ χ̄^{-1} ≠ 1 mod ϖ, so uniqueness holds. The paper's exception list is therefore incomplete exactly by case (3).

2. Defence attempted.

Read 'conductor-minimal deformation ring' charitably, as 'lifts with determinant χ_φ that are twists of level-Γ_1(N) lifts'. Then sentence 1 is tautologically R_{v,φ}. But the 'Equivalently ... uniquely' sentence cannot be saved: uniqueness is exactly the property the authors use to separate harmless primes, where every twist has conductor 2.

3. Consequences: the passage is load-bearing.

- Uniqueness is what makes f ↦ ρ_f ⊗ ψ_f^{-1/2} injective from eigenforms in S_φ to points of R_φ. Given two such forms f, f', the twisted representations coincide iff ρ_{f'} = ρ_f⊗θ, with θ ≡ 1 mod ϖ ramified only at non-harmless primes. Uniqueness at each such prime forces θ to be unramified everywhere, so θ = 1.
- Case (3) breaks this. Let θ be a Dirichlet character of conductor v and p-power order, and let f1 ∈ S_φ be ordinary with ρ_{f1}|I_v ≅ θ ⊕ 1. Such f1 exists by the paper's own claim that every component of R_{v,φ} lies in the support of S_φ. Set f2 = f1⊗θ^{-1}. Then ρ_{f2}|I_v ≅ 1 ⊕ θ^{-1}, which still has conductor exponent 1. The nebentypus of f2 is χ1θ^{-2}, and its restriction to Φ is still φ. So f2 ∈ S_φ, it is ordinary, and it lies in the m-part.
- Computation: ψ2 = ψ1θ^{-2}. Since the square root is unique in a p-group with p odd, ψ2^{-1/2} = ψ1^{-1/2}θ. Hence ρ_{f2}⊗ψ2^{-1/2} = ρ_{f1}⊗ψ1^{-1/2}. The twisted U_p-eigenvalues also agree.
- So f1 and f2 have distinct Hecke eigensystems: a_l(f2) = θ^{-1}(l)·a_l(f1), and the nebentypus at v is θ versus θ^{-1}. Yet they give the same Q̄_p-point of R_φ, and of R̃.
- Therefore R_φ[1/p] → T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] is not surjective, and the asserted isomorphism R_φ[1/p] ≃ T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] (p. 363) is false whenever N has a case-(3) prime. The same holds for R̃ ≃ T_{φ,m} (p. 365).
- The conclusions drawn from it are then unproven in that case: T_{φ,m} Cohen–Macaulay with dim ω/m = 3, hence the same for T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ], hence dim J_1(N*)[m] = 2.
- Lemma 4.11 treats case (3) explicitly, and Theorem 4.8 does not exclude it.

The statement of Theorem 4.8 is not shown false. The repair looks plausible: use a conductor-≤1 local ring over O[Δ_v] that should be Cohen–Macaulay. So I rate affects as 'the proof', not 'nothing' as the candidate proposed. Confidence is high that the passage is wrong, and medium-high on the exact extent of the damage to the proof. I transcribed the text from 220-dpi renders of PDF pp. 68–69 (pp. 364–365). Setup: v ≠ p, p odd, and R_v is the unrestricted framed deformation ring with fixed determinant. By the local Euler characteristic, dim Z^1 = 3 + h^2(ad^0ρ̄). So R_v is not smooth exactly when H^0(G_v, ad^0ρ̄(1)) ≠ 0.

Redoing the classification for ρ̄ minimal among twists gives four cases, not three:
- v≡1, split, χ ramified.
- v≡−1, induced from the unramified quadratic extension.
- v≡1, ramified unipotent.
- v≡−1, ρ̄ ≅ μ⊗(ω̄ *; 0 1) with * ramified.
The fourth case is missing. It is minimal: the conductor exponent is 1 and no twist lowers it. In this case e = (0 1; 0 0) spans H^0(ad^0ρ̄(1)), because G_v acts on it by ω̄^2 and ω̄(Frob_v) = −1. Also H^0(ad^0ρ̄) = 0: e is inertia-fixed, but Frobenius acts on it by −1. So h^2 = 1 and dim Z^1 = 4. That exceeds the relative dimension 3, so R_v is not formally smooth.

I checked the extra lifts. Take ρ(τ) = (ζ 1; 0 ζ^{−1}) with ζ ≠ 1, ζ^{v+1} = 1, of p-power order, and S = (d1, (d2−d1)/δ; d1δ, −d1) with δ = ζ^{−1}−ζ. Then S ρ(τ) S^{−1} = ρ(τ)^v; I verified this numerically for (q,v) = (3,2), (3,5), (3,11), (9,17), (5,19). Taking d1 ≡ −1 and d2−d1 ∈ δO, the lift reduces to ρ̄. Hensel's lemma lets det S hit the fixed determinant.

Lemma 4.11 itself still holds. At Steinberg points H^0(ad^0ρ(1)) = 0, since Frobenius acts on e by v^{±2} ≠ 1. At the induced points, ad^0ρ(1) = ηε ⊕ Ind(ψ/ψ^σ)⊗ε. Frobenius acts on ηε by −v^{±1}, and the second summand has no inertia invariants because ζ^2 ≠ 1.

I believe such ρ̄ exist within the §4.1 scope: unramified at p with scalar Frob_p (Thm 4.8). One route is an S4-quartic construction with p=3, v=2. I have not verified an explicit example. The submitter's elliptic-curve example is only local, since det ρ̄_{E,3} is ramified at 3.

The submitter says the case-(3) argument covers this "verbatim". That is not quite right: the description of the generic points has to change.

Lemma 4.11 is used only in the proof of Thm 4.8 (p. 363); grep finds no other citations. There is a related, more serious flaw that should be a separate item. On p. 363 the paper claims that for non-harmless v every lift is twist-equivalent to a conductor-minimal one, and that the only exception is v≡1 with ρ̄ having trivial I_v-invariants. The induced lifts above have conductor v^2 and cannot be twisted down to conductor v. So the claim that every component of R_{v,φ} lies in the support of S_φ (level Γ1(N*)) fails at such v. The likely repair is to use the smooth Steinberg quotient at such v. So I rate this as affecting the proof, not the stated results.

Minor side point: in footnote 5, "primitive q-th root of unity" should be "q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1". Otherwise the count (q−1)/2 is wrong when q = p^2. Setting. By p. 365 of the paper, p ≥ 3 and v ≠ p. R_v is the unrestricted framed ring with fixed determinant. Here χ_φ|G_v is unramified at every v that is not harmless. The only condition the paper imposes at v | N is that ρ̄ has minimal conductor among its twists, and the mod-p Steinberg type (conductor exponent 1) satisfies it. The local Euler characteristic gives dim Z¹(G_v, ad⁰ρ̄) = 3 + h²(ad⁰ρ̄) − h⁰(ad⁰ρ̄) + h⁰(ad⁰ρ̄) = 3 + h⁰(G_v, ad⁰ρ̄(1)). R_v has relative dimension 3, so it fails to be formally smooth exactly when H⁰(G_v, ad⁰ρ̄(1)) ≠ 0.

Missing case. Take v ≡ −1 mod p and ρ̄ = (ω̄ *; 0 1) with * ramified. Such an extension exists and is unique: h¹(G_v, ω̄) = h⁰(ω̄) + h⁰(ω̄^{-1}·ω̄) = 0 + 1, and the unramified part is ω̄/(Frob−1) = 0. Conjugating by the unipotent ρ̄(τ) shows H⁰(I_v, ad⁰ρ̄) = k·e with e = (0 1; 0 0), since p is odd. Frobenius acts on e by ω̄(Frob) = −1, so H⁰(ad⁰ρ̄) = 0. On e⊗ω̄ it acts by (−1)(−1) = 1, so H⁰(ad⁰ρ̄(1)) = k·e. Hence h² = 1, dim Z¹ = 4 > 3, and R_v is not smooth. This case is none of (1)–(3): v ≢ 1, and ρ̄|G_v is reducible.

Checks. I brute-forced H⁰ over F_p. It has dimension 1 for (p,v) = (3,2), (3,5), (5,19), (7,13). It has dimension 0 for v ≢ ±1, e.g. (5,7) and (7,5). Redoing the classification (irreducible, split, and non-split types) gives exactly four non-smooth twist-minimal cases, so only this one is missing.

Lemma 4.11 survives. The lifts are of two kinds.
- Steinberg twists. H⁰(ad⁰ρ(1)) = 0 because Frobenius acts on e by v² ≠ 1.
- The extra points, with ρ(τ) = (ζ 1; 0 ζ^{-1}), ζ^{v+1} = 1, ζ ≠ 1 of p-power order, and ρ(σ) = S swapping the eigenlines. I checked S·T = T^v·S numerically for (q,v) = (3,2), (3,5), (3,11), (9,17), (5,19), (3,8), (9,26). These lifts reduce to ρ̄. Here ad⁰ρ(1) = ηε ⊕ Ind(ψ/ψ^σ)ε. Frobenius acts on the first summand by −v ≠ 1. The second has no inertia invariants, since ζ^{±2} ≠ 1.

So the error is in the proof only. The submitted corrections are right. H-part1b-2 says the argument covers the new case "verbatim", which is slightly off: the generic-point description must change. X-K5-8's correction states it correctly.

Could the case be excluded? Nothing in §4.1 rules it out. Examples plausibly exist: take the mod-3 reduction of an odd octahedral Artin representation (projective image S4 ≅ PGL2(F3)) that is tamely ramified of index 3 at some v ≡ 2 mod 3, with 3 split completely. Projectively, D_v = S3 is the Borel subgroup, and this forces ρ̄|G_v to be of the missing type. I have not verified an explicit example.

Consequences. Lemma 4.11 is cited only in the proof of Thm 4.8, on p. 363, and it is used implicitly on p. 365 through Lemma 4.2. The consequence is serious but separate, and it deserves its own item, distinct from C-K5-0. For this local type, p ∤ v−1, so no nebentypus twist is available at v. The Ind components have conductor v² and cannot be twisted down. So the p. 363 claim that every component of R_{v,φ} lies in the support of S_φ (level Γ1(N*), v ∥ N*) fails at such v. The natural repair is to use the minimally ramified (Steinberg) quotient there, which is formally smooth (CHT §2.4). The stated results are unaffected. - **Gap** at §1, Corollary 1.5, hypothesis (1), p. 304 (same in arXiv v1 Cor. 1.4 and v2) (it affects a stated result). The source says `We immediately deduce from Theorem 1.4 the following: Corollary 1.5 Suppose that p ≥ 3. Suppose also that ρ : G_Q → GL_2(O) is a continuous representation satisfying the following conditions. (1) For all primes v, either ρ(I_v) ~→ ρ̄(I_v) or dim(ρ^{I_v}) = dim(ρ̄^{I_v}) = 1. (2) ρ̄ is odd and irreducible. (3) ρ is unramified at p. Then ρ is modular of weight one.`; it should be `Hypothesis (1) must say that ρ is minimal up to twist, which is all that Theorem 1.4 can give. The fix: first twist ρ̄ by a character ε̄, and ρ by its Teichmüller lift, so that ρ̄^{I_v} ≠ 0 whenever ρ̄|G_v is ramified and reducible (§3.1). Then require, for every prime v: (a) if ρ̄ is unramified at v, then ρ is unramified at v; (b) if ρ̄^{I_v} = 0, then ρ(I_v) ⥲ ρ̄(I_v); (c) if ρ̄^{I_v} is a line, then rank ρ^{I_v} = 1 and det ρ|I_v = ⟨det ρ̄⟩|I_v. Put ψ = det ρ·⟨det ρ̄⟩^{-1}. This character has finite order, being unramified at p. Under (a)–(c), ρ⊗ψ^{-1/2} is minimal in the sense of Def. 3.1, so Theorem 1.4 applies and twisting back gives the corollary. Equivalently, simply assume that some finite-order twist of ρ is a minimal deformation of the correspondingly twisted ρ̄. The correction proposed in X-K1-0 is right, given that it twists ρ̄ first as it states. The correction in H-part1a-12, which adds only the determinant condition, is not enough, because it misses the unipotent-reduction case (ii) below.`. Rendered PDF p.8 = p.304; the printed text matches the transcription. The same statement appears in arXiv v2. I checked the setup the corollary relies on. Def. 3.1(1) (p.307) fixes det ρ = Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄, and R^min is taken with Q=∅. Theorem 1.4 is proved with X_U = X_1(N)/H, where H is the p-part of (Z/N)^× (§3.3). In §3.9, U_x at x ∈ P(ρ̄) requires d to have p-power order. So T_m only sees forms whose nebentypus has order prime to p.

Redoing the counterexample. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_v = 1 ⊕ χ̄, χ̄ ≠ 1. Frobenius fixes the trivial isotypic line, so ρ̄|G_v is reducible, v ∈ S−T, and dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1. Let ρ|I_v = 1 ⊕ [χ̄]θ with θ ≠ 1 of p-power order. Then dim ρ^{I_v} = 1, so (1) holds. Put ψ = det ρ/[det ρ̄], which has p-power order and ψ|I_v = θ. Any twist ρ⊗ε that lifts ρ̄⊗ε̄ with the fixed determinant forces ε = [ε̄]·ψ^{-1/2}, because squaring is bijective on 1+m when p is odd. The standing hypothesis ρ̄^{I_v} ≠ 0 forces ε̄|I_v ∈ {1, χ̄^{-1}}. In both cases (ρ⊗ε)|I_v has characters [ε̄]θ^{-1/2} and [ε̄χ̄]θ^{1/2}, and neither is trivial, so there are no inertia invariants and Def. 3.1(4) fails. So no twist of ρ is a point of any R^min covered by Theorem 1.4. The Hecke side agrees: the twist has conductor v² at v, and the untwisted ρ has non-p'-order nebentypus.

A global example exists. Take p=3, v=13, K=Q(√−14): 13 splits, 3 is unramified, and O_K^× = ±1. Let ψ be a character of order 6 on I_w, unramified at w' and elsewhere. ψ_w(−1) = 1 because 12/6 is even, so ψ extends to a Hecke character. Then ρ = Ind_K ψ is odd, ρ̄ is irreducible (ψ̄ ≠ ψ̄^c at w), ρ is unramified at 3, and (1) holds at 2, 7 (order-2 inertia) and at 13. ρ is modular, but only on X_1(728), not on X_U. So the claimed "immediate" deduction fails for part of the hypothesis. The paper itself says non-minimal lifting is hard (p.304 text after Cor. 1.6).

Corollary 1.5 is not cited again in the paper (grep). Corollary 1.6 assumes minimality, so it is unaffected. The candidate's gap is correct. Its correction's "equivalently" and "only at v ≡ 1 mod p" are overstated, as the correction field explains. I checked the Steinberg case only locally and did not construct a global example. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED. Theorem 1.4 is proved in §3 for R^min as defined in Def. 3.1 with Q = ∅. That ring has a fixed determinant, equal to the Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄ (Def. 3.1(1)), and it requires ρ^{I_x} to be a rank-one direct summand at every x ∈ S−T where ρ̄|G_x is reducible (Def. 3.1(4)). T_m lives on X_U = X_1(N)/H, where H is the p-part of (Z/N)^× (§3.3, p. 2141 of the text). At x ∈ P(ρ̄), the group U_x forces d to have p-power order (§3.9). So T_m sees only forms of conductor dividing N whose nebentypus has no p-part.
The intended deduction runs: twist by ψ^{-1/2}, get a minimal deformation, conclude modularity, twist back. This only works if hypothesis (1) makes some twist of ρ minimal. Two cases show that it does not.

(i) DETERMINANT CASE. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_v = 1⊕χ̄, χ̄ ≠ 1, and ρ|I_v = 1⊕[χ̄]θ, with θ ≠ 1 of p-power order. The second alternative of (1) holds. Consider any twist ρ⊗ε that lifts ρ̄⊗ε̄ with the fixed determinant. Since squaring is bijective on 1+m, this forces ε = [ε̄]ψ^{-1/2}. On I_v the twist then has characters [ε̄]θ^{-1/2} and [ε̄χ̄]θ^{1/2}, and neither is trivial. So Def. 3.1(4) fails for every such twist.
A global example, which I re-checked: p = 3, K = Q(√−14), in which 13 splits, 3 is unramified and O_K^× = ±1. Take ψ of order 6 on I_w for one prime w | 13; since ψ_w(−1) = 1, ψ extends to a Hecke character. Then ρ = Ind_K ψ is odd, ρ̄ is irreducible (ψ̄ ≠ ψ̄^c), ρ is unramified at 3, and (1) holds at 2, 7 and 13. This ρ is modular (it is dihedral), but no twist of it is a point of T_m.

(ii) UNIPOTENT-REDUCTION CASE. Take x ≡ ±1 mod p with ρ̄|I_x unipotent and nontrivial, so ρ̄(I_x) ≅ Z/p. Let ρ|I_x = ζ⊕ζ^{-1} with ζ of order p. This occurs as a non-split lattice; I checked the lattice explicitly. Here ρ(I_x) ⥲ ρ̄(I_x), so the first alternative of (1) holds, and det ρ|I_x = 1. But ρ^{I_x} = 0 and the conductor is x^2. Any p-power twist still has no inertia invariants, and a prime-to-p twist destroys ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0.
In fact, at a Steinberg-type x the first alternative never yields a minimal ρ. Minimal lifts there have infinite inertia image and satisfy the second alternative instead. I expect global examples to exist (for instance p = 3 tetrahedral or octahedral forms with inertia of order 3 at some prime), but I did not construct a specific one.

In both cases ρ is a non-minimal lift. The paper itself says (p. 304–305) that its method cannot handle such lifts. So the word "immediately" is unjustified for part of the range of hypothesis (1). The conclusion is probably true, as predicted by Fontaine–Mazur, and the examples above are modular by classical results. That makes this a gap rather than a false statement.

CONSEQUENCES. Corollary 1.5 is not used later in the paper. Corollary 1.6 assumes minimality outright, and Theorem 1.4 is unaffected. Only the corollary, as a stated result, is not established in the generality stated. The source says `Footnote 5, p. 365 (PDF p. 69), checked on a 300 dpi render: "One may take r to be C(T) − T, where C is the Chebyshev-type polynomial determined by the relation C(t + t^{−1}) = t^v + t^{−v}, and T is the trace of a generator of tame inertia (note that T − 2 ∈ m_{R_v}). The generic fibre of R_v has (q + 1)/2 geometric components, where q is the largest power of p dividing v − 1 (see also Theorem 1.0.1(A2.2) of [55]). One component corresponds to lifts of ρ̄ on which inertia is nilpotent, and in particular has trace T = 2. The remaining (q − 1)/2 components correspond to representations which are finitely ramified of order dividing q, on which T = ζ + ζ^{−1} for some primitive q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1." The arXiv v2 footnote 5 (cg-v2.txt l. 2716–2721) has the same wording, "primitive" included.`; it should be `Replace "for some primitive q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1" with "for some q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1", i.e. ζ ∈ μ_q \ {1}, taken up to ζ ↔ ζ^{−1}. The candidate's second change, "inertia is nilpotent" → "inertia is unipotent" (or "acts unipotently"), is fine as a wording fix. The paper says "unipotent" elsewhere (e.g. p. 297 text line 205, and §5 conditions), but "nilpotent" here can also be read loosely as "σ − 1 is nilpotent / N is nilpotent", so on its own it is not a mathematical error.`. I redid the computation. Set t^v + t^{−v} − t − t^{−1} = (t^v − t)(1 − t^{−v−1}). So C(T) = T at T = t + t^{−1} exactly when t^{v−1} = 1 or t^{v+1} = 1. C(T) − T is separable of degree v in T: its roots are ±2, (v−3)/2 values from t^{v−1} = 1 and (v−1)/2 values from t^{v+1} = 1. The condition T − 2 ∈ m forces t ≡ 1, so t is a 1-unit root of unity of p-power order. Since v ≡ 1 mod p and p is odd, p does not divide v + 1, so t^{v+1} = 1 gives only t = 1, and t^{v−1} = 1 gives t ∈ μ_q.

The T-values in the residue disc are therefore T = 2 plus ζ + ζ^{−1} for ζ ∈ μ_q \ {1} modulo inversion. That is 1 + (q−1)/2 = (q+1)/2 values, matching the footnote's count. Each ζ ≠ 1 gives one geometric component: σ is regular semisimple with eigenvalues ζ^{±1}, Frobenius lies in its centralizer torus with fixed determinant, and the result is irreducible of dimension 3.

If only primitive ζ were allowed there would be φ(q)/2 = p^{s−1}(p−1)/2 such components, fewer than (q−1)/2 once q = p^s with s ≥ 2. Concrete check: p = 3, v = 19, so q = 9. ζ_3 + ζ_3^{−1} = −1 satisfies T − 2 = −3 ∈ m and is a genuine root, giving 4 = (9−1)/2 non-trivial values against 3 primitive ones.

The sentence itself points the same way. It says "finitely ramified of order dividing q", and "ζ ≠ 1" would be redundant for a primitive q-th root, since q ≥ p > 1. So "primitive" is a slip. The counts (q+1)/2 and (q−1)/2 are correct; only this adjective is wrong. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. (That known defect does appear on the same page in "R_v ≅ O[x1,…,x4]/(r)", which should read O⟦x1,…,x4⟧/(r), but that is separate.) This is confirmed on the page image, and arXiv v2 has the same wording. O[Φ] is the group ring of a finite group, so it is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Both justifications given in the paper fail:
(1) Being local does not force the image into T_{1,m}⊗O[Φ]. Take T_{1,m}=O, Φ=Z/p and O=Z_p[ζ_p]. The ring A={(a_φ)∈⊕O : all a_φ congruent mod ϖ} is local and contains O[Φ]. It also contains (ϖ,0,…,0) = (ϖ/p)Σ[g], which is not in O[Φ] because v_ϖ(p)=p−1≥2.
(2) An injection of ϖ-torsion-free lattices that becomes an isomorphism after ⊗K need not be onto. O[Φ] ⊂ ⊕_φ O is itself an example. Torsion-freeness gives only injectivity.
So the printed reasons prove at most an inclusion of finite index. I checked the candidate's replacement argument myself, including the twisting convention, the images T_l ↦ T_l⊗[l] and ⟨d⟩ ↦ 1⊗[d]^2 for d∈Φ, and that squaring is bijective on Φ. It is correct, apart from the small base-change caveat noted in the correction.
On 'affects', I disagree with the candidate's "nothing". The proof of Theorem 4.8 as printed does not establish the isomorphism, and a different argument is needed, so it affects the proof. Theorem 4.8 still holds, because the intermediate isomorphism is true. Only the multiplicity-two statement of Thm 4.8 uses this step, together with Remark 4.12 ("a similar argument"), and neither is changed. I tried to defend the printed argument and could not.

(1) "Since T_m is local, the image lands inside T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]" does not follow. A local subring of T_{1,m} ⊗ ⊕_φ O need not lie in T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]. Take T_{1,m} = O, Φ = Z/p, O = Z_p[ζ_p]. The ring A = {(a_φ) : all a_φ congruent mod ϖ} is local and contains O[Φ]. It also contains (ϖ,0,…,0) = (ϖ/p)Σ_g[g], and this is not in O[Φ] because v_ϖ(p) = p−1 ≥ 2. The containment is true only because of the explicit images of the generators, and the paper never states them.

(2) "Isomorphism after ⊗K + ϖ-torsion free" gives only an injection of lattices of the same rank. O[Φ] ⊂ ⊕_φ O is itself such an injection, and it is not onto.

I looked for other readings:
- a Nakayama argument would need surjectivity onto target/m_{T_m}·target, not just onto the residue field;
- an integral module isomorphism S_2(Γ_1(N*),O)_m ≅ S_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ] would still leave the same generator argument to be made;
- nothing elsewhere in the paper supplies the step (I searched every twisting passage and the 2022 Correction).

The step cannot be skipped. Lemma 4.2 (p. 334) gives CM-ness and the number of generators of ω only for an actual B ⊗_O C, and a finite-index subring of T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ] inherits neither. Without the equality, the proof of dim ω_{T_m}/m = 3, and so of multiplicity two, is incomplete.

I checked the repair myself, including the twisting direction (on S_{φ²}, ⟨d⟩ for d ∈ Φ acts by φ²(d), so it matches 1⊗[d²]) and that U_l = 0 for l | M. The repair is sound, so the stated result is correct.

Consequences: Theorem 4.8 is used nowhere else. §4.1 opens with "Although this is not needed for our main results". Remark 4.12 ("a similar argument shows…") inherits the same step. I checked the page image (PDF p. 70 = p. 366); the display is exactly as quoted, and arXiv v2 has the same wording. I recomputed the parts. G^0 = T_pG^0 ⊗ Q_p/Z_p has Pontryagin dual Hom(T_pG^0, Z_p) = T_pG^e ≅ ω, so dim G^0[m] = dim ω/m = 3. G^e has dual Hom(T_pG^e, Z_p) = T_pG^0 ≅ T_m (free of rank 1), so dim G^e[m] = 1. Both values are correct. The additivity dim G[m] = dim G^0[m] + dim G^e[m] needs G[m] → G^e[m] to be onto. The obstruction lives in Ext^1_T(k, G^0), which is Pontryagin dual to Tor_1^T(k, ω). That group is nonzero because ω needs 3 generators (T_m is not Gorenstein), so additivity is not automatic, and the proof gives no argument for it. The paper only cites the Tate-module exact sequence from Gross 12.9/12.10. In Gross's multiplicity-one setting only the upper bound is needed, and here the "=" is simply asserted. The equality is true after the fact: the image of G[m] in the 1-dimensional G^e[m] is either 0 or everything, and 0 would force dim G[m] = 3, which is odd and contradicts BLR. So Theorem 4.8 is unaffected. The candidate's correction and its two side remarks are right. I disagree only on 'affects': the printed proof has an unjustified step that is false in general and needs a one-line repair (parity via BLR, or Wiese's d ≥ 2 from Remark 4.9), so I rate it 'the proof', not 'nothing'. No stated result changes. Theorem 4.8 is a standalone application and nothing later depends on it (grep finds only the introduction and Remarks 4.9/4.12). Remark 4.12's "similar argument" would need the same repair. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The page image confirms the display. The two dimensions are right. Pontryagin duality gives G^0[m]^∨ = Hom(T_pG^0,Z_p)/m = T_pG^e/m ≅ ω_{T_m}/m, which has dimension 3. Likewise G^e[m]^∨ = T_pG^0/m ≅ T_m/m, which has dimension 1.

The additivity dim G[m] = dim G^0[m] + dim G^e[m] is the step in question. It holds only if G[m] → G^e[m] is surjective. Dually, T_m/m → T_pG^∨/m must be injective in 0 → T_m → T_pG^∨ → ω → 0, where the obstruction is the connecting map Tor_1^{T_m}(ω,k) → k. That group is nonzero because T_m is not Gorenstein (ω needs 3 generators). So the equality is not formal, and the proof gives no argument for it. Its only input is the Tate-module sequence of Gross, Prop. 12.9/12.10. In Gross's Gorenstein case only the upper bound is needed.

Defence attempts:
(a) Gross's exact sequence is for Tate modules, and those sequences do not stay exact after taking [m].
(b) Nothing in §4.1 splits the sequence of T_m-modules. Ext^1_T(ω, T) can be nonzero, and the Galois structure is not used.
(c) The strongest charitable reading is Remark 4.9, just before the proof. It says Wiese proved multiplicity ≥ 2 and that "our contribution … is to show that the multiplicity is exactly two". With that bound only "≤" is needed. But the proof never invokes it; it asserts "=" and concludes "= 2" from the display alone.
So the printed proof has an unjustified step. It is not an error: the equality is true here by parity or by Wiese's bound, so the stated result is unaffected.

Consequences: I grepped the published text. Theorem 4.8 is used nowhere later. It is cited only in the Introduction (p. 305) and in Remarks 4.9/4.12/4.13. Remark 4.12 (J_H(N*)[m], "a similar argument shows…") inherits the same step and the same one-line repair.

Affects: "the proof" rather than "nothing", because the repair needs an ingredient absent from the proof (BLR parity or Wiese's bound). This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the Correction (2022) does not address it.
